discussion_title: Q&A and casual open discussion on RFC-0012 (CVM)
author: mjprager
text:
Re: Q&A and casual open discussion on RFC-0012 (CVM)

mjprager: Hi Pete,

As the ConMon lead for a large CSP, this standard is probably the one that affects me the most.

It seems like the keys really are:
* what constitutes a credibly-exploitable vuln
* whether something is internet-reachable or not.

I'm doing my best to parse the definitions and game plan how they would apply.

My interpretation of FRR-CVM-TM-05 "Providers SHOULD fully mitigate or remediate credibly exploitable vulnerabilities in internet-reachable resources promptly, within three calendar days of detection" is that these are likely equivalent to things that may have been a CISA Emergency Directive (and in our case, were always already an internally-declared incident for "all hands on deck" expedited patching even before the CISA ED). Is that the intent? Is setting a "Max Time" helpful in this case, or should it actually just be "Promptly", which was defined in FRD-CVM-10 as "As quickly as possible and without unnecessary delay."?

I think it's good that FRR-CVM-TM03 for CISA KEVs is a "should" and not a "must". Known exploited in public doesn't necessarily mean exploitable in our environment with the substantial defense-in-depth, and the original CISA KEV deadlines didn't recognize that. 

I'm still personally wrestling with whether this delineation between "internet-reachable or not" is the right thing to focus on from a security perspective, given "assume breach" mentalities, insider threat, lateral movement... it's not magically safer because you aren't on the true perimeter. 

Will of course follow proper process for formal comments, but you invited musings, so here are some of mine!

By the way, the organization of this RFC (like having the definitions, requirements, and timelines spelled out with indexed identifiers) really resonated with me... but I'm the kind who always reads the table of contents before diving in. Thank you!

Melissa

pete-gov [FEDRAMP-OFFICIAL]: Hey Melissa! Some quick responses:

> My interpretation of FRR-CVM-TM-05 "Providers SHOULD fully mitigate or remediate credibly exploitable vulnerabilities in internet-reachable resources promptly, within three calendar days of detection" is that these are likely equivalent to things that may have been a CISA Emergency Directive

I would say generally credibly exploitable vulnerabilities in internet-reachable resources would be treated like an incident by many providers but wouldn't necessarily result in a CISA ED - those are generally reserved for broad specific circumstances (like a zero day in a firewall), whereas this would apply to context specific issues. I think, generally, a good security program probably already treats these like incidents though, things like leaked API keys or SQL injection issues would be included.

> Is setting a "Max Time" helpful in this case, or should it actually just be "Promptly"

Honestly this is an example of the type of scarring that exists around government policies - everyone assumes that if we don't specify a max time, there will be a bunch of people who decide that "as soon as possible" means "five years from now because I'm busy right now."  🤷  So we put specific max timeframes to force escalation and discussion if folks want to exceed those, so AOs can make an informed decision about continued authorization of the service.

> I'm still personally wrestling with whether this delineation between "internet-reachable or not" is the right thing to focus on from a security perspective

This is a point that came up in a lot of internal discussions too - generally, I'd point out that we also prioritized credibly exploitable vulnerabilities that aren't internet-reachable with aggressive timelines for mitigation compared to previously, they just aren't _as_ prioritized as the internet-reachable ones. 

> By the way, the organization of this RFC (like having the definitions, requirements, and timelines spelled out with indexed identifiers) really resonated with me...

One of the things I'm excited about with [FedRAMP Machine Readable Docs](https://github.com/FedRAMP/docs) is that people will be able to mashup and enrich these materials to fit whatever their preferred way of consuming them is. 🚀  

eclectiqus: Your comment about "max time" and "promptly" is an important one, thank you for making it and committing it to this thread. When I worked on World Economic Forum guidance and white papers for cyber resilience in the oil and gas industry, I spent two years trying to get the word "continuous" inserted in front of the word "monitoring" and yet *still* there are folks who have varying interpretations of the word continuous. I was the CISO at SecurityScorecard at the time and definitely wanted folks to step away from annual risk assessment cadence and move to "event-based" risk assessments informed by continuous monitoring. For some like me, it's 5 minute timeseries data for a monitoring check. For others (in government DoD for example) they believe that they perform continuous monitoring by performing an audit. Every three years!

discussion_title: Q&A and casual open discussion on RFC-0012 (CVM)
author: cpelote
text:
Re: Q&A and casual open discussion on RFC-0012 (CVM)

cpelote: In Section 3.0 of the current [CSP_Vulnerability_Scanning_Requirements ](https://www.fedramp.gov/assets/resources/documents/CSP_Vulnerability_Scanning_Requirements.pdf)publication, there are requirements for CVSS risk scoring: 

> For any vulnerability with a CVSSv3 base score assigned in the latest version of the NVD, the CVSSv3 base score must be used as the original risk rating. If no CVSSv3 score is available, a CVSSv2 base score is acceptable where available. If no CVSS score is available, the native scanner base risk score can be used.

With FRR-CVM-04 it says: 

> Providers MUST adjust the risk and severity of vulnerabilities using CVSS base scores (if applicable) AND the context of the vulnerability, factoring for at least criticality, reachability, exploitability, detectability, prevalence, and mitigation, to determine if vulnerabilities are credibly exploitable and the potential adverse impact of exploitation

Are these requirements still the same? How can we interpret 'if applicable' with FRR-CVM-04? 

With the current requirement (rev5), we generally follow the logic as CVSS-v3, else CVSS-v2, else Native scanner. Does the new requirement (FRR-CVM-04) enable us to leverage Native scanner analysis (which is usually more up to date than NVD).

pete-gov [FEDRAMP-OFFICIAL]: > Are these requirements still the same?

When formalized for Rev5, the Continuous Vulnerability Management Standard will replace related historical FedRAMP policies.

> How can we interpret 'if applicable' with FRR-CVM-04?

Not all vulnerabilities will have a CVSS base score - things like misconfiguration, leaked credentials, etc. 

cpelote: Let me try to simplify the question(s) - may not have been clear:

1. Will we [still] be required to use the CVSS score if one is present?
2. If we have confidence in the score/severity determined by the scanner, can we use it instead? 

pete-gov [FEDRAMP-OFFICIAL]: Ah, I'll try again too! :D

(1) The CVSS score is a factor that should be used _but not alone._ It should be a convenient starting point, not an end result. There are circumstances where a max CVSS score vulnerability can be risk and severity adjusted into something that is not credibly exploitable and would have a very low potential adverse impact and is thus not urgent to address. Or vice versa (low CVSS score vuln that is a huge massive problem). The adjusted risk and severity should be used to determine next steps.

(2) This really depends on the "scanner" - if it can effectively factor for context to estimate if a vulnerability is credibly exploitable and the potential adverse impact of exploitation then yes. If it just outputs CVSS scores then no, it is insufficient to use alone.

discussion_title: Q&A and casual open discussion on RFC-0012 (CVM)
author: kelseymcmichael
text:
Re: Q&A and casual open discussion on RFC-0012 (CVM)

kelseymcmichael: #Discussion Topic: Reconciling RFC 0008 Flexibility with RFC 0012 KEV-Based Remediation Requirements

## Background

This post is intended to clarify how providers, 3PAOs, and agencies should interpret the remediation expectations outlined in RFC 0008 in relation to the newer requirements introduced in RFC 0012, specifically around the CISA Known Exploited Vulnerabilities (KEV) catalog.

## RFC 0008: Mitigation-Based Risk Management

RFC 0008 allows cloud providers to carry vulnerabilities beyond the defined remediation windows when the associated risk has been mitigated. The language explicitly states:

> “Providers MAY carry mitigated vulnerabilities beyond FedRAMP remediation windows for the original risk rating without penalty but MUST remediate such vulnerabilities once it is reasonable to do so.”

This reflects a pragmatic posture: if the operational or security risk has been sufficiently mitigated — for example, through isolation, configuration changes, or compensating controls — then full remediation (e.g., patch deployment) can be deferred, provided it is eventually addressed.

## RFC 0012: Continuous Vulnerability Management and the CISA KEV Catalog

RFC 0012 introduces a formal continuous vulnerability management standard aligned with the CISA KEV catalog. It requires remediation of any KEV-listed vulnerability by the timeline specified in the KEV — typically within 15 to 30 days.

There is no indication in RFC 0012 that mitigation without remediation is acceptable for KEVs. This aligns with broader federal cybersecurity directives that elevate the urgency of KEVs due to their known active exploitation.

## Current Interpretation - please confirm this understanding below:

- **RFC 0008** allows for mitigated non-KEV vulnerabilities to be carried forward when risk is lowered and remediation is tracked appropriately.
- **RFC 0012** mandates strict remediation deadlines for KEV vulnerabilities, regardless of local mitigations.

**Therefore, RFC 0012 takes precedence over RFC 0008 for KEV vulnerabilities.**

## Implementation Suggestion: Tiered Model or similar for clarity

### Tier 1 – KEV Vulnerabilities
- Must be patched by the KEV-defined due date.
- Mitigations do not extend the timeline.
- Exceptions must come from CISA or the PMO.

### Tier 2 – Non-KEV Vulnerabilities
- Follow RFC 0008 guidance.
- Risk-based mitigation can extend remediation timelines.
- Document rationale and mitigation clearly in POA&M and CM deliverables.

##  Supporting Materials Recommendation

Per the FedRAMP site statement that "*Standards will be supported separately by templates, best practices, technical assistance, and other materials*", I suggest the PMO prioritize:

###  Additional Suggested Materials

- **POA&M templates for KEV tracking**, including deadline and remediation fields.
- **Decision tree or flowchart** to determine applicable standard based on CVE source/type.
- **Sample dashboard views** or tagging models to separate KEV and non-KEV vulnerabilities.
- **Integration examples** for CM/POA&M systems and vulnerability management platforms.

**Request for Confirmation**  
Please confirm whether this interpretation — that RFC 0012 requirements supersede RFC 0008 flexibility in the case of KEV vulnerabilities — aligns with PMO expectations, or provide adjustments to clarify any gaps in understanding.

pete-gov [FEDRAMP-OFFICIAL]: > Please confirm whether this interpretation — that RFC 0012 requirements supersede RFC 0008 flexibility in the case of KEV vulnerabilities — aligns with PMO expectations, or provide adjustments to clarify any gaps in understanding.

RFC-0012's proposed Continuous Vulnerability Management Standard builds on and replaces RFC-0008's proposed Continuous Reporting Standard.

This is briefly mentioned in the Summary & Motivation section where RFC-0012 states: "This RFC builds on stakeholder feedback to FedRAMP’s recent [RFC-0008 Continuous Reporting Standard](https://www.fedramp.gov/rfcs/0008/) and incorporates previous plans to update the [Continuous Monitoring Performance Management Guide](https://www.fedramp.gov/assets/resources/documents/CSP_Continuous_Monitoring_Performance_Management_Guide.pdf) for 20x."

There's a bit more [background on our roadmap for this item here](https://github.com/FedRAMP/roadmap/issues/38).

**Please note, whatever you used to generate this summary completely misunderstood RFC-0012.** It does not at all apply only to KEVs; KEVs are simply included in a much vaster scope.

kelseymcmichael: ## Follow-Up: Clarification on RFC-0012 Scope, Timelines, and Supersession of RFC-0008

Thank you for the response and clarification. It’s now understood that:

- RFC-0012 replaces RFC-0008 as the proposed standard for continuous vulnerability and configuration management under FedRAMP 20x.
- RFC-0012 is not limited to KEV vulnerabilities — its scope applies to all vulnerabilities, with KEVs called out as one critical subset. 

### 📍 Clarifying One Point on Engagement

I want to respectfully address the note suggesting that a tool was used to generate the post which “completely misunderstood” RFC-0012. While a tool was used for markdown making it appear machine-generated, the post was the result of a **close, manual read of the RFC by multiple people at Mark43** — myself included — who are actively working to understand how to operationalize these evolving requirements.

To be clear: **yes, tools were used to assist to format markdown, especially as we prepare automation-friendly frameworks — but the interpretation itself was human-led**. The very reason this post exists is because we found the document introduced **genuine ambiguity**, particularly around:

- How KEV remediation timelines differ in urgency and enforcement.
- Whether non-KEV vulnerabilities retain the mitigation flexibility described in RFC-0008, or if that option has been removed altogether under RFC-0012.

This is a sincere effort to engage deeply with the material, and I want to emphasize that assumptions about tooling, while understandable, risk overlooking the very real implementation questions security teams are navigating. 

### Remaining Clarification Requested

To ensure alignment with PMO intent, we would appreciate clarification on the following:

- Are KEVs the **only** vulnerability type within RFC-0012’s scope that are subject to externally enforced remediation deadlines (via CISA)?
- Do non-KEV vulnerabilities continue to follow the FedRAMP baseline remediation windows (e.g., 30/90/180 days), with some allowance for mitigated risk and POA&M deferral?


### Operational Impact: High Effort for KEV Requirements

This is one of several areas identified by my team that will have a **high operational impact**. Specifically, the requirement:

> *“Remediate vulnerabilities in the CISA Known Exploited Vulnerabilities (KEV) catalog by the CISA-defined due date.”*

makes adherence to the KEV catalog a **mandatory practice**. KEV due dates are often **much shorter than 30 days** (e.g., 7 or 14 days), requiring a **highly agile patching and response capability**.

While it is understood the requirement currently is drafted as "SHOULD", as it is not currently final - we are assessing all impacts. I am also wondering how this will be implemented within each agency, if the verbiage remains as "SHOULD" and what, if any, implications that can have (I could be overthinking here).

Meeting this requirement across multiple environments will require **significant updates to tooling, alerting, internal workflows, and compliance processes** — representing a **high level of effort (LOE)** for our team. This is precisely why it is so important that we **fully understand the intent and structure of RFC-0012** from the outset.

###  Suggested Reference Matrix

To support consistent implementation, a requirements matrix could clarify differential handling based on vulnerability type:

| Vulnerability Type     | Required Remediation Timeline        | Mitigation Without Patch? |
|------------------------|--------------------------------------|----------------------------|
| **CISA KEVs**          | Per KEV due date (e.g., 7–30 days)   | **No** — Full remediation required |
| **High – non-KEV**     | FedRAMP baseline (30 days)           | Possibly, if risk is mitigated |
| **Moderate/Low – non-KEV** | 90/180 days                     | Possibly, if risk is mitigated |



mjprager: Hi, just wanted to share my perspective on this, since that's the goal of the informal discussions :)

A vuln being on the CISA KEV list is a useful "hey, you might want to especially pay attention to this!" but it's only one threat signal. And just because a vuln is on that list doesn't necessarily mean that it's exploitable in MY environment with all the defense-in-depth we have, so I'd really like to see this not get written in the FedRAMP standards so firmly as a YOU MUST FIX IT BY CISA KEV DEADLINE. We need a more balanced approach - because there's an opportunity cost of spinning up resources to fix something that isn't exploitable in my environment.  

kelseymcmichael: Thanks for this input. I completely agree that the verbiage should remain "SHOULD". My 'overthinking' on this is "what if the agency requires this as a MUST". While it is easily defensible if the KEV is mitigated due to your point above about defense-in-depth (compensating controls, overlays, etc.), that will require significant more effort (POA&M etc.) I am curious how the standards will be finalized with the understanding some agencies _may_ require above and beyond the standards intention.

pete-gov [FEDRAMP-OFFICIAL]: Sorry, the focus on KEVs was weird to me since they're only mentioned in FRR-CVM-TM-03 and everything else in the standard is focused elsewhere. Is it possible your team is conflating "credibly exploitable vulnerabilities" with "known exploited vulnerabilities?"

> Are KEVs the only vulnerability type within RFC-0012’s scope that are subject to externally enforced remediation deadlines (via CISA)?

As written, yes.

> Do non-KEV vulnerabilities continue to follow the FedRAMP baseline remediation windows (e.g., 30/90/180 days), with some allowance for mitigated risk and POA&M deferral?

No, this standard includes updated requirements for handling non-KEVs in extensive detail, including remediation windows. Every single requirement in this draft standard except for FRR-CVM-TM-03 refers to non-KEVs. 

> adherence to the KEV catalog a mandatory practice

This is a carry-forward of current policy.

CISA has already determined this to be the case for federal agencies under [BOD 22-01 using their legal authority to bind all agency information systems](www.cisa.gov/news-events/directives/bod-22-01-reducing-significant-risk-known-exploited-vulnerabilities). FedRAMP already expects CSPs to comply with BOD 22-01.

In short, a government agency isn't allowed to use a system that isn't in compliance with BOD 22-01. 


pete-gov [FEDRAMP-OFFICIAL]: > We need a more balanced approach - because there's an opportunity cost of spinning up resources to fix something that isn't exploitable in my environment.

Honestly, agreed - but the law has a specific requirement that DHS concurs with changes FedRAMP makes to continuous monitoring, and CISA feels quite strongly about KEVs! That said, formal public comment has changed hearts and minds in the past... ;)

mswilson: My personal perspective (speaking for myself) is that there is room for a balanced approach, if we can all agree what "remediation" means for KEVs, and that CSPs have (and, IMO, should be _required_ to have) the capability to determine if there is _even a vulnerability at all_ in the context of their in-use software systems.

"Remediation without patch" in the suggested matrix above (where it seems the remediation of a KEV is deemed impossible without a software change) lacks the balance that we need.

The only way to "remediate" a vulnerability is if a vulnerability is present in an in-use software system. All software systems of any meaningful complexity have numerous defects. In one software system, a defect may compromise security objectives, and thus there is a vulnerability present. In another software system, the same identified defect may have no effect on security objectives and there is no vulnerability to remediate. This "_there is no vulnerability present_" condition may be due to an identified input in source code that isn't compiled into a deployed artifact, or modular functionality that is present in storage but not loaded (and not loadable by an attacker), among many other causes.

One problem with the KEV is how we identify _potential weaknesses_ (defects that may compromise security objectives) in software-intensive systems (using CVEs). We have a goal to map one identified weakness to one identifier via a CVE ID. Entries in the KEV are [required to have a CVE](https://www.cisa.gov/known-exploited-vulnerabilities#:~:text=The%20vulnerability%20has%20an%20assigned%20Common%20Vulnerabilities%20and%20Exposures%20(CVE)%20ID.). KEV entries must also [have clear remedation action](https://www.cisa.gov/known-exploited-vulnerabilities) such as a vendor-provided update.

When a CVE reads on widely reused software, such as the Linux Kernel, the notion that a KEV entry can crisply articulate the remediation actions goes out the window. Let's look at [CVE-2024-50302](https://tuxcare.com/blog/when-cvss-scores-dont-tell-the-full-story-the-case-of-cve-2024-50302/) as a case study. I'll leave [CVE-2023-44487](https://www.cisa.gov/news-events/alerts/2023/10/10/http2-rapid-reset-vulnerability-cve-2023-44487) (HTTP/2 Rapid Reset) for another day.

CVE-2024-50302 is part of a vulnerability chain commercialized in Cellebrite mobile device data exfiltration tools. In the context of Android-based devices, it is [known to have been used to target phone of a Serbian student activist.
](https://securitylab.amnesty.org/latest/2025/02/cellebrite-zero-day-exploit-used-to-target-phone-of-serbian-student-activist/)

CISA added CVE-2024-50302 to the KEV on 2025-03-04 with the "Required Action" of "Apply mitigations per vendor instructions, follow applicable BOD 22-01 guidance for cloud services, or discontinue use of the product if mitigations are unavailable." There is an "additional note" on the KEV record, which is not displayed by default on CISA's web site:
> This vulnerability affects a common open-source component, third-party library, or a protocol used by different products. For more information, please see: https://lore.kernel.org/linux-cve-announce/2024111908-CVE-2024-50302-f677@gregkh/ ; https://source.android.com/docs/security/bulletin/2025-03-01 ; https://nvd.nist.gov/vuln/detail/CVE-2024-50302

As an information conveyance tool, I find this KEV entry ineffective at advancing the goal of closing this particular known exploited vulnerability. Compare to the New York State Office of Information Technology Services [advisory 2025-025](https://its.ny.gov/2025-025), which is syndicated from the Multi-State Information Sharing and Analysis Center (MS-ISAC) [advisory](https://www.cisecurity.org/advisory/multiple-vulnerabilities-in-google-android-os-could-allow-for-remote-code-execution_2025-025), which is very usable information.

I sincerely doubt that adding CVE-2024-50302 to the KEV meaningfully improved the security posture of any in-use system, whereas adding "Android OS levels prior to 2025-03-05" to a KEV _may_ have made a meaningful difference. But there's no way for the KEV to do this, because it only identifies vulnerabilities via CVEs, not end-user accessible software identifiers.

The KEV generally works at the "least common denominator" level of information for both vulnerabilities and remediation guidance ("Apply mitigations per vendor instructions, follow applicable BOD 22-01 guidance for cloud services, or discontinue use of the product if mitigations are unavailable."). That might work when you're dealing primarily with COTS software where there is a single vendor that is responsible for issuing pre-packaged software updates or other end-user-consumable instruction to resolve security concerns about their products (e.g., Sharepoint).

But for something like CVE-2024-50302, software composition analysis is generally going to match on Linux kernel version numbers, not even look at if the affected code in the USB HID driver is compiled or not, or (if so) if the affected module is loaded on a given asset or not, etc. etc. The database will say there is a "fixed version" available, so the effect of the KEV and BOD 22-01 today is forced upgrades of (and reporting on) non-vulnerable software, rather than expediting vulnerable Android OS updates.

What you want to know for effective vulnerability management is if this known-exploited version of **Android** is running, and what CISA should want to know with the BOD 22-01 reporting requirements is if agencies are managing **that** risk present in their in-use software inventory effectively via their processes.

(apologies for the length, I feel quite strongly about KEVs too!)

discussion_title: Q&A and casual open discussion on RFC-0012 (CVM)
author: mjprager
text:
Re: Q&A and casual open discussion on RFC-0012 (CVM)

mjprager: Pete and team, 

When circulating this doc internally, the most repeated question has been around "credibly exploitable vulnerability" and "what does that mean", so I refer them to the definition:

FRD-CVM-02
Credibly exploitable vulnerability: A vulnerability where a likely threat actor with knowledge of the vulnerability would likely be able to gain unauthorized access, cause harm, disrupt operations, or otherwise have an undesired adverse impact; vulnerabilities must be reachable and not fully mitigated to be credibly exploitable.

And then their next question is "great, so who defines what 'credibly exploitable'" means? My take is that "my security team does, because they are the ones that have the best knowledge of our architecture and overlays that against this vuln to determine whether it is credibly exploitable". Is that the intent of this, or do we have to 100% defer to outside sources like the CISA KEV list?

Melissa

pete-gov [FEDRAMP-OFFICIAL]: > My take is that "my security team does, because they are the ones that have the best knowledge of our architecture and overlays that against this vuln to determine whether it is credibly exploitable". Is that the intent of this

Yeah, the owner of the cloud service offering is responsible for determining what's credibly exploitable based on the unique context of their environment and how this is assessed. 

Generally, engineering teams are best positioned for this, and as we heard in our Vulnerability Management Special Event this week it's common for tech companies to empower engineering teams to collaborate with security teams to follow processes similar to that required by FRR-CVM-04. There might be other ways to go about it that make sense though!

discussion_title: Q&A and casual open discussion on RFC-0012 (CVM)
author: aj327
text:
Re: Q&A and casual open discussion on RFC-0012 (CVM)

aj327: Quick question, there was some discussion of timelines for implementing RFC-0012 into FedRAMP 20x and eventually Rev 5 yesterday on the webinar. Will RFC-0012 apply to just FedRAMP Low to start (when the Rev 5 Beta begins) or will apply to Low, Moderate, and High?

pete-gov [FEDRAMP-OFFICIAL]: We don't distinguish between authorization impact levels for most standards, unless there is a specific need. Right now the only standard that is limited by impact level is the Key Security Indicators.

aj327: Okay, I think I'm perhaps missing something. 

The only KSIs that have been shared for now (I believe in RFC-0006) are for FedRAMP Low. In those KSIs, there is a section on Monitoring, Logging, and Auditing, which alludes to continuous monitoring standards (#3, 4, and 6). Does that mean RFC-0012 only applies to the KSIs for FedRAMP Low and there will be future KSIs for Moderate + High that have separate continuous monitoring standards? Apologies in advance if I'm being dense here and mis-understanding your response. 

pete-gov [FEDRAMP-OFFICIAL]: Note that RFCs are just requests for comments, not standards/etc. - the [formal KSI Standard is here](https://github.com/FedRAMP/docs/blob/main/markdown/FRMR.KSI.key-security-indicators.md) and you'll note that **only** applies to FedRAMP 20x. Other standards like the [Significant Change Notification Requirements](https://github.com/FedRAMP/docs/blob/main/markdown/FRMR.SCN.significant-change-notifications.md) apply to both 20x and Rev5 via the [Balance Improvement process](https://github.com/fedRAMP/community/discussions/38).

There's no intent to separate continuous monitoring requirements or other standards by impact level at this time. A FedRAMP 20x authorized service will need to meet the SCN, CVM, and other requirements as they are finalized, just like a Rev5 one will need to.

As FRR-CVM-01 states: "these requirements supplement controls in FedRAMP Rev5 Baselines and Key Security Indicators in FedRAMP 20x."

tl;dr RFC-0012 will apply as a blanket across any impact level.

aj327: Really helpful, thanks Pete

discussion_title: Q&A and casual open discussion on RFC-0012 (CVM)
author: eclectiqus
text:
Re: Q&A and casual open discussion on RFC-0012 (CVM)

eclectiqus: Regarding FRR-CVM-03: "Providers MUST make vulnerability reports available to all necessary parties in similar human-readable and compatible machine-readable formats, including at least FedRAMP, CISA, and all agency customers." I'm curious to know what are the compatible machine-readable formats? STIX/TAXII v2.1 or are there other desired machine-readable formats beyond just XML, CSV, and JSON? I'm thinking about structured formats such as:

- Vulnerability Exploitability eXchange (VEX)
- Vulnerability Disclosure Reports (VDR)
- Open Vulnerability and Assessment Language (OVAL)
- Security Content Automation Protocol (SCAP)
- Common Weakness Enumeration (CWE)

Lastly, I'm curious to know where things sit with adding NIST OSCAL as a requirement versus nice-to-have.



pete-gov [FEDRAMP-OFFICIAL]: FedRAMP isn't specifying machine-readable formats during pilots/beta tests to encourage innovative solutions that aren't constrained by existing preconception - I expect a few different standards to emerge and GRC automation tools to broker communication between standards as needed. 

More important than the format itself will be how folks make this information available, since there's not much point in having a massive datafile that has to be downloaded and parsed to see updates/etc. I expect folks will lean towards API driven models here. At least _some_ sort of standard will be added prior to wide release.

> Lastly, I'm curious to know where things sit with adding NIST OSCAL as a requirement versus nice-to-have.

So far OSCAL has been showing up here and there in our 20x pilot but it hasn't been the preferred choice for most of industry when given the option to innovate. I'm curious to see how this will continue to play out over time as well.

discussion_title: Q&A and casual open discussion on RFC-0012 (CVM)
author: jbrenton-fits
text:
Re: Q&A and casual open discussion on RFC-0012 (CVM)

jbrenton-fits: Hi Pete,
As I reviewed RFC-12, a few questions came up where some added clarity would be helpful.
	• Previously FedRAMP required that scans cover at least OS/Infrastructure, databases, Web Applications, and container images. However, RFC-12 gives no guidelines on which parts of the CSO environment must be scanned. Will the previous requirements still apply going forward?
	• Will sampling assets for scanning continue to be permissible as it is now or will there be any new scan requirements/guidelines for sampling?
	• Do raw vulnerability scans and/or inventory scans need to be provided to FedRAMP any longer, or is only the vulnerability report with the information detailed in FRR-CVM-02 required to be delivered?
	• RFC-12 has much more aggressive timeframes for fully mitigating/remediating credibly exploitable vulnerabilities, but it also makes no mentions of the previous FedRAMP thresholds for overdue High and Moderate vulnerabilities that would automatically place a CSP into Corrective Action Plan (CAP) territory. Will missing the new timelines be formally counted against CSPs in any way, or is the intention here to give agencies more insight into the current risk posture of the CSO and allow each agency to determine whether or not it meets their needs?
	• Finally, regarding the updated guidance on scanning cadence, my understanding is that many CSPs already struggle with performing authenticated scans of their full FedRAMP environment every 30 days. I suspect that with the increased scanning cadence many will be concerned that this could lead to a significant degradation in performance.


pete-gov [FEDRAMP-OFFICIAL]: > Previously FedRAMP required that scans cover at least OS/Infrastructure, databases, Web Applications, and container images. However, RFC-12 gives no guidelines on which parts of the CSO environment must be scanned. Will the previous requirements still apply going forward? 

See FRD-CVM-01 - RFC-0012 requires management of _all_ “weakness in an information system, system security procedures, internal controls, or implementation that could be exploited or triggered by a threat source.”

Traditional "vulnerability scans" are only the tip of the iceberg in a modern security program.

> Will sampling assets for scanning continue to be permissible as it is now or will there be any new scan requirements/guidelines for sampling? 

This would depend on the context and should be part of the documented program established in FRR-CVM-01. (edit: generally, if there's a high degree of confidence that sampling is appropriate, then sampling should be encouraged, yes)

> Do raw vulnerability scans and/or inventory scans need to be provided to FedRAMP any longer, or is only the vulnerability report with the information detailed in FRR-CVM-02 required to be delivered?

RFC-0012 does not require raw data, just reports. 

> Will missing the new timelines be formally counted against CSPs in any way, or is the intention here to give agencies more insight into the current risk posture of the CSO and allow each agency to determine whether or not it meets their needs? 

FRR-CVM-05 requires CSPs to carry POA&Ms (or future equivalents) to explain how vulnerabilities will eventually be addressed so agencies can make their own ongoing authorization decisions, yep.

CSPs who abuse this may have to deal with additional assessments or have their FedRAMP authorization revoked, but we're not particularly concerned about making up punitive policies in advance. Anyone acting in good faith and communicating appropriately will just have their risk score adjusted.

> Finally, regarding the updated guidance on scanning cadence, my understanding is that many CSPs already struggle with performing authenticated scans of their full FedRAMP environment every 30 days. I suspect that with the increased scanning cadence many will be concerned that this could lead to a significant degradation in performance.

This policy is intended to send a clear signal that CSPs should reassess their architecture and security approaches and invest appropriately to ensure they can protect information at a level that matches modern threats.

discussion_title: Q&A and casual open discussion on RFC-0012 (CVM)
author: badgerinspace
text:
Re: Q&A and casual open discussion on RFC-0012 (CVM)

badgerinspace: Can I cheat the system and ask for casual discussion on the following post? https://github.com/FedRAMP/community/discussions/59#discussioncomment-14011556

While CVSS is not a cure-all, it's a known standard, widely implemented, widely understood, and repeatable. It's also flexible by design and provides analytical methods for determining severity. Allowing branching options outside of such standards and processes will cause distrust in the system through a loss of standardization and an increase in subjectivity. When researchers talk about a new vulnerability, they aren't determining severity based on subjectivity of their engineers, they're determining it based off of a standardized process known around the world. Think of threat intelligence feeds or vendor-provided severities, it's in use everywhere. Allowing alternative processes with high levels of subjectivity will decrease trust.

pete-gov [FEDRAMP-OFFICIAL]: > Can I cheat the system and ask for casual discussion on the following post? https://github.com/FedRAMP/community/discussions/59#discussioncomment-14011556

FedRAMP is strictly limited from directly influencing public comment, which makes things like this a bit weird. 

A couple comments to share in general that have been made elsewhere:

- Relying only on CVSS scores means ignoring low scored or unscored vulnerabilities that present existential risks in specific environments due to the context in which they exist. This happens way too much right now.
- Automated reactive tooling is only a single aspect of the change FedRAMP is signalling here. To meet these requirements at scale, CSPs will need to design more resilient architectures with default mitigation and better management and deployment tools. The example of someone deploying a KEV is a perfect example of something that _should never be allowed to happen_ and should be stopped far before any vulnerability scan is done on a production system.
- This policy generally signals meaningful expected change; the intent is to transition the space away from the current behaviors that do not meet modern threats. It needs to push, which is why folks can carry POA&Ms and not receive explicit penalties as long as they're acting in good faith.
- You can expect this to override any previous timelines when it's formally adopted.





badgerinspace: Apologies for making that weird, appreciate the feedback you were able to provide though. I also appreciate the open discussion happening here and on the Zoom calls. Some thoughts on comments:

- Relying only on CVSS can have drawbacks for sure, but the general guidance we've followed for a while now is CVEs without CVSS data are regarded as a high severity. This is guidance directly from FedRAMP's info@. That's not a very flexible approach for sure, so wouldn't a good compromise be to utilize CVSS when it's available and utilize the CSP's own internal exploit credibility determination when not?
  - Expanding on this point, there are numerous flaws with a purely CSP-managed credible exploitability determination:
    - The process will be extremely subjective and bottlenecked by the technical capability and realistically the staffing level of the CSPs. I know FedRAMP is actively talking with CSPs across the board and across these RFC and 20X topics, but does that include the developers at these CSPs? Does that include the engineers that are responsible for fixing vulnerabilities as they come up? If so, you'd likely find that they are maxing out their capabilities already, as things stand today. They're spending countless hours every month chasing down fixes, applying them, testing them, and merging them into the larger codebase, followed by even more testing. Rarely do they have time to look into if or how the vulnerability could be exploited and instead spend their time managing the complexities of fixing these vulnerabilities. And realistically, there's often not even enough public information posted about a vulnerability to determine if it is exploitable or not. If a CSP is seeing 50+ new vulnerabilities every month (which is by no means uncommon), with the guidance as it stands today, they would need to switch from spending time fixing vulnerabilities to spending time researching if they're exploitable and then fixing them anyways either within 3 days or pushing the can down the road by as much as 6 months (based on my understanding of the RFC language). All this assumes the CSP has engineers on hand with the technical knowledge to analyze exploitability and get into the weeds on each and every vulnerability that comes up.
    - Agencies will need to somehow have trust in a subjective system. Agencies at the end of the day are left holding the bag if vulnerabilities are not remediated on time. With the existing CVSS process, they align with a known process, known standard, and repeatability. These base scores are created from professional researchers whose job it is to determine exploitability, impact, and several other details. It's as scientific of a process as we've got and it's by no means perfect, but that's why CSPs have the option to adjust the vector data based on their environment and protections in place. With this new approach, agencies will now need to inherently trust that each CSO they buy will be staffed with sufficient personnel and _sufficiently capable_ personnel to research each and every vulnerability to determine exploitability. I can't be the only one thinking this level of trust is unfounded and extremely risky to the government. If the goal is to promote zero trust, wouldn't the better approach be to assume the worst and let the CSP prove otherwise? In other words, go with a known standard, CVSS, and let them prove that each vulnerability is more or less of a risk, rather than put inherent trust that they'll be able to handle the entire exploitability determination on their own.

- On another point brought up on today's Zoom call:
  - CSPs should code better. This is a summarized point brought up on today's Zoom call and while yes, that would solve some issues from the start, it would not be a cure-all and simplifies a topic that is far more complex. Modern cloud systems are built with countless 3rd party packages and every new service and feature that gets built for the government gets built from these packages. Or built from combinations of packages. Or packages that are forked, modified heavily, and then built for more bespoke purposes. The branching complexities and possible combinations from using different packages in different ways are endless. Tracking down how a CVE affects one package could result in a determination that an update must be made on line X of the code, but once that chance is made, it propagates issues down the chain and a simple "version update" or "change one line of code" can turn into days or weeks of work to ensure everything works perfectly still. Adding a requirement for CSPs to determine exploitability every time on every CVE will slow down existing processes even further.

mjprager: I wrestle with that too, Badger. Yes, we could extensively review the vulns and risk adjust. I do this today for our FedRAMP reports, and have automation that does most of it based on the original CVSS vector strings, looking at what services the vulns were detected on, some metadata about the services (do they contain customer data? are they externally facing? plus other secret sauce...) and auto-populate the RA justifications for each change I'm making in the vector string. I do this because we are still subject to the ConMon Performance Management guide's limits for overdue vulnerabilities. We've debated whether this approach should be taken more internally to help prioritize vulns - there are mixed opinions, but _mine_ is that we need to design our engineering process to still patch all VMs, containers, etc. within a period of time (a month? three months?), and if you're going to patch it, patch ALL the things, not just the highs and then circle around next week for the moderates. 

The other thing to note is that this CVM doc really is expanding the definition of vulns beyond just CVE-based things - "This includes software vulnerabilities, misconfigurations, exposures, weak credentials, insecure services, and other weaknesses". Those aren't going to have CVSS scores then. So there will be an element of subjectivity there.

In summary, I like that this is being more respectful of what presents a true risk and allows us to focus our efforts on the work that makes a tangible security difference. But yep, there's a risk that we evaluate it differently - or worse, wrongly.

mswilson: responding to https://github.com/FedRAMP/community/discussions/60#discussioncomment-14026843
> The other thing to note is that this CVM doc really is expanding the definition of vulns beyond just CVE-based things - "This includes software vulnerabilities, misconfigurations, exposures, weak credentials, insecure services, and other weaknesses". Those aren't going to have CVSS scores then. So there will be an element of subjectivity there.

+1 to this observation. That said, CVEs don't just apply to software, they also apply to Internet protocols (among other things). See HTTP/2 Rapid Reset ([CVE-2023-44487](https://nvd.nist.gov/vuln/detail/cve-2023-44487)).

> But yep, there's a risk that we evaluate it differently - or worse, wrongly.

This is risk in all human efforts of analyzing highly complex systems-of-systems, and correctly understanding the hazards that are the _emergent properties_ of those systems. Even experts are going to inevitably disagree in their assessments, and collectively come to conclusions that are wrong in hindsight.

The question in my mind is: as a tool, does CVSS help or hinder the work of making *risk assessments* of these emergent properties of complex systems? I'm sure that those closest to the coordinated vulnerability disclosure processes are well aware, but many who may read this are not, so I will say it here plainly: [CVSS is **not a tool that measures risk**](https://nvd.nist.gov/vuln-metrics/cvss#:~:text=CVSS%20is%20not%20a%20measure%20of%20risk.).

When I am doing the work of evaluating a disclosed vulnerability in the context of a given system, I have never found the CVSS vectors, or the score summary, useful in that process. In my experience, more often than not the scores that have been made available are plainly incorrect. Sometimes this is because a CVE has been allocated to an open source library without the involvement of the maintainer, the text of the CVE is vague, and the NVD enrichment process scores it 9.8 or 10 because of "[incomplete data](https://nvd.nist.gov/vuln-metrics/cvss#:~:text=NVD%20enrichment%20efforts%20will%20assess%20that%20vulnerability%20as%20a%2010.0%20(the%20highest%20rating).)".

In [2014, researchers found](https://dl.acm.org/doi/10.1145/2630069) that patching software just because it had a high CVSS score was equivalent to randomly picking vulnerabilities to fix. This is aligned with my personal experience.

responding to OP https://github.com/FedRAMP/community/discussions/60#discussioncomment-14011694
> While CVSS is not a cure-all, it's a known standard, widely implemented, widely understood, and repeatable. 

Sometimes the NIST-produced score in the NVD has a 9.8 score for no apparent reason, like https://nvd.nist.gov/vuln/detail/CVE-2025-1446. This should pretty clearly be [CVSS:3.1/AV:N/AC:L/PR:H/UI:N/S:C/C:L/I:N/A:N](https://www.first.org/cvss/calculator/3-1#CVSS:3.1/AV:N/AC:L/PR:H/UI:N/S:C/C:L/I:N/A:N) for a 4.1 "MEDIUM" score, as confirmed by CISA ADP Vulnrichment. This is one of many examples where independent application of the CVSS system yields two different scores, despite the system's design to distill and communicate the intrinsic characteristics of a vulnerability.

[Research from the Software Engineering Institute at CMU](https://www.sei.cmu.edu/documents/574/2018_019_001_538372.pdf) found that:
> There are substantive problems in assigning scores, with various kinds of inconsistency (variability and inflation), vague guidelines, and technical details of scores. Based on available evidence, CVSS v3.0 concepts are understood with wide variability, even by experienced security professionals. The most accurate 50% of security professionals surveyed mis-score vulnerabilities in a range of 2–4 points. Note four points is wider than the whole recommended “high” range. More than half of survey respondents are not consistently within an accuracy range of four CVSS points.

Note that this report is pre-CVSSv4, which could offer some improvements. We have to see how it shakes out in practice.

> When researchers talk about a new vulnerability, they aren't determining severity based on subjectivity of their engineers.

In practice, this is often a point of contention between Finders and Vendors [in the Coordinated Vulnerability Disclosure process](https://certcc.github.io/CERT-Guide-to-CVD/), at least in the Open Source world. Researchers that disclose vulnerabilities in open source software often have exaggerated impact claims that go undisputed, or the dispute of the claims are merely appended to the CVE record in a "report both sides so that the reader can come to their own conclusions" approach.

See also
* D. Richard Hipp's summary of his experience with [SQLite and CVEs](https://www.sqlite.org/cves.html).
* Cathy Almond's [presentation](https://www.isc.org/docs/ReportingDNSCVEsOARC43.v4.pdf) of how CVSS doesn't work well for the DNS software and protocol ecosystem

There are others, in particular in the open source community where resource and power gradients can be extreme compared to commercially developed proprietary software.

badgerinspace: I understand why people think CVSS doesn't do a good enough job at determining risk and everyone and every company's experiences will be different as the products are all different, the pipelines are different and the teams are different. There is no question that it doesn't work for everyone.

However, from my understanding of the language presented in this RFC, the requirement will force every company participating in FedRAMP to have sufficient staff on hand to determine exploitability for every vulnerability detected. What was once a duty that could (accurately or not) be handed off to professionals to determine risk will now need to be done by every CSP, regardless of company size and staff proficiency in the matter. This is likely a non-issue for some larger companies, but I very much believe it will be a huge issue for the majority of companies that are not in the top percentile of market share on the platform. Many will not have the resources or the capability to pursue this with rigor and will default to labeling vulnerabilities as lower severities than they actually should be as a way of saving time and money.

If nothing else, I'm advocating that CSPs should have the choice to stick with CVSS (and account for internet reachability still, given it's part of the vector data) or go their own way and determine exploitability through internal methodologies. Forcing every CSP, regardless of size, to comply with this will likely result in security being dropped for the sake of staying in business.

ghost: Badger, I'm reading the language the same in regards to the burden of review. I think this reading seems correct given Pete's comment about lows going ignored that have a higher true severity in a given environment.  When pulling static scanning, STIG, web/api, etc all into the mix as needing individual tailored review for a CSP, on a frequent enough occasion to be able to mitigate within 3 days, this seems like a massive human resource burden. 

pete-gov [FEDRAMP-OFFICIAL]: > However, from my understanding of the language presented in this RFC, the requirement will force every company participating in FedRAMP to have sufficient staff on hand to determine exploitability for every vulnerability detected. 

Humans should not be looking at scan reports and making decisions based off the output. It should not involve a human to assess the criticality of the affected resource, if the resource is reachable by a potential threat, if the vulnerability is in a service/library/etc. in active use, if the vulnerability is detectable, how prevalent the vulnerability is inside the environment, and if the vulnerability is mitigated. 

These are all things for the computers to do. In most cases even a simple rules engine can apply the required factors. This is a security issue to be addressed with superior tools, not more people to argue over spreadsheets.

author: kcarr91
text:

kcarr91: Have there been collaborative discussions with DISA to ensure these updated Vulnerability Management standards (once finalized) align with future IL4/5 requirements? discussion_title: Q&A and casual open discussion on RFC-0012 (CVM)
author: brandonganem
text:
Re: Q&A and casual open discussion on RFC-0012 (CVM)

brandonganem: First of all, thank you for providing the opportunity to deliver feedback on FedRAMP’s direction. Overall, FedRAMP is moving in a direction that aligns with how GitHub thinks about risk management, namely the prioritization of `credibly exploitable` vulnerabilities and their actual impact to our organization. This alignment does enable a few positive things to happen:

- We can properly prioritize actual risk to our organization over and above other vulnerabilities that are mitigated or not impactful.  
- Hygiene patching remains important, but we gain a great deal of flexibility with the longer timelines afforded for `All detected vulnerabilities`.  
- Alignment (or enablement) of logical grouping of vulnerabilities. This is already how we operate as an organization, but we have to instead group by asset & CVE for our current con-mon reporting.

The move away from previously difficult to parse language is also greatly appreciated.

That said, we do have some specific feedback that would be useful to drive further clarification within the standard.

## Definitions

### `Credibly Exploitable Vulnerability`

We believe the intent behind `Credibly Exploitable Vulnerability (CEV)` is good. Our concerns stem from a lack of clarity on what constitutes a `CEV`. The way the standard is written, a good deal is left up to the organization and security program to determine. This *is* a good thing, we worry however that this will devolve into requiring large justifications for many vulnerabilities.

A sample criteria or recommendation in an appendix could be a useful tool to guide the conversation between organizations and their sponsoring agencies. While it’s obvious that anything on the CISA KEV list likely belongs as a `CEV`, and likewise if we have another intelligence source giving us reason to believe there is an exploit available then it qualifies. On the less clear side of things, EPSS is a useful tool for triaging and ranking priorities. Is there an EPSS (Exploit Prediction Scoring System) score that should escalate a finding to `CEV`? Probably, but the methodology here is likely to vary highly between organizations.

How does physical access play into this? Do we consider physical exploits as `CEV`? Should we include notes about the security of our datacenters? What about when utilizing cloud vendors?

### Remediation & Mitigation

We think directly referencing the definition in `NIST SP 800-216` makes more sense than re-defining it in this standard.

### False Positives

We often see scanning vendors detect all possible CVEs against a kernel, even when the exploitable kernel module is not present. For example, bluetooth vulnerabilities on Ubuntu kernels. This code is not loaded or present, but due to the way scanning vendors detect CVEs, often they are just included in as a result of basic version matching. Would these be considered `Fully Mitigated` or `False Positives`? We currently consider these `False Positives`.

### Risk Adjustment

Something not covered in the document is the ability to risk adjust vulnerabilities. Currently, we are only allowed to adjust the risk score of a vulnerability by one level (High \-\> Moderate for example). Clarifying that we have greater control to make risk based decisions here would be helpful.

pete-gov [FEDRAMP-OFFICIAL]: Hey Brandon, thank you for sharing this! I just want to quickly point out that if you want this to be explicitly considered as part of the public comment for this RFC, you should also post it [in the formal RFC discussion thread](https://github.com/FedRAMP/community/discussions/59). ;)

> This is a good thing, we worry however that this will devolve into requiring large justifications for many vulnerabilities.

I'm aware that there's a lot of scarring in the FedRAMP community about previous interactions with AOs and their representatives as well as the JAB, the PMO, etc. It's important to note though that from FedRAMP's perspective this information is shared from the CSP to agency customers as a courtesy in a business relationship to ensure the agency customer has sufficient information to understand ongoing risks to their information and make decisions related to how they use those systems.

Justifications really shouldn't be a back and forth - the CSP says what they are doing and why. The agency can say that might not be good enough for them and ask for something that goes beyond the standard set by FedRAMP, then the CSP can choose if they want to do something differently as a result, but that's a business relationship issue and is unrelated to FedRAMP's role as a standardizer of the process.

> Probably, but the methodology here is likely to vary highly between organizations.

In early adoption we somewhat encourage this - approach variance at the beginning tends to encourage innovation. There **will** be changes to these policies as the community puts them into practice and we see the results either way though.

 > How does physical access play into this?

Any gap or vulnerability related to a control or other risk is included in the definition, so yes, definitely.

> We think directly referencing the definition in NIST SP 800-216 makes more sense than re-defining it in this standard.

We do also reference those, but had some initial feedback about those definitions being unclear in a previous RFC.

> This code is not loaded or present, but due to the way scanning vendors detect CVEs, often they are just included in as a result of basic version matching. Would these be considered Fully Mitigated or False Positives? We currently consider these False Positives.

Agreed this would be a False Positive, just always important that it include confirmation that the code isn't loaded rather than just saying "our policy is that we don't start bluetooth modules so we can ignore this." For example, you might have one random machine where someone did enable the bluetooth module and then it's legit. 

> Something not covered in the document is the ability to risk adjust vulnerabilities.

FRR-CVM-04 describes a process that can (and should) be continuous and circular. As the context of the vulnerability changes, the risk and severity should be adjusted (upward or downward). No stepping limit exists in this policy. ;)

discussion_title: Q&A and casual open discussion on RFC-0012 (CVM)
author: mjprager
text:
Re: Q&A and casual open discussion on RFC-0012 (CVM)

mjprager: I know the focus is to move away from being incredibly prescriptive, but we were wondering what checks and balances will exist to ensure that a CSP doesn't have a crappy vuln scanner, with half the detections turned off, or misconfigurations, or delayed signature updates, yet produces a POAM report / AO dashboard that shows a shiny wonderful picture?

pete-gov [FEDRAMP-OFFICIAL]: > I know the focus is to move away from being incredibly prescriptive, but we were wondering what checks and balances will exist to ensure that a CSP doesn't have a crappy vuln scanner, with half the detections turned off, or misconfigurations, or delayed signature updates, yet produces a POAM report / AO dashboard that shows a shiny wonderful picture?

FedRAMP isn't currently designed to detect and prevent fraud or attempts from businesses to deliberately mislead auditors or government users. Especially with the current 3PAO process, there is a _significant_ amount of reliance on self attestation. 

Our expectation is that by requiring meaningful information to be sent we can make informed decisions that will help us truly assess the overall risk to government information. In a situation like the above, with proper amounts of data flowing in across services, one would hope FedRAMP and/or CISA would rapidly detect a cloud service provider that routinely underreports vulnerabilities compared to their peers with similar configurations and make an informed decision about digging into why with them.

discussion_title: Announcing two Rev5-focused Continuous Vulnerability Management special events!
author: pete-gov
text:
Announcing two Rev5-focused Continuous Vulnerability Management special events! Last week we released [RFC-0012, a proposed FedRAMP Continuous Vulnerability Management Standard](https://github.com/FedRAMP/community/discussions/59). Similar to the [Significant Change Notification Standard](https://www.fedramp.gov/20x/standards/) for 20x, this standard is a significant shift fueled by the expectations in [M-24-15](https://www.fedramp.gov/assets/resources/documents/FedRAMP_Policy_Memo.pdf). After public comment, this standard will be carefully and deliberately tested and evaluated with Rev5 cloud service providers in both closed and open betas prior to wide release. FedRAMP is hosting two events to spur conversation around the changes in RFC-0012 and encourage formal public comment, with both events focused primarily on Rev5-based FedRAMP authorizations and currently authorized cloud service providers. --- ## Rev5 Community Working Group Special Event w/ the FedRAMP TAG **When:** Wednesday, August 6, from 1pm to 2pm Eastern **Sign Up:** Register for the [recurring Rev5 Community Working Group meeting here](https://www.fedramp.gov/community/) (if you're already signed up then you're good to go!). The FedRAMP Technical Advisory Group (TAG) is a core part of FedRAMP's success. At this session, you'll hear from some of the TAG members about vulnerability management in government, why this updated standard is important, and in some cases where they disagree or think it fell short. We'll also host open Q&A with the audience about Rev5-related topics and share an update on the Significant Change Notification Closed Beta progress. --- ## FedRAMP Vulnerability Management Special Event

| Info | Details | | -- | --| |**When**| Wed, July 30, from 1pm to 2:30pm Eastern| |**Who's Speaking**| [Representatives from industry including Palo Alto Networks, Okta, Cisco, Wiz, Salesforce, GitHub, Amazon, StackArmor, UberEther!](https://github.com/FedRAMP/community/discussions/62#discussioncomment-13890983)| FedRAMP has assembled a panel of industry experts to answer burning questions about how leading cloud service providers approach vulnerability management in 2025. Inspired by the recently released [RFC-0012 for FedRAMP’s proposed Continuous Vulnerability Management Standard](https://www.fedramp.gov/rfcs/0012/), this event will explore industry best practices, FedRAMP pain points, and how the proposed standard fits into existing security programs - and where it doesn’t! **If you missed it, you can watch the recording of this Special Event on YouTube here: https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=Z8-9Ef2cnNQ**

discussion_title: Partnerships
author: DrSC-IA
text:
Partnerships

Does the FedRAMP PMO consider a 3PAO using a GRC tool to offer its assessment services the same as being a partner with that vendor?  In the assessment guidance, it states that when a 3PAO partners with a vendor who has a GRC tool, that the 3PAO cannot perform assessments for the CSP that uses that tool.  What does the PMO consider as a partnership? discussion_title: Partnerships
author: jsantore-cgc
text:
Re: Partnerships

jsantore-cgc: When I was a 3PAO not that long ago, the way we interpreted it was this way:
I cannot make you use some specific automated assessment tool.  If I require the use of that tool, and or make you purchase it, or otherwise have a business relationship with that tool, that violates independence and therefore we could not assess.  Particularly agent based tools, or something they must host in boundary.  I could not say 'if you happen to use GRC tool X' I will give you a 10% discount, either.  Anything that even has the appearance of pushing a particular solution is not appropriate.

That's NOT the same thing as 'upload your evidence to this respository/tool' because in that case, the 3PAO would bear the cost of the tool (which again, cannot be deployed within the CSP boundary).  And even there there, there were quirks about the assessment tools themselves.  While they didn't specifically need to be FedRAMP Authorized, we couldn't just use some random thing either.  

I will say that over the years, many GRC tools tried to partner up with us, and in all cases, I could not find a way to make that work withouth violating independence.  Even if we purchased the tool, their licensing model was often such that they would to charge us to use the tool on behalf of a CSP, it was always $X per project which we could not pass along to the customer.  Also, it didn't really speed up or add efficiency to the assessment itself, either.


troyfine: @DrSC-IA what assessment guidance are you referring to?

iteuscher: I believe they are talking about Section 5.2.4 F.3 of the R311 which is the [Specific Requirements: Federal Risk and Authorization
Management Program (FedRAMP)](https://a2la.qualtraxcloud.com/ShowDocument.aspx?ID=5621) from the A2LA. Essentially the rules for 3PAOs doing FedRAMP audits. Here is the relevant section:

> 5.2.4 F.3 Tools owned or developed by a 3PAO that provide any type of direct service or support to a
> CSP including, but not limited to, creating FedRAMP documentation are considered a form
> of consulting. Therefore, to maintain the independence of an assessment, 3PAOs are not
> permitted to perform assessment services for the same CSP that has directly utilized tool(s)
> that are owned or developed by the 3PAO for any purpose. In scenarios where a tool being
> used is owned or developed by a company with an affiliation to a 3PAO or its management
> team, employees, or subcontractors, the 3PAO must document the rationale for how it
> maintains its impartiality from the CSP when the CSP is using the tool owned or developed
> by the entity affiliated with the 3PAO and how it does not infringe upon the boundaries
> between providing consulting and assessing services to the CSP. This rationale must be
> approved by both A2LA and the FedRAMP PMO.


Here is another helpful resource: https://help.fedramp.gov/hc/en-us/articles/28889328488859-3PAO-Readiness-Assessment-Report-Guide-Version-3-1

troyfine: Thank you! 

@DrSC-IA the assessment guidance that @iteuscher referenced doesn’t say “ when a 3PAO partners with a vendor who has a GRC tool, that the 3PAO cannot perform assessments for the CSP that uses that tool.”

It states that a 3PAO can’t assess a CSP that is also using tools owned or developed by said 3PAO that provide direct services to the CSP to help them with FedRAMP.

It says 3PAOs can assess CSPs that use a tool owned or developed by a third party that provides assistance with FedRAMP that said 3PAO is affiliated with as long as they document their rationale for why it doesn’t infringe upon assessment and consulting boundaries and obtains approval of the rationale from A2LA and FedRAMP.

GRC tools providing FedRAMP readiness services are going to have business relationships with 3PAOs where they refer clients to each other, there is no question about that. I definitely think this guidance needs to be visited and updated to clearly document what is or isn’t allowed.

I am curious what the PMO’s current position is regarding the 3PAOs that performed FedRAMP assessments for GRC software providers that provide FedRAMP readiness services when the 3PAO has a business relationship with those GRC software providers. If 3PAOs are getting client referrals from the GRC software provider they assessed, it is pretty difficult to say that a conflict of interest doesn’t exist.
