Our company is listed as "FedRAMP Ready" on the FedRAMP Marketplace, but we not entirely cloud-native or fully authorized. Which also means we do not have a sponsor yet.

discussion_title: Participation in the Phase 2 Pilot
author: kyhu65867
text:
Re: Participation in the Phase 2 Pilot

kyhu65867: So one clarification is that your company itself doesn't need to be FedRAMP Authorized, only the underlying architecture. So, if your offering was deployed using a FedRAMP authorized hosting platform, you still qualify for the pilot. 

In terms of sponsorship, the 20x path is one that does not require an agency sponsor. 

In terms of not entirely cloud native services, the details around the phase 2 pilot haven't quite been ironed out, but you should expect clarification and guidance on eligibility once we've finished phase one and pinned down the details :)

discussion_title: 20x Pilot Review Feedback Friday (Phase 1)
author: emu-gov
text:
20x Pilot Review Feedback Friday (Phase 1)

We here at FedRAMP have seen a number of 20x pilot packages and have started noticing some trends. We want to start sharing this info with the greater 20x Community.

discussion_title: 20x Pilot Review Feedback Friday (Phase 1)
author: dan-fedramp
text:
Re: 20x Pilot Review Feedback Friday (Phase 1)

dan-fedramp [FEDRAMP-OFFICIAL]: When you're sending in your 20x package, remember to reference the Key Security Indicator (KSI) using its exact id from the official KSI documentation [here](https://github.com/FedRAMP/docs/blob/main/FRMR.KSI.key-security-indicators.json). Each element in the JSON document has a unique identifier in the 'id' field. It makes things a lot simpler if you use the full id as written.  For example, KSI-CED-01 is spot on, but steer clear of formats like KSI-CED-1 or ksi-ced-01 - those won't match due to the case sensitivity and need for a leading zero.

I'd suggest CSPs check their submissions against the most recent KSI JSON file as part of their automated system. This helps in keeping up with any KSI changes and helps us review packages quicker and smoother.

The submissions we've seen so far have impressed us with their focus on security and efficiency. While there haven't been any major hiccups, nailing these small details like getting the KSI ids right will help us grow the 20x program and support future efforts in automation.

discussion_title: 20x Pilot Review Feedback Friday (Phase 1)
author: emu-gov
text:
Re: 20x Pilot Review Feedback Friday (Phase 1)

emu-gov [FEDRAMP-OFFICIAL]: The KSI family `KSI-RPL` is for **Recovery Planning** which is an area near and dear to my heart as someone who has spent much of my career elbows deep in outage and/or incident response.

Some excellent examples of what we have received include not only a Business Continuity & Disaster Recovery Plan or Service Level Agreement where targets for RPO & RTO are initially established, but also an automated calculation of the RPO based on actual database and storage backup configuration and a boolean output of if it maths out.

RPO seems to be a commonly misinterpreted metric. [Defined by NIST](https://csrc.nist.gov/glossary/term/recovery_point_objective) as _"The point in time to which data must be recovered after an outage"_ - an alternate way to view is the maximum amount (in time) of acceptable loss of customer and/or service data.

If your data backup frequency (24hrs) is greater than your RPO target (8hrs), you are probably not going to consistently meet that target...

discussion_title: 20x Pilot Review Feedback Friday (Phase 1)
author: kyhu65867
text:
Re: 20x Pilot Review Feedback Friday (Phase 1)

kyhu65867: A little late to the party here, but we have been very excited to see scripts and script-generated output provided as evidence, as it is very much in the spirit of 20x automated assessments!

That being said, to facilitate our review process, we recommend the following: If you are using custom scripts, you should include the script code with the output. If the output is generated by a tool from a PaaS/IaaS/SaaS provider or another third party, you should provide the name of the tool and the provider as metadata with the evidence. Providing this information greatly assists us in understanding and assessing the results effectively :)

discussion_title: 20x Pilot Review Feedback Friday (Phase 1)
author: dan-fedramp
text:
Re: 20x Pilot Review Feedback Friday (Phase 1)

dan-fedramp [FEDRAMP-OFFICIAL]: Piggybacking off of [kyhu65867’s](https://github.com/FedRAMP/community/discussions/69#discussioncomment-13993332) post, it's a good idea to include some context with each piece of KSI evidence. At a minimum you should include the following elements:

Provide an explanation of how the evidence satisfies the KSI and what the criteria is for the Pass, Fail or Partial decision.
Include information about where the KSI applies specifically for the cloud service offering (scope).
When referencing a document, provide either excerpts or specific locations (section numbers for example) that show the KSI is met
For each artifact, indicate if it was collected manually or automatically.  Remember one of the goals for the 20x program is to automate as much of the security assessment as possible.
When providing evidence that a policy or procedure exists also provide evidence that the process is being executed. If no evidence of execution is available, indicate that.   

This context will really help anyone understand how the KSI is achieved and the connection between the KSI implementation and the KSI evidence. It is also important to remember that an agency or FedRAMP reviewer may not be familiar with the CSP offering or the specific services being used from the cloud hosting provider. So if you are making use of specific cloud services it is helpful to include a short explanation of what the service does and/or links to additional information.

discussion_title: 20x Pilot Review Feedback Friday (Phase 1)
author: emu-gov
text:
Re: 20x Pilot Review Feedback Friday (Phase 1)

emu-gov [FEDRAMP-OFFICIAL]: We've been getting lots of questions about where the submission package should be located 👀 

For the 20x-P1 Pilot, we are not leveraging connect.gov or a FedRAMP hosted centralized location. The expectation is that the submission be hosted by the CSP and access provided to the FedRAMP review team.

Ideally this would also be the Trust Center or central shared location as described in [RFC-0011](https://www.fedramp.gov/rfcs/0011) which can then be used to grant access to future agency customers, but this is a pilot and we have tried to be as flexible as possible.

So far we have accessed submissions via file shares on Trust Repositories, directly connected to a GRC Audit Tool or CSP hosted application, or via private Git repositories. 

We support public facing submissions as much as possible as it gives the community a way to learn, contribute, and iterate from one another ❤️ - but we absolutely understand that certain KSI validation information and evidence may be proprietary or non-public.

discussion_title: 20x Pilot Review Feedback Friday (Phase 1)
author: emu-gov
text:
Re: 20x Pilot Review Feedback Friday (Phase 1)

emu-gov [FEDRAMP-OFFICIAL]: What a week! Even with our Phase 1 Pilot submission window closed (more on that next week from @pete-gov 🎸 🔥 ) -  we are going to continue to post our reviewers' thoughts, observations and advice here as it is relevant for the upcoming Phase 2 Pilot and will help to shape our future standardized approach.

A quick sneak peak on an upcoming Phase 2 requirement will be the inclusion of a CSP group email address. This helps us to streamline comms and ensures that you have the right folks receiving email every time.

This can absolutely be an existing security or support group you already use or a custom one just for 20x.

discussion_title: 20x Pilot Review Feedback Friday (Phase 1)
author: nicole-gov
text:
Re: 20x Pilot Review Feedback Friday (Phase 1)

nicole-gov [FEDRAMP-OFFICIAL]: Thanks so much for everyone's patience as we chip away at the overwhelming response to the Phase 1 Pilot! As always, an influx of packages generates new feedback, so stay tuned for our general thoughts as we work to close out Phase 1 and look forward to Phase 2 later this fall. 

In the theme of sneak peeks for Phase 2 requirements, this week's focus is automated validation and supporting evidence. The intent of FedRAMP 20x is to move toward continuous real-time evaluation of a CSP's security posture. Manual evidence collection doesn't quite meet the bar that we're setting. Some of the really cool pilot efforts we've seen have solved this with real-time trust centers and/or APIs that report on the current state of the service, but those certainly aren't the only ways to solve this problem. For Phase 2, you can expect a remarkably heightened threshold for automated validation and evidence (in other words, fewer screenshots please!). 

In a similar vein, as you're preparing your submission, independent assessors should be reviewing BOTH your evidence AND your automated validation that produced it (is it complete, is it accurately polling the cloud service offering's configuration, is it automated or human-generated, does it fully meet the KSI, etc.). Your independent assessor should be validating that the evidence accurately demonstrates a true/false/partial response to the KSI and also that the method that produced that evidence is a valid and complete approach for your particular cloud service offering. Also, don't be surprised if we here at FedRAMP also want to see your automated validation as we work through evaluating this pilot effort together!

discussion_title: 20x Pilot Review Feedback Friday (Phase 1)
author: emu-gov
text:
Re: 20x Pilot Review Feedback Friday (Phase 1)

emu-gov [FEDRAMP-OFFICIAL]: We heard you loud and clear on KSI-IAM-05 during the Phase One pilot - that it is nebulous, that zero trust principals don't just apply to Identity and Access Management, and that it was generally confusing.

We also saw this KSI being used as almost a rollup of the other IAM KSI validations. What was *Apply zero trust design principles* is now **Design identity and access management systems that assume resources will be compromised**.

Some examples of the thought process for this KSI are below and this update is included in [RFC-014](https://www.fedramp.gov/rfcs/0014) which is currently open for feedback!

- What protections are in place to mitigate a hijacked JWT? 
- Are your SSO and trust relationships well configured? 
- Are all resources explicitly locked down or are insecure direct object reference vulnerabilities possible?
- What about permission propagation and inheritance? 

The ask for this KSI is to think about ways your IdP, trust chain and any services that manage access to information resources could be compromised and how based on your specific architecture, movement within your environment would be limited.

We also have `3` other Request for Comments active 🙀 - checkout our [RFC Page](https://www.fedramp.gov/rfcs).

discussion_title: Aligning FedRAMP POA&Ms with M-24-15: A PO&AM for POA&Ms
author: pete-gov
text: Aligning FedRAMP POA&Ms with M-24-15: A PO&AM for POA&Ms **Bottom Line Up Front:** Policy requirements for plans of action and milestones (POA&Ms) related to information resources apply to federal agencies and their implementation and use of secure systems. These requirements are based on 25 year old procedures for capital planning and long term oversight of agency decision making and should not be directly applied to cloud service providers. FedRAMP intends to align POA&M expectations for cloud service providers with the requirements set out in M-24-15 and encourage the development of a modern approach to product security roadmaps that align with commercial best practices and enable agencies to integrate with government POA&Ms as needed. # **A Brief History of the POA&M** The Government Information Security Reform Act (GISRA) was passed in the year 2000 as [Subtitle G in Public Law 106-398](https://www.govinfo.gov/content/pkg/PLAW-106publ398/html/PLAW-106publ398.htm), adding requirements to Federal agency responsibilities under 44 USC § 3534 subsections (c) and (d) for agencies to examine their information resources and report any significant deficiencies as a material weakness. This law also required agencies to include information on the time periods and resources required to resolve these weaknesses. In response to GISRA, [OMB Memorandum M-01-24](https://bidenwhitehouse.archives.gov/wp-content/uploads/legacy_drupal_files/omb/memoranda/2001/m01-24.pdf) instructed agencies to “develop a plan of action with milestones to correct any security weaknesses identified by the annual program reviews and independent evaluations” that “1) describes how the agency plans to address any issues/weaknesses; and 2) identifies obstacles to address known weaknesses.” [OMB Memorandum M-02-01](https://georgewbush-whitehouse.archives.gov/omb/memoranda/m02-01.html) followed in late 2001 establishing the initial plans of action and milestones (POA&M) requirements and templates. Many aspects of the law, policies, and regulations related to information security have changed since then, but the POA&M has broadly carried forward in government information security as a required planning item for agencies with little consideration for its original purpose: ensuring federal agencies properly planned for the time and resources required to remediate weaknesses when building their capital asset plans. Over time, NIST reintroduced plans of action and milestones as a risk management tool rather than a capital asset planning tool. The modern POA&M used by federal agencies is an awkward mash-up of both use cases built over many years of multi-organizational attempts to align on a single magical spreadsheet-based tool for both information security and business planning needs. Under the original 2011 FedRAMP memo’s requirements to predominantly lift and shift the government’s approach directly to commercial cloud service providers, POA&Ms were awkwardly applied to commercial businesses as well. FedRAMP’s current [Plan of Actions and Milestones (POA&M) requirements](https://www.fedramp.gov/assets/resources/documents/CSP_POAM_Template_Completion_Guide.pdf) are complex and do not effectively give agency authorizing officials meaningful information that allows simple ongoing risk assessments or effectively map to ongoing risk assessment and prioritization for cloud service providers. They have become a maintenance burden that distracts from security outcomes for both agencies and industry by carrying forward this strange historical mashup approach of government systems and applying them to industry. # **Realigning the FedRAMP POA&M** M-24-15 identified a new vision for FedRAMP, where it is “a bridge between industry and the Federal Government, and is expected to thoughtfully navigate situations where unthinking adherence to standard agency practices in a commercial cloud environment could lead to unexpected or undesirable security outcomes.” This memorandum further charged FedRAMP with ensuring the continuous monitoring framework for cloud services is redesigned “to one that primarily monitors the CSP’s change process itself, rather than individual changes.” As FedRAMP seeks to realign its POA&M process under the new vision, FedRAMP is considering the following factors: 1. FedRAMP should not apply statutory or OMB requirements for POA&Ms related to agency capital planning to service providers, including any definition of fields, required information, method of updating, locked fields, etc. provided by OMB for federal agencies. These government capital planning requirements apply *only* to the agency implementation of third-party services. 2. Cloud service providers should be encouraged to develop their own process for creating, managing, and implementing plans of action and milestones as part of their standard product lifecycle (see [SP 800-37 Task A-6](https://nvlpubs.nist.gov/nistpubs/SpecialPublications/NIST.SP.800-37r2.pdf#%5B%7B%22num%22%3A321%2C%22gen%22%3A0%7D%2C%7B%22name%22%3A%22XYZ%22%7D%2C88%2C219%2C0%5D)), while ensuring their process is clear to authorizing officials during the authorization process. 3. FedRAMP should strongly encourage mitigation of risk such that properly mitigated POA&Ms can be removed from risk registers or similar ongoing tracking. 4. Following M-24-15’s direction to “generally empower CSPs to deploy changes and fixes at their own pace, without requiring advance approval from FedRAMP or an authorizing official” organizations should manage POA&Ms transparently without negotiating permission from government customers. In summary, POA&Ms should reflect a cloud service provider's organizational approach to risk management, integrate with their own business processes for decision making and planning, and allow them to demonstrate organizational intent for and progress towards mitigating and remediating (or not) large scale weaknesses in their service that may affect federal customers. The information shared with federal customers should be limited to truly impactful information that the federal customer must be aware of to either inform ongoing authorization decisions or take action to address resulting weaknesses in their own information security posture. Finally, in keeping with recent changes to avoid persistent confusion from the reuse of formal federal terms, any future FedRAMP POA&M policy should use separate terminology with clear differentiation from the current terminology (e.g. “Product Security Roadmap” or similar instead of “Plans of Action and Milestones”). # **Charging the Federal Secure Cloud Advisory Committee** The POA&M is deeply embedded in both federal information security culture and the existing FedRAMP ecosystem; changes to POA&Ms must take into account the impact on all FedRAMP stakeholders, including agencies, cloud service providers, third-party assessment organizations, third-party vendor relationships, integrated tools and compliance documentation services, and FedRAMP itself. The [Federal Secure Cloud Advisory Committee (FSCAC)](https://www.gsa.gov/technology/government-it-initiatives/federal-secure-cloud-advisory-committee) was established in the FedRAMP Authorization Act to determine ways the authorization process can continuously be improved and serve as a forum for communication and collaboration among these stakeholders. The FedRAMP Director, on behalf of the GSA Administrator, has charged the FSCAC with providing advice and recommendations on the specific topic of POA&Ms in its [upcoming public meeting on Thursday, August 14, 2025 from 1:30pm to 4:00pm](https://www.federalregister.gov/documents/2025/07/25/2025-14078/federal-secure-cloud-advisory-committee-notification-of-upcoming-meeting). The purpose of this meeting is included in the linked Federal Register notice and duplicated below for convenience: The August 14, 2025, public meeting will be dedicated to advice and recommendations for reducing the burden and cost of managing Plans of Action and Milestones (POA&Ms) for cloud services and agencies and to develop recommendations for an updated standard. FSCAC is to propose key elements of this standard by addressing at least the following questions: 1. What are the major pain points with the current POA&M implementation for CSPs and agencies? 2. What are the security gaps and increased risks (including missed opportunities) that result from the current model? 3. What are the benefits of the current model? 4. What would a new set of FedRAMP POA&M requirements that addresses the major pain points and gaps while maintaining or increasing the benefits of such a process for all parties look like? # **Next Steps** This community working group thread will be included in the scope of public comment for the upcoming FSCAC meeting. The public may comment on any or all of this topic related to POA&Ms on this thread, [via the public comment form provided on the FSCAC home page](https://www.gsa.gov/technology/government-it-initiatives/federal-secure-cloud-advisory-committee), or in the meeting itself during the appropriate time slot. ### Planned Milestones * **August 14, 2025:** FSCAC meeting to provide advice and recommendations for POA&Ms. * **Late August, 2025:** FedRAMP plans to release a draft updated POA&M standard for comment. * **October, 2025:** FedRAMP plans to formalize an updated POA&M standard for FedRAMP 20x authorizations and begin beta testing for Rev5. * **February, 2026:** FedRAMP plans to announce a Rev5 transition plan for an updated POA&M standard for Rev5 based on testing and evaluation in the beta periods. Progress for this standard can be monitored in the [POA&M Standard FedRAMP Roadmap item](https://github.com/orgs/FedRAMP/projects/25/views/1?pane=issue&itemId=113842723&issue=FedRAMP%7Croadmap%7C40).

discussion_title: Aligning FedRAMP POA&Ms with M-24-15: A PO&AM for POA&Ms
author: austinsonger
text:
Re: Aligning FedRAMP POA&Ms with M-24-15: A PO&AM for POA&Ms

austinsonger: I feel doing it on here is way more productive with more input, but it is what it is.


### What are the major pain points with the current POA&M implementation for CSPs and agencies?

- Manual entry, tracking, and updating in large spreadsheets can be time-consuming and error-prone.
- Duplication of effort when multiple agencies leveraging the same CSP require independent POA&M reviews ￼.
- Variability in how weaknesses, milestones, and remediation details are documented leads to rework during reviews.
- Missing or unclear risk ratings, false positive justifications, and deviation rationales delay closure.
- Monthly POA&M submissions can overwhelm CSP and agency resources, especially for large cloud environments with hundreds of findings ￼.
- Most CSPs do not have direct integration between vulnerability scanning tools and the POA&M format, creating manual data transformation work.
- Agencies may apply different urgency or acceptance criteria for similar findings, creating conflicting remediation demands for CSPs.
- Significant changes trigger POA&M updates even when risks are already documented elsewhere


### What are the security gaps and increased risks (including missed opportunities) that result from the current model?

- Manual review and update cycles can lead to slow closure of high-risk vulnerabilities 
- Lack of centralized POA&M management across leveraging agencies can result in missed follow-up or inconsistent monitoring
- Dependencies on third-party products may linger without adequate tracking or escalation, leaving exploitable vulnerabilities open 
- Without automated historical tracking, systemic or repeat weaknesses may be underreported.
- Inconsistent application of deviation requests, operational requirements, and false positive claims can mask true risk posture.


### What are the benefits of the current model?

- The FedRAMP POA&M format ensures consistent reporting fields (weakness description, remediation plan, milestones, vendor dependencies, risk adjustments) across CSP
- Every weakness has a unique POA&M ID, facilitating auditability and lifecycle tracking from detection to closure.
- Agencies can see exactly what weaknesses exist, planned remediation steps, and responsible parties.
- POA&Ms are central to monthly ConMon reviews and annual assessments, allowing agencies to verify progress
- CSPs can document operational requirements and vendor dependencies, ensuring risk-based rather than purely compliance-based remediation.



### What would a new set of FedRAMP POA&M requirements that addresses the major pain points and gaps while maintaining or increasing the benefits of such a process for all parties look like?

- Allow CSPs to submit POA&M updates via secure APIs linked to scanning, ticketing, and CMDB tools.
- Integrate NIST CVSSv3 scoring directly into the POA&M to ensure consistent severity assessments.
- Single authoritative POA&M for each FedRAMP-authorized system, accessible to all leveraging agencies, to eliminate duplicate reviews
- Build on the existing Collaborative ConMon approach to centralize monthly POA&M reviews and approvals.
- Require monthly updates only for high-risk/open operational requirements; lower risks can be updated quarterly.
- Reduce redundant fields and clarify milestone formatting to cut down on manual work.
- Uniform acceptance guidelines to avoid agency-by-agency interpretation differences.
- Require documented timelines and escalation paths for vendor fixes.
- **Automatic POA&M Entry on Significant Changes**: For high-impact changes, auto-generate POA&M entries from the significant change request process to ensure visibility 
- **Risk Reduction KPIs**: Track closure rates, recurrence rates, and mean time-to-remediate to measure security improvement, not just compliance activity.
- Clear Escalation Path: Mandate a defined escalation procedure when remediation milestones are repeatedly missed.

MY FAVORITE IDEA
**FedRAMP Contextual Exploitability Grading:**  
- Instead of just reporting the CVSS base score, calculate an **Adjusted Exploitability Score** that accounts for:  
  - **Exposure** (*FRD-CVM-07*)  
    - Internet-reachable vs. not internet-reachable.  
    - Accessible by authenticated users only vs. anonymous access.  
  - **Asset Criticality**  
    - Whether the asset handles sensitive federal data (e.g., PII, CUI).  
  - **Mitigating Controls** (*FRD-CVM-04, FRD-CVM-05*)  
    - Runtime container security (AppArmor, seccomp, SELinux).  
    - Network segmentation, WAF, IDS/IPS.  
  - **Exploit Maturity** (*FRD-CVM-02, FRD-CVM-08*)  
    - Is there a known working exploit in the wild?  
    - Is it listed on the CISA Known Exploited Vulnerabilities (KEV) list?  
  - **Patch Availability**  
    - Vendor patch available vs. pending vendor release (VD scenario).  

**Formula Could Be Something Like:**  
`Exploitability Grade = (CVSS Base Score × Exposure Factor × Criticality Factor × Exploit Maturity Factor) - Mitigation Credit`  

**5-Level FedRAMP Exploitability Grade**  

| Grade        | Meaning                                                                                                                                                   | Remediation Urgency (Aligned to FRR-CVM-TM)            |
|--------------|-----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------|--------------------------------------------------------|
| **E5 – Critical**   | Credibly exploitable, internet-reachable, high or very high potential adverse impact, no full mitigation, may be in CISA KEV or have active exploitation. | Fully mitigate or remediate within 3 calendar days     |
| **E4 – High**       | Credibly exploitable with moderate skill, high-value target, partial mitigation in place, or moderate potential adverse impact if internet-reachable. | Fully mitigate or remediate within 7 days (non-internet) or 3 days (internet-reachable) |
| **E3 – Moderate**   | Limited exposure or mitigations in place, low data impact, no active exploitation but exploitable in theory.                                        | Fully mitigate or remediate within 21 days if Low impact, 7 days if Moderate+ |
| **E2 – Low**        | Minimal exposure, strong compensating controls, low or very low potential adverse impact.                                                          | Fully mitigate or remediate within 6 months            |
| **E1 – Negligible** | Theoretical exploit only, very low potential adverse impact, or validated false positive.                                                           | Address when feasible; may be informational only       |

**EXAMPLE in POA&M:**  
   - **CVE**: CVE-2025-12345 (OpenSSL vuln in base image)  
   - **CVSS Base Score**: 9.8  
   - **Environment**: Internal microservice container, only reachable from a VPC.  
   - **Mitigations**: Mutual TLS between services, read-only FS, non-root container user.  
   - **Exploit Maturity**: Public PoC exists, not actively exploited in the wild.  
   - **Exploitability Calculation**: 9.8 × 0.5 (internal only) × 0.8 (low criticality) × 1.0 (PoC only) - 2.0 (mitigations) = 3.9 → **Grade E2 – Low**  
   - **POA&M Action**: Track as low risk, remediation within 180 days unless KEV listing changes.

discussion_title: RFC-0013 SC-7 Boundary Protection Balance Improvement Release
author: pete-gov
text:
RFC-0013 SC-7 Boundary Protection Balance Improvement Release

# RFC-0013 SC-7 Boundary Protection Balance Improvement Release


# **RFC Front Matter**

* **Status:** Closed 
* **Created By:** FedRAMP  
* **Start Date:** 2025-08-11  
* **Closing Date:** 2025-09-11  
* **Short Name:** rfc-0013-sc-7-boundary-protection

In addition to this markdown, this RFC is available in the following formats:

- **PDF file:** [0013-sc-7-boundary-protection.pdf](https://github.com/FedRAMP/rfcs/raw/main/rfc/assets/0013-sc-7-boundary-protection.pdf)
- **Word file:** [0013-sc-7-boundary-protection.docx](https://github.com/FedRAMP/rfcs/raw/main/rfc/assets/0013-sc-7-boundary-protection.docx)

## Where to Comment

Members of the public may submit multiple different comments on different issues during the public comment period. The public is asked to please refrain from including documents or spreadsheets (especially those with in-line comments or suggested changes) in public comment as this creates a significant additional review burden.

Formal public comment for official consideration by FedRAMP can be made via the following mechanisms in order of preference:

1. GitHub Post: [https://github.com/FedRAMP/community/discussions/71](https://github.com/FedRAMP/community/discussions/71)   
2. Public Comment Form: [https://forms.gle/vgHHybwHwEe3Z6an7](https://forms.gle/vgHHybwHwEe3Z6an7)   
3. Email: [pete@fedramp.gov](mailto:pete@fedramp.gov) with the subject "**RFC-0013 Feedback**"

Note: FedRAMP will review and publicly post all public comments received via email, but will not otherwise respond. Email submissions from federal agencies will not be made public unless requested.

## Summary & Motivation

[FedRAMP does not plan to provide updated technical assistance](https://www.fedramp.gov/20x/faqs/) or guidance for implementations of the Rev5 baselines but [balancing Rev5 against improvements to FedRAMP 20x](https://github.com/fedRAMP/community/discussions/38) remains important. SC-7 Boundary Protection requirements are currently imbalanced across these approaches: FedRAMP 20x Key Security Indicators encourage logical separation of network resources to prevent unwanted network traversal while Rev5 baselines limit network separation to Layer 3 subnetting as defined in IETF RFC-950.

To ensure consistency in a modern approach to boundary protection between FedRAMP 20x and Rev5, FedRAMP will begin an urgent Balance Improvement Release for Rev5 as follows:

1. On August 8, 2025, FedRAMP rescinded the “[Subnets White Paper](https://www.fedramp.gov/assets/resources/documents/FedRAMP_subnets_white_paper.pdf)” to begin bringing Rev5 into balance with 20x by removing past guidance that prevented cloud service providers from using other technical capabilities that meet control SC-7. 

2. FedRAMP will formalize updated SC-7 Boundary Protection guidance in all FedRAMP baselines to clarify how this control should be met for Rev5 authorizations. That proposed updated guidance is the primary content of this RFC.

3. When formalized after public comment, this Balance Improvement Release will ***immediately*** apply to all Rev5 baselines and authorizations. There will not be a separate beta period for this release. Stakeholders can expect this change to the Rev5 baselines to occur within 30 days of completing the public comment period.

## Effective Date(s) & Overall Applicability

This is a draft baseline update released for public comment; it does not apply to any FedRAMP authorization and MUST NOT be used in draft form.

* FedRAMP **20x**:

  * This baseline update clarifies underlying expectations for FedRAMP 20x controls but does not apply directly to FedRAMP 20x.

* FedRAMP **Rev5**:

  * This baseline update will apply immediately to all Rev5 baselines and authorizations when formally released.


# **NIST SC-7 Boundary Protection Control Statement**

The NIST SP 800-53 Rev5 contains the following text for the SC-7 Boundary Protection control:

a. Monitor and control communications at the external managed interfaces to the system and at key internal managed interfaces within the system;

b. Implement subnetworks for publicly accessible system components that are [Selection: physically; logically] separated from internal organizational networks; and

c. Connect to external networks or systems only through managed interfaces consisting of boundary protection devices arranged in accordance with an organizational security and privacy architecture.

# **FedRAMP SC-7 Boundary Protection Control Expectations**

The following updates will apply to all FedRAMP baselines under SC-7 Boundary Protection (current guidance or procedures will be entirely replaced with the updated guidance or procedures):

## SC-7 Control Requirement(s)

### Current FedRAMP Guidance:

**SC-7 (b) Additional FedRAMP Requirements and Guidance:** SC-7 (b) should be met by subnet isolation.  A subnetwork (subnet) is a physically or logically segmented section of a larger network defined at TCP/IP Layer 3, to both minimize traffic and, important for a FedRAMP Authorization, add a crucial layer of network isolation. Subnets are distinct from VLANs (Layer 2), security groups, and VPCs and are specifically required to satisfy SC-7 part b and other controls. See the FedRAMP Subnets White Paper (https://www.fedramp.gov/assets/resources/documents/FedRAMP_subnets_whitepaper.pdf) for additional information.

### Updated FedRAMP Guidance:

**SC-7 (b) Additional FedRAMP Requirements and Guidance:** SC-7 (b) may be met by using any technical capability that ensures logical separation between publicly accessible components and internal networks by preventing traversal without inspection and authorization; traffic may not flow unrestricted from publicly accessible components to internal networks.

## SC-7 Assessment Plan/Procedures

### Current Assessment Procedure:

Determine if: 

* subnetworks for publicly accessible system components are physically; logically separated from internal organizational networks; and

### Updated Assessment Procedure: 

Determine if: 

* publicly accessible system components are logically separated from internal organizational network devices; and

discussion_title: RFC-0013 SC-7 Boundary Protection Balance Improvement Release
author: BPFanelli
text: Re: RFC-0013 SC-7 Boundary Protection Balance Improvement Release BPFanelli: SC-7(b) applies equally to customer access as well as administrator access. Since the discussion seems to be centering on admin access, I have limited my comments to this use case. While focused on the constraints of SC-7(b), by necessity these comments incorporate elements of several other control parts and enhancements. Tracking down the specific controls is left as an exercise for someone getting paid to do this. ;) The following refers to this diagram. **Admin Endpoint** - Generally intended to be considered outside the authorization boundary **Network Device(s)** - Not generally generating content-specific responses to the Admin Endpoint - Therefore do not meet the intent of a publicly accessible component for the purposes of the protections in SC-7(b) **Admin Access Point** - First authentication of Admin within the boundary - May or may not have public IP address(es) - Requirements - Inside an authorized boundary - Audit all access traffic - Traffic from administrators to the access point is authenticated at the appropriate AAL - Implements authentication and authorization separate from any interface being accessed - That is, it is only an access point - The same device should not host any other functionality **Logical Separation** - SC-7(b) calls for a physical or logical subnetwork separation - We will allow a deviation from that here on the presumption that: - Subnet separation is intended to direct network traffic to a device where access controls can and will be applied - Software defined networking (SDN) in most IaaS/PaaS environments now supports access control application at any and all interfaces - Requirements: - Deny all; permit by exception access rules - Applied to all interfaces on the access point - Presumes application to each interface on the access point in an SDN environment - A CSO built in a non-SDN environment (such as a co-lo facility) should hew closer to the original NIST requirement of subnetting with equivalent demonstrated access controls - At a minimum applied to address and port - Preferably also applied at the protocol level - Sufficient SDN example: - Security groups with appropriate rules on all access point interfaces - Typical configurations: - Within a VPC - From a customer VPC to an authorized service from the same IaaS/PaaS - From a customer VPC to an external authorized service from a different CSO - Can be allowed - Similar access rules must be applied from the access point to the external service **Access Point Configuration Console (when required)** - May or may not be required - A bastion host typically is configured locally - An identity proxy is often configured from a console located separately - sometimes even a cloud service - Requirements - Inside an authorized boundary - Traffic from console to the access point is mutually authenticated - Sufficient example: - mTLS **Internal Component** - Any internal component lacking public accessibility - Requirements: - User access must be uniquely identified - User authentication may be single factor when authenticated against the same user domain as used on the access point - Federation is sufficient to meet this requirement - For example, the following is sufficient: - CSO leverages an external, authorized identity management provider (IdP) CSO - External IdP users are federated to a user directory internal to the boundary - Admin authenticates to external IdP - External IdP presents authentication token to access point - Admin authenticates to internal component - Internal component leverages federated, internal directory to authenticate the admin - Note: It is insufficient for an admin to authenticate as a local user on an internal component without meeting the full AAL requirements on that device - Device to device authentication is sufficient when both: - Traffic from the access point to the internal interface is mutually authenticated and authorized at the device level - Unique user identity is presented and logged at the internal component vennemp: @BPFanelli Welcome back to the fold! I think I speak for most security folks when I say, this is a great reference for how it should be done and it certainly makes sense. I recall the PMO (probably driven by you) taking a similar position 2-3 years ago, so my following comments will include a lot of that historical context. My problem is the position tries to be a blog when it really needs to be a white paper. Given the abundance of options at each layer, coupled with the the dogmatic, black-and-white approach of auditors, it's tough to know which implementations are compliant without a lot of reference architectures to eliminate confusion. For example - you say `admin access point and internal interface should be mutually authenticated and authorized at device level`. What constitutes mutual authentication? I recall evaluating Google's IAP and feeling it met the above requirements - but I was met with push back; practically everyone thought mutual authentication meant "mTLS", despite there being other options. Even when we reached out to the PMO 2-3 years ago asking this question - the only example were we given was mTLS. Google IAP does support generating cryptographically signed headers and passing those to the backend application for authentication - the app could be configured to only accept requests with headers signed by IAP -- to me the constitutes mutual authentication but given the PMOs reluctance to admit that - people were frozen. At same time, what if you are using a COTS product like Splunk Enterprise or Nessus as the backend - those don't support cryptographically signed header based authn and we have no capability to add that in. We'd only be able to restrict traffic between admin access point and internal face at network layer - was that sufficient? The previous iteration of this guidance suggested the mutual authn was only required when it was possible but we got contradictory information from PMO when asking if network layer restrictions like AWS Security Groups/Google VPC Firewall were sufficient. This is NOT meant as an attack or some sort of historical "gotcha" - I get this s*** is complicated and the PMO was likely stretched thin back then, as it is now. My point is: in practice, this level of detail leaves a lot of questions unanswered and without that additional clarification, innovation and progress will freeze. It might be obvious to you what is acceptable - but the unfortunate reality is there is a ton of subjectivity in the world of compliance - not because compliance is inherently subjective, but because of people. I tend to think this is the reasoning behind the new minimalist direction of FR20x -- perhaps it is an overcorrection that will introduce with its own inherent risks basically asking the question-- can CSPs be trusted to construct complete threat models around privileged access and secure against them? But the previous iteration had its own risks that stymied innovation and left agencies without state-of-the-art-tech for far too long. I'd bet 5-10 years from now if the robots haven't taken over, the next iteration of FR will revert to the "more prescriptive guidance" model. BPFanelli: > * User authentication may be single factor when authenticated against the same user domain as used on the access point I want to add a comment about the seeming complexity of the single-factor authentication allowance for components downstream of the Admin Access Point as referenced above. IA-2(1) and IA-8(2) in SP 800-53 require MFA for "for access to privileged accounts". There is no exception carved out for only MFA to the first hop, and then less-than-MFA is sufficient for downstream components. In addition, EO 14028 and subsequent CISA guidance on zero trust architecture (ZTA) (both of which are still in effect) underscore the need for full user authentication for access to each networked resource. Given the above, the JAB crafted the single factor downstream allowance as a significant relaxation of the guidance as written in the IA controls and amplified in the ZTA directives. Single factor is allowed downstream - but with the constraint that is is against the same user domain. If the admin crosses into a new user domain, then the AAL must be re-established with MFA. I think the JAB did a decent job of balancing security and usability, and some flavor of this should be retained going forward. BPFanelli: > For example - you say `admin access point and internal interface should be mutually authenticated and authorized at device level`. What constitutes mutual authentication? Matt, I share your concern about the vagaries of mutual authentication. The mutual authentication requirement was adopted from the original CISA guidance around DHS BOD 23-02. Someone asked the PMO about it (probably you) and I went back to CISA to get clarification on what they were anticipating would meet the requirement. CISA responded that they really had no idea, and admitted that they could not even locate the source for how that got written into their guidance. Given the above, I consciously changed the wording around mutual authentication in my comment from the previous PMO guidance. Specifically: - **Dropped** the "where possible" suggestion of mutual authentication of traffic between the access point and internal components - **Kept** the requirement for mutual authentication between a console (when used) and the access point - This is the same for any remote configuration architecture - When configuration changes are being sent: - The sender has to prove their identity to the receiver - The receiver has to prove their identity to the sender - For example, every endpoint protection agent has to be similarly mutually authenticated to their console - **Added** the requirement for mutual authentication when relying on device to device authentication - Device to device authentication is severely frowned upon under zero trust when a user is accessing a resource - I suggest allowing it as a practicality - That said, it comes with the additional constraint of user identification - Otherwise you will have eight different admins all logged in as 'root' at different times - This is an incident responder's worst nightmare - Launching a session under the admin's unique login is a little more work on setup, but can be completely transparent to the admin in practice Finally, I offer the following as at least the beginning of a more flexible definition of mutual authentication: - Any configuration where both of the following are met prior to initiating a session: - The resource initiating a session is fully authenticated to the resource being accessed - The resource being accessed is fully authenticated to the resource initiating the session - A resource can be a user, device, system service, etc. - Full authentication of a human must meet SP 800-63 requirements - Authentication of a non-human resource has not (yet) been defined in a NIST standard - Generally the PMO has looked for an authentication mechanism that is substantially equivalent in strength to the applicable AAL if a human was involved - Usually this involves establishing a trust relationship via some previously shared and protected secret - Adding the user ID to the .rlogin file would usually be considered insufficient protection - A host firewall rule only allowing rlogin connections from the access point would usually be considered insufficient identification - The expectation would be that a secure mechanism for trust establishment would be used such as a handshake using PKI certificates Hope that helps. vennemp: Thanks for the response! (Also appreciate your comment about the single factor authn above, was gonna ask for clarification around that on my previous comment but didn't want to turn my post into a full on diatribe). Ahh yes you are correct - I remember BOD 23-02.. Perhaps I'm missing the point, but to me the whole discussion around mutual authentication here is to answer the question: How are you ensuring that the internal interfaces are only accessible via the Admin Access Point (bastion, IAP, VPN etc)? While I agree that this *should* be cryptographically secure and not reliant on network layer restrictions, the reality is making that a hard requirement really limits your options. I can only think of a few solutions that meet that requirement -- Teleport being one that comes to mind for all protocols, and Google IAP for internal Web UIs (but even that has a limitation around whether the app supports signed headers for authentication - a refactor for an built in-house app would be possible but not necessarily for a COTS product.). Even a bastion host couldn't meet that requirement (I'm not aware of any client VPN that could either but I'll admit it's been a while since I explored this) - it would require application-level authentication to the internal interface (SSH/RDP/SAML for webUI) with AWS Security Groups/VPC Firewall rules etc to only allow traffic from the Bastion. To me that doesn't meet the definition of mutual authentication as stated - the internal interface is not cryptographically authenticating the connection; the user's requests are authenticated but that is only after a network firewall (and only a network firewall) allows the traffic through. This position all but forces *everyone* to use Teleport and specs out industry-standard options like Google IAP, AWS SSM, Azure Bastion, Zscaler, etc. Rather than requiring mutual authentication between admin access point and internal interface, I would propose saying "the admin access point individually authorizes each request" so that if user A wants to access interface A and is authorized, the access point allows the connection, but if user A wants to access interface B and is not authorized, it will not be allowed. That is something all the above solutions support - though for a bastion you would need dedicated bastions for each interface. BPFanelli: > Perhaps I'm missing the point, but to me the whole discussion around mutual authentication here is to answer the question: How are you ensuring that the internal interfaces are only accessible via the Admin Access Point (bastion, IAP, VPN etc)? I am suggesting dropping the mutual authentication when a user authenticates with single factor to a downstream component. Even in the CISA guidance it is only a "where possible" suggestion. I say drop it altogether. For example, in the case where an admin uses MFA to access a bastion, and then supplies a password to SSH to a downstream component, there is no requirement for mutual authentication anywhere. vennemp: I guess I was having flashbacks from BOD 23-02 and imagining it was still there. Thank you! ryangmsi: While I support the effort to rebalance SC-7(b) between FedRAMP 20x and Rev5, I recommend the following clarifications and refinements for administrator access scenarios: **Scope of SC-7(b) – Customer vs. Administrator Access** SC-7(b) applies equally to customer-facing and administrator-facing components. Current guidance and much of the discussion has centered on admin access. I recommend FedRAMP explicitly call out that both use cases must be addressed, as the risks and technical implementations differ significantly. **Admin Access Points** - Should be considered inside the authorization boundary, with no dual-purpose hosting of other functionality. - All inbound traffic to the access point should be audited, authenticated, and authorized at the appropriate AAL. - Logical separation should ensure that publicly accessible networks cannot traverse to internal components without explicit inspection/authorization. **Logical Separation Requirements** - While the rescission of the Subnets White Paper provides flexibility beyond strict Layer 3 subnetting, updated guidance should continue to require deny-all / permit-by-exception rules at all access point interfaces. - In SDN-enabled environments, this means applying granular rules at every interface; in non-SDN environments (e.g., co-lo facilities), implementers should hew closer to traditional subnetting with demonstrable equivalent controls. **Downstream Authentication** - Current allowances for single-factor authentication to downstream components (after MFA at the access point) should be revisited. - NIST SP 800-53 controls (IA-2(1), IA-8(2)) and EO 14028/CISA ZTA guidance emphasize MFA for privileged access to each networked resource. - I recommend FedRAMP clarify whether single-factor downstream is a deliberate policy relaxation, and if so, define the conditions under which it is acceptable (e.g., same user domain, auditable federated identity). **Mutual Authentication Language** The requirement for “mutual authentication” between admin access points and internal components is currently vague and risks excluding industry-standard solutions (e.g., AWS SSM, Azure Bastion, Google IAP, Zscaler). I suggest refining this requirement to: “The admin access point must individually authorize each request to internal resources. Authorization decisions should be enforced at the access point, preventing unauthorized traversal even where mutual authentication is not feasible.” This maintains the intent of zero-trust enforcement while preserving flexibility across architectures. **Closing Thought** The Balance Improvement Release is a positive step toward harmonizing FedRAMP Rev5 with operational practices. The final guidance should provide flexibility for modern SDN-based and managed service architectures, while ensuring that SC-7(b) continues to drive strong separation, auditable access, and consistent enforcement of zero-trust principles.

discussion_title: RFC-0013 SC-7 Boundary Protection Balance Improvement Release
author: Rene2mt
text:
Re: RFC-0013 SC-7 Boundary Protection Balance Improvement Release

Rene2mt: Bottom line up front (BLUF), the proposed change to **SC-7 (b) Additional FedRAMP Requirements and Guidance** is much needed, as it provides CSPs more modern and innovative options for satisfying the intent of SC-7(b), which IMO is ensuring systems establish strong network segmentation and isolation of (public-facing) resources.  SC-7(b) is very prescriptive when it states _"Implement subnetworks for publicly accessible system components that are [Selection: physically; logically] separated from internal organizational networks"_ however, this is grounded in an era that predates modern cloud computing and when DMZs were generally implemented via subnetting. We have lots of cloud-native tools nowadays that can be used (e.g., in combination) for implementing network segmentation and trust boundaries including VPCs, WAFs, ALB/ELBs, subnets, identity-based policies, security groups, network ACLs, IAP, ZTNA, and more. Subnet, while still very important, is one of many tools in the toolbox.

#### Recommendation 1

This is very minor, but consider updating  SC-7(b) updated guidance to "SC-7 (b) may be met by any **set of technical capabilities** that ensures..." as a way to emphasize that its not necessarily implementation of one technical capability that is required; there may be many cases where CSP implement several (cloud-native) capabilities that collectively provide the logical separation intended by SC-7(b).  

#### Recommendation 2

It may be worthwhile to establish a common FedRAMP definition for "publicly accessible" in the context of SC-7(b) to ensure that CSPs, 3PAOs, and federal agency customers are all aligned when assessing this control.  

I've seen some stakeholders interpret "publicly accessible" in a number of ways including:

- Directly accessible from the public internet (i.e., public IP, open port) without a mediating boundary (e.g., firewall, WAF, API gateway).
- Reachable from the internet without requiring authentication or identity enforcement.
- Even if residing in a private subnet, components that serve public traffic (via a public WAF, reverse proxy, or API gateway) are still functionally exposed and may meet the intent of "publicly accessible."

We need a common FedRAMP definition so that we're all on the same page.  Hopefully FedRAMP will establish a common definition that CSPs can demonstrate via (future) 20x KSIs.

discussion_title: RFC-0013 SC-7 Boundary Protection Balance Improvement Release
author: vedigaurav
text:
Re: RFC-0013 SC-7 Boundary Protection Balance Improvement Release

vedigaurav: 1: Insufficient Guidance for Non-HTTP(S) Protocols

Gap Identified: Most discussions and examples have centered around web-based access methods (e.g., Google IAP, mTLS, identity proxies), yet many CSPs support operational workflows over non-web protocols such as SSH, RDP, SNMP, syslog, or database ports. These protocols pose unique challenges in meeting SC-7(b) without traditional inspection or proxy enforcement mechanisms.

Recommendation: FedRAMP should provide explicit examples and acceptable methods for enforcing logical separation, inspection, and authorization for non-HTTP(S) protocols. These examples should include guidance for SSH, RDP, SQL-based access, and agent-based communication, addressing how traversal control and access logging can be enforced when identity-aware proxying is not feasible.

2: Ambiguity Around the Terms "Inspection" and "Authorization"

Gap Identified: The updated guidance requires "preventing traversal without inspection and authorization" but does not clearly define either term, nor explain whether they must be co-located or sequential. This creates confusion for architectures where inspection and authorization are decoupled across different layers.

Recommendation: Clarify definitions of:

- Inspection: Does this mean deep packet inspection, metadata analysis, or logging?
- Authorization: Does this include identity-based rules, ACLs, or service-level RBAC?
Specify whether inspection and authorization must occur together at the same boundary control point or whether they can be distributed across layers, provided the traversal is still controlled and auditable.

3: No Consideration for Multi-Cloud or Hybrid Deployments

Gap Identified: The guidance assumes a single-cloud or homogenous environment. However, many CSPs operate multi-cloud platforms or hybrid-cloud infrastructures that include on-prem components or other federal networks. SC-7(b) implementation becomes more complex in these cases, especially for ensuring consistent boundary protections across providers.

Recommendation: Include guidance on how to implement and assess logical separation across cloud-to-cloud and cloud-to-on-prem boundaries. This should address:

- Cross-cloud identity enforcement
- Federated network control and inspection
- Minimum evidence or control parity expectations across environments

4: No Specific Treatment of Third-Party Administrator Access

Gap Identified: The updated guidance focuses on internal admin access points but does not address scenarios involving third-party administrators, such as Managed Service Providers (MSPs), contractors, or shared services (e.g., agency SOCs or FedRAMP-authorized security tools).

Recommendation: Define expectations for external administrative access, including:

- Required controls at the boundary between external providers and internal systems
- Identity federation, trust establishment, and logging requirements
- Whether third-party access must traverse an internal admin access point or can be direct with equivalent controls

5: Ambiguity Around SC-7(b) Applicability to Multi-Tenant SaaS

Gap Identified: The current update does not clarify whether SC-7(b) applies in multi-tenant SaaS or PaaS environments where boundaries are between tenants rather than public vs. internal. This leads to uncertainty about whether tenant isolation must meet the same standard as public-to-internal boundary separation.

Recommendation: Clarify whether SC-7(b) applies to inter-tenant boundaries in multi-tenant architectures. If so, provide guidance on:

- How logical separation and traversal control must be enforced between tenants
- Whether other controls (e.g., SC-4, AC-6, AC-3) are more appropriate for tenant boundary enforcement
- Acceptable tenant isolation mechanisms (e.g., namespace isolation, access policies, per-tenant microservices)

wisecryptic: I appreciate the comprehensiveness of these suggestions. In lieu of expanding the policy to cover every possible situation, I would bias towards scoping the policy to the primary intended use case.

author: nicole-gov

nicole-gov [FEDRAMP-OFFICIAL]: Public comment received via email from Schellman reproduced in its entirety here:

---
**Section:** SC-7 Control Requirement(s)

**Quote:** "Updated FedRAMP Guidance: SC-7 (b) Additional FedRAMP Requirements and Guidance: SC-7 (b) may be met by using any technical capability that ensures logical separation between publicly accessible components and internal networks by preventing traversal without inspection and authorization; traffic may not flow unrestricted from publicly accessible components to internal networks."

discussion_title: RFC-0013 SC-7 Boundary Protection Balance Improvement Release
author: nicole-gov
text:
Re: RFC-0013 SC-7 Boundary Protection Balance Improvement Release

nicole-gov [FEDRAMP-OFFICIAL]: Public comment received via form from Ryan Gutwein reproduced in its entirety here:

---
While I support the effort to rebalance SC-7(b) between FedRAMP 20x and Rev5, I recommend the following clarifications and refinements for administrator access scenarios:

Scope of SC-7(b) – Customer vs. Administrator Access
SC-7(b) applies equally to customer-facing and administrator-facing components. Current guidance and much of the discussion has centered on admin access. I recommend FedRAMP explicitly call out that both use cases must be addressed, as the risks and technical implementations differ significantly.

Admin Access Points

Should be considered inside the authorization boundary, with no dual-purpose hosting of other functionality.

All inbound traffic to the access point should be audited, authenticated, and authorized at the appropriate AAL.

Logical separation should ensure that publicly accessible networks cannot traverse to internal components without explicit inspection/authorization.

Logical Separation Requirements

While the rescission of the Subnets White Paper provides flexibility beyond strict Layer 3 subnetting, updated guidance should continue to require deny-all / permit-by-exception rules at all access point interfaces.

In SDN-enabled environments, this means applying granular rules at every interface; in non-SDN environments (e.g., co-lo facilities), implementers should hew closer to traditional subnetting with demonstrable equivalent controls.

Downstream Authentication

Current allowances for single-factor authentication to downstream components (after MFA at the access point) should be revisited.

NIST SP 800-53 controls (IA-2(1), IA-8(2)) and EO 14028/CISA ZTA guidance emphasize MFA for privileged access to each networked resource.

I recommend FedRAMP clarify whether single-factor downstream is a deliberate policy relaxation, and if so, define the conditions under which it is acceptable (e.g., same user domain, auditable federated identity).

Mutual Authentication Language

The requirement for “mutual authentication” between admin access points and internal components is currently vague and risks excluding industry-standard solutions (e.g., AWS SSM, Azure Bastion, Google IAP, Zscaler).

I suggest refining this requirement to:

“The admin access point must individually authorize each request to internal resources. Authorization decisions should be enforced at the access point, preventing unauthorized traversal even where mutual authentication is not feasible.”

This maintains the intent of zero-trust enforcement while preserving flexibility across architectures.

Closing Thought
The Balance Improvement Release is a positive step toward harmonizing FedRAMP Rev5 with operational practices. The final guidance should provide flexibility for modern SDN-based and managed service architectures, while ensuring that SC-7(b) continues to drive strong separation, auditable access, and consistent enforcement of zero-trust principles.

discussion_title: Q&A and open casual discussion on RFC-0013 (SC-7)
author: pete-gov
text:
Q&A and open casual discussion on RFC-0013 (SC-7)

This general thread is intended for casual open discussion and Q&A on [RFC-0013 SC-7 Boundary Protection Balance Improvement Release](https://github.com/FedRAMP/community/discussions/71). The discussion in this thread will not be considered as part of the formal public comment process by FedRAMP so participants can have a chill place to discuss the RFC.

discussion_title: Q&A and open casual discussion on RFC-0013 (SC-7)
author: ajay-stratus
text:
Re: Q&A and open casual discussion on RFC-0013 (SC-7)

ajay-stratus: The required used of Bastions Hosts by 3PAOs have pointed to the rescinded Subnets Whitepaper. The new RFC should explicitly call out not having to use Bastion Hosts if that is the intent. 

ghost: I'm unclear if the 'publicly accessible components' in the updated guidance is meant to be full compute instances (bastion hosts, web proxies, etc), or if that can now be something else like a next-gen firewall doing break/inspect, an identity aware proxy service, a load balancer, etc.   The whitepaper called some of these out as not being allowed. 



pete-gov [FEDRAMP-OFFICIAL]: To avoid repeats of confusion like the one being referenced, FedRAMP doesn't plan to explicitly call out specific technical capabilities that meet or don't meet requirements; historically this leads to hyper-fixation on those documented capabilities and causes people to avoid adopting better modern alternatives, which is how we got to a place where everyone has just decided that you can't meet SC-7 without bastion hosts. 🤷 

The updated guidance is intended to ensure the spirit of the NIST RMF is put into play and novel approaches that meet the requirements can be argued for and adopted. FedRAMP is definitely down for improving the wording to ensure it's clear that any technical capability that meets those conditions works though!



ajay-stratus: That sounds great!

pete-gov [FEDRAMP-OFFICIAL]: > I'm unclear if the 'publicly accessible components' in the updated guidance is meant to be full compute instances (bastion hosts, web proxies, etc), or if that can now be something else like a next-gen firewall doing break/inspect, an identity aware proxy service, a load balancer, etc. The whitepaper called some of these out as not being allowed.

It's squishy depending on the environment. The whitepaper was rescinded because the things it called out as not being allowed are now allowed and over-fixated on compute instances in a way that does not account for individual technology architectures.

One environment might have a firewall that allows everything over port 80 to go through to a load balancer that does TCP passthrough to a web server which means it's effectively publicly accessible. 

Another environment as described might break/inspect, filter, proxy, and restrict traffic to that webserver in a way that means it is not publicly accessible and either the next-gen firewall or proxy service is the publicly accessible component.

Raikiri1310: From an architecture standpoint, I don't find this squishy at all, which is perplexing. 

Both examples that you've given thus far, have an outside and an inside interface, both are beholden to the rules of publicly routable IP space, and both end up using subnetting which is necessary piece if utilizing internet protocol. They're both part of a logical piece of the cloud network, complete with a routing table and a gateway that does network address translation. 

I understand cleaning up language to make it more flexible to the spirit and intent of the control, but by negating the core concept of subnetting primarily, FedRAMP has given the green light to interpret "logical separation" in whatever way is convenient. 

Technically speaking, a virtual private cloud is used to logically separate away a private part of cloud away from the public at large. Using this logic, just having a VPC means that I'm good right? 

Even though, under the hood.. if I want to communicate using IP, publically routable IP space needs to be translated into private, and the data plane is going to be split by subnet. So we're back to where we started. 

This feels like a document that needs more input from cloud architects. 


pete-gov [FEDRAMP-OFFICIAL]: > Both examples that you've given thus far, have an outside and an inside interface, both are beholden to the rules of publicly routable IP space, and both end up using subnetting which is necessary piece if utilizing internet protocol. 

All the devices in both examples could be on the same subnet without changing the risk of unauthorized traversal (versus them being split across multiple subnets). 

> I understand cleaning up language to make it more flexible to the spirit and intent of the control, but by negating the core concept of subnetting primarily, FedRAMP has given the green light to interpret "logical separation" in whatever way is convenient.

This is the intent.

> Technically speaking, a virtual private cloud is used to logically separate away a private part of cloud away from the public at large. Using this logic, just having a VPC means that I'm good right?

It would depend on the configuration of traffic within the VPC, the updated guidance requires inspection and authorization of traffic to traverse networks. If a VPC is configured with a bunch of open routing between networks then it's not meeting the requirement, but if security groups and NACLs are implemented then it might.

> Even though, under the hood.. if I want to communicate using IP, publically routable IP space needs to be translated into private, and the data plane is going to be split by subnet. So we're back to where we started.

There are plenty of ways to logically separate traffic within the same subnet. That is the point of this update - splitting a data plane by subnet should be done to organize traffic and is not an effective way to limit unwanted traversal by itself. Logical separation between devices is necessary and sufficient.
 
> This feels like a document that needs more input from cloud architects.

Yes, please. That is the purpose of an RFC.

author: BPFanelli
text:
Re: Q&A and open casual discussion on RFC-0013 (SC-7)

BPFanelli: A bastion host has never been the only option. There are many FedRAMP authorized CSOs that satisfy SC-7b as described in the white paper using AWS System Manager, Azure Bastion, Zscaler, Teleport server in boundary, AWS or Google Workspaces, and many others. 

wisecryptic: This is true fundamentally, but every 3PAO/advisory group I have known always requests/advises a Bastion to fulfill the requirements, and I have always been challenged when forgoing a traditional bastion, even when the novel architecture is more efficient and secure (noting also in fairness that the 3PAOs have always eventually accepted the novel architecture upon explanation of control implementation). My hope is that this provides a welcome reset to a 3PAOs standard expectation.

ajay-stratus: @wisecryptic Same situation here. Sounds like this will be a welcome reset for all parties.

discussion_title: Q&A and open casual discussion on RFC-0013 (SC-7)
author: BPFanelli
text:
Re: Q&A and open casual discussion on RFC-0013 (SC-7)

BPFanelli: A bastion was the easy button. For any other configuration, the access point needed to:
- Be inside an authorized boundary - not necessarily the instant CSO's boundary (see below)
- Audit all access traffic
- Meet the appropriate AAL requirements to authenticate users

When accessing a CSO boundary from another CSO, the access should be network adjacent, for example:
- Access from AWS Workspace into an AWS VPC is acceptable
- Access from Google Workspace into an AWS VPC is questionable

Questionable means it did not happen very often, and there was no defined rule established. In general, the question was - If the connection is going to be made over the Internet (rather than remaining within a single CSO's authorized environment):
- Can it be considered as having met the SC-7b requirement, or
- Does it need to meet SC-7b within the boundary
If the former, at a minimum, there needs to be very tight controls on the connection over the Internet to prevent spoofing

I suggest any new guidance take these points into account. After I take input here, I will move my final comments to the comment page. 

Raikiri1310: What gave CSPs the impression that a bastion was required? 

BPFanelli: No idea. We tried very hard to get the same message out that Pete is touting above - novel approaches that meet the requirements are welcome. 

BPFanelli: I will make this guess:
- The white paper was primarily focused on getting across the point about **_publicly accessible system components_**
- Publicly accessible is different than only devices with public IP addresses
- For ease of explanation, it uses a bastion as an **_example_**
- Examples are often mistaken for **_The Way_** 

mjprager: Hah, that's probably why Pete is so reluctant to give examples :) even though we press for them (since they help humans contextualize and understand things)

ajay-stratus: It wasn't CSPs interpreting it this way, it was 3PAOs that would give out High findings for it and CSPs would just have to comply. 

BPFanelli: Can't blame that on the white paper or the PMO.

Raikiri1310: I was part of the technical review team for my 3PAO. I reviewed many many RARs, and none of them had an obligatory bastion host. Some of them had innovative solutions for meeting the subnetting guidance for "publicly reachable", using access brokers, cloud-native features like AWS systems manager tunneling, or zscaler. 

At the end of the day, we had to evaluate whether or not they were easily reachable via the context of network routing, if they were sufficiently segmented logically from a network perspective, and if they met the rest of the SC requirements. 

I don't understand how this is controversial, but SC-7(4), which should be a responsibility for on-premise data centers or the cloud provider.. isn't. 

BPFanelli: > Hah, that's probably why Pete is so reluctant to give examples :) even though we press for them (since they help humans contextualize and understand things)

As Pete has mentioned, examples are an enormous amount of work. But in the long run, the real reason is that they are almost always taken as templates and used verbatim. Witness the ABD example that was promulgated under the title of "VA Job Aid". It was intended only to make a few points about how to build up an ABD. To do that, it broke the ABD into several layers so the example could focus on just a few data flows at a time. 

The result was 80% of the diagrams submitted in SSPs after that had ABDs with separate layers. It was (and still is) awful! That was never the intent. The PMO generally wanted just a single ABD. The layers were just to make it easier to explain. Instead, it became the template for ABDs. 

BPFanelli: > I don't understand how this is controversial, but SC-7(4), which should be a responsibility for on-premise data centers or the cloud provider.. isn't.

I get your concern there, but SC-7(4) only addresses interfaces at the point of connection of a telecom provider. SC-7b addresses any "publicly accessible system components" and these can be buried behind a firewall, NAT server, and a load balancer.

Raikiri1310: we're speaking the same language, but I think you misunderstood my example use here. I find sc-7.b not controversial, I find SC-7(4) highly controversial. 

One of these has a rescinded white paper and an RFC, the other gets no attention. 

I asked the Noblis folks when FR PMO was still FR PMO, and even they gave me a wishy washy answer.  

BPFanelli: > we're speaking the same language, but I think you misunderstood my example use here. I find sc-7.b not controversial, I find SC-7(4) highly controversial.

You are correct. I missed your meaning. What do you find controversial about SC-7(4)?



lesley-hess: > Can't blame that on the white paper or the PMO.

I can see how 3PAOs in general could be an easy scapegoat here, however, we operate based on published guidance, direct feedback from the former PMO package reviewers, Agency reviewers, etc. Absolutely there is variance on interpretations of requirements. When there is room for interpretation, all the 3PAOs I know seek guidance from government representatives, and the reality is - they are not always aligned.  I don't think it's reasonable or conductive to what we're trying to accomplish here to place blame solely on one entity.  

BPFanelli: > I don't think it's reasonable or conductive to what we're trying to accomplish here to place blame solely on one entity.

Good point, Lesley. It is really the responsibility of the PMO to get the word out consistently to all stakeholders. There were lots of discussions about how to get more of the internal guidance published, but it never happened. 

Raikiri1310: > > we're speaking the same language, but I think you misunderstood my example use here. I find sc-7.b not controversial, I find SC-7(4) highly controversial.
> 
> You are correct. I missed your meaning. What do you find controversial about SC-7(4)?

How, or in what form, does a CSP need or procure an external telecommunications service? This control has no guidance in rev5. In rev4, it spoke to providing data and voice communication services. That sounds most directly like ordering a leased line or additional ISP connection. Which, would be more often than not applicable in an on-premise implementation. Not that many CSPs are going to be architecting MPLS or SDWAN into their design. 

This is why I find this control more controversial than sc-7.b

BPFanelli: > How, or in what form, does a CSP need or procure an external telecommunications service? 
> 
> This is why I find this control more controversial than sc-7.b

I think you are correct. A CSO built on an authorized PaaS will almost always just inherit this control enhancement. 

If a CSP has their own data center - or is using a co-location facility - they will need to take responsibility for SC-7(4).   

ajay-stratus: > > I don't think it's reasonable or conductive to what we're trying to accomplish here to place blame solely on one entity.
> 
> Good point, Lesley. It is really the responsibility of the PMO to get the word out consistently to all stakeholders. There were lots of discussions about how to get more of the internal guidance published, but it never happened. 

Absolutely! This is what is critical to ensure that all stakeholders are well aligned in the process. We're all in this together.

jsantore-cgc: @ajay-stratus well said.  

I want to also mirror something I've said repeatedly in FedRAMP related discussions.
All parties need to presume good faith and work collaboratively, and not treat things as adversarial.  We all want the same end goals.
A good faith disagreement should never be cause for corrective action, but instead a launching place to find an answer together.  Once you add in adversarial, you get people 'playing defense,' and that sucks all around.

text:
