discussion_title: RFC-0017 Persistent Validation and Assessment Standard
author: pete-gov
text:
RFC-0017 Persistent Validation and Assessment Standard

# RFC-0017 Persistent Validation and Assessment Standard

---

# **RFC Front Matter**

* **Status:** Closed 
* **Created By:** FedRAMP  
* **Start Date:** 2025-09-15  
* **Closing Date:** 2025-11-17
* **Short Name:** rfc-0017-persistent-validation


In addition to this markdown, this RFC is available in the following formats:

- **PDF file:** [0017-persistent-validation.pdf](https://github.com/FedRAMP/rfcs/raw/main/rfc/assets/0017-persistent-validation.pdf)
- **Word file:** [0017-persistent-validation.docx](https://github.com/FedRAMP/rfcs/raw/main/rfc/assets/0017-persistent-validation.docx)

## Where to Comment

Members of the public may submit multiple different comments on different issues during the public comment period. The public is asked to please refrain from including documents or spreadsheets (especially those with in-line comments or suggested changes) in public comment as this creates a significant additional review burden.

Formal public comment for official consideration by FedRAMP can be made via the following mechanisms in order of preference:

1. GitHub Post: [https://github.com/FedRAMP/community/discussions/88](https://github.com/FedRAMP/community/discussions/88)   
2. Public Comment Form: [https://forms.gle/yYiCUCYt3WruZRBQ6](https://forms.gle/yYiCUCYt3WruZRBQ6)   
3. Email: [pete@fedramp.gov](mailto:pete@fedramp.gov) with the subject "**RFC-0017 Feedback**"

Note: FedRAMP will review and publicly post all public comments received via email, but will not otherwise respond. Email submissions from federal agencies will only be made public when requested by the agency.

## Summary & Motivation

Governance, Risk, and Compliance (GRC) should be integrated directly into engineering and security programs within modern cloud services instead of added on at the end by a separate part of the organization with different goals, expectations, and levels of responsibility and accountability. Automation should be used to align engineering teams with security goals and empower them to rapidly develop and deploy changes and capabilities in an environment where secure outcomes are encouraged or enforced by the engineering tools, pipelines, and workflows they normally follow.

In a modern threat environment it simply takes too long and costs too much to make changes at the engineering level then wait for a future audit by entirely separate parts of the organization to review those changes or enforce policies that are not directly informed by engineering. Development and operations teams began to work more closely together fifteen years ago to ensure that decisions made early in the engineering process align with delivery; the only way to scale modern secure systems is to ensure security and compliance is integrated early into the engineering process as well, including native integration into processes and tools wherever possible.

This proposed Persistent Validation and Assessment Standard formalizes the core vision for FedRAMP 20x authorizations that separates 20x from Rev5 by requiring providers to directly and deeply integrate the security and compliance process within their engineering activities instead of tacking GRC onto the end. It also outlined the requirements and recommendations for assessing the capabilities and completeness of persistent validation as the core activity required for FedRAMP 20x authorization.

All FedRAMP 20x Moderate authorizations will be required to demonstrate their commitment to defining security objectives in code and implementing the persistent validation of these objectives within their infrastructure and practices. This standard does create an additional burden for cloud service providers but is designed to deliver clear business value that will incentivize the adoption of secure practices within commercial services instead of building separate government services to follow these practices.

## Effective Date(s) & Overall Applicability

This is a draft standard released for public comment; it does not apply to any FedRAMP authorization and MUST NOT be used in draft form.

* FedRAMP **20x**:  
  * This standard will initially apply to all FedRAMP 20x authorizations when formalized.  
  * Phase One Pilot participants have one year from authorization to fully implement this standard but must demonstrate continuous quarterly progress.  
  * Phase Two Pilot participants must demonstrate significant progress towards implementing this standard prior to authorization.  
* FedRAMP **Rev5**:  
  * This standard DOES NOT apply to FedRAMP Rev5 authorizations.

## Documentation Guidelines

The following FedRAMP documentation guidelines apply to this document:

* The capitalized key words "MUST", "MUST NOT", "REQUIRED", "SHALL", "SHALL NOT", "SHOULD", "SHOULD NOT", "RECOMMENDED", "MAY", and "OPTIONAL" in this document are to be interpreted as described in [IETF RFC 2119](https://datatracker.ietf.org/doc/html/rfc2119).  
* FedRAMP-specific terms defined in [FRD-ALL (FedRAMP Definitions)](https://github.com/FedRAMP/docs/blob/main/markdown/FRMR.FRD.fedramp-definitions.md) are italicized throughout this document for reference.

---

**Background & Authority**  
[OMB Circular A-130: Managing Information as a Strategic Resource](https://whitehouse.gov/wp-content/uploads/legacy_drupal_files/omb/circulars/A130/a130revised.pdf) defines continuous monitoring as *“maintaining ongoing awareness of information security, vulnerabilities, threats, and incidents to support agency risk management decisions.”*

[The FedRAMP Authorization Act (44 USC § 3609 (a) (7))](https://www.govinfo.gov/app/details/USCODE-2023-title44/USCODE-2023-title44-chap36-sec3609) directs the Administrator of the General Services Administration to *“coordinate with the FedRAMP Board, the Director of the Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency, and other entities identified by the Administrator, with the concurrence of the Director and the Secretary, to establish and regularly update a framework for continuous monitoring…”* 

## Purpose

FedRAMP 20x is built around the core concept that secure cloud service providers will persistently and automatically validate that their security decisions and policies are being implemented continuously within their cloud service offering. The activities and operational state of a secure service should be intentional, understood, documented, and in a state that is always known and understood by the provider.

Secure providers will design their business processes and technical procedures to maximize the use of persistent validation and reporting across the entirety of their cloud service offering. This reduces cost by increasing efficiency, enables fast agile delivery of new capabilities through automation, and prevents unintended drift between the cloud service offering in practice and the business goals for the offering. Secure providers will not be worried when an audit comes around that it might result in unexpected findings and frustration.

All FedRAMP 20x Authorized providers are expected to implement persistent validation programs as part of their core engineering workflow. These programs should be optimized to deliver value to the provider and their engineering teams first and foremost, though agencies and other customers will benefit from the improved security and insight resulting from high quality persistent validation programs.

To obtain and maintain a FedRAMP 20x authorization, providers will be required to have their persistent validation programs assessed regularly for effectiveness and completeness.

## Expected Outcomes

* Cloud service providers will operate effective persistent validation programs to always understand the state of their services.  
* Assessors will prioritize technical review of validation programs to ensure the quality and effectiveness of a cloud service provider’s security programs are documented accurately.  
* Federal agencies will have significantly increased confidence in the quality and effectiveness of cloud service provider’s security programs.

---

# **Definitions**

**FRD-PVA-01**

**All Necessary Assessors:** All entities who participate in the FedRAMP assessment of a *cloud service offering* in the context of a FedRAMP authorization. This always includes FedRAMP and any FedRAMP recognized Third-Party Assessment Organization (3PAO) contracted by a provider to perform a FedRAMP assessment; this does not include agency assessment teams by default as completed FedRAMP assessments are presumed adequate for their use.

**FRD-PVA-02**

**Persistent Validation:** The systematic and *persistent* process of validating that *information resources* within a *cloud service offering* are operating in a secure manner as expected by the goals and objectives outlined by the provider for meeting Key Security Indicators.

**FRD-PVA-03**

**Initial FedRAMP Assessment (IFRA):** The first full assessment of a *cloud service offering* seeking FedRAMP authorization, coordinated by the provider with *all necessary assessors*, that results in a FedRAMP authorization.

**FRD-PVA-04**

**Persistent FedRAMP Assessment (PFRA):** Follow-on assessments of a *cloud service offering* focused on Key Security Indicators, coordinated by the provider with *all necessary assessors*, to maintain a FedRAMP authorization or change its *impact categorization*; this assessment is limited to assessing the *significant changes* made by the provider since the previous assessment.

# **Requirements**

## FRR-PVR

These requirements apply ALWAYS to ALL FedRAMP Authorized cloud services based on the current Effective Date(s) and Overall Applicability of this standard.

**FRR-PVA-01**

Providers MUST maintain simple high-level summaries of at least the following for each Key Security Indicator:

1. Goals for how it will be implemented and validated, including clear pass/fail criteria and traceability  
2. The consolidated *information resources* that will be validated (this should be a high-level consolidated summary such as “all employees with privileged access that are members of the Admin group”)  
3. The machine-based processes for validation and the *persistent* cycle on which they will be run  
4. The human-based processes for validation and the *persistent* cycle on which they will be run  
5. Current implementation status  
6. Any clarifications or responses to the assessment summary  
   

**FRR-PVA-02**

Providers MUST *persistently* run automated and non-automated validation processes on the cycle documented in their Key Security Indicators, following the requirements and recommendations outlined in FRR-PVA-TF regarding timeframes for *persistent* validation and reporting; this process is called *persistent validation* and is part of *vulnerability detection.*

**FRR-PVA-03**

Providers MUST treat failures *detected* during *persistent validation* or failures of the *persistent validation* process as *vulnerabilities* and follow the requirements and recommendations in the FedRAMP Vulnerability Detection and Response Standard for such findings.

**FRR-PVA-04**

Providers MUST include *persistent validation* activity in the reports on *vulnerability detection* and *response* activity required by the FedRAMP Vulnerability Detection and Response Standard.

**FRR-PVA-05**

Providers MUST track *significant changes* that impact their Key Security Indicator goals and validation processes while following the requirements and recommendations in the FedRAMP Significant Change Notification Standard; if such *significant changes* are not properly tracked and supplied to *all necessary assessors* then a full *Initial FedRAMP Assessment* may be required in place of the expected *Persistent FedRAMP Assessment.*

## FRR-PVA-TF-LO

This section provides guidance on timeframes that apply specifically to FedRAMP Low authorizations for activities required or recommended in this standard; these timeframes are thresholds that secure providers should consistently strive to exceed by significant margins.

**FRR-PVA-TF-LO-01**

Providers MUST complete the validation processes for Key Security Indicators of non-machine-based *information resources* at least once every 3 months.

**FRR-PVA-TF-LO-02**

Providers MUST complete the validation processes for Key Security Indicators of machine-based *information resources* at least once every 7 days.

**FRR-PVA-TF-LO-03**

Providers MUST complete a *Persistent FedRAMP Assessment* at least once every 12 months.

## FRR-PVA-TF-MO

This section provides guidance on timeframes that apply specifically to FedRAMP Moderate authorizations for activities required or recommended in this standard; these timeframes are thresholds that secure providers should consistently strive to exceed by significant margins.

**FRR-PVA-TF-MO-01**

Providers MUST complete the validation processes for Key Security Indicators of non-machine-based *information resources* at least once every 3 months.

**FRR-PVA-TF-MO-02**

Providers MUST complete the validation processes for Key Security Indicators of machine-based *information resources* at least once every 3 days.

**FRR-PVA-TF-MO-03**

Providers MUST complete a *Persistent FedRAMP Assessment* at least once every 9 months.

## FRR-PVA-PA

This section provides requirements and recommendations for providers about *Initial FedRAMP Assessment* and *Persistent FedRAMP Assessment* of a *cloud service offering* for a FedRAMP 20x authorization. These assessments are performed by a FedRAMP recognized 3PAO or by FedRAMP directly.

**FRR-PVA-PA-01**

Providers MUST have the implementation of their goals and validation processes assessed by a FedRAMP recognized Third-Party Assessment Organization OR by FedRAMP directly, AND MUST include the results of this assessment in the *authorization data* for their Key Security Indicators without modification.

**FRR-PVA-PA-02**

Providers MUST allow a complete assessment of validation procedures (including underlying code, pipelines, configurations, automation tools, etc.) by *all necessary assessors*.

**FRR-PVA-PA-03**

Providers SHOULD be prepared and willing to provide technical explanations, demonstrations, and proof to *all necessary assessors* regarding their assertions of the technical capabilities they employ to meet Key Security Indicators and to provide validations.

**FRR-PVA-PA-04**

Providers MUST be responsive to recommendations and requests from FedRAMP during initial assessment and authorization; otherwise they will be removed from authorization review and barred from submitting an updated authorization request for at least six months.

**FRR-PVA-PA-05**

Providers MAY ask for and accept advice from their third-party assessor during assessment regarding techniques and procedures that will improve the effectiveness, clarity, and accuracy of their validation and reporting procedures for Key Security Indicators, UNLESS doing so might compromise the objectivity and integrity of the assessment (see also FRR-PVA-AA-07).

**FRR-PVA-PA-06**

Providers MUST include in their *authorization data* a high-level summary of any advice from their third-party assessor that was received and acted upon during assessment.

**FRR-PVA-PA-07**

Providers MUST consult with FedRAMP, in collaboration with their assessor, if their assessor determines the provider has not maintained sufficient information about *significant changes* to properly scope a *Persistent FedRAMP Assessment.*

## FRR-PVA-AA

This section provides requirements and recommendations for assessors about *Initial FedRAMP Assessment* and *Persistent FedRAMP Assessment* of a *cloud service offering* for a FedRAMP 20x authorization. These assessments are performed by a FedRAMP approved 3PAO or by FedRAMP directly.

**FRR-PVA-AA-01**

Assessors MUST evaluate the underlying processes (both machine-based and human-based) that providers use to validate Key Security Indicators; this evaluation should include at least:

1. The effectiveness, completeness, and integrity of automated processes that perform validation  
2. The effectiveness, completeness, and integrity of human processes that perform validation  
3. The coverage of these processes within the *cloud service offering*, including if all of the consolidated *information resources* listed are being validated

**FRR-PVA-AA-02**

Assessors MUST evaluate the accuracy of the Key Security Indicator goals against actual implementation of the process to determine whether or not the provider has accurately documented their process.

**FRR-PVA-AA-03**

Assessors MUST evaluate whether or not the underlying processes are consistently creating the desired security outcome documented by the provider.

**FRR-PVA-AA-04**

Assessors MUST perform evaluation using a combination of quantitative and expert qualitative assessment as appropriate AND document which is applied to which aspect of the assessment.

**FRR-PVA-AA-05**

Assessors SHOULD engage provider experts in discussion to understand the decisions made by the provider and inform expert qualitative assessment, and SHOULD perform independent research to test such information as part of the expert qualitative assessment process.

**FRR-PVA-AA-06**

Assessors MUST NOT rely on screenshots, configuration dumps, or other point-in-time output as evidence EXCEPT when evaluating the accuracy and reliability of a process that generates such point-in-time output.

**FRR-PVA-AA-07**

Assessors MUST assess whether or not procedures are consistently followed, including the processes in place to assure this occurs; assessors MUST NOT rely solely on the existence of a procedure document for assessing if appropriate processes and procedures are in place

**FRR-PVA-AA-08**

Assessors MAY share advice with providers they are assessing about techniques and procedures that will improve the effectiveness, clarity, and accuracy of their validation and reporting procedures for Key Security Indicators, UNLESS doing so might compromise the objectivity and integrity of the assessment (see also FRR-PVA-AA-05).

NOTE: This is intended to provide some leeway that allows an assessor to explain when and why something doesn’t make sense or is hard to understand, or to share pro-tips or similar based on previous experience; it does not allow assessors to consult on the security of a system in general during an assessment.

**FRR-PVA-AA-09**

Assessors MUST deliver a high-level summary of their assessment process and resulting findings for each Key Security Indicator that is intended for inclusion in the provider’s *authorization data.*

**FRR-PVA-AA-10**

Assessors MUST NOT deliver an overall recommendation on whether or not the *cloud service offering* meets the requirements for FedRAMP authorization; this will be determined by FedRAMP based on the assessment findings for each Key Security Indicator.

**FRR-PVA-AA-11**

Assessors MUST limit the assessment during a *Persistent FedRAMP Assessment* to *significant changes* made by the *cloud service offering* since the most recently completed FedRAMP assessment UNLESS the provider is unable to supply the necessary information to do so.

**FRR-PVA-AA-12**

Assessors MUST consult with FedRAMP, in collaboration with the provider, if they determine a provider has not maintained sufficient information about *significant changes* to properly scope a *Persistent FedRAMP Assessment.*

discussion_title: RFC-0017 Persistent Validation and Assessment Standard
author: kcarr91
text:
Re: RFC-0017 Persistent Validation and Assessment Standard

kcarr91: >  FRR-PVA-AA-11
> Assessors MUST limit the assessment during a Persistent FedRAMP Assessment to significant changes made by the cloud service offering since the most recently completed FedRAMP assessment UNLESS the provider is unable to supply the necessary information to do so.

**Recommended Change**
In addition to reviewing significant changes, I recommend implementing a rotating annual re-assessment of approximately one-third of the Key Security Indicators (KSIs) each year. This would ensure that assessors evaluate the overall service offering holistically on an annual basis, not solely incremental changes.

Given the introduction of automated testing capabilities and the reduced number of KSIs compared to NIST 800-53 controls, this approach represents a reasonable expansion of the assessment scope that would significantly enhance security assurance.

**Rationale**:

1. Assessment Coverage Gaps: Despite best efforts, assessors may inadvertently overlook certain areas during initial assessments or significant change reviews. A rotating re-assessment provides a systematic quality control mechanism.
2. Scope Creep and Cumulative Changes: Significant changes may not always be scoped with complete precision. Additionally, minor changes that individually fall below the significance threshold can accumulate over time, potentially creating security gaps as Cloud Service Offerings (CSOs) evolve.
3. Assessor Transitions: When CSOs change 3PAOs, periodic re-assessment ensures continuity and validates that prior findings remain accurate under fresh review.
4. Security Best Practice: Regular re-validation of existing controls aligns with defense-in-depth principles and continuous monitoring best practices.

This rotating approach balances the need for comprehensive ongoing assurance with practical resource constraints, ensuring that the entire control baseline receives fresh scrutiny at least once every three years.

> FRR-PVA-TF-MO-03
> [High] Providers MUST complete a Persistent FedRAMP Assessment at least once every 9 months.

**Recommended Change**: Extend the assessment frequency requirement to once every 12 months (annually).

**Rationale**:
1.	Industry Standard Alignment: Annual assessment cycles are widely recognized and accepted across the cybersecurity and compliance industries as a balanced cadence that provides meaningful oversight without excessive burden. This alignment would simplify planning and resource allocation for both CSPs and 3PAOs.
2.	Complementary Coverage Through Significant Change Process: The existing FedRAMP Significant Change Notification Requirements already mandate third-party assessor testing prior to implementing transformative changes. This requirement, documented at https://github.com/FedRAMP/docs/blob/main/markdown/FRMR.SCN.significant-change-notifications.md, ensures that material modifications receive timely independent validation outside the regular assessment cycle.
3.	Enhanced Baseline Review (cross-reference to FRR-PVA-AA-11): When combined with my proposed rotating annual re-assessment of one-third of KSIs, a 12-month cycle would provide comprehensive coverage while maintaining continuous assurance.
4.	Resource Optimization: The shift from 9 to 12 months would allow for more thorough preparation and execution of assessments, potentially improving quality while reducing scheduling friction for all stakeholders.

**Alternative Consideration**: If the PMO determines that more frequent oversight is necessary for High impact systems, a mid-cycle review at 6 months post-assessment could focus specifically on significant changes implemented during that period. However, given the existing significant change requirements for transformative and how they should have 3PAO reivew, this additional touchpoint may be redundant and represents unnecessary overhead.


> FRR-PVA-PA-01
> Providers MUST have the implementation of their goals and validation processes assessed by a FedRAMP recognized Third-Party Assessment Organization OR by FedRAMP directly, AND MUST include the results of this assessment in the authorization data for their Key Security Indicators without modification.

 i think **OR by FedRAMP directly** should be removed
 
Having FedRAMP directly conduct assessments conflicts with the program's strategic direction and creates inefficiencies. This seems counter intuitive to the direction the PMO has taken in 2025 (e.g. be the ones more providing guidance and policy and stopping formal package reviews).  Testing should always be done by a 3PAO who are trained and accredited to perform such work. 

The PMO has identified their staffing as "the single biggest risk to FedRAMP today." Using limited staff to duplicate 3PAO work is inefficient when those resources could focus on oversight, policy development, and authorization decisions.

> FRR-PVA-AA-10
> Assessors MUST NOT deliver an overall recommendation on whether or not the cloud service offering meets the requirements for FedRAMP authorization; this will be determined by FedRAMP based on the assessment findings for each Key Security Indicator.

If FedRAMP will make final determinations on what constitutes acceptable for authorization, the program must publish clear, objective standards defining requirements for each impact level (Low, Moderate, and High). Without transparent, publicly available criteria, CSPs and 3PAOs cannot design compliant solutions with confidence, leading to inconsistent outcomes, unnecessary rework, and reduced trust in the authorization process. Official standards would provide the predictability and accountability necessary for an efficient, fair authorization program.


mhungate-schellman: Agreed with @kcarr91 thoughts above, especially around FRR-PVA-AA-11 and the FRD-PVA-04 definition. 

Limiting the scope of persistent FedRAMP assessments to only include “significant changes made by the provider since the previous assessment” creates a risk of unintended consequences for the overall security posture of authorized cloud services. While it seems as if the intent is to rely on cloud service providers’ change control processes, this assumption cannot guarantee that all security capabilities continue to operate as expected between assessments.

Unintended changes may occur that are not formally classified as an SCR under the FedRAMP SCN standard, yet still materially impact security. In addition, insider threats or intentional misconfigurations could circumvent ongoing KSI validation checks. For example, if Infrastructure-as-Code baselines are modified as part of a routine change and inadvertently disable a security safeguard that falls outside of the automated validation pipeline, this weakness could remain undetected without an independent recurring assessment.

Additionally, FRR-PVA-02 states “Providers MUST persistently run **_automated and non-automated_** validation processes…” However, without recurring independent review, these non-automated processes would lack even more oversight and accountability, creating a blind spot in assurance.

Recurring assessments conducted by an independent third party are standard practice across nearly all major commercial security frameworks (SOC, ISO, PCI, etc.). These reassessments provide assurance to downstream customers that the cloud service provider’s environment continues to meet baseline security expectations. Without such a requirement, FedRAMP risks lowering its assurance standard below widely accepted industry norms. To maintain confidence in the security of federal systems, FedRAMP should ensure persistent validation includes recurring, independent third-party assessments so that trust is preserved in both the program and the cloud services it authorizes.

discussion_title: RFC-0017 Persistent Validation and Assessment Standard
author: mhungate-schellman
text:
Re: RFC-0017 Persistent Validation and Assessment Standard

mhungate-schellman: > FRR-PVA-01
Providers MUST maintain simple high-level summaries of at least the following for each Key Security Indicator:
> 1. Goals for how it will be implemented and validated, including clear pass/fail criteria and traceability

> FRR-PVA-03
Providers MUST treat failures detected during persistent validation or failures of the persistent validation process as vulnerabilities and follow the requirements and recommendations in the FedRAMP Vulnerability Detection and Response Standard for such findings.

We support the intent of FRR-PVA-01 and FRR-PVA-03 in ensuring that failures in persistent validation are treated as vulnerabilities and managed under the FedRAMP Vulnerability Detection and Response (VDR) Standard. However, as currently written, these requirements risk creating gaps in how agencies understand and act on risk.

1. Pass/Fail Criteria May Not Capture Risk:
The current model emphasizes binary pass/fail results for KSIs. While efficient, this approach may obscure meaningful risk. For example, a CSP could define a KSI implementation as “all data flows are encrypted except for X flow.” The validation logic would pass because it aligns with the CSP’s stated implementation, but the exception (X flow unencrypted) represents a real residual risk. Agencies would not see this context unless they performed additional follow-up, which undermines the purpose of persistent validation.
2.	Oversight in Risk Classification:
CSPs are currently able to classify and assign risk ratings under VDR with minimal oversight. Given the subjectivity involved in contextualizing vulnerability risk, there is a need for structured, ongoing oversight. 3PAOs are already embedded in the assessment of KSIs and are well-positioned to provide authoritative input on the severity of KSI failures and their corresponding risk to federal data.

> FRR-PVA-AA-01
> Assessors MUST evaluate the underlying processes (both machine-based and human-based) that providers use to validate Key Security Indicators; this evaluation should include at least:
> 3. The coverage of these processes within the cloud service offering, including if all of the consolidated information resources listed are being validated

This requirement (# 3) is ambiguous in how CSPs are expected to demonstrate compliance. Specifically, there is no clear requirement for a CSP to present a centralized, structured artifact (e.g., a system-level diagram) that shows which information resources (systems, subsystems, data flows, roles) are in scope and how they will be validated.

Without such a requirement, 3PAOs must rely on unstructured, conversational descriptions and ad hoc artifacts from CSPs. This becomes highly problematic (or even unworkable) for large or complex CSPs, where multiple teams contribute to system architecture, data flows, identity management, configuration, and monitoring.

FedRAMP should require CSPs to produce a **FedRAMP system architecture diagram** to (a) reduce assessor dependence on loosely defined descriptions, (b) improve consistency and transparency across CSPs, and (c) make assessments more scalable and reliable even in complex environments.

> FRR-PVA-AA-02
> Assessors` MUST evaluate the accuracy of the Key Security Indicator goals against actual implementation of the process to determine whether or not the provider has accurately documented their process.

This phrasing creates uncertainty about the intended object of evaluation. Specifically:
- It first directs 3PAOs to evaluate KSI goals against **_actual implementation_** (suggesting a process effectiveness / implementation audit).
- It then instructs 3PAOs to determine whether the CSP has **_accurately documented_** the process (suggesting a documentation / alignment check).

It is unclear whether the KSI requires validation of (a) the CSP’s documentation against its stated goals, or (b) the CSP’s actual operational implementation against those goals. Both are important, but they require different evidence and evaluation methods. Without clarity, 3PAOs may apply different interpretations - some focusing on document accuracy, others on process execution - leading to inconsistent assessments across CSPs.

> FRR-PVA-AA-09
Assessors MUST deliver a high-level summary of their assessment process and resulting findings for each Key Security Indicator that is intended for inclusion in the provider’s authorization data.

The current requirement directs assessors to provide a high-level summary of their assessment process and findings for each KSI, but does not specify a consistent format. This lack of standardization will likely result in varied reporting styles across 3PAOs.

FedRAMP should provide a standardized summary template for 3PAOs to use. A common format would reduce variability, decrease agency confusion, and limit repetitive follow-up questions –  improving both efficiency and clarity in the authorization process.

> FRR-PVA-AA-10
Assessors MUST NOT deliver an overall recommendation on whether or not the cloud service offering meets the requirements for FedRAMP authorization; this will be determined by FedRAMP based on the assessment findings for each Key Security Indicator.

FedRAMP should publish clear expectations on which assessment outcomes or deficiencies are considered unacceptable for authorization. This would give 3PAOs consistent direction, prevent confusion during assessments, and ensure CSPs understand the potential impact of significant findings.

author: cbaerschellman

cbaerschellman: > **FRD-PVA-01**
> **All Necessary Assessors:** All entities who participate in the FedRAMP assessment of a _cloud service offering_ in the context of a FedRAMP authorization. This always includes FedRAMP and any FedRAMP recognized Third-Party Assessment Organization (3PAO) contracted by a provider to perform a FedRAMP assessment; this does not include agency assessment teams by default as completed FedRAMP assessments are presumed adequate for their use.
 
Does "FedRAMP recognized" 3PAO mean a 3PAO accredited by the A2LA? The PMO should consider clarifying if "FedRAMP recognized" means a 3PAO accredited by the A2LA.

> **FRR-PVA-PA-01**
> Providers MUST have the implementation of their goals and validation processes assessed by a FedRAMP recognized Third-Party Assessment Organization OR by FedRAMP directly, AND MUST include the results of this assessment in the _authorization data_ for their Key Security Indicators without modification.

Are there specific use cases for an assessment by a 3PAO or by FedRAMP directly? The PMO should consider clarifying when a FedRAMP recognized 3PAO would perform an assessment and when FedRAMP would perform the assessment directly.

> **FRR-PVA-PA-02**
> Providers MUST allow a complete assessment of validation procedures (including underlying code, pipelines, configurations, automation tools, etc.) by _all necessary assessors_.

FRR-MAS-01 states that "Providers MUST identify a set of information resources to assess for FedRAMP authorization that includes all information resources that are likely to handle federal information or likely to impact the confidentiality, integrity, or availability of federal information handled by the cloud service offering." 

Does FRR-PVA-PA-02 only apply to information resources that are considered in scope based on FRR-MAS-01? The PMO should consider clarifying if the scope of FRR-PVA-PA-02 only applies to information resources in scope as defined by FRR-MAS-01.

> **FRR-PVA-PA-03**
> Providers SHOULD be prepared and willing to provide technical explanations, demonstrations, and proof to _all necessary assessors_ regarding their assertions of the technical capabilities they employ to meet Key Security Indicators and to provide validations.

This may lead to assessors being unable to obtain assurance that technical capabilities have been employed to meet KSIs. The PMO should consider mandating that providers be prepared and willing to provide technical explanations, demonstrations, and proof to all necessary assessors regarding their assertions to all technical capabilities they employ to meet KSIs.

> **FRR-PVA-PA-04**
> Providers MUST be responsive to recommendations and requests from FedRAMP during initial assessment and authorization; otherwise they will be removed from authorization review and barred from submitting an updated authorization request for at least six months.

This statement might be interpreted that the CSP must implement all requests and recommendations from the FedRAMP PMO even if the CSP believes the requests goes beyond the rules and regulations of the FedRAMP 20x requirements and KSIs. The PMO should consider clarifying the requirement to provide room for dialogue with the CSP: "Providers should be responsive to recommendations and requests from FedRAMP during the initial assessment. If there is a disagreement regarding whether the recommendations or requests align with FedRAMP 20x rules and regulations, including KSIs, providers should document their rationale and submit it to the FedRAMP PMO for discussion."
 
> **FRR-PVA-AA-02**
> Assessors MUST evaluate the accuracy of the Key Security Indicator goals against actual implementation of the process to determine whether or not the provider has accurately documented their process.

It's not clear how an assessor would capture discrepancies with the manner in which the provider has documented their process. In a Rev. 5 assessment, this would typically lead to a PL-2 finding with a discrete list of documentation discrepancies. The PMO should consider clarifying how an assessor would capture discrepancies related to a provider's documentation around their process for meeting the KSI goals.

> **FRR-PVA-AA-04**
> Assessors MUST perform evaluation using a combination of quantitative and expert qualitative assessment as appropriate AND document which is applied to which aspect of the assessment.

Current methodology is only qualitative and all current PMO guidance only works with qualitative assessments. If quantitative assessments are needed how will methodologies need to change and will the PMO provide a quantitative framework. The PMO should consider that current methodology is only qualitative and without the proper framework, training, and guidance changing to a hybrid methodology will be difficult and this switch could result in lower quality assessments.

> **FRR-PVA-AA-05**
> Assessors SHOULD engage provider experts in discussion to understand the decisions made by the provider and inform expert qualitative assessment, and SHOULD perform independent research to test such information as part of the expert qualitative assessment process.

It's not clear what would constitute a "provider expert". If a CSO is being assessed, the individuals who designed, built, and manage the CSO would typically be considered the experts.  The PMO should consider clarifying the role of "provider experts" and their interaction with the assessment organization.

> **FRR-PVA-AA-06**
> Assessors MUST NOT rely on screenshots, configuration dumps, or other point-in-time output as evidence EXCEPT when evaluating the accuracy and reliability of a process that generates such point-in-time output.

Non-technical KSIs will be difficult to evaluate without relying on screenshots, configuration dumps, or other point-in-time output as evidence. For example, there is no reliable way of evaluating KSI-PIY-06 without screenshots or other point in time output. For reference:  "KSI-PIY-06: Have staff and budget for security commensurate with the size, complexity, scope, executive priorities, and risk of the service offering that demonstrates commitment to delivering a secure service." The PMO should consider limiting FRR-PVA-AA-06 to specific technical KSIs where it is possible not to rely on  screenshots, configuration dumps, or other point-in-time output.

> **FRR-PVA-AA-09**
> Assessors MUST deliver a high-level summary of their assessment process and resulting findings for each Key Security Indicator that is intended for inclusion in the provider’s _authorization data._

This does not clarify if the assessor is to assign a level of risk for any resulting findings. The PMO should consider clarifying if assessors are to assign a level of risk to any resulting findings.

pete-gov [FEDRAMP-OFFICIAL]: > Does "FedRAMP recognized" 3PAO mean a 3PAO accredited by the A2LA? The PMO should consider clarifying if "FedRAMP recognized" means a 3PAO accredited by the A2LA.

For public awareness, "FedRAMP recognized 3PAO" has been a standard term used in FedRAMP and A2LA materials for many years. It means the 3PAO has been accredited by the A2LA and that FedRAMP has officially recognized the 3PAO after A2LA accreditation. 

This is explained by A2LA on their [FedRAMP accreditation page](https://a2la.org/accreditation/fedramp/):"Under the Security Assessment Framework, 3PAOs are required to be accredited by A2LA in order to be recognized by FedRAMP. " 

It is furthermore explained in A2LA's R311 Specific Requirements: FedRAMP in **5.3**: "A2LA accreditation is the first step in gaining FedRAMP recognition. A2LA provides evidence to the FedRAMP PMO, but that does not imply acceptance to the FedRAMP 3PAO program. A2LA submits the entire 3PAO assessment package (including the assessor report, corrective actions, correspondences and any Accreditation Council comments) to the FedRAMP PMO for final recognition. A 3PAO is not recognized by FedRAMP until the 3PAO receives an official recognition letter signed by the FedRAMP Director and is listed publicly on [www.FedRAMP.gov](http://www.fedramp.gov/)."

The FedRAMP Marketplace lists FedRAMP recognized 3PAOs (as stated on the Marketplace), and there's an entire section of the [3PAO Obligations and Performance Guide ](https://www.fedramp.gov/resources/documents/3PAO_Obligations_and_Performance_Standards.pdf) on FedRAMP Recognition.

```
FRR-PVA-AA-07
Assessors MUST assess whether or not procedures are consistently followed, including the processes in place to assure this occurs; assessors MUST NOT rely solely on the existence of a procedure document for assessing if appropriate processes and procedures are in place
```
How do we audit a procedure that does not or has not occurred, e.g. user termination/onboarding? 
```
FRR-PVA-AA-08
Assessors MAY share advice with providers they are assessing about techniques and procedures that will improve the effectiveness, clarity, and accuracy of their validation and reporting procedures for Key Security Indicators, UNLESS doing so might compromise the objectivity and integrity of the assessment (see also FRR-PVA-AA-05).
NOTE: This is intended to provide some leeway that allows an assessor to explain when and why something doesn’t make sense or is hard to understand, or to share pro-tips or similar based on previous experience; it does not allow assessors to consult on the security of a system in general during an assessment.
```
This provision is going to be misused by every 3PAO and auditor. The current standard of "no advice" should be retained. 
```
FRR-PVA-AA-09
Assessors MUST deliver a high-level summary of their assessment process and resulting findings for each Key Security Indicator that is intended for inclusion in the provider’s authorization data.
```
So.... the 3PAO writes up a summary of how the KSI was assessment and the results. Maybe we call it "Assessment Test Procedure." Instead of having a standardized KSI matrix, we are going to have a customized KSI defined by the CSP that the 3PAO then has to write to. How are we going to forecast LOE for an assessment when every client is going to have a different standard? How are assessors going to be expected to learn a new KSI matrix every few weeks? 
```
FRR-PVA-AA-10
Assessors MUST NOT deliver an overall recommendation on whether or not the cloud service offering meets the requirements for FedRAMP authorization; this will be determined by FedRAMP based on the assessment findings for each Key Security Indicator.
```
Good. Keep this in here. 
```
FRR-PVA-AA-11
Assessors MUST limit the assessment during a Persistent FedRAMP Assessment to significant changes made by the cloud service offering since the most recently completed FedRAMP assessment UNLESS the provider is unable to supply the necessary information to do so.
```
So the annual audit is only going to include significant changes. How would we know that the KSIs are actually being monitored and that their magic KSI tool isn't just spitting out garbage data? Do we check the KSI tool for valid output? Who makes sure that all 475+ FedRAMP systems have valid KSI tool outputs? How do we figure out LOE for an assessment every year when the scope constantly changes? 
```
FRR-PVA-AA-12
Assessors MUST consult with FedRAMP, in collaboration with the provider, if they determine a provider has not maintained sufficient information about significant changes to properly scope a Persistent FedRAMP Assessment.
```
This was undefined in FRR-PVA-05, should probably be defined there too.

discussion_title: RFC-0017 Persistent Validation and Assessment Standard
author: vedigaurav
text:
Re: RFC-0017 Persistent Validation and Assessment Standard

vedigaurav: Please consider below gaps and recommendation:

FRR‑PVA‑01 (“Providers MUST maintain … summaries … for each KSI”)
Gap: The clause requires both “machine‑based processes …” and “human‑based processes …” for each KSI. It is ambiguous when either/or might suffice. Some KSIs may only realistically have one type of validation.
Recommendation: Clarify whether both machine‑based and human‑based validation must always apply, or allow “one or the other” if appropriate. Add “or” option where valid.

FRR‑PVA‑02 (“Providers MUST persistently run automated and non‑automated validation processes …”)
Gap: The dual requirement of “automated and non‑automated” may be burdensome or impractical for certain KSIs that naturally lend to one type only. Also lacks guidance on how to define the cycle, or tool maturity.
Recommendation: Permit flex‑model: “automated or non‑automated validation (or both) depending on KSI nature, with justification included”. Provide tool‑maturity guidance or criteria when automation is required.

FRR‑PVA‑03/04 (treat failures as vulnerabilities; include activity in VDR reports)
Gap: No remediation timeframe specified for validation failures, and no escalation path defined for recurring or systemic failures.
Recommendation: Add requirement: define maximum time to remediate persistent‑validation failures (e.g., within X days/hours by severity), and require escalation to senior management or external assessors if repeated failures occur.

FRR‑PVA‑T F‑LO / T F‑MO (timeframes)
Gap: Timeframes are defined for Low and Moderate impact systems—no timeframes are defined for High impact systems (if/when applicable).
Recommendation: If High impact (or “High” baseline) is in scope, define appropriate shorter validation cycles and assessment intervals for High impact systems. If High not in scope, clarify explicitly.

FRR‑PVA‑PA‑02 (assessment must allow full access to code/pipelines/etc)
Gap: Does not clearly define scope of “underlying code, pipelines, configurations, automation tools” in outsourced/hybrid arrangements—i.e., how to handle third‑party components or managed services.
Recommendation: Add requirement: providers must identify outsourced/hybrid service components, and ensure contractual/access arrangements permit assessors to verify underlying validation tooling/processes even in managed or third‑party contexts.

FRR‑PVA‑AA‑04 (assessors must use combination of quantitative and expert qualitative assessment)
Gap: Lack of defined quantitative metrics, benchmarks, or methodology; without guidance, quantitative component may be inconsistent or subjective across assessors.
Recommendation: Provide a reference or appendix with suggested quantitative metrics (e.g., % validated assets, time to detection/remediation, coverage %, false‑positive/false‑negative rates) and require providers to capture and report these metrics, with assessors evaluating them.

FRR‑PVA‑AA‑06 (assessors must not rely on screenshots/config dumps except when evaluating process that generates them)
Gap: Some KSIs (especially non‑technical ones, human/process ones) may inherently rely on point‑in‑time artifacts. The blanket prohibition could limit feasible assessment of non‑automated processes.
Recommendation: Clarify that for non‑technical/human KSIs, assessors may rely on structured evidence (logs, reports, process execution records) rather than only avoiding “point‑in‑time” screenshots; define acceptable formats for human‑process evidence.

discussion_title: 20x Phase Two Pilot Q&A (old)
author: ElaineFR
text:
Re: 20x Phase Two Pilot Q&A (old)

ElaineFR: Good afternoon @pete-gov ! Question: are there any specific requirements for bringing AI products into scope for FR20x? 

pete-gov [FEDRAMP-OFFICIAL]: > Good afternoon @pete-gov ! Question: are there any specific requirements for bringing AI products into scope for FR20x?

The [Minimum Assessment Standard](https://github.com/FedRAMP/docs/blob/main/markdown/FRMR.MAS.minimum-assessment-standard.md) applies regardless. 

FedRAMP doesn't have LLM-related specific requirements (e.g. "AI safety" etc.). FedRAMP is focused on information flows and risk to federal customer data; that's universally applied any time any service is likely to handle federal customer data or impact the confidentiality, integrity, or available of federal customer data. The thing that matters about AI-based services is what they do with customer data and how information flows are protected, not that there is an LLM involved or not. 

Services that leverage LLMs can do a very wide variety of things in a wide variety of ways and unlike many other traditional services are likely to put federal customer data at risk in a very different way. If customer data is flowing to a third-party AI-based service then you should expect additional scrutiny on your justification, mitigation measures, compensating controls, and the potential impact of using such a service (FRR-MAS-03). For example if an LLM-based service is given permissions to do crazy stuff then it will get flagged the same as any other service that has permissions to do crazy stuff.

discussion_title: RFC-0018 FedRAMP Security Inbox Requirements
author: pete-gov
text:
RFC-0018 FedRAMP Security Inbox Requirements

# **RFC Front Matter**

* **Status:** Closed  
* **Created By:** FedRAMP  
* **Start Date:** 2025-09-29  
* **Closing Date:** 2025-11-17  
* **Short Name:** rfc-0018-fedramp-security-inbox

In addition to this markdown, this RFC is available in the following formats:

- **PDF file:** [0018-fedramp-security-inbox.pdf](https://github.com/FedRAMP/rfcs/raw/main/rfc/assets/0018-fedramp-security-inbox.pdf)
- **Word file:** [0018-fedramp-security-inbox.docx](https://github.com/FedRAMP/rfcs/raw/main/rfc/assets/0018-fedramp-security-inbox.docx)

## Where to Comment

Members of the public may submit multiple different comments on different issues during the public comment period. The public is asked to please refrain from including documents or spreadsheets (especially those with in-line comments or suggested changes) in public comment as this creates a significant additional review burden.

Formal public comment for official consideration by FedRAMP can be made via the following mechanisms in order of preference:

1. GitHub Post: [https://github.com/FedRAMP/community/discussions/92](https://github.com/FedRAMP/community/discussions/92)  
2. Public Comment Form: [https://forms.gle/JkQ7oQtTZPUSjztVA](https://forms.gle/JkQ7oQtTZPUSjztVA)  
3. Email: [pete@fedramp.gov](mailto:pete@fedramp.gov) with the subject "**RFC-0018 Feedback**"

Note: FedRAMP will review and publicly post all public comments received via email, but will not otherwise respond. Email submissions from federal agencies will only be made public when requested by the agency.

## Summary & Motivation

FedRAMP recently sent an emergency notification to the security contact addresses for all cloud service providers as part of the government-wide response to [CISA’s Emergency Directive 25-03](https://www.cisa.gov/news-events/directives/ed-25-03-identify-and-mitigate-potential-compromise-cisco-devices) and discovered a systemic problem within the FedRAMP marketplace: a significant number of FedRAMP Authorized cloud services have failed to maintain their security contact information, have gated contact behind customer portals with required registration, or have otherwise cut themselves off from direct emergency communication from FedRAMP.

This proposed standard outlines clear requirements for cloud service providers to maintain a path for open communication from FedRAMP and government customers, especially during an emergency. It also explicitly outlines the punitive actions FedRAMP will take in the future against providers who do block critical communications and plans for FedRAMP to regularly assess the effectiveness of all provider’s ability to receive communications from FedRAMP.

Once formalized, providers will have a limited time to adopt this policy and should expect an initial FedRAMP-wide assessment of compliance by the end of FY26 Q2.

## Effective Date(s) & Overall Applicability

This is a draft standard released for public comment; it does not apply to any FedRAMP authorization and MUST NOT be used in draft form.

* FedRAMP **20x**:  
  * This standard will immediately apply to all FedRAMP 20x authorizations when formalized.  
* FedRAMP **Rev5**:  
  * This standard will immediately apply to all FedRAMP Rev5 authorizations when formalized.

## Documentation Guidelines

The following FedRAMP documentation guidelines apply to this document:

* The capitalized key words "MUST", "MUST NOT", "REQUIRED", "SHALL", "SHALL NOT", "SHOULD", "SHOULD NOT", "RECOMMENDED", "MAY", and "OPTIONAL" in this document are to be interpreted as described in [IETF RFC 2119](https://datatracker.ietf.org/doc/html/rfc2119).  
* FedRAMP-specific terms defined in [FRD-ALL (FedRAMP Definitions)](https://github.com/FedRAMP/docs/blob/main/markdown/FRMR.FRD.fedramp-definitions.md) are italicized throughout this document for reference.

---

**Background & Authority**  
[OMB Memorandum M-24-15 on Modernizing FedRAMP](https://www.fedramp.gov/assets/resources/documents/FedRAMP_Policy_Memo.pdf) section VII (a) (17) states that GSA must *“position FedRAMP as a central point of contact to the commercial cloud sector for Government-wide communications or requests for risk management information concerning commercial cloud providers used by Federal agencies.”*

## Purpose

FedRAMP and agency customers must have a reliable way to directly contact senior security and public sector staff operating all FedRAMP Authorized cloud service offerings without maintaining separate accounts, login procedures, or other processes for individual cloud service providers. These requirements for a FedRAMP Security Inbox apply to all cloud service providers to ensure that this direct reliable path remains open.

Once finalized, FedRAMP will perform quarterly assessments of all FedRAMP Authorized cloud service offerings by sending test messages to the FedRAMP Security Inbox on file requesting a simple human response. Cloud service offerings that fail to meet these requirements (during quarterly tests or other communications) will be **immediately suspended from the FedRAMP Marketplace for a minimum of 30 days and publicly placed on a Corrective Action Plan.**

To recover from this Corrective Action Plan and return to full service on the FedRAMP Marketplace, the providers for affected cloud services will need to demonstrate they have resolved the gap in meeting these requirements. Cloud service offerings that are unable to address such a Corrective Action Plan within 30 days may lose their FedRAMP authorization entirely.

## Expected Outcomes

* Cloud service providers will prioritize review and response of emergency time-sensitive messages from FedRAMP or other agency customers.  
* Federal agencies will have a reliable way to contact security teams at cloud service providers.

# **Definitions**

**FRD-FSI-01**

**FedRAMP Security Inbox (FSI):** An email address that meets the requirements outlined in the FedRAMP Security Inbox requirements.

# **Requirements**

## FRR-FSI

These requirements apply ALWAYS to ALL FedRAMP Authorized cloud services based on the current Effective Date(s) and Overall Applicability of this standard.

**FRR-FSI-01**

Providers MUST establish and maintain an email address to receive email regarding urgent security notifications from *all necessary parties*; this inbox is a *FedRAMP Security Inbox (FSI)*. The *FedRAMP Security Inbox* is listed in the FedRAMP Marketplace as the “Security E-mail.” 

**FRR-FSI-02**

Providers MUST persistently ensure their *FedRAMP Security Inbox* receives email messages from .gov or.mil emails without any disruption, including meeting ALL of the following requirements when receiving an email originating from a .gov or .mil email address:

1. Messages MUST be routed to at least one senior security official who has authority to respond on behalf of the organization  
2. Messages MUST NOT require manual verification from the sender, logins to a web-based system, or any other sort of authentication by the sender  
3. Messages MUST NOT be automatically resolved, closed, rejected, or otherwise addressed without human review

**FRR-FSI-03**

Providers MUST follow the requirements and recommendations outlined in FRR-FSI-TF regarding timeframes for acknowledging and addressing messages received in their *FedRAMP Security Inbox.*

**FRR-FSI-04**

Providers MUST immediately notify FedRAMP of any changes in addressing for their *FedRAMP Security Inbox* by emailing [info@fedramp.gov](mailto:info@fedramp.gov) with the name and FedRAMP ID of the cloud service offering and the updated email address.

## FRR-FSI-TF

This section provides guidance on timeframes that apply to all impact levels of FedRAMP authorization for activities required or recommended in this standard; these timeframes are thresholds that secure providers should consistently strive to exceed by significant margins.

**FRR-FSI-TF-01**

Providers SHOULD immediately and automatically acknowledge the receipt of messages received from *all necessary parties* in their *FedRAMP Security Inbox*.

## FRR-FSI-TF-LO

This section provides guidance on timeframes that apply specifically to FedRAMP Low authorizations for activities required or recommended in this standard; these timeframes are thresholds that secure providers should consistently strive to exceed by significant margins.

**FRR-FSI-TF-LO-01**

Providers MUST have a human acknowledge and address messages sent by FedRAMP (including any @[fedramp.gov](http://fedramp.gov) address) to their *FedRAMP Security Inbox* within 3 business days.

**FRR-FSI-TF-LO-02**

Providers MUST have a human acknowledge and address messages sent by *all necessary parties* (other than FedRAMP) to their *FedRAMP Security Inbox* within 5 business days.

## FRR-FSI-TF-MO

This section provides guidance on timeframes that apply specifically to FedRAMP Moderate authorizations for activities required or recommended in this standard; these timeframes are thresholds that secure providers should consistently strive to exceed by significant margins.

**FRR-FSI-TF-MO-01**

Providers MUST have a human acknowledge and address messages sent by FedRAMP (including any @[fedramp.gov](http://fedramp.gov) email address) to their *FedRAMP Security Inbox* within 1 business day.

**FRR-FSI-TF-MO-02**

Providers MUST have a human acknowledge and address messages sent by *all necessary parties* (other than FedRAMP) to their *FedRAMP Security Inbox* within 3 business days.

## FRR-FSI-TF-HI

This section provides guidance on timeframes that apply specifically to FedRAMP High authorizations for activities required or recommended in this standard; these timeframes are thresholds that secure providers should consistently strive to exceed by significant margins.

**FRR-FSI-TF-HI-01**

Providers MUST have a human acknowledge and address messages sent by FedRAMP (including any @[fedramp.gov](http://fedramp.gov) email address) to their *FedRAMP Security Inbox* within 12 hours.

**FRR-FSI-TF-HI-02**

Providers MUST have a human acknowledge and address messages sent by *all necessary parties* (other than FedRAMP) to their *FedRAMP Security Inbox* within 1 business day.

discussion_title: RFC-0018 FedRAMP Security Inbox Requirements
author: vedigaurav
text:
Re: RFC-0018 FedRAMP Security Inbox Requirements

vedigaurav: Please consider below Gaps and recommendation.

Gap 1: Lack of Defined Escalation Protocols
Relevant Requirements: FRR-FSI-02: Messages must be routed to a senior security official, FRR-FSI-TF-*: Require human acknowledgment within strict timeframes
Issue: The RFC assumes a senior official will always be available to respond. But in reality, availability varies due to PTO, turnover, or off-hours.
Recommendation: Add a requirement that CSPs must define escalation paths and backup contacts to ensure coverage (especially for 12-hour and 1-day SLAs). Include language around escalation continuity plans to meet response timelines.

Gap 2: No Requirement for Inbox Monitoring/Auditing
Relevant Requirements: FRR-FSI-03: Requires timely response, FRR-FSI-TF-01: Suggests immediate acknowledgment
Issue: There is no mention of monitoring, tracking, or auditing to ensure emails are received, triaged, or escalated effectively.
Recommendation: Add a requirement for monitoring and logging access to the inbox, including:
Message receipt timestamp
Timestamp of acknowledgment and response
Responsible responder
This supports auditability and enforcement of SLAs.

Gap 3: Risk of Email Spoofing and Lack of Anti-Spam Guidance
Relevant Requirements: FRR-FSI-02: Must accept emails from .gov/.mil reliably
Issue: The RFC doesn't address security protections to prevent spoofed or malicious emails appearing to come from .gov/.mil addresses.
Recommendation: Add a control for email authentication (e.g., SPF, DKIM, DMARC) and optionally a .gov/.mil allowlist to prevent spoofing, phishing, and denial-of-service attacks via the FSI.

Gap 4: No Explicit Uptime or Redundancy Requirement
Relevant Requirements: FRR-FSI-01: Inbox must be maintained, FRR-FSI-02: Must receive email “without disruption”
Issue: "Without disruption" is vague. There is no specific requirement for email availability uptime, redundancy, or failover mechanisms.
Recommendation: Clarify that providers must implement high-availability (HA) configurations or email continuity mechanisms (e.g., fallback MX records, cloud email monitoring) to minimize downtime.

Gap 5: Ambiguity Around "Address" vs. "Acknowledge"
Relevant Requirements: FRR-FSI-TF-HI-01 to LO-02: Require human to "acknowledge and address"
Issue: "Address" and "acknowledge" are not clearly defined. Does a reply like “We’re looking into it” count as full compliance?
Recommendation: FedRAMP should define: "Acknowledge" = confirm receipt by a human, "Address" = begin action or triage with intent to resolve
This will eliminate confusion and improve SLA enforcement consistency.

Gap 6: Overloaded Use of a Single Security Email Address
Relevant Requirements: FRR-FSI-01: Single inbox listed in Marketplace, FRR-FSI-TF-HI/LO/MO: Apply to all types of messages
Issue: A single inbox may become cluttered with both routine and urgent messages, especially in large orgs with multiple FedRAMP offerings.
Recommendation: Permit CSPs to implement email aliases or internal routing rules behind the FSI (e.g., high-priority tagged messages sent to on-call staff) — as long as all routing and response requirements are met.

Gap 7: No Requirement for Email Testing or Health Monitoring by Providers
Relevant Requirements: FRR-FSI-01/02: Must always be reachable
Issue: While FedRAMP will conduct quarterly tests, there’s no requirement for providers to self-monitor or self-test inbox functionality.
Recommendation: Encourage or require CSPs to implement automated test emails or synthetic monitoring to ensure FSI functionality between FedRAMP’s quarterly tests.

wisecryptic: I understand that this could be structured with more detail, but I would recommend we make sure that these are problems that actually need to be solved before adding them in the guidance. All of these would improve a CSPs response capability, but I question if including them will have measurable effect on the specific outcome or if they are adding items which are already implemented or are not highly impactful issues.

author: pete-gov
text:
Re: RFC-0018 FedRAMP Security Inbox Requirements

pete-gov [FEDRAMP-OFFICIAL]: The following public comment was received via email from Salesforce:

Section: FRR-FSI-01,
FRR-CCM-04

Text: Providers MUST establish and maintain an email address to receive email regarding urgent security notifications from all necessary parties; this inbox is a FedRAMP Security Inbox (FSI). The FedRAMP Security Inbox is listed in the FedRAMP Marketplace as the “Security E-mail.”,

Providers MUST establish and share an asynchronous mechanism for all necessary parties to provide feedback or ask questions related to each Ongoing Authorization Report; all such feedback and questions from agencies, along with responses from the provider, MUST be available to FedRAMP.

Comment: RFC-0016 mentions that CSPs must have an async comms mechanism set for parties to communicate regarding Ongoing Authorization Reports. Can the e-mail required in RFC-0018 be the same as the async comms channel required in RFC-0016. We are proposing that yes, they can be one and the same, and that this should be reflected in technical assistance for either one of these standards.
Section: FRR-FSI-TF-MO-01

Text: Providers MUST have a human acknowledge and address messages sent by FedRAMP (including any @[fedramp.gov](http://fedramp.gov/) email address) to their FedRAMP Security Inbox within 1 business day.

Comment: Proposing that this is changed to "...by the end of the following business day" to remove any confusion about what "within 1 business day" means (does it mean by end of same business day? does it mean by end of the next? Does it mean by the same time the following day? etc.)
Section: FRR-FSI-TF-HI-01

Text: Providers MUST have a human acknowledge and address messages sent by FedRAMP (including any @[fedramp.gov](http://fedramp.gov/) email address) to their FedRAMP Security Inbox within 12 hours.

Comment: Proposing that this is changed to "...within 12 business hours" to account for alerts sent late on a given day or weekend. If the expectation is that this inbox is monitored 24x7, then this should be explicitly added to the standard.
Section: Various

Text: Providers MUST have a human acknowledge and address messages sent by FedRAMP (including any @[fedramp.gov](http://fedramp.gov/) email address) to their FedRAMP Security Inbox within X.

Comment: Proposing that, for each impact level, we separate this statement into two statements - one for human acknowledgement within a defined time period, and then one for addressing/resolving the message "as promptly as possible" or something similar. Human acknowledgement is straightforward to standardize, but each security-related message may involve different timelines for resolution on a case-by-case basis.

By breaking out SLAs where one is for acknowledgement and one is for addressing, this provides customers with the initial assurances that the message was received by the CSP and is being worked on.
Section: FRR-FSI-TF-LO-01,
FRR-FSI-TF-MO-01,
FRR-FSI-TF-HI-01

Text: Providers MUST have a human acknowledge and address messages sent by FedRAMP (including any @[fedramp.gov](http://fedramp.gov/) email address) to their FedRAMP Security Inbox within X.

Comment: Proposing that a separate statement is added for scenarios where the same message is sent to all levels of CSPs. If an urgent security matter such as an emergency directive is sent to Low, Moderate, and High CSPs, then the timeline for resolution should be the same for all CSPs.

discussion_title: RFC-0018 FedRAMP Security Inbox Requirements
author: pete-gov
text:
Re: RFC-0018 FedRAMP Security Inbox Requirements

pete-gov [FEDRAMP-OFFICIAL]: The following public comment was received via email from Crowdstrike:

REQUEST FOR COMMENT RESPONSERFC-0018 FEDRAMP SECURITY INBOX REQUIREMENTS. October 3, 2025

 

INTRODUCTION

In response to FedRAMP’s request for comment on the FedRAMP Security Inbox Requirements (“draft standard”), CrowdStrike offers the following views.  We approach these questions from the standpoint of a leading international, US-headquartered, cloud-native cybersecurity provider that defends globally distributed enterprises from globally distributed threats. CrowdStrike offers insights informed by multiple practice areas: cyber threat intelligence; proactive hunting, incident response and managed security services; and an AI-powered software-as-a-service cybersecurity platform and marketplace. Accordingly, this perspective is informed by CrowdStrike’s role in protecting organizations from data breaches and a variety of other cyber threats.

COMMENTS

CrowdStrike understands the importance of timely responses to FedRAMP inquiries, and that a quick response is necessary in times of emergency. We appreciate FedRAMP's efforts to address the critical communication gaps identified during the response to CISA Emergency Directive 25-03. The request for comment correctly notes that many providers have inadvertently created barriers to emergency communications through outdated contact information and gated access systems. This creates unacceptable risks during security incidents that require immediate coordination and response. We welcome the opportunity to offer feedback that may be of value to FedRAMP as it considers the draft standard.

 

Operational Implementation Challenges

The draft standard's response time requirements, particularly the 12-hour timeframe for High authorization providers such as CrowdStrike, create significant operational burdens that require dedicated weekend and holiday staffing by senior personnel. This necessitates a fundamental shift from business-hour operations to a 24/7/365 model that many organizations have not structured or budgeted to support. The requirement for senior officials with "authority to respond" to monitor communications creates bottlenecks at the executive level rather than enabling rapid response through established security teams, potentially slowing response times during critical incidents when senior leadership should focus on strategic decision-making.

 

Business Continuity

The immediate 30-day marketplace suspension for non-compliance represents a disproportionately severe penalty that could significantly impact revenue streams and damage customer relationships. The potential escalation to complete loss of FedRAMP authorization creates an existential threat to cloud service providers' government business over what might be communication process failures rather than actual security deficiencies. These penalties do not account for legitimate technical failures or provide graduated enforcement mechanisms. The draft standard creates severe penalties without proportionate consideration of technical failures or good faith compliance efforts. Ideally, enforcement would include graduated penalties that account for the nature and cause of communication failures. Conversely, the current framework does not distinguish between willful non-compliance and technical issues beyond provider control. The standard should include a dispute resolution process that defines appeal procedures, creates clear timelines for resolution, and provides mechanisms for addressing technical failures.

 

Regulatory Ambiguity & Scope Concerns

FedRAMP should reconsider the "all necessary parties" construct within the draft standard. As written, this definition is unclear and may lead to system abuse or overwhelming security teams with non-critical requests. The distinction between "acknowledging" and "addressing" messages remains ambiguous, potentially creating compliance uncertainty.

 

Specifically:

·         'All necessary parties' should be explicitly defined to include only FedRAMP, CISA, and designated federal agency security contacts to prevent abuse.

·         'Address messages' should clearly distinguish between acknowledgement requirements and full resolution expectations.

·         Emergency versus routine communications should have clear categorization criteria to ensure appropriate resource allocation.

 

The objective of these proposed clarifications is to maintain focus on legitimate emergency communications while providing sufficient clarity for compliance.

 

CONCLUSION

We believe reliable emergency communication capabilities are essential for effective cybersecurity coordination. As the Standard moves forward and evolves, we recommend continued engagement with stakeholders to balance emergency preparedness with operational feasibility. Finally, because emergency response scenarios vary significantly, we recommend that any final framework establish realistic timeframes that account for business operations while maintaining emergency responsiveness, such as business-hour focused requirements or tiered emergency classifications that distinguish between true emergencies requiring immediate response and urgent communications that can be addressed within standard business timeframes.

discussion_title: Does FedRAMP have a reference page on its website for all of the GSA, OMB, and its own publications to easily reference for Cloud Guidance (Also applies for FedRAMP 20x)?
author: pete-gov
text:
Re: Does FedRAMP have a reference page on its website for all of the GSA, OMB, and its own publications to easily reference for Cloud Guidance (Also applies for FedRAMP 20x)?

pete-gov [FEDRAMP-OFFICIAL]: > It will depend on the purpose of the document one is creating the reference section for but in general, does FedRAMP keep a reference page which someone could leverage to point to all of the applicable FedRAMP, OMB, GSA, DoD, and NIST publications related to cloud computing?

From a FedRAMP perspective we're only really concerned about FedRAMP specific policies; that is, generally a cloud service does not need to meet any other government requirements except those required by FedRAMP for a FedRAMP authorization, so we don't need to collect and reference such policies. Our section of the law only requires us to maintain materials and publish information about the FedRAMP authorization process; under current executive policy that means we're limited to doing that.

You can see this in [44 USC § 3609](https://www.law.cornell.edu/uscode/text/44/3609) (b) (1) where it states: "The Administrator shall maintain a public website to serve as the authoritative repository for FedRAMP, including the timely publication and updates for all relevant information, guidance, determinations, and other materials required under subsection (a)." (Subsection (a) outlines all of the things that FedRAMP needs to create)

That said, [Executive Order 13694 (amending EO 14144) on Sustaining Select Efforts to Strengthen the Nation's Cybersecurity](https://www.federalregister.gov/documents/2025/06/11/2025-10804/sustaining-select-efforts-to-strengthen-the-nations-cybersecurity-and-amending-executive-order-13694) charges NIST, CISA, and OMB with establishing a pilot program to make all cybersecurity policy and guidance available in a machine-readable format. I'm certainly looking forward to seeing how that plays out, but it will likely also be focused entirely on government-specific requirements.
