discussion_title: RFC-0026 Clarifying CA-7 Continuous Monitoring Expectations for Rev5 Providers
author: rhoesing
text:
Re: RFC-0026 Clarifying CA-7 Continuous Monitoring Expectations for Rev5 Providers

rhoesing [FEDRAMP-OFFICIAL]: Comment from Raj P.

Please find below my public comments on RFC-0026: Clarifying CA-7 Continuous Monitoring Expectations for Rev5 Providers.

Comment 1 — General / Meeting Standards

Generally Supportive of this RFC. The proposed corrective action ladder is a step towards clarity from the current gray area. However there is one gap I wanted to highlight. The failure metric for RV5-CA07-CCM states Providers shall host a monthly meeting open to all agency customers, but there is no definition of what "hosting a meeting" entails, what baseline content/topics must be covered in the meeting, or how a provider can document that the meeting took place. Without clarity on those 3 aspects it will be difficult for 3PAOs to consistently evaluate and providers have no clear bar to work towards. Would recommend adding minimum expectations for meeting content and how it should be documented before this is finalized.

Comment 2 — Agency Perspective

Supportive of this RFC. The proposed corrective action "framework" definitely moves the ball forward when it comes to holding CSP's accountable. However from an agency perspective there is a gap in that when a CSP reaches each "strike", the onus is solely on them to take action to correct and retry. If an agency receives a "strike three" and logs into the Marketplace to see their provider is now in Remediation, there is no explanation of what that means for them moving forward. Are they expected to reassess their determination, suspend use of AWS.org, or just wait for AWS to meet any required remediation criteria? This RFC does a good job of putting the burden of information sharing on the CSP but leaves agencies in the dark about their own responsibilities. Would recommend that the final rule mention at minimum that agencies have a set of responsibilities they need to meet when they receive failure notifications.

Comment 3 — Provider Perspective

In Support of this RFC and appreciate the increase in transparency the corrective action ladder will provide. Enforcement concern: Due to the 12 month window resetting after each failure, a CSP needs to go 12 consecutive months without any failure to clear their slate. All failure measures will apply to all agency customers at once with no partial points awarded. So if your provider has 30 agency customers and meets the requirement to share ConMon data with 29 of them but fails to due to a technical glitch or admin oversight on 1, you still fail and are treated the same as a provider who didn't share with any agencies. Considering the fact that the motivation of this RFC admits the requirements were changed with little notice in July of 2024, some leeway for partial compliance or a cure period of less than 30 days would better balance the framework risk without losing the strength of enforcing this requirement.

Thank you for the opportunity to comment on this RFC.

discussion_title: RFC-0026 Clarifying CA-7 Continuous Monitoring Expectations for Rev5 Providers
author: WhalerMike
text:
Re: RFC-0026 Clarifying CA-7 Continuous Monitoring Expectations for Rev5 Providers

WhalerMike: Supportive of this RFC. The five-strike corrective action framework is a meaningful step toward accountability, and the distinction between RV5-CA07-VLN and RV5-CA07-CCM correctly separates the data-sharing obligation from the collaborative engagement obligation.

One intersection I haven't seen raised in the comments: BOD 25-01 now requires FCEB agencies to deploy CISA's ScubaGear to assess M365 tenant configuration against SCuBA Secure Configuration Baselines and report results into CyberScope. ScubaGear is a point-in-time assessment tool. This RFC is formalizing the continuous monitoring expectation above that assessment. But there's a practical gap between "ScubaGear scanned clean last Tuesday" and "the tenant is still compliant today" that neither tool nor policy currently fills.

Configuration drift in a multi-admin GCC Moderate tenant can happen hours after a clean scan -- a Conditional Access policy change, a SharePoint external sharing default, a Defender policy override. The monthly ConMon cadence this RFC establishes is the right governance rhythm for collaborative reporting, but it doesn't address what happens to configuration state between those monthly checkpoints.

Building on @austinsonger's point about a "minimum viable shared ConMon dataset" -- I'd argue that dataset needs to include canonical desired-state definitions (what the tenant configuration *should* look like per the applicable SCuBA baseline) alongside continuous drift detection evidence, not just vulnerability and POA&M status. That gives agencies an ongoing authorization signal they can act on, rather than a monthly snapshot that may already be stale.

We've been working on this exact problem in GCC Moderate environments -- a governance layer that consumes ScubaGear output as the assessment baseline, maintains canonical desired state, runs continuous drift detection, and tracks remediation with owner accountability and SLA timelines. The enforcement teeth this RFC adds will create real demand for that kind of persistent compliance evidence. CSPs and agencies will need more than periodic scans and monthly meetings to stay on the right side of the corrective action ladder -- they'll need machine-trackable proof that configuration state was maintained between touchpoints.

discussion_title: RFC-0026 Clarifying CA-7 Continuous Monitoring Expectations for Rev5 Providers
author: acloudcj
text:
Re: RFC-0026 Clarifying CA-7 Continuous Monitoring Expectations for Rev5 Providers

acloudcj: Removing the JAB references is overdue and welcome. That language has been a source of confusion since M-24-15 dropped and the practical effect was CSPs explaining to agencies why their authorization letters referenced an entity that no longer existed in the same capacity.
The substantive question is about the enforcement structure. The tiered corrective action model, notification escalating through remediation plans to potential certification revocation after five failures in 12 months, sounds reasonable on paper. But the details matter.
What constitutes a “failure”? If a CSP conducts a collaborative monitoring meeting with 47 of 48 agency customers because one agency’s ISSO is unresponsive for three months, is that a gap? The requirement says CSPs must conduct recurring meetings with “all agency customers.” CSPs don’t control agency participation. If the obligation is to offer and document the attempt, that’s workable. If it’s to ensure meetings actually occur, that shifts agency accountability onto CSPs without giving them any enforcement mechanism of their own. Please clarify whether “conduct” means “facilitate and document good faith attempts” or “ensure completion.”
VDR vs. traditional pathway clarity. The RFC frames VDR and traditional monthly scanning as parallel options, but it’s unclear whether a CSP can choose one pathway globally or whether individual agency customers can demand one or the other. If Agency A wants VDR and Agency B insists on traditional monthly POA&M updates, the CSP is running both, which isn’t a reduction in burden but an increase. Is the pathway selection a CSP level decision, or does each agency customer relationship get its own pathway?
The grace period is well designed, effective immediately on publication with no corrective action through December 31, 2026, and enforcement starting January 2027. That’s the right structure. One ask: consider publishing example scenarios during the grace period that illustrate what FedRAMP considers compliant vs. noncompliant under CA-7, similar to how the IRS publishes revenue rulings. Real world examples calibrate expectations far better than control language alone, and the grace period is the natural window to do that before enforcement begins.
3PAO treatment of gaps as high impact findings. This is a significant change with cost implications. Annual assessments already run six figures for complex environments. If 3PAOs must now treat any CA-7 gap as high impact, that expands remediation timelines, potentially delays reauthorization, and increases assessment costs, all for a control that’s fundamentally about process cadence rather than technical vulnerability. Is the high impact classification mandatory regardless of context, or can 3PAOs exercise judgment about severity based on the nature and duration of the gap?

discussion_title: RFC-0026 Clarifying CA-7 Continuous Monitoring Expectations for Rev5 Providers
author: CSP-AB
text:
Re: RFC-0026 Clarifying CA-7 Continuous Monitoring Expectations for Rev5 Providers

CSP-AB: CSP-AB submits the following comment to RFC-0026:

**Requirement RV5-CA07-VLN (Vulnerability Reporting)** - Sharing Operating System, Database, Web Application, Container, and Service Configuration Scans, at least monthly; AND sharing updated Plans of Action and Milestones (POA&Ms), at least monthly; AND sharing all scans performed by an Independent Assessor, at least annually.

- This reads as the traditional path under RV5-CA07-VLN requiring CSPs to share raw Operating System, Database, Web Application, Container, and Service Configuration scans monthly with all agency customers. This creates a significant and unexplained asymmetry with the VDR BIR, which explicitly prohibits irresponsible disclosure of sensitive vulnerability details that would likely lead to exploitation (VDR-RPT-NID), and instead requires only structured, risk-contextualized reporting. If VDR is considered an acceptable — and arguably superior — alternative to traditional ConMon, the traditional path should not impose a more expansive and security-degrading disclosure burden by default.

We recommend the following changes to RV5-CA07-VLN:

1. Raw scan sharing should not be a baseline requirement. Unprocessed scan output provides limited value to most agency customers, who generally lack the tooling and expertise to interpret it. Validation of scan results by a 3PAO during annual assessments is the appropriate mechanism for independent verification. Monthly raw scan distribution to all agencies does not meaningfully improve risk awareness and may increase attack surface by broadly distributing detailed exploitability information. FedRAMP should remove the requirement to share raw scans with all agency customers and treat scan artifacts as 3PAO review materials, not agency deliverables. Sharing with agency customers beyond the lead agency should be governed by individual agency contracts, not mandated uniformly.

2. Scan results shared with any party — including 3PAOs and lead agencies — should explicitly be permitted to be redacted. CSPs should be permitted to redact specific details from scan results (including plugin IDs, CVE identifiers, and exploit path details) when disclosure of those details would likely facilitate exploitation of an unmitigated vulnerability. Redacted findings must retain a CSP-assigned unique tracking identifier, affected component classification, and risk level sufficient to support risk-based decision-making. This aligns with the responsible disclosure principle already established in VDR-RPT-NID and VDR-FRP-ADV. Full unredacted details should be available for correlation by the CSP in the event of a CISA-directed response, legal hold, or FedRAMP corrective action — consistent with the existing FedRAMP authority to require additional sensitive information under those circumstances — but should not be required for routine distribution.

3. FedRAMP should clarify the disclosure asymmetry between the traditional path and VDR explicitly. As currently written, CSPs on the traditional path face a stricter and less security-conscious disclosure posture than those adopting VDR. If the intent is for VDR to represent a modernization and improvement, the traditional path should be updated to match VDR's responsible disclosure principles, not left in a state that inadvertently penalizes CSPs who have not yet adopted VDR.

judgecspab-max: I completely support CSP-AB’s position. This comment correctly identifies an asymmetry where the "traditional path" inadvertently forces a less secure disclosure posture than the modernized VDR approach.
For example, an IaaS provider has a responsibility is to maintain the security of the shared environment. Mandating the broad distribution of raw, unredacted scans to every agency customer creates unnecessary  systemic risk. If an IaaS provider’s foundational layer is exposed through over-sharing, every SaaS provider and government agency sitting on top of that infrastructure also inherits that risk.  Aligning these requirements with VDR’s risk-contextualized reporting ensures that agencies receive actionable intelligence without forcing the CSP to affect security--which is prohibited in VDR.

rgaffey: Completely concur with the CSP-AB, especially around the release of raw scans, vulnerability data to many people.  These are potentially files in TB's of information for hyerscalers and for others just incredibly large files.  Secondly, what value does the average person and Agency X gain from seeing raw vuln scans? ZERO.  That is why there are summaries, taking into account the risk and rating of the vulns. Lastly this absolutely increases the attack surface for malicious actors. 

mjprager: I completely agree with the CSP-AB's feedback. Hyperscalers' raw monthly packages are terabytes in size - it's barely practical for the 3PAO to pull down the files and process them through the parsers, let alone expecting agencies to also do so. Nor do we have any assurance that the agency will adequately protect this very sensitive information which literally says what vulnerability exists on a specific system. This is a tremendous risk. The aggregated information is adequate and is what is actually useful for agencies to assess the security posture of a CSP.

cb-axon: We strongly support the CSP Advisory Board's comment on RV5-CA07-VLN, and echo concerns raised by other commenters in this thread.
The traditional path as written inadvertently forces a less secure disclosure posture than the modernized VDR approach. VDR explicitly prohibits disclosure of details likely to facilitate exploitation (VDR-RPT-NID) — the traditional path should not impose a stricter and less security-conscious standard than the path FedRAMP is actively promoting.

It is worth noting that in practice, this requirement was historically associated only with JAB-authorized systems. Codifying it now as a uniform requirement for all CSPs to provide to all agency customers would represent a significant and operationally unsafe expansion of existing expectations.

Several practical realities reinforce why this requirement is unsafe as written:

- Raw scans are impractical and dangerous to distribute broadly. 3PAOs with dedicated tooling already struggle to process them, and the FedRAMP ConMon team previously struggled to parse them for the JAB — agencies cannot reasonably be expected to do the same, and there is no assurance they can adequately protect this data once obtained.
- Raw scans provide no actionable value to agencies. Risk-contextualized summaries are what agencies can actually act on. Unprocessed output identifying specific vulnerabilities on specific systems increases attack surface without improving agency decision-making.
- Systemic risk compounds for IaaS providers. Over-sharing at the foundational layer exposes every SaaS provider and agency tenant sitting on top of that infrastructure.

We support the CSP-AB's recommendations that raw scans be treated as 3PAO review materials, that CSPs be permitted to redact sensitive exploitability details while preserving risk-level information, and that the traditional path be aligned with VDR's responsible disclosure principles.  If FedRAMP determines that raw scan access must remain available outside of VDR, we strongly recommend it be limited to a single designated lead agency that has demonstrated the capability and controls to responsibly manage this data — and that even then, sharing be governed by agency contract rather than uniform mandate.

discussion_title: RFC-0026 Clarifying CA-7 Continuous Monitoring Expectations for Rev5 Providers
author: mjschroeder1
text:
Re: RFC-0026 Clarifying CA-7 Continuous Monitoring Expectations for Rev5 Providers

mjschroeder1: Strong support for this RFC. The existing CA-7 guidance has carried the JAB reference for the twenty months since M-24-15, and the ambiguity has produced real operational drift across CSPs with multiple agency customers. Clarifying that all agency customers must have access to the same ConMon data is correct in principle and aligns with what the FedRAMP model promises agencies that leverage authorizations.

Agency-side perspective on the all-agency access requirement. I directed Agency Authorization lifecycle work for 60+ enterprise cloud deployments across the VA, representing $3.8B in federal contracts. In practice, the JAB-path vs. Agency-path distinction in the old CA-7 language produced visibility tiers where lead agencies received richer ConMon feeds than downstream agencies leveraging the same service. Downstream agencies making ongoing authorization decisions were doing so with materially less current information than the FedRAMP model promised. This RFC corrects that. Please keep the all-agency access baseline.

On the raw scan sharing pathway. The community discussion in the general thread surfaced a legitimate operational concern: most downstream agencies lack the capability or staffing to parse raw scan outputs at cadence. That observation is accurate and worth acknowledging **without walking the requirement back**. Making scan data available is a data-provisioning requirement, not a customer-enablement requirement. Consider adding an explicit clarification that CSPs meet the requirement by making the data accessible through their standard ConMon channels, and that agency capacity to consume that data is an agency responsibility. The distinction matters because it prevents CSPs from over-investing in customer education and correctly scopes the cost.

On the corrective action schedule. The graduated five-failure structure is well-designed, with predictable off-ramps and proportional consequences. One clarification worth building in: how does the process handle documented good faith disruptions during BIR transition activity, partial VDR adoption, or coordination-driven meeting slips where no agency customer attends a scheduled meeting? I would suggest either explicit exception language or clear confirmation that the initial Corrective Action Plan submission at first failure is the correct venue to document and resolve those conditions. Either answer works; removing ambiguity is what matters.

On the effective date. The alignment with CR26 publication, Q3–Q4 2026 grace period, and January 1, 2027 enforcement is sensible and gives CSPs a real implementation window. The BIR incentive structure is correctly oriented: CSPs that adopt VDR and CCM BIRs inherit cleaner ConMon alignment and exit the traditional corrective action schedule. That is the right direction of travel. 

Thank you to the PMO for closing a guidance gap that has been structurally out of sync with M-24-15 for almost two years. This is meaningful cleanup.

Michael Schroeder

author: badgerinspace
text:
Re: RFC-0026 Clarifying CA-7 Continuous Monitoring Expectations for Rev5 Providers

badgerinspace: - RV5-CA07-VLN states that providers must follow either the VDR standard or traditional Rev 5 processes including scan file and POA&M uploads. This contracts with Notice 0009, which states “Mandatory adoption of the Vulnerability Detection and Response process for all Rev5 cloud services” with an anticipated deadline of 6/1/2027. Which is the correct guidance?
- Likewise, RV5-CA07-CCM states that providers have options for meeting ConMon, either the Collaborative BIR approach, or the traditional approach. However, Notice 0009 states “Mandatory adoption of the Collaborative Continuous Monitoring process for all Rev5 cloud services” with an anticipated deadline of 4/2/2027. Which is the correct guidance?
- RV5-CA07-VLN uses the term “Service Configuration Scans” without defining what these should be run on. The scope of this term has been loosely defined in FedRAMP and causes unnecessary confusion during assessments and ConMon. Some CSPs will only run such scans against Hosts, others will include Databases, and others still will also include Container Images, but it’s left up to 3PAOs to attempt to enforce a consistent approach and different 3PAOs think differently on this subject. CM-6 does not explicitly state asset types either, so referencing CM-6 language does not help here. FedRAMP’s vulnerability scanning requirements for containers does reference CM-6, but this language is often ignored by 3PAOs, causing inconsistent enforcement of service configuration scans. Please provide clear guidance directly in this or another control on what types of assets these scans should be run on to ensure a level playing field and consistent assessments across 3PAOs.

Alliancefordigitalinnovation: ADI appreciates the opportunity to comment on RFC-0026, Clarifying CA-7 Continuous Monitoring Expectations for Rev5 Providers.
To help in FedRAMP’s efforts to provide greater clarity around CA-7 continuous monitoring expectations for Rev5 providers, ADI offers the following recommendations: 

• FedRAMP should clarify what it means to host a monthly ConMon meeting and to share the required information with all agency customers and FedRAMP.
• FedRAMP should also clarify whether a provider would incur a failure if it made the meeting available and shared the required materials, but an agency did not act or respond. If agency participation or acknowledgment is required, the RFC should say so clearly.

This could be problematic for providers supporting a growing number of agencies before reaching the scale needed to initiate the collaboration group model.

Thank you for your consideration on this matter.

Re: RFC-0026 Clarifying CA-7 Continuous Monitoring Expectations for Rev5 Providers

nicolagsa: I concur with the comments above, and find that sharing what is beneficial to agency customers at a cadence that is useful and to s degree that is useful should be the goal of these changes. In particular, sharing raw scans seems to be overscoped, and ConMon material production should be audited by 3PAO to ensure alignment between scans and submitted materials, as it seems impractical for any agency using a moderate to large sized CSP to be able to develop the pipelines to process this data in a useful way. 

Unless, the idea is that something like a local LLM run federally is to be used to identify risk across the entire government (hey LLM, find me all CSPs that have a log4j in their scans and write me an email telling them to fix or explain now, etc). Whether or not this is true, there is certainly a growing realization that there should be some reciprocity in terms of ensuring that raw scan data is treated confidentially once it leaves a CSP system, as CSP's take great lengths to ensure is true for federal data that we are entrusted with.

author: nicole-gov
text:
Re: RFC-0026 Clarifying CA-7 Continuous Monitoring Expectations for Rev5 Providers nicole-gov [FEDRAMP-OFFICIAL]: The following public comment was received via email from Salesforce on Wed April 22: I am copy/pasting into the public comment record on their behalf as required by the FedRAMP public comment process. This is not an endorsement of the commenter or the content within the comment. This was converted from a table to markdown, apologies for any formatting issues. Text should all be intact. --- | Requirement_ID | Title/Section | Salesforce Comment | |----------------|------------------------------|--------------------| | RV5-CA07-VLN | CA-07: Continuous Monitoring | _"Sharing Operating System, Database, Web Application, Container, and Service Configuration Scans, at least monthly; AND sharing updated Plans of Action and Milestones (POA&Ms), at least monthly; AND sharing all scans performed by an Independent Assessor, at least annually."_

**Concern:** Requiring monthly raw scans under RV5-CA07-VLN creates a security risk inconsistent with the VDR BIR, which prioritizes risk-contextualized reporting over sensitive data exposure (VDR-RPT-NID). Sharing of raw scan files has historically been limited to JAB authorized service offerings due to the PMO's ConMon support through monthly summary reports which was then disseminated to Agencies. Salesforce has major concerns over increasing the sharing radius of this data:

- Providing raw scan data on a broad scale is inefficient and perilous, as it lacks necessary context while simultaneously increasing the attack surface and risk of sensitive data exposure. Further do Agency customers have the tooling to process and accurately digest these files? Many agency customers struggle to accurately read and digest our monthly POA&M.
- Raw scans provide no actionable value to agency customers and require processing to accuratly understand risk and security status. Providing customers with context-rich summaries ensures that agencies receive actionable insights that they can actually act on.
- Lack of assurance that Agency customers will limit further sharing and adequately protect this sensitive scan data.

**Recommendation:** The sharing of raw scans should not be a default requirement, instead this should be an optional requirement. CSPs that feel comfortable in providing raw scans to agency customers should feel empowered and this should potentially be reflected on the FedRAMP Marketplace. |

nicole-gov [FEDRAMP-OFFICIAL]: The following public comment was received via email from Netskope on April 17:

I am copy/pasting into the public comment record on their behalf as required by the FedRAMP public comment process. This is not an endorsement of the commenter or the content within the comment.

---

**Requirement RV5-CA07-VLN (Vulnerability Reporting)**

Providers MUST share vulnerability information with all agency customers and FedRAMP using one of the following two processes:
1.	Implementing the Vulnerability Detection and Response Balance Improvement Release for Rev5 (either in Beta or Wide Release); or
2.	Sharing Operating System, Database, Web Application, Container, and Service Configuration Scans, at least monthly; AND sharing updated Plans of Action and Milestones (POA&Ms), at least monthly; AND sharing all scans performed by an Independent Assessor, at least annually.

**Feedback:** 

**From my experience independent assessors do not perform scans during an annual assessment. They witness a CSP run their scans live.**

discussion_title: RFC-0027 FedRAMP Rev5 Security Controls Baseline Update for AC, AT, AU, CA, and CM Control Families
author: rhoesing
text:
RFC-0027 FedRAMP Rev5 Security Controls Baseline Update for AC, AT, AU, CA, and CM Control Families

# RFC-0027 FedRAMP Rev5 Security Controls Baseline Update for AC, AT, AU, CA, and CM Control Families

❓   **Please note that FedRAMP will not answer questions in this thread as it is reserved for public comment. If you would like to ask a question or generally discuss this RFC informally, please use the [General discussion and Q&A for RFCs related to Rev5 Updates (RFCs 0026, 0027, 0028, 0029, & 0030) thread](https://github.com/FedRAMP/community/discussions/129). Thank you!**

**Status:** Closed
**Start Date:** March 19, 2026
**Closing Date:** April 22, 2026
---

## **Summary**

This is a technical RFC that proposes updates to the Additional FedRAMP Security Technical Controls Requirements and Guidance for FedRAMP Rev5 baselines.

To save space and to limit the breadth of a single RFC, this technical document shows only the proposed changes to the current baseline document and is restricted to a few control families. If verbiage is being updated, only the specific wording that is to be changed is identified in the old verbiage section. If the verbiage to be added is not replacing previous verbiage, but being added, it will be identified as “NEW” in the old verbiage section.  

Since this spreadsheet covers hundreds of controls across multiple tabs and sections, only those specific controls, sections, and tabs identified are being proposed for updates.  If it is not mentioned below, changes are NOT being proposed.  

**Commenters are advised to please mention specific controls in their comments\!**

This RFC addresses controls in the following families:

* Access Control (AC)  
* Awareness and Training (AT)  
* Audit and Accountability (AU)  
* Assessment, Authorization and Monitoring (CA)  
* Configuration Management (CM)

## **Motivation**

Many Rev5 FedRAMP Requirements and Guidance statements are based on outdated approaches that predated the release of the FedRAMP Authorization Act and M-24-15. This set of Requirements and Guidance needs a refresh to match FedRAMP’s current rules and approach.

The updates formalized after this RFC will be included in the FedRAMP Consolidated Rules for 2026\. That set of rules will be valid until December 31, 2028\. FedRAMP will provide a transition plan for adopting any new guidance that will enable cloud service providers to update their approach as part of their annual assessment as appropriate.

These changes are designed to lower the burden for cloud service providers and eliminate previous pain points.

Additionally, NIST released 800-53 Rev 5.2.0 in August of 2025\.  While this update was minor, control updates from NIST will require updates to FedRAMP Security Control Baseline in order to reflect this update. These changes will happen without public comment through FedRAMP since these are direct reflections of NIST changes. As subsequent iterations of the FedRAMP Security Control Baseline are published, it is FedRAMP’s intent only to carry over the following information from NIST 800-53; Control Family, Control Name, and Control ID. Following this will be FedRAMP-Defined Assignment / Selection Parameters and additional FedRAMP Requirements and Guidance.

## **Proposed Changes to Access Control Family**

This section contains proposed changes to the FedRAMP Requirements and Guidance section for each of these controls.

### **AC-02: Account Management**

**Tabs Affected:** High Baseline, Moderate Baseline, Low Baseline  
**Sections Affected:** Additional FedRAMP Requirements and Guidance  
**Current Verbiage:** NEW  
**Proposed Change**: a. Accounts types should align to those accounts identified within the FedRAMP Secure Configuration Guidance where applicable.  
**Rationale:** Alignment with the FedRAMP Secure Configuration Guidance (SCG).

### **AC-10: Concurrent Session Control**

**Tabs Affected:** High Baseline  
**Sections Affected:** FedRAMP-Defined Assignment / Selection Parameters  
**Current Verbiage:** AC-10-2 \[three (3) sessions for privileged access and two (2) sessions for non-privileged access\]  
**Proposed Change:** AC-10-2 \[one (1) session for Top-level administrative, three (3) sessions for privileged access, and two (2) sessions for non-privileged access\]  
**Rationale:** Alignment with the FedRAMP Secure Configuration Guidance (SCG).

## **Proposed Changes to Awareness and Training Family**

This section contains proposed changes to the FedRAMP Requirements and Guidance section for each of these controls.

### **AT-03 Role-based Training:**

**Tabs Affected:** High Baseline, Moderate Baseline, Low Baseline  
**Sections Affected:** Additional FedRAMP Requirements and Guidance  
**Current Verbiage:** NEW  
**Proposed Change:** a. Top-Level Administrative and Privileged Accounts Secure Configuration Guidance must be included as part of role based training where applicable.  
Rationale: Alignment with the FedRAMP Secure Configuration Guidance (SCG)**.**

## **Proposed Changes to Audit and Accountability Family**

No changes are being proposed

## **Proposed Changes to Assessment, Authorization, and Monitoring Family**

This section contains proposed changes to the FedRAMP Requirements and Guidance section for each of these controls.

### **CA-05: Plan of Action and Milestones**

**Tabs Affected:** Low Baseline, Moderate Baseline, High Baseline  
**Sections Affected:** FedRAMP-Defined Assignment / Selection Parameters  
**Current Verbiage:** CA-5 (b) \[at least monthly\]  
**Proposed Change:** CA-5 (b) \[at least monthly for traditional FedRAMP Processes\] \[every three months if opting into Collaborative Continuous Monitoring BIR\] \[Monthly Activity Report in lieu is due every month if opting into Vulnerability and Detection Response BIR\]  
**Rationale:** Updated based on BIRs

### **CA-05: Plan of Action and Milestones**

**Tabs Affected:** Low Baseline, Moderate Baseline, High Baseline  
**Sections Affected:** Additional FedRAMP Requirements and Guidance  
**Current Verbiage:** CA-5 Requirement: POA\&Ms must be provided at least monthly. CA-5 Guidance: Reference FedRAMP-POAM-Template  
**Proposed Change:** CA-5 Requirement: POA\&Ms must be provided at least monthly for traditional FedRAMP processes. For those opting into Collaborative Continuous Monitoring BIR, Ongoing Authorization Reports must be provided every three months. For those opting into Vulnerability Detection and Response BIR, a Monthly Activity Report is also required.  
CA-5 Guidance: Reference FedRAMP-POAM-Template \[traditional\], CCM-OAR-AVL for those opting into Collaborative Continuous Monitoring BIR, and VDR-TFR-MHR for those opting into Vulnerability Detection and Response BIR  
**Rationale:** Updated based on BIRs

### **CA-05: Plan of Action and Milestones**

**Tabs Affected:** Low Baseline, Moderate Baseline, High Baseline  
**Sections Affected:** Continuous Monitoring Periodicity  
**Current Verbiage:** CA-5 (b) \[at least monthly\]

This requirement applies to CSOs authorized via the Agency path as each agency customer is responsible for performing ConMon oversight.

This section contains proposed changes to the FedRAMP Requirements and Guidance section for each of these controls.

CM-6 (a) Requirement 2: The service provider shall ensure that checklists for configuration settings are Security Content Automation Protocol (SCAP) validated or SCAP compatible (if validated checklists are not available).  
**Proposed Change:** CM-6 (a) Requirement 1:  The service provider shall use Security Configuration Guidelines (See CM-6) to establish instructions on how to securely access, configure, operate, and decommission top-level administrative accounts within the cloud service offering.  This MUST include explanations of security-related settings that can be operated only by top-level administrative accounts and their security implications. This SHOULD include explanations of security-related settings that can be operated only by privileged accounts and their security implications.  
CM-6 (a) Requirement 2:  The service provider shall use the DoD STIGs or Center for Internet Security guidelines to establish configuration settings;  
CM-6 (a) Requirement 3: The service provider shall ensure that checklists for configuration settings are Security Content Automation Protocol (SCAP) validated or SCAP compatible (if validated checklists are not available).  
**Rationale:** Updated based on SCG BIR

### **CM-07: Least Functionality**

**Proposed Change:** CM-7 (b) Requirement: The service provider shall use Security Configuration Guidelines (See CM-6) to establish instructions on how to securely access, configure, operate, and decommission top-level administrative accounts within the cloud service offering as well as provide a list of prohibited or restricted functions, ports, protocols, and/or services or establishes its own list of prohibited or restricted functions, ports, protocols, and/or services if STIGs or CIS is not available.

discussion_title: RFC-0027 FedRAMP Rev5 Security Controls Baseline Update for AC, AT, AU, CA, and CM Control Families
author: wisecryptic
text:
Re: RFC-0027 FedRAMP Rev5 Security Controls Baseline Update for AC, AT, AU, CA, and CM Control Families

wisecryptic: CM-06/CM-07

**In short:** I recommend finding a different home for the SCGs because they do not follow the spirit of configuration management under those controls. If they must reside in a control, AC‑2 or AC‑6 are a better fit( My parameter choices would be AC-2d3 or AC-2(7)add'l requirement). This may sound like a small distinction, but getting this right will save a lot of headache in the future for agencies implementing the control, assessors keeping scope of the control, and CSPs tracking the control.

**The longer rationale**
**theoretical discussion**
This proposal represents a significant shift in how these controls are conceptualized. The CM family—Configuration Management—was designed to address baseline configuration control. CM begins with the initial configuration baseline(CM-2), continues with change control (CM-3), and then breaks into more detailed expectations around the state and management of those changes.

CM‑06 is about standardized system configuration settings—establishing what standard configurations are and determining how an organization adheres to them. NIST specifically calls out USGCB, STIGS, etc as examples. 
In contrast, “instructions” that describe the “how to” of accessing, configuring, operating, and decommissioning top‑level accounts are typically part of what most CSPs refer to as implementations. If this material must live in a configuration setting control, we should be looking for recommended configurations, not operational instructions.

CM-07, least function is slightly more nuanced but follows the same basic reasoning. parameters should focus on limiting functionality. "accessing, configuring, operating, and decommissioning" is information far beyond the scope of what CM-07 should be.

**Practical implementation**
CM‑06
CM‑06 Looking at the big picture, I believe that CM-06 could benefit from more flexibility. While STIG implementation should remain an acceptable standalone response, it should also fit into a broader configuration schema that contributes to the configuration baseline (if we are focusing on security practice, not security theatre, that is).
However, the SCG should not live here unless the customer is providing machine‑implementable artifacts or tools that directly configure elements referenced in the SCG. CM‑06 is not the place for instructions or walkthroughs.
CM‑07
CM‑07 Again, thinking big picture, I would change the STIG requirement from “shall” to “may” because:

- STIGs are already required in CM‑06, making the CM‑07 inclusion redundant.
- NIST’s discussion and intent for CM‑07 do not include STIG expectations.
- While STIGs can help satisfy the control, they are not the sole or even primary focus here; the enhancements to CM‑07 clearly point toward a more composite, multi‑layered approach.

Regardless, the SCG should not be inserted in CM-07 either. It distracts from the core intent of least functionality. The SCG is about secure implementation—not least functionality. While the two can overlap, instructions and detailed how‑tos are not examples of least functionality.

So where should the SCG go?
For this particular requirement, I would place it under the AC family, where responsibility for customer‑administered accounts is already delegated. AC‑2 or AC‑6 remain the most logical fits.
However, if FedRAMP anticipates future SCG‑type requirements that fall outside the AC scope but still require explicit assessment, there are two possible approaches:

**Approach 1:** Align each SCG requirement with its corresponding NIST control complement.

- This preserves alignment with NIST’s structure and the community’s shared mental model.
- The downside is fragmentation—SCG content would be distributed across multiple controls.
- A separate guide would be needed to identify where SCG‑related parameters live.



**Approach 2:** Add the SCG requirement to PL‑2 or attach it as a required appendix in the SSP template.

- This keeps related material in one place.
- It also aligns with existing FedRAMP patterns, for better or worse.



This may feel like a small placement issue, but I strongly believe we should not distort the original NIST intent of CM‑06 and CM‑07 with requirements of this nature. While occasionally forcing a “square peg into a round hole” helps expose the need for a new square hole, in this case I think existing compliance scaffolding already provides the right home for this content without bending the CM controls out of shape.

discussion_title: RFC-0027 FedRAMP Rev5 Security Controls Baseline Update for AC, AT, AU, CA, and CM Control Families
author: vedigaurav
text:
Re: RFC-0027 FedRAMP Rev5 Security Controls Baseline Update for AC, AT, AU, CA, and CM Control Families

vedigaurav: Gap #1: Fragmented Control Update Visibility
Issue: The RFC presents changes across multiple control families in a spreadsheet-style, partial update format, making it difficult to understand cumulative impact across the baseline.
Recommendation: Provide a consolidated “redlined baseline view” or diff summary showing all updates in context to improve traceability and review efficiency.

Gap #2: Insufficient Rationale Depth for Control Changes
Issue: Many updates cite “alignment with Secure Configuration Guidance (SCG)” or BIRs without explaining risk-based justification or expected security outcomes.
Recommendation: Include risk rationale and intended security impact for each control change to help CSPs and assessors interpret intent consistently.

Gap #3: Ambiguity in BIR vs Traditional Path Equivalence
Issue: The RFC introduces alternative requirements for BIR participants (e.g., reduced reporting frequency) without clarifying equivalence in assurance levels.
Recommendation: Define equivalency criteria or assurance benchmarks to demonstrate that BIR-based approaches meet or exceed traditional control objectives.

Gap #4: Lack of Implementation Examples
Issue: Updated requirements (e.g., account types alignment, role-based training enhancements) lack practical implementation examples, increasing interpretation variability.
Recommendation: Provide reference implementations or sample evidence artifacts for selected controls to standardize adoption.

Gap #5: No Explicit Impact on Assessment Procedures
Issue: While control requirements are updated, there is limited guidance on how these changes affect 3PAO assessment methods, test cases, or evidence expectations.
Recommendation: Include assessment guidance updates or mappings to ensure consistent evaluation across assessors.

Gap #6: Incomplete Coverage of Inter-Control Dependencies
Issue: Changes to controls (e.g., AC, CM, CA families) may introduce dependencies or conflicts across control implementations, but these are not addressed.
Recommendation: Document key inter-control relationships and dependency considerations to avoid inconsistent implementations.

Gap #7: Limited Guidance on Automation Alignment
Issue: The RFC aligns with modernization goals but does not explicitly address how updated controls should support automation or machine-readable compliance (e.g., OSCAL).
Recommendation: Include guidance on automation-ready control implementation and reporting, aligning with broader FedRAMP modernization efforts.

Gap #8: Transition Timing and Phasing Ambiguity
Issue: While a transition plan is mentioned, there is no clarity on prioritization, sequencing, or phased adoption of control updates.
Recommendation: Provide a phased adoption roadmap (e.g., control families by priority or impact level) to reduce implementation risk.

discussion_title: RFC-0027 FedRAMP Rev5 Security Controls Baseline Update for AC, AT, AU, CA, and CM Control Families
author: rhoesing
text:
Re: RFC-0027 FedRAMP Rev5 Security Controls Baseline Update for AC, AT, AU, CA, and CM Control Families

rhoesing [FEDRAMP-OFFICIAL]: Comment from Raj P.

Please find below my public comments on RFC-0027: FedRAMP Rev5 Security Controls Baseline Update for AC, AT, AU, CA, and CM Control Families.

Comment 1 
AC-02 — Account Management
No comment. Matching account types defined in account management to those referenced in FedRAMP Secure Configuration Guidance will increase consistency during assessments and minimize ambiguity during authorization review.
AC-10 — Concurrent Session Control
Limiting top level administrative accounts to single session is fair. FedRAMP needs to provide guidance if this control is meant to be enforced at the OS/network layer, application layer, or both. Additionally, FedRAMP should provide guidance as to how this control is implemented/enforced for IaaS, PaaS, and SaaS models.
AT-03 — Role-Based Training
FedRAMP should specify if this applies to all users with privileged account access or if this only applies to dedicated administrators. Along those lines, FedRAMP needs to provide a standard that better defines "where applicable" so that organizations can apply it consistently and in a manner that is proportionate.

Comment 2
AU — Audit and Accountability
No change suggested. No comment. Future Recommendation: Provide guidance around acceptable automated audit analysis capabilities and their effects on ConMon reporting requirements.
CA-05 — Plan of Action and Milestones
Separate tracks for traditional, CCM BIR, and VDR BIR reporting is greatly appreciated. FedRAMP should specify the mapping of traditional POA&M components to the newly developed reporting standards for adequate oversight.
CM-06 — Configuration Settings
Requirement 1 is required and supported. FedRAMP needs to specify what SHOULD be included in Security Configuration Guidance. Is the Security Configuration Guidance a standalone document, or is it part of the SSP? Does the language of SHOULD allow assessors to elevate findings if guidance is not present?

Comment 3
CM-07 — Least Functionality
Clear, concise. No additional comment. Matches CM-06.
CM-08 — System Component Inventory
Allows vendors to opt-out of inventory for VDR/BIR which lessens burden. Need FedRAMP to define minimum acceptable automated inventory standards to meet this requirement. This would include minimum discovery cycles, ephemeral/container components, and tie into CM workflow.
CM-12 — Information Location
Revision ties CM-12 control to MAS BIR boundary framework. No additional comment.
CM-12(1) — Automated Tools to Support Information Location
This special parameter has already been defined in CP-2(8). Consider revising the language to "CM-12(1) — [essential]"
IA-8 — Identification and Authentication Through Mobile Devices
Requiring an OTP is in-line with industry best practices. FedRAMP needs to allow for compliance of legacy applications that do not support OTP without major rewrites.

discussion_title: RFC-0027 FedRAMP Rev5 Security Controls Baseline Update for AC, AT, AU, CA, and CM Control Families
author: acloudcj
text:
Re: RFC-0027 FedRAMP Rev5 Security Controls Baseline Update for AC, AT, AU, CA, and CM Control Families

acloudcj: A few specific observations at the control level.
AC-10 (Concurrent Session Control): Limiting top level administrative accounts to one concurrent session at the High baseline makes sense as a security measure. The operational question is how this interacts with break glass procedures. If a critical incident requires two administrators to access the same service account simultaneously (one performing remediation while another monitors) does this control require denying the second session? If so, the incident response playbook and the access control policy are in direct tension. Consider adding language that addresses emergency access scenarios, or explicitly state whether break glass accounts are subject to this limit.
CA-05 (Plan of Action and Milestones): The differentiated timelines for BIR participants versus traditional processes are a good idea in principle. But the RFC introduces multiple acronyms (BIR, CCM, VDR, SCN) without a single place that maps them to concrete CSP obligations. A CSP reading CA-05 needs to cross reference RFC-0026, the BIR guidance, the VDR framework, and the CCM playbook just to understand what frequency applies to them. This isn’t a comment about the policy; it’s about navigability. Consider a decision tree or lookup table: “If you are [pathway], your CA-05 cadence is [X].”
CM-06 and CM-07 (Configuration Settings / Least Functionality): Both now reference the Security Configuration Guidelines (SCG). This is the third RFC in the current batch that introduces SCG as a dependency, as it also appears in AT-03 and AC-02. What’s the status of the SCG itself? If it’s still in draft or hasn’t been published, CSPs are being asked to comment on controls that reference a document they can’t yet read. Please confirm whether the SCG is published and where to find it, or clarify the timeline for its release relative to these control updates taking effect.
CM-08 (System Component Inventory): Exempting VDR and CCM BIR participants from monthly reporting is a meaningful burden reduction, but only if the alternative reporting cadence is clearly defined somewhere. The RFC says what VDR participants don’t have to do (monthly reports) without specifying what they do have to do instead. If the answer is “see the BIR guidance,” a cross reference would help.
CM-12(1): The RFC adds an undefined parameter referencing “CP-2(8) [essential].” This appears to be a copy and paste from a different control family (Contingency Planning). Is this intentional cross referencing or an error? If intentional, the relationship between information location tracking and essential contingency planning functions should be explained.

text:

CSP-AB: CSP-AB submits the following comments to RFC-0027:

We respectfully request clarification from the PMO regarding whether the parameter assignment for CP-2(8) should be listed under the Contingency Planning (CP) control family rather than the Configuration Management (CM) control family to ensure proper alignment and organizational clarity.

mjprager: I concur with the CSP-AB's comments. 

rgaffey: Agree, that this opportunity for standardization across CSP, 3PAO's in a standardized configuration guide would be a huge for all parties concerned, including the PMO!

discussion_title: RFC-0027 FedRAMP Rev5 Security Controls Baseline Update for AC, AT, AU, CA, and CM Control Families
author: mjschroeder1
text:
Re: RFC-0027 FedRAMP Rev5 Security Controls Baseline Update for AC, AT, AU, CA, and CM Control Families

mjschroeder1: Strong support for this cleanup work. The SCG alignment across AC, AT, and CM is overdue, and the BIR integration into CA-05 reporting cadence and CM-08 inventory requirements correctly reflects where the program is moving. A few specific comments follow.

On CM-12(1) Information Location – Automated Tools to Support Information Location. The proposed change body reads "CP-2 (8) - [essential]" which appears to be an incorrect copy from the adjacent CP-2(8) change in RFC-0028. The control being updated is CM-12(1), not CP-2(8). The parameter value for CM-12(1) should reference the CM-12(1) control family, and the FedRAMP-defined assignment should be specified **explicitly**. Recommend rewriting this change block so that the control ID and the parameter value align, and confirming the intended parameter value for CM-12(1) is established clearly in the published baseline.

On CM-06 Configuration Settings. The proposed introduction of a new Requirement 1 specifying Security Configuration Guideline instructions for top-level administrative account access, configuration, operation, and decommissioning is a meaningful substantive addition, not a simple SCG alignment. Suggest the Initial Outcome make this visibility explicit, and that the published materials flag this as a net-new CM-06 requirement for CSPs to scope in their implementation updates. Proactive CSPs will scope it correctly regardless. Making the addition visible up front prevents surprise during assessment.

On CA-05 Plan of Action and Milestones. The three-cadence structure tied to BIR adoption (monthly traditional, Ongoing Authorization Reports every three months for CCM BIR, Monthly Activity Report for VDR BIR) is a reasonable reflection of the pathway options. Recommend that CSPs be expected to document their pathway selection explicitly in the SSP so that the reporting cadence for any given service is unambiguous to assessors and agency customers at any point in time.

On AT-03 Role-based Training. Adding SCG content to role-based training is appropriate. The practical question is implementation timing. Suggest confirming that CSPs have until their next annual assessment cycle after CR26 publication to incorporate the updated content into their role-based training materials. Training content updates are a slow-cycle change, and the grace period should reflect that reality.

General posture. These changes are consistent with the direction of travel in RFC-0024, RFC-0026, and the BIR structure. The complexity introduced through pathway dependence is real, but manageable if the pathway selection is documented clearly at the SSP level - which will remain critical to agency customers. Thank you to the PMO for taking the time to sweep through these control families with a consistent lens.

Michael Schroeder

discussion_title: RFC-0027 FedRAMP Rev5 Security Controls Baseline Update for AC, AT, AU, CA, and CM Control Families
author: badgerinspace
text:
Re: RFC-0027 FedRAMP Rev5 Security Controls Baseline Update for AC, AT, AU, CA, and CM Control Families

badgerinspace: - CM-6 does not define what asset types Service Configuration Scans should be run on and even with RFC-0026’s updated CA-7 language, neither does CA-7. The scope of this term has been loosely defined in FedRAMP and causes unnecessary confusion during assessments and ConMon. Some CSPs will only run such scans against Hosts, others will include Databases, and others still will also include Container Images, but it’s left up to 3PAOs to attempt to enforce a consistent approach and different 3PAOs think differently on this subject. FedRAMP’s vulnerability scanning requirements for containers does reference CM-6, but this language is often ignored by 3PAOs, causing inconsistent enforcement of service configuration scans. Please provide clear guidance directly in this or another control on what types of assets these scans should be run on to ensure a level playing field and consistent assessments across 3PAOs. A similar request has been posted to RFC-0026, where it may be more directly appropriate.
- CM-6 language states “STIGs or Center for Internet Security guidelines”, which uses “or” language, rather than a hierarchical order. However, RFC-0030’s SA-4(5) proposed changes reference the hierarchical order of STIGs > CIS > custom baselines, per standard FedRAMP process. This issue will be cross-posted on RFC-0030 as well. Recommend ensuring a standard hierarchical order is used across both controls.
- CM-8/CM-12 proposed changes have slightly different verbiage than previous controls (such as how CA-5 is worded), when referencing the traditional Rev 5 approach vs the new BIR approaches. Recommend standardizing language when referencing traditional vs new BIR approaches.
- CM-12(1) proposed changes reference CP-2(8), though these controls are disparate in nature. Recommend clarifying what FedRAMP’s intended changes are to this control.

discussion_title: RFC-0027 FedRAMP Rev5 Security Controls Baseline Update for AC, AT, AU, CA, and CM Control Families
author: Alliancefordigitalinnovation
text:
Re: RFC-0027 FedRAMP Rev5 Security Controls Baseline Update for AC, AT, AU, CA, and CM Control Families

Alliancefordigitalinnovation: ADI appreciates the opportunity to comment on RFC-0027, FedRAMP Rev5 Security Controls Baseline Update for AC, AT, AU, CA, and CM Control Families.

To support FedRAMP’s efforts in clarifying and updating the Rev5 baseline requirements, ADI recommends that FedRAMP clarify who is responsible for providing the training in AT-03. The proposed language states that “Top-Level Administrative and Privileged Accounts Secure Configuration Guidance must be included as part of role-based training where applicable,” but it is unclear whether that responsibility falls to the cloud service provider (CSP), the agency, or both.

While the wording suggests this is a CSP responsibility, agency customers also share responsibility for secure configuration under the shared security model. FedRAMP should clearly specify whether the CSP, the agency, or both are responsible for providing this training to Top-Level Administrative and Privileged Accounts.

Thank you for your consideration on this matter.

text:
RFC-0028 FedRAMP Rev5 Security Controls Baseline Update for CP, IA, IR, MA, and MP Control Families

# RFC-0028 FedRAMP Rev5 Security Controls Baseline Update for CP, IA, IR, MA, and MP Control Families

❓   **Please note that FedRAMP will not answer questions in this thread as it is reserved for public comment. If you would like to ask a question or generally discuss this RFC informally, please use the [General discussion and Q&A for RFCs related to Rev5 Updates (RFCs 0026, 0027, 0028, 0029, & 0030) thread](https://github.com/FedRAMP/community/discussions/129). Thank you!**

**Status:** Closed
**Start Date:** March 19, 2026
**Closing Date:** April 22, 2026
---

# FedRAMP Rev5 Security Controls Baseline Update for CP, IA, IR, MA, and MP Control Families

---

## **Summary**

This is a technical RFC that proposes updates to the Additional FedRAMP Security Technical Controls Requirements and Guidance for FedRAMP Rev5 baselines.

To save space and to limit the breadth of a single RFC, this technical document shows only the proposed changes to the current baseline document and is restricted to a few control families. If verbiage is being updated, only the specific wording that is to be changed is identified in the old verbiage section. If the verbiage to be added is not replacing previous verbiage, but being added, it will be identified as “NEW” in the old verbiage section.  

Since this spreadsheet covers hundreds of controls across multiple tabs and sections, only those specific controls, sections, and tabs identified are being proposed for updates. If it is not mentioned below, changes are **not** being proposed.  

**Commenters are advised to please mention specific controls in their comments!**

This RFC addresses controls in the following families:

* Contingency Planning (CP)  
* Identification and Authentication (IA)  
* Incident Response (IR)  
* Maintenance (MA)  
* Media Protection (MP)

## **Motivation**

Many Rev5 FedRAMP Requirements and Guidance statements are based on outdated approaches that predated the release of the FedRAMP Authorization Act and M-24-15. This set of Requirements and Guidance needs a refresh to match FedRAMP’s current rules and approach.

The updates formalized after this RFC will be included in the FedRAMP Consolidated Rules for 2026. That set of rules will be valid until December 31, 2028. FedRAMP will provide a transition plan for adopting any new guidance that will enable cloud service providers to update their approach as part of their annual assessment as appropriate.

These changes are designed to lower the burden for cloud service providers and eliminate previous pain points.

Additionally, NIST released 800-53 Rev 5.2.0 in August of 2025.  While this update was minor, control updates from NIST will require updates to FedRAMP Security Control Baseline in order to reflect this update.  These changes will happen without public comment through FedRAMP since these are direct reflections of NIST changes.  As subsequent iterations of the FedRAMP Security Control Baseline are published, it is FedRAMP’s intent only to carry over the following information from NIST 800-53; Control Family, Control Name, and Control ID. Following this will be FedRAMP-Defined Assignment / Selection Parameters and additional FedRAMP Requirements and Guidance.

## **Proposed Changes to Contingency Planning Family**

This section contains proposed changes to the FedRAMP Requirements and Guidance section for each of these controls.

### **CP-02: Contingency Plan**

**Tabs Affected:** High Baseline, Moderate Baseline, Low Baseline  
**Sections Affected:** Additional FedRAMP Requirements and Guidance  
**Current Verbiage:** CP-2 Requirement: CSPs must use the FedRAMP Information System Contingency Plan (ISCP) Template (available at: https://www.fedramp.gov/assets/resources/templates/SSP-A06-FedRAMP-ISCP-Template.docx).   
**Proposed Change**: CP-2 Requirement: CSPs must use the FedRAMP Information System Contingency Plan (ISCP) Template (available at:   
https://www.fedramp.gov/resources/templates/SSP-Appendix-G-Information-System-Contingency-Plan-(ISCP)-Template.docx).  
**Rationale:** Update existing link to active link.

### **CP-02(8): Contingency Plan | Identify Critical Assets**

**Tabs Affected:** High Baseline, Moderate Baseline   
**Sections Affected:** FedRAMP-Defined Assignment / Selection Parameters  
**Current Verbiage:** NEW  
**Proposed Change:** CP-2 (8) - [essential]  
**Rationale:** Parameter previously undefined.

### **CP-03: Contingency Training**

**Tabs Affected:** High Baseline, Moderate Baseline, Low Baseline  
**Sections Affected:** Additional FedRAMP Requirements and Guidance  
**Current Verbiage:** CP-3 (a) Requirement: Privileged admins and engineers must take the basic contingency training within 10 days. Consideration must be given for those privileged admins and engineers with critical contingency-related roles, to gain enough system context and situational awareness to understand the full impact of contingency training as it applies to their respective level. Newly hired critical contingency personnel must take this more in-depth training within 60 days of hire date when the training will have more impact.  
**Proposed Change**: CP-3 (a) Requirement: Privileged admins (to include TLAs) and engineers must take the basic contingency training within 10 days. Consideration must be given for those privileged admins and engineers with critical contingency-related roles, to gain enough system context and situational awareness to understand the full impact of contingency training as it applies to their respective level. Newly hired critical contingency personnel must take this more in-depth training within 60 days of hire date when the training will have more impact.  
**Rationale:** Adjustment due to verbiage updates within SCG.

## **Proposed Changes to Identification and Authentication Family**

This section contains proposed changes to the FedRAMP Requirements and Guidance section for each of these controls.

### **IA-02: Identification and Authentication**

**Tabs Affected:** High Baseline, Moderate Baseline, Low Baseline  
**Sections Affected:** Additional FedRAMP Requirements and Guidance  
**Current Verbiage:** IA-2 Requirement: For all control enhancements that specify multifactor authentication, the implementation must adhere to the Digital Identity Guidelines specified in NIST Special Publication 800-63B.  
IA-2 Requirement: Multi-factor authentication must be phishing-resistant.  
IA-2 Requirement: All uses of encrypted virtual private networks must meet all applicable Federal requirements and architecture, dataflow, and security and privacy controls must be documented, assessed, and authorized to operate.  
IA-2 Guidance: “Phishing-resistant" authentication refers to authentication processes designed to detect and prevent disclosure of authentication secrets and outputs to a website or application masquerading as a legitimate system.   
**Proposed Change:** IA-2 Requirement: For all control enhancements that specify multifactor authentication, the implementation must adhere to the Digital Identity Guidelines specified in NIST Special Publication 800-63B.  
Multi-factor authentication must be phishing-resistant. Per CISA, One-time password (OTP), Mobile push notification with number matching and Token-based OTP are NOT phishing resistant.  
https://www.cisa.gov/sites/default/files/publications/fact-sheet-implementing-phishing-resistant-mfa-508c.pdf  
IA-2 Requirement: Authentication Factors and their applicable protocols must be explicitly identified within applicable control documentation to include the System Security Plan. When following traditional Rev 5 processes, the Architecture Boundary Diagram must show every instance of MFA to include protocol, where applicable. This should, at a minimum, be at every ingress point  into the boundary.    
IA-2 Requirement: All uses of encrypted virtual private networks must meet all applicable Federal requirements and architecture, dataflow, and security and privacy controls must be documented, assessed, and authorized to operate.  
**Rationale:** This update was added to address a common issue seen during the authorization/certification process.

### **IA-02(1): Identification and Authentication (organizational Users) | Multi-factor Authentication to Privileged Accounts**

**Tabs Affected:** High Baseline, Moderate Baseline, Low Baseline  
**Sections Affected:** Additional FedRAMP Requirements and Guidance  
**Current Verbiage:** Multi-factor authentication must be phishing-resistant.  
**Proposed Change:** Multi-factor authentication must be phishing-resistant. Per CISA, One-time password (OTP), Mobile push notification with number matching  
and Token-based OTP are NOT phishing resistant.  
https://www.cisa.gov/sites/default/files/publications/fact-sheet-implementing-phishing-resistant-mfa-508c.pdf  
**Rationale:** This update was added to address a common issue seen during the authorization/certification process.

### **IA-02(2): Identification and Authentication (organizational Users) | Multi-factor Authentication to Non-privileged Accounts**

**Tabs Affected:** High Baseline, Moderate Baseline, Low Baseline  
**Sections Affected:** Additional FedRAMP Requirements and Guidance  
**Current Verbiage:** Multi-factor authentication must be phishing-resistant.  
**Proposed Change:** Multi-factor authentication must be phishing-resistant. Per CISA, One-time password (OTP), Mobile push notification with number matching  
and Token-based OTP are NOT phishing resistant.  
https://www.cisa.gov/sites/default/files/publications/fact-sheet-implementing-phishing-resistant-mfa-508c.pdf  
**Rationale:** This update was added to address a common issue seen during the authorization/certification process.

### **IA-11: Reauthentication**

**Tabs Affected:** High Baseline, Moderate Baseline, Low Baseline  
**Sections Affected:** Additional FedRAMP Requirements and Guidance  
**Current Verbiage:** The fixed time period cannot exceed the limits set in SP 800-63.  
**Proposed Change:** The fixed time period cannot exceed the limits set in SP 800-63B.  
**Rationale:** Updated to accurately reflect the correct Publication.

## **Proposed Changes to Incident Response Family**

This section contains proposed changes to the FedRAMP Requirements and Guidance section for each of these controls.

### **IR-02: Incident Response Training**

**Tabs Affected:** High Baseline, Moderate Baseline, Low Baseline  
**Sections Affected:** FedRAMP-Defined Assignment / Selection Parameters  
**Current Verbiage:** IR-2 (a) (1) [ten (10) days for privileged users, thirty (30) days for Incident Response roles]  
**Proposed Change:** IR-2 (a) (1) [ten (10) days for privileged users (to include TLA), thirty (30) days for Incident Response roles]  
**Rationale:** Alignment with the FedRAMP Secure Configuration Guidance (SCG).

### **IR-06: Incident Reporting**

**Tabs Affected:** High Baseline, Moderate Baseline, Low Baseline  
**Sections Affected:** Additional FedRAMP Requirements and Guidance  
**Current Verbiage:** IR-6 Requirement: Reports security incident information according to the guidance in the FedRAMP Continuous Monitoring Playbook.  
**Proposed Change:** IR-6 Requirement: Reports security incident information according to the guidance in the FedRAMP Continuous Monitoring Playbook or Vulnerability Detection and Response (VDR) guidance (as applicable).  
**Rationale:** Alignment with the FedRAMP Vulnerability Detection and Response (VDR) guidance.

### **IR-07: Incident Response Assistance**

**Tabs Affected:** High Baseline, Moderate Baseline, Low Baseline  
**Sections Affected:** Additional FedRAMP Requirements and Guidance  
**Current Verbiage:** NEW  
**Proposed Change:** CSPs must maintain a centralized point of contact and appropriate response rates to FedRAMP incidents as identified within FedRAMP Secure Inbox Guidance.  
**Rationale:** Alignment with the FedRAMP Secure Inbox (FSI) guidance.

## **Proposed Changes to Maintenance Family**

This section contains proposed changes to the FedRAMP Requirements and Guidance section for each of these controls.

### **MA-05: Maintenance Personnel**

**Tabs Affected:** Low Baseline, Moderate Baseline, High Baseline  
**Sections Affected:** Additional FedRAMP Requirements and Guidance  
**Current Verbiage:** NEW  
**Proposed Change:** CSPs should clearly document nationality requirements for maintenance personnel, where applicable.  
**Rationale:** Added due to recent events

## **Proposed Changes to Media Protection Family**

This section contains proposed changes to the FedRAMP Requirements and Guidance section for each of these controls.

### **MP-06(1): Media Sanitization | Review, Approve, Track, Document, and Verify**

**Tabs Affected:** High Baseline  
**Sections Affected:** Additional FedRAMP Requirements and Guidance  
**Current Verbiage:** MP-6 (1)  Requirement: Must comply with NIST SP 800-88  
**Proposed Change:** MP-6 (1)  Requirement: Must comply with NIST SP 800-88 Rev 2  
**Rationale:** Administrative update.

### **MP-06(3): Media Sanitization | Nondestructive Techniques**

**Tabs Affected:** High Baseline  
**Sections Affected:** Additional FedRAMP Requirements and Guidance  
**Current Verbiage:** MP-6 (3)  Requirement: Must comply with NIST SP 800-88  
**Proposed Change:** MP-6 (3)  Requirement: Must comply with NIST SP 800-88 Rev 2  
**Rationale:** Administrative update.

discussion_title: RFC-0028 FedRAMP Rev5 Security Controls Baseline Update for CP, IA, IR, MA, and MP Control Families
author: p4gs
text:
Re: RFC-0028 FedRAMP Rev5 Security Controls Baseline Update for CP, IA, IR, MA, and MP Control Families

p4gs: Given the hyperactive threat environment around credential theft, the commoditization of e.g. phishing kits, and the ease with which people can be socially engineered, I think we need to start treating phishing-resistant MFA like we treat encryption protocols: be explicit about which kinds of MFA protocols/standards/patterns qualify as phishing-resistant, instead of specifying which kinds are **not** phishing resistant. FIDO2-based implementations of authentication credentials are really the only well known, well understood, easily accessible, and well vetted protocols/schemes for phishing-resistant authenticators (PIV/CAC PKI-based credentials can be considered phishing resistant but are really only common within government organizations). 

Let's be more explicit here about what is considered phishing-resistant to avoid instances of organizations "rolling their own" or rolling a vendor's purported "phishing-resistant MFA" product that uses proprietary protocols or implementation patterns that make it prone to remote credential theft. It would also make sense to explicitly define existing forms of hardware-backed authentication credential devices, such as PIV/CAC cards, as qualifying as phishing-resistant MFA.

Here's an example of what I mean (bolded text is my recommendation):

> IA-2 Requirement: For all control enhancements that specify multifactor authentication, the implementation must adhere to the Digital Identity Guidelines specified in NIST Special Publication 800-63B.
Multi-factor authentication must be phishing-resistant. Per CISA, One-time password (OTP), Mobile push notification with number matching and Token-based OTP are NOT phishing resistant. **Likewise, FIDO2-based authenticators and PKI-based authenticators, wherein a hardware-bound cryptographically-generated credential is used, are considered phishing resistant**
https://www.cisa.gov/sites/default/files/publications/fact-sheet-implementing-phishing-resistant-mfa-508c.pdf

jtpickering: I do like specifying FIDO2, but as more products come onto the market and new methods are established, we may find that we dislike the specificity in the suggestion (enumerating approved/preferred solutions). In addition, this might end up as an untenable or unwanted administrative burden on the FedRAMP team (to maintain which kinds of MFA protocols/standards/patterns qualify as phishing-resistant when new standards emerge, old ones are deprecated, industry consensus shifts, or weaknesses appear in approved items). Lastly, FedRAMP aligns to NIST for requirements/baselines and CISA for implementation guidance. FedRAMP publishing specific "approved or preferred" items would deviate from established practice and potentially put oil on that slope. $0.02.

discussion_title: RFC-0028 FedRAMP Rev5 Security Controls Baseline Update for CP, IA, IR, MA, and MP Control Families
author: vedigaurav
text:
Re: RFC-0028 FedRAMP Rev5 Security Controls Baseline Update for CP, IA, IR, MA, and MP Control Families

vedigaurav: Gap #1 – Limited guidance on shared responsibility in cloud-native environments
Issue: The RFC does not sufficiently clarify how updated controls (especially in IA, IR, and CP families) should be applied in shared responsibility models across IaaS, PaaS, and SaaS. This creates ambiguity in control ownership and assessment boundaries.
Recommendation: Include a mapping or explanatory guidance that distinguishes CSP versus customer responsibilities for each affected control family across different service models.

Gap #2 – Insufficient integration with automation and continuous monitoring
Issue: While controls are updated, there is minimal emphasis on how requirements should be implemented using automated or continuous monitoring approaches, which are central to modern FedRAMP practices.
Recommendation: Incorporate expectations or examples for automation (e.g., machine-readable evidence, APIs, continuous diagnostics) to align control implementation with ongoing authorization and real-time monitoring goals.

Gap #3 – Ambiguity in evidence expectations for assessments
Issue: The RFC updates control language but does not clarify what constitutes sufficient or acceptable evidence for assessors, increasing the risk of inconsistent 3PAO interpretations.
Recommendation: Provide supplemental assessment guidance or example evidence artifacts for updated controls to improve consistency across assessments and reduce rework.

Gap #4 – Transition guidance for existing authorizations
Issue: There is no clear direction on how currently authorized systems should transition to the updated requirements, including timelines, reauthorization triggers, or delta assessment expectations.
Recommendation: Define a transition strategy outlining applicability to existing ATOs, expected timelines, and whether updates can be incorporated through continuous monitoring or require formal reassessment.

Gap #5 – Interdependencies across control families not addressed
Issue: Updates to CP, IA, IR, MA, and MP controls may have operational dependencies (e.g., incident response tied to identity systems), but these relationships are not explicitly addressed.
Recommendation: Highlight key interdependencies and provide cross-references or implementation considerations to ensure cohesive and effective control implementation.

Gap #6 – Limited consideration for operational scalability
Issue: Some updated expectations may be difficult to operationalize at scale (e.g., in large, distributed, or multi-tenant environments) without additional clarification.
Recommendation: Include scalability considerations or implementation patterns for large CSP environments to ensure requirements remain practical and achievable.
