discussion_title: RFC-0030 FedRAMP Rev5 Security Controls Baseline Update for RA, SA, SC, SI, and SR Control Families
author: cb-axon
text:
Re: RFC-0030 FedRAMP Rev5 Security Controls Baseline Update for RA, SA, SC, SI, and SR Control Families

cb-axon: Overall, we welcome the updates proposed in this RFC. The alignment of RA-5 parameters with the VDR BIR, the cleanup of outdated references, and the clarifications around configuration baselines and operational directives represent meaningful progress in modernizing FedRAMP's Rev5 requirements. We appreciate FedRAMP's continued effort to reduce burden on CSPs while maintaining rigorous security expectations.

**RA-5 -** The proposed language for the traditional Rev5 path under RA-5(a) reads:

> [monthly operating system/infrastructure; monthly web applications (including APIs) and databases for traditional Rev5 processes]

This same scan type enumeration appears repeatedly throughout this RFC — across the FedRAMP-Defined Assignment/Selection Parameters, Additional FedRAMP Requirements and Guidance, and Continuous Monitoring Periodicity sections — and the concern below applies to all instances.
Container scanning is absent from this language. This is not new — the original Rev5 baseline predated FedRAMP's separate container scanning guidance and was never updated to explicitly include containers alongside OS/infrastructure, web application, and database scans. This RFC represents an opportunity to correct that gap, and we strongly urge FedRAMP to do so.
FedRAMP should explicitly confirm in this RFC whether container scans are required for CSPs on the traditional Rev5 path. If they are — which we believe they should be given the prevalence of containerized workloads in modern cloud architectures and the existence of FedRAMP container scanning guidance — every instance of the traditional Rev5 scan type enumeration in this RFC must be updated to include containers explicitly. Implicit coverage under "infrastructure" is insufficient; OS/infrastructure, web applications, and databases are each called out as distinct scan types, and containers warrant the same explicit treatment.
Proposed language wherever this enumeration appears for the traditional Rev5 path:

> [monthly operating system/infrastructure; monthly web applications (including APIs) and databases; monthly containers for traditional Rev5 processes]

Leaving containers unaddressed in this update would perpetuate an existing gap at exactly the moment FedRAMP has the opportunity to close it.

**SI-8 -** The SI-8 guidance — both current and proposed — addresses DMARC only in the context of outbound email sent on behalf of the government, but leaves several common CSO email scenarios unaddressed. We request FedRAMP explicitly clarify the following:

Spam protection (SI-8): Is spam protection required only when the CSO sends email, only when it receives email, or both? Is there any SI-8 obligation for CSOs that neither send nor receive email as part of their offering?
DMARC (outbound): Does the policy=reject requirement apply only when sending on behalf of the government, or also when the CSO sends email from CSP-owned domains for any purpose?
DMARC (inbound): If a CSO accepts inbound email and controls its own spam filtering — without delegating that control to customers — is the CSO expected to enforce DMARC rejection on inbound mail failures?

The existing guidance is explicit for the government-email-sending scenario but silent on these adjacent cases, creating inconsistency in how CSPs implement SI-8 and how 3PAOs assess it.

**SC-13 -** We applaud the addition of explicit guidance directing CSPs to follow FedRAMP instructions for cryptographic modules listed as "historical" in the CMVP database. This has been a recurring source of confusion during the authorization process, and surfacing it directly in the baseline makes compliance expectations more evident to both CSPs and assessors.



mjschroeder1: Support for the SI-8 insights and feedback, especially the DMARC commentary. Highly insightful.

discussion_title: RFC-0030 FedRAMP Rev5 Security Controls Baseline Update for RA, SA, SC, SI, and SR Control Families
author: acloudcj
text:
Re: RFC-0030 FedRAMP Rev5 Security Controls Baseline Update for RA, SA, SC, SI, and SR Control Families

acloudcj: This RFC carries the most operational weight in the batch. The VDR pathway and cryptographic module guidance in particular will reshape how CSPs run their vulnerability and compliance programs.
RA-05 (Vulnerability Monitoring and Scanning), VDR Pathway:
The VDR pathway is the headline change across the entire RFC batch, and I support the direction. Moving from calendar based scanning to detection and response cadences reflects how mature security programs actually operate. A few concerns about the specifics:
The detection frequency ranges (every 7 days at Low to daily at High) with evaluation timelines compressed from 7 to 2 days are aggressive but achievable for CSPs with modern tooling. The question is what happens at the boundary. If a CSP detects a vulnerability on day 1 and evaluates it by day 2, the remediation timeline then varies by impact, exploitability, and internet reachability. That’s three variables producing a matrix of possible deadlines. Is FedRAMP publishing that matrix, or is the CSP expected to define its own remediation SLAs within guardrails? If the latter, the acceptable range of those guardrails needs to be specified; otherwise 3PAOs will interpret “reasonable” differently across engagements.
For CSPs not on the VDR pathway, the traditional monthly scanning cadence is maintained. But the RFC doesn’t address what happens when a CSP wants to transition from traditional to VDR midcycle. Is that a decision that takes effect at the next annual assessment? Can a CSP adopt VDR for specific system components while maintaining traditional scanning for others? Or is it all or nothing at the authorization boundary level?
SC-13 (Cryptographic Protections), Historical CMVP Modules:
Adding guidance for modules listed as “historical” in the CMVP database addresses a real pain point. CSPs have been caught in a bind where modules they deployed in good faith transition to historical status due to certificate expiration or algorithm deprecation, and the previous guidance was effectively “replace it,” which for embedded crypto modules in production infrastructure is a multiquarter effort, not a patch.
What’s the expected posture? If a module goes historical, is there a grace period to transition, or does the CSP need to document it as a POA&M immediately? And does the guidance distinguish between modules that went historical due to administrative expiration (vendor didn’t renew) versus algorithmic deprecation (the underlying crypto is actually weaker)? Those are very different risk profiles and should warrant different response timelines.
SI-05 (Security Alerts), CISA EDs and BODs:
Aligning with CISA Emergency Directives and Binding Operational Directives through the FSI process makes sense. One clarification: CISA directives are binding on federal agencies, not on commercial entities. When FedRAMP requires CSPs to comply with EDs and BODs via FSI response timelines, that’s FedRAMP extending CISA’s authority to CSPs through the authorization relationship. That’s a legitimate policy choice, but the RFC should be explicit about it rather than implying that EDs and BODs directly apply to CSPs. The legal basis matters for CSP counsel evaluating compliance obligations, and clarity here avoids unnecessary exchanges during assessments.
SR (Supply Chain Risk Management), No Changes:
Noted. Given the current emphasis on supply chain security across the federal government (EO 14028, CISA SBOM guidance, the C-SCRM requirements in NIST 800-161 Rev 1) the absence of any SR updates is surprising. Is FedRAMP planning a dedicated SR focused RFC, or is the assessment that the existing SR controls are adequate as is? Not requesting changes for the sake of changes, but the gap between federal supply chain policy momentum and the “no changes” here is worth acknowledging.

discussion_title: RFC-0030 FedRAMP Rev5 Security Controls Baseline Update for RA, SA, SC, SI, and SR Control Families
author: CSP-AB
text:
Re: RFC-0030 FedRAMP Rev5 Security Controls Baseline Update for RA, SA, SC, SI, and SR Control Families

CSP-AB: CSP-AB submits the following comments for RFC-0030:

**RA-05: Vulnerability Monitoring and Scanning - Proposed Change: RA-5 (a) [monthly operating system/infrastructure; monthly web applications (including APIs) and databases for traditional Rev 5 processes] [For those opting into the Vulnerability Detection and Response:**

- _[monthly operating system/infrastructure; monthly web applications (including APIs) and databases for traditional Rev5 processes]_

Container scanning is absent from this language. This is not new — the original Rev5 baseline predated FedRAMP's separate container scanning guidance and was never updated to explicitly include containers alongside OS/infrastructure, web application, and database scans. This RFC represents an opportunity to correct that gap, and we strongly urge FedRAMP to do so.
FedRAMP should explicitly confirm in this RFC whether container scans are required for CSPs on the traditional Rev5 path. If they are — which we believe they should be given the prevalence of containerized workloads in modern cloud architectures and the existence of FedRAMP container scanning guidance — the traditional Rev5 parameter for RA-5(a) must be updated to say so explicitly. Implicit coverage under "infrastructure" is insufficient; OS/infrastructure, web applications, databases, and containers are each called out as distinct scan types in other FedRAMP contexts, and consistency demands the same treatment here.
Proposed language for the traditional Rev5 path:

- _[monthly operating system/infrastructure; monthly web applications (including APIs) and databases; monthly containers for traditional Rev5 processes]_

Leaving containers unaddressed in this update would perpetuate an existing gap at exactly the moment FedRAMP has the opportunity to close it.

**RA-05: Vulnerability Monitoring and Scanning**

- "Representative samples": For large-scale cloud providers with millions of information resources, we request FedRAMP define what constitutes a "representative sample" — whether by percentage, statistical methodology, or host-class coverage — to ensure consistent implementation and assessment.

- "Likely to drift": We request clarification on how "information resources that are likely to drift" applies to cloud-native architectures where infrastructure is immutable (e.g., AMI-based deployments that are replaced rather than patched in place). Resources that are never modified post-deployment may not fit the traditional "drift" model.

**Proposed Changes to Systems and Services Acquisition Family - Custom baselines shall be used if CIS is not available and must be documented and validated during independent assessment**

- Please provide guidance on the minimum documentation expectations for custom baselines (e.g., baseline rationale, security control mapping, deviation justification) to ensure consistent 3PAO assessment criteria across CSPs.

**SC-13: Cryptographic Protections
Tabs Affected: High Baseline, Moderate Baseline, Low Baseline
Sections Affected: Additional FedRAMP Requirements and Guidance
Current Verbiage: New
Proposed Change: For Cryptographic Modules list as "historical" in the CMVP database, please ensure Service Providers follow FedRAMP instructions here: https://www.fedramp.gov/archive/2022-12-22-crypto-modules-historical-status/
Rationale: This update was added to address a common issue seen during the authorization/certification process.**

- Highly supportive of this and please confirm this guidance remains current and consider publishing it at a non-archive URL to avoid confusion about its validity.

**Proposed Change: SI-8 Guidance:**

- The SI-8 guidance — both current and proposed — addresses DMARC only in the context of outbound email sent on behalf of the government, but leaves several common CSO email scenarios unaddressed. We request FedRAMP explicitly clarify the following:

Spam protection (SI-8): Is spam protection required only when the CSO sends email, only when it receives email, or both? Is there any SI-8 obligation for CSOs that neither send nor receive email as part of their offering?
DMARC (outbound): Does the policy=reject requirement apply only when sending on behalf of the government, or also when the CSO sends email from CSP-owned domains for any purpose?
DMARC (inbound): If a CSO accepts inbound email and controls its own spam filtering — without delegating that control to customers — is the CSO expected to enforce DMARC rejection on inbound mail failures?

The existing guidance is explicit for the government-email-sending scenario but silent on these adjacent cases, creating inconsistency in how CSPs implement SI-8 and how 3PAOs assess it.


cb-axon: I strongly concur with the CSP Advisory Board's comments on RFC-0030.
Container scanning has been an expected practice for years and its absence from the traditional Rev5 scan enumeration has created real inconsistency in how CSPs implement and 3PAOs assess it — this needs to be made explicit.
SI-8 ambiguity is a genuine pain point. Without clarity on when spam protection and DMARC apply, assessment outcomes vary significantly across 3PAOs for what should be a straightforward control.

mjschroeder1: Supporting the CSP-AB comments, I expand on this in my comment.

rgaffey: In agreement here, we MUST close the gap around containers in the r5 track.  Please do NOT miss this opportunity!!

discussion_title: RFC-0030 FedRAMP Rev5 Security Controls Baseline Update for RA, SA, SC, SI, and SR Control Families
author: mjschroeder1
text:
Re: RFC-0030 FedRAMP Rev5 Security Controls Baseline Update for RA, SA, SC, SI, and SR Control Families

mjschroeder1: This is the most substantive RFC in the March batch, and the VDR integration work in RA-05 is well-structured. The impact-tiered cadences correctly reflect the VDR philosophy, and the evaluation windows are operationally tight but appropriate for Class D commitments. Several specific comments follow.

On RA-05(a) container scanning. The proposed parameter text references operating system/infrastructure, web applications (including APIs), and databases. It does not reference containers. Current FedRAMP guidance in the Continuous Monitoring Playbook requires container scanning, and leaving the RA-05(a) parameter silent about containers while being explicit about other resource types creates an asymmetric reading that invites CSPs to deprioritize container scans.

From agency-side authorization experience, I directed Agency Authorization lifecycle work for 60+ enterprise cloud deployments at the VA, including systems with heavy container usage. Container-native architectures do not have their vulnerabilities surfaced by OS and infrastructure scanning. The community discussion captured this correctly: for CSPs doing container scans, a majority of identified vulnerabilities come from that scanner type, and there is no substitute pathway for containerized workload findings.

Recommend one of two fixes. Either explicitly include containers in the RA-05(a) parameter text for the traditional pathway (preserving status quo and eliminating the asymmetric reading), or explicitly confirm in the VDR pathway language that containers are machine-based resources subject to the representative sampling approach. The latter is the stronger long-term answer because it treats containers as first-class machine-based resources under VDR’s philosophy. Either way, the silence in the current proposed text should be closed.

On SI-05 security alerts, advisories, and directives. Support for FSI process integration for Emergency Directive and Binding Operational Directive responses. Consistent with the IR-07 FSI alignment in RFC-0028. Recommend that specific response timelines be referenced from the FSI guidance, with the guidance itself carrying those definitions. That keeps the baseline durable as FSI guidance evolves with operational experience.

On SI-02(2) and SI-03 persistent language for VDR participants. Correct use of the existing FRMR definition of persistent. This aligns with how the VDR BIR describes continuous monitoring and avoids introducing a second definition.

On SA-15 Authorization/Certification terminology. Useful transition marker consistent with RFC-0023’s Initial Outcome. Consider a note that the terminology will remain “Authorization/Certification” through the CR26 transition so CSPs understand the durable shape of the language.

On SC-13 Cryptographic Modules historical status. The referenced page is a 2022 archive. Recommend the PMO confirm whether that archive remains the authoritative guidance or whether it should be refreshed into a current Rev. 5/20x document.

On SC-07 and SA-04(5). Supportive. The MAS BIR accommodation in SC-07(8) and the documentation/validation requirement for custom baselines in SA-04(5) are both appropriate alignments.

General note - The VDR pathway integration across SI-02(2), SI-03, and RA-05 is good work and the right direction. Closing the container scanning gap in RA-05 makes the pathway coherent for traditional and VDR-track providers alike.

One structural concern remains across the VDR framework that this RFC surfaces but does not resolve. The Phase 2 VDR design gives CSPs significant latitude to classify and contextualize their own vulnerability risk. Public comments on the 20x requirements have recommended that independent assessors be given more formal oversight authority here: assessors embedded in KSI validation are well-positioned to provide input on the severity of KSI failures, and that role has not been formalized in the published requirements. The control updates in this RFC extend VDR's reach further into Rev5 without addressing that gap. As CR26 finalizes the VDR pathway, formalizing IA oversight of CSP risk classification decisions would meaningfully strengthen the pathway's integrity.

Michael Schroeder

discussion_title: RFC-0030 FedRAMP Rev5 Security Controls Baseline Update for RA, SA, SC, SI, and SR Control Families
author: rhimbrittany
text:
Re: RFC-0030 FedRAMP Rev5 Security Controls Baseline Update for RA, SA, SC, SI, and SR Control Families

rhimbrittany: SAP NS2 Compliance Team:
One concern I would like to raise in the RA-5 family is the operational impact of the accelerated vulnerability scanning timelines, particularly for organizations managing large, complex, or hybrid environments. While the move towards continuous monitoring is understandable, the increased scan frequency for Low, Moderate, and High systems may create challenges around tool capacity, network performance, false-positive management, and staffing resources needed to triage findings within the required evaluation windows. Another concern is the absence of specific guidance related to containerized environments. As organizations continue adopting Kubernetes, ECS, AKS, and other container platforms, containers represent a significant portion of modern infrastructure and application deployments. Without defining scanning cadence, remediation expectations, or assessment parameters for container images, registries, orchestrators, and running workloads, there is room for inconsistent interpretation across CSPs and assessors. 

Suggestion: It may be helpful to provide additional implementation guidance or flexibility for organizations transitioning from traditional monthly scanning models, especially where compensating controls or existing mature monitoring capabilities are already in place. Clarification on how agencies and assessors should evaluate reasonable expectations, scalability constraints, and phased adoption would help support consistent implementation across environments. 

It would be beneficial for FedRAMP to clarify how RA-5 requirements should apply to container ecosystems, including image vulnerability scanning, runtime monitoring, and responsibility boundaries between the platform, host, and application layers.

nicole-gov [FEDRAMP-OFFICIAL]: The following public comment was received via email from Netskope on April 17:

I am copy/pasting into the public comment record on their behalf as required by the FedRAMP public comment process. This is not an endorsement of the commenter or the content within the comment.

---

Current Verbiage: RA-5 (a) [monthly operating system/infrastructure; monthly web applications (including APIs) and databases]

RA-5 (d) [high-risk vulnerabilities mitigated within thirty (30) days from date of discovery; moderate-risk vulnerabilities mitigated within ninety (90) days from date of discovery; low-risk vulnerabilities mitigated within one hundred and eighty (180) days from date of discovery]

Proposed Change: RA-5 (a) [monthly operating system/infrastructure; monthly web applications (including APIs) and databases for traditional Rev 5 processes]

RA-5 (d) [high-risk vulnerabilities mitigated within thirty (30) days from date of discovery; moderate-risk vulnerabilities mitigated within ninety (90) days from date of discovery; low-risk vulnerabilities mitigated within one hundred and eighty (180) days from date of discovery for traditional Rev 5 processes][

**Feedback:** 

**Guidance should be provided on the word “mitigated”. Is this a partially mitigated or fully mitigated, per the FedRAMP definitions? What is a misconception is that high-risk vulnerabilities have to be remediated within 30 days from the date of discovery.**

**There should be guidance that a risk mitigation is required vs vulnerability remediation.**

**Ref:** 
- **[https://www.fedramp.gov/docs/rev5/balance/fedramp-definitions/#remediated-vulnerability](https://www.fedramp.gov/docs/rev5/balance/fedramp-definitions/#remediated-vulnerability)**
- **[https://www.fedramp.gov/docs/rev5/balance/fedramp-definitions/#partially-mitigated-vulnerability](https://www.fedramp.gov/docs/rev5/balance/fedramp-definitions/#partially-mitigated-vulnerability)**
- **[https://www.fedramp.gov/docs/rev5/balance/fedramp-definitions/#fully-mitigated-vulnerability](https://www.fedramp.gov/docs/rev5/balance/fedramp-definitions/#fully-mitigated-vulnerability)**

SA-04(5): Acquisition Process | System, Component, and Service Configurations

Current Verbiage: SA-4 (5) (a) The service provider shall use the DoD STIGs to establish configuration settings; Center for Internet Security up to Level 2 (CIS Level 2) guidelines shall be used if STIGs are not available; Custom baselines shall be used if CIS is not available.

Proposed Change: SA-4 (5) (a) The service provider shall use the DoD STIGs to establish configuration settings; Center for Internet Security up to Level 2 (CIS Level 2) guidelines shall be used if STIGs are not available; Custom baselines shall be used if CIS is not available and must be documented and validated during independent assessment.

**Feedback:**

**This is not consistent with the CM-6 (a) Requirement 2 Proposed Change. In this control, DOD STIGs are the leading requirement whereas in CM-6 (a) Requirement 2: _The service provider shall use the DoD STIGs or Center for Internet Security guidelines to establish configuration settings_**

SA-05: System Documentation

Proposed Change: a. (1) in conjunction with the FedRAMP Security Configuration Guidance

**Feedback:**

**It should be made clear in this control that the scope of the control requirement pertains to the FedRAMP Security Configuration Guidance document, not to a CSP’s internal administrator documentation pertaining to infrastructure.**

So if a Moderate offering can use the GH Li-SaaS offering to manage our SSP and appendices that would be an excellent option.

pete-gov [FEDRAMP-OFFICIAL]: It's important to note that templates and documentation for the FedRAMP process are not equivalent in risk to a filled out system security plan for a system, so don't make any assumptions based on how FR makes documentation available!

That said, the [Minimum Assessment Scope](https://www.fedramp.gov/docs/20x/minimum-assessment-scope/) is designed to allow flexibility in how cloud services leverage third-party independent services based on risk. A key aspect of this is establishing compensating controls with information flows to lower risk.

In general, a responsibly prepared system security plan and related continuous monitoring materials for a secure cloud service should not be high-risk sensitive materials; in fact, generally one should assume at least a loss of confidentiality when preparing those materials and it's impossible for a cloud service provider to maintain control over them once released to a single party. Integrity can very easily be verified (even automatically) with checksums, and lower availability objectives for security materials can be risk accepted as they don't need to be available 99.999% of the time etc.

In an extreme example, there is absolutely nothing against the rules with a Class D (High) Certified offering publicly publishing their security materials for the world to see on a non-FR certified service. Done responsibly, especially with a good Vulnerability Disclosure Policy and similar strong vulnerability detection and response policies, they might even be able to prove that doing so increases the security of their service. It's always important to remember that the most of the widely relied-upon critical software that cloud services uses is open-source (linux, kubernetes, etc.). 

Just like people shouldn't check API keys into their open-source code, people shouldn't put sensitive information that would likely to lead to compromise into security materials. 🤷 

meagankwhite: Thank you for the rapid and thorough explanation!

judgecspab-max:  Hello PMO!   After the JAB was dissolved in 2024, FedRAMP assigned several CSPs a “designated lead” for continuous monitoring.   It is my understanding that under FedRAMP Rev5 CR 2026, the lead agency model for continuous monitoring has been replaced by the Collaborative Continuous Monitoring (CCM) process, and that the Significant Change Notification (SCN) process will now serve as the cross-agency mechanism for reporting changes to the boundary. I’d like to confirm that once the CCM and SCN processes are implemented, the Lead Agency for any given CSP will no longer serve as the primary federal agency responsible for leading continuous monitoring of FedRAMP certifications, or approval of changes/services.

pete-gov [FEDRAMP-OFFICIAL]: Hey judgecspab-max - The "designated lead" situation in late 2024 was a temporary short-term step on the transition to full collaborative continuous monitoring for former JAB CSPs, with the expectation that like all other FedRAMP authorized (at the time) CSPs they would properly implement the [CA-7 controls following the Collaborative ConMon Playbook](https://www.fedramp.gov/docs/rev5/playbook/csp/continuous-monitoring/collaborative-monitoring/). Providers with more than one customer were expected to bring Significant Changes to their entire Collaborative ConMon group, etc.

We found that some providers chose to only work with a single agency instead of meeting this requirement, out of habit, ignorance, or whatever reason... FR doesn't monitor all of the continuous monitoring of 500+ providers so we only catch this when agencies come to us because a provider is refusing to properly run their Collab ConMon. Collab ConMon is not new and replaced the lead agency model over a year ago!

The updated Collaborative Continuous Monitoring (CCM) and Significant Change Notification (SCN) rulesets (and the Vulnerability Detection and Response ruleset) are designed to add prescriptive guardrails around this and make it very clear via explicit requirements that there is no such thing as a lead agency and that cloud service providers must support the security programs of all customers. It's also intended to ease the burden for agency customers (and providers) by allowing a more continuous stream of information supported by quarterly meetings that focus on security. 

And they requires CSPs to make information available in a way that FedRAMP can hopefully monitor centrally at scale, so we are not in the dark about CSPs that don't follow the rules to maintain their Certification.

> I’d like to confirm that once the CCM and SCN processes are implemented, the Lead Agency for any given CSP will no longer serve as the primary federal agency responsible for leading continuous monitoring of FedRAMP certifications, or approval of changes/services.

This is the case the moment a CSP establishes a legacy Collab ConMon charter and/or implements the CCM process, yep.

discussion_title: General discussion / Q&A on Rev5 improvements and changes in 2026
author: meagankwhite
text:
Re: General discussion / Q&A on Rev5 improvements and changes in 2026

meagankwhite: I say the following in my personal professional capacity and do not represent the opinion of my employer in any way.

As a FedRAMP Audit SME and a private citizen I am raising a Conscientious Objection to both this decision and the way it was made.  

In summary, the removal of minimum requirements in the form of FedRAMP-specific Parameters and Requirements without a dedicated Request-For-Comment period is a sharp decline in the quality of the FedRAMP Certification as well as a direct violation of the requirement for dedicated public feedback.

1. The FedRAMP-specific Parameters and Requirements represent a significant portion of the absolute minimum-security standard that any Cloud Service must adhere to when selling to the Federal Government.  Summarily removing those Parameters and Requirements means that you are removing that minimum.  Removing the minimum means that Federal Agencies can no longer expect any solid security requirements associated with FedRAMP.
2. A market-driven approach to regulation is a misunderstanding of the market and regulation.  Regulations exist to protect the consumer, in this case Federal Agencies and the data of US citizens that they hold.  The market exists to make money.  The two can be aligned, but frankly often are not.  A company can choose to sacrifice security and privacy for cost savings if there is no regulation.  The customers may not even know about this until their information has been compromised.  By the time the market corrects, the data is already exposed and damage has already been done.  The customers are USA Federal Agencies and the data at risk is from USA Federal Agencies and the taxpayers that support them.  Regulation exists to prevent that from even being an option to companies serving the Federal Government.
3. Humans are lazy and not all companies are security-centric.  I still have to have conversations with employees about why multi-factor authentication is necessary.  I still have to explain why STIGs are better than CIS Level 2 in most cases.  I still have to use FedRAMP requirements as justifications for the business to choose the more expensive, but more secure and private route.  Removing the FedRAMP Parameters and Requirements is hamstringing those discussions.
4. FedRAMP exists to make a uniform approach for Federal Agencies to select Cloud Service Providers with a minimum set of security and privacy requirements.  The uniformity of parameters and requirements is a large part of the uniformity of the overall security and privacy that was the goal of FedRAMP.
5. The Notice that includes this massive change to the program is referencing a tangentially related topic.  The original RFC was about specific verbiage changes to the FedRAMP Parameters and Guidance, not their total removal.  The public was not given the opportunity to directly comment on this change.  Isolated comments that suggest this change may be desirable is analogous to the situation with putting pricing information on the marketplace.  Assorted commentary from interested parties made it seem like that would be the best way forward, but a dedicated forum on the subject showed the outright rejection of the premise.  In this case we were not even given that opportunity.

I am very supportive of VDR, CCM, SCG, and most other changes represented in CR26 because they will be an improvement to the security and privacy of the Cloud Service Offerings.  Careful risk-based assessments of a broader definition of vulnerabilities, and a focus on mitigating that risk is a big step forward for securing the software, configurations, and supply-chain.  Bringing together all USA Federal agencies with a stake in the Cloud Service Offering to understand the security and compliance of the offering is a big step forward in relationships with Federal agencies and transparency on security and compliance.  However, the removal of FedRAMP-specific parameters and requirements can only result in a sharp decline in the security and privacy of those Cloud Service Offerings to the detriment of the FedRAMP program, the USA Federal Agencies, and the taxpayers that both serve.  I am sorry, but I must object to this decision.

pete-gov [FEDRAMP-OFFICIAL]: I'd like to address a few of these points while acknowledging that we understand that every decision FedRAMP makes won't land well with every stakeholder. Like everyone else, FR follows direction from higher level stakeholders and often that includes direction on pace and urgency.

> The FedRAMP-specific Parameters and Requirements represent a significant portion of the absolute minimum-security standard that any Cloud Service must adhere to when selling to the Federal Government. Summarily removing those Parameters and Requirements means that you are removing that minimum. Removing the minimum means that Federal Agencies can no longer expect any solid security requirements associated with FedRAMP.

In the Consolidated Rules for 2026, FedRAMP has established nearly 250 specific rules designed to ensure that clear information is shared about security decisions and that FedRAMP Certified cloud services meet a minimum set of critical security expectations (especially around managing vulnerabilities). This will ensure a significant level of transparent assurance about what a cloud service provider does or doesn't do as part of its security program.

Some cloud services will operate extremely complex and highly effective security architectures and increase their effort and investment in security to meet the assurance requirements of higher FedRAMP Certification Classes, while others may reduce the amount of effort put into overall security (and will be unable to meet the assurance requirements of higher FedRAMP Certification Classes).

This is ok. There are very many use cases (such as the one we're interacting on right now) for the federal government to use systems that provide very little assurance about their security capabilities. Civil servants should not be limited to highly secure services that have invested millions of dollars in gov-specific implementations to perform basic daily tasks that are not sensitive.

> A market-driven approach to regulation is a misunderstanding of the market and regulation. 

FedRAMP is **not** a regulator. FedRAMP does not protect consumers or regulate companies. FedRAMP operates an assessment process that does not require any company to do anything unless they want to obtain or maintain a certification that makes government-wide use easier.

> A company can choose to sacrifice security and privacy for cost savings if there is no regulation. The customers may not even know about this until their information has been compromised. 

FedRAMP still requires companies to report their decisions. For current FedRAMP Certified cloud service offerings, changing a control parameter would require a significant change in most circumstances and customers would know about it or the cloud service provider would lose their FedRAMP Certification.

> I still have to use FedRAMP requirements as justifications for the business to choose the more expensive, but more secure and private route. 

This is an example of something that goes against the idea of ensuring civil servants have access to appropriate tools with appropriate capabilities at appropriate prices. If everyone follows a more expensive path then we don't have access to cheaper tools to use when a less secure or less private route is unnecessary.

> FedRAMP exists to make a uniform approach for Federal Agencies to select Cloud Service Providers with a minimum set of security and privacy requirements. 

FedRAMP exists to provide a _standardized, reusable approach to security assessment and authorization_, yes. That does not mean the implementation of the things being assessed or authorized should be standardized or uniform. 

> the removal of FedRAMP-specific parameters and requirements can only result in a sharp decline in the security and privacy of those Cloud Service Offerings to the detriment of the FedRAMP program, the USA Federal Agencies, and the taxpayers that both serve.

The historical and current evidence we have indicates the opposite; FedRAMP-assigned parameters have lead to stagnation, increased risk, poorer security outcomes, and many cloud service providers who are unwilling or unable to modernize their operational security procedures because their business is unwilling to invest in continuous incremental improvement since there was no recognition or incentive for doing so from FedRAMP or the federal government.


meagankwhite: Thank you very much for taking the time to do a thorough review and answer to my points.  I appreciate the time you have put into the conversation and respect your perspective.  I'm still very worried and do not agree with the decision, but I respect the work involved and will hope this works out as you expect it to.

discussion_title: General discussion / Q&A on Rev5 improvements and changes in 2026
author: vennemp
text:
Re: General discussion / Q&A on Rev5 improvements and changes in 2026

vennemp: I strongly support FedRAMP's strategic direction with the new Vulnerability Detection and Response framework. Given the current threat environment, including the increasing speed and automation of exploitation activity, a more risk-based and responsive approach to vulnerability management is clearly needed.

That said, I wanted to raise a practical implementation concern that may affect CSPs' ability to meet the required timelines, particularly where agency approval processes do not yet align with the newer Significant Change Notification approach.

The current timeline for CSP adoption, including the December 7 implementation date and the subsequent 90-day grace period, appears to assume that agencies will broadly accept the SCN process for VDR-related system changes. In practice, CSPs may still encounter agency-specific expectations that require use of the more traditional Significant Change Request process (we are seeing this with many agencies on other less significant changes). This creates a potential disconnect between FedRAMP's intended modernization path and how implementation may actually occur across different agency authorization environments.

There are three areas where additional PMO guidance or engagement could materially reduce implementation risk.

### 1. Agency Alignment on SCN Usage

FedRAMP's updated approach to significant changes provides an important opportunity to move from pre-approval-heavy processes toward more continuous, notification-based governance. However, some Agency Authorizing Officials and security teams may continue to require SCRs for changes that CSPs believe are appropriate for SCN handling.

For CSPs working with agencies that take a more conservative approach, the challenge is not unwillingness to comply with VDR expectations. Rather, it is that agency-specific change management expectations may materially extend implementation timelines.

Additional PMO clarification on when VDR-related changes should be handled through SCN, and perhaps even direct engagement with agencies to encourage consistent adoption of that approach, would be very helpful.

### 2. 3PAO Capacity and Cost Considerations

If VDR-related changes are treated as SCRs by many agencies, CSPs may be required to obtain additional 3PAO assessment support. This could create two practical challenges.

First, the cost of additional 3PAO assessment activity can be significant, especially for small and mid-sized SaaS providers that may not have budgeted for a major assessment cycle on this timeline.

Second, the 3PAO ecosystem has finite capacity. If a large number of CSPs are simultaneously directed into SCR-driven assessment activities, there is a real possibility of scheduling backlogs that could delay implementation even for CSPs acting in good faith.

This does not reduce the importance of the VDR requirement, but it does suggest that the success of the rollout may depend on ensuring that the change process is scaled appropriately.

### 3. Avoiding Unintended Marketplace Impact

A rigid enforcement posture, without accounting for agency-level process dependencies or 3PAO capacity constraints, could have unintended consequences for the FedRAMP marketplace.

Some specialized or smaller CSPs may face delays that are outside their direct control. Larger providers may also view repeated high-friction compliance changes as a factor in evaluating the cost and predictability of continued participation in the FedRAMP ecosystem.

The concern is not that enforcement should be weakened. Rather, enforcement should distinguish between CSPs that are not engaging and CSPs that are actively implementing VDR but are delayed by agency process requirements, assessment scheduling, or other documented dependencies.

### Suggested PMO Actions

To support successful adoption while preserving the security intent of the VDR framework, I would respectfully suggest the following:

1. **Provide additional agency-facing guidance on SCN applicability.**
   Clarify that VDR-related implementation changes should generally be handled through SCN where the nature of the change supports that path, unless there is a specific risk-based reason to require an SCR.

2. **Engage directly with Agency AOs and security teams.**
   Help ensure agencies are aligned with FedRAMP's modernization goals and are not unintentionally creating implementation barriers through inconsistent change management expectations.

3. **Establish a conditional safe harbor for good-faith implementation.**
   Consider allowing CSPs that have documented implementation plans, active milestones, and evidence of progress to remain in good standing where delays are caused by agency-directed SCR requirements, 3PAO scheduling constraints, or similar dependencies.

4. **Clarify enforcement expectations.**
   Distinguish between CSPs that are not taking action and CSPs that are actively working toward compliance but require additional time due to factors outside their direct control.

5. **Consider phased enforcement where appropriate.**
   A phased or risk-based enforcement model could help preserve the urgency of VDR adoption while avoiding unnecessary disruption to agencies and the CSP marketplace.

Overall, I fully support the goal of improving vulnerability detection and response across FedRAMP-authorized systems. My concern is that the implementation path needs to account for how agency change management and 3PAO assessment capacity work in practice. With additional PMO guidance and agency alignment, FedRAMP can maintain the urgency of the VDR transition while reducing the risk of avoidable delays, unnecessary costs, or unintended marketplace disruption.

pete-gov [FEDRAMP-OFFICIAL]: Hi Matt,

Every single agency is required by law, under the Binding Operational Directive issued by CISA in BOD 26-04, to ensure all federal information systems transition to a risk-based approach by December 7, 2026. The entire federal government is beginning a mad scramble to implement. Cloud service providers should expect maximum support from agency authorizing officials and their representatives to take all appropriate actions to support significant changes presented by cloud services and approve them in a timely manner **because all agencies are required to meet the same deadline.** This isn't a whimsical CSP thing, it's the Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security agency telling all agencies that there is an absolutely urgent need for all federal information to be protected differently. 

I guarantee that agency authorizing officials will start placing immense pressure on CSPs as a result of this BOD and FedRAMP is working as designed to standardize this and encourage implementation across all FedRAMP Certified CSPs in a predictable way without per-agency expectations and timelines.

FedRAMP has already indicated that we will provide a 3 month grace period before revoking FedRAMP Certification but CISA has not provided any agency with such a grace period. Cloud service providers who do not implement by December 7, 2026 will answer to their agency customers because the agency will be out of compliance with BOD 26-04 by continuing to use their cloud service.

I would expect these to be the most in-demand fastest SCR approvals in the history of pretty much any such request, given the environment, deadlines from CISA, and expectations. Start moving.
