For example, would FedRAMP engage directly with each CSP, or would verification follow a process similar to quarterly testing, using submitted evidence and/or agency reporting?

It would also be helpful to understand how FedRAMP is thinking about supporting agencies that may still be establishing the processes needed to receive, process, and evaluate VDR data. Will FedRAMP provide interim guidance, a phased approach, or other implementation support as agencies build those capabilities?

Finally, how will FedRAMP evaluate a CSP's progress toward implementation? If a CSP has a documented action plan and is actively taking steps to implement the applicable CR26 requirements by the deadline, would that be sufficient to avoid a corrective action plan, or is full implementation expected by December 7/March 7th? 

pete-gov [FEDRAMP-OFFICIAL]: > As we work to understand the implementation expectations and plan accordingly, could FedRAMP provide additional context on how it intends to verify that CSPs have implemented VDR by the December 7 deadline?

We simply need to ask you and review your required vulnerability detection and response activity reports to confirm.

> It would also be helpful to understand how FedRAMP is thinking about supporting agencies that may still be establishing the processes needed to receive, process, and evaluate VDR data. 

You should work with your agency customers to supply information in a way that optimizes their experience. The default requirements in the VER are not very different from historical information that cloud service providers were expected to share. Agencies generally manually review spreadsheets and summaries, and they will be able to continue to do this if they do not have tools, expertise, or interest in reviewing more detailed information. 

Remember that agencies are also simultaneously rebuilding all of their own internal processes and tooling to comply with BOD 26-04 and are figuring all of this out on the fly as well.

> Finally, how will FedRAMP evaluate a CSP's progress toward implementation? If a CSP has a documented action plan and is actively taking steps to implement the applicable CR26 requirements by the deadline, would that be sufficient to avoid a corrective action plan, or is full implementation expected by December 7/March 7th?

We are not planning on evaluating progress. Cloud service providers are capable of managing their own progress and don't need to report to us along the way. 

Yes, full implementation is expected by December 7. If full implementation is not completed on that date then the cloud service provider will be expected to supply a corrective action plan to complete the implementation by March 7. This process is explained on the [Rev5 Deadlines](https://www.fedramp.gov/2026/providers/updating/deadlines/rev5/) page.

Please remember that CISA BOD 26-04 requires every single agency to transition to this risk-based approach by December 7. On that date, agencies will need to report their status and the status of the cloud services they use. Historically, there may be a bit of flexibility in a CISA BOD deadline but we have seen circumstances where within a few months of such a deadline agencies have been forced to turn off services that do not comply. The grace period that FedRAMP provided is **only** for FedRAMP Certification itself, it is entirely possible that failure to comply with the VDR/VER will result in agencies turning off your service on that date and considering you in breach of contract (depending on how that's written).

We wrote VDR and VER in a way that would allow any mildly competent cloud service provider to rapidly switch over to it while gaining all of the benefits of the risk-based approach to vulnerability management, at a potential negative cost of needing to massively accelerate response to extremely rare circumstances (like this week's php2shell) _which any secure cloud service was already doing._

MichaelLAllen: Thanks, Pete. That confirms the December 7 expectation. A few follow-ups to close the operational gaps:

Many Class C VDR timeframe rules are SHOULDs (for example, VDR-TFR-PVR and VDR-TFR-PSD). For a Class C CSP, does “full implementation” mean meeting every SHOULD? Or does it mean meeting every MUST and documenting the rationale for any SHOULD deviation?

On December 8, does FedRAMP send a request to each CSP, or does the CSP submit its activity report on its own? If FedRAMP sends a request, what is the response window?

pete-gov [FEDRAMP-OFFICIAL]: > For a Class C CSP, does “full implementation” mean meeting every SHOULD? Or does it mean meeting every MUST and documenting the rationale for any SHOULD deviation?

A "full implementation" means all applicable rules are addressed - additional explanation of what this means is here: https://www.fedramp.gov/2026/providers/implement/rules/

_"Any time we say that a cloud service provider or agency must "address" a FedRAMP rule, we mean that you need to demonstrate you have read the rule, understood it, and implemented whatever is necessary within the context of the Consolidated Rules to follow the rule and explain how you are following it (or to document a decision not to follow it and your reasoning)."_

Remember, this is for meeting FedRAMP Certification requirements. You may have agency contracts that say you have to implement other things, and may have agency customers that expect you to implement some of the SHOULD rules in various ways for various reasons. 

> On December 8, does FedRAMP send a request to each CSP, or does the CSP submit its activity report on its own? 

You will submit your activity report on cadence that month with your continuous monitoring, the same way you submit any or all continuous monitoring information.

> If FedRAMP sends a request, what is the response window?

The [Addressing FedRAMP Communication](https://www.fedramp.gov/2026/reference/addressing-fedramp-communication/) rules went into effect for all cloud service providers at the beginning of 2026 and the grace period for addressing these rules is over. These rules explain how FedRAMP will communicate with cloud service providers formally and what the default expectations for response times are.




MichaelLAllen: Thank you.

discussion_title: Rev5 questions and discussion on the Consolidated Rules for 2026 (or Legacy)
author: MAHavens
text:
Re: Rev5 questions and discussion on the Consolidated Rules for 2026 (or Legacy)

MAHavens: VER-EVA-EFP requires that false positives are identified but does not state a specific way that they should be reported.  Neither VER-RPT-VDT nor VER-RPT-AVI include a section for false positive reporting.  Is it up to each CSP to decide how they want to report false positives (with input from agency customers)?  Does FedRAMP want to see false positives reported as N0 vulnerabilities?  While this is an option, not all N0 vulnerabilities will be false positives, so using this label without further clarification seems like it could introduce confusion.  

I apologize if this has been addressed elsewhere.  I looked around for a while before posting.  

pete-gov [FEDRAMP-OFFICIAL]: The theory with false positive vulnerabilities is that since they're still there and they show up and will presumably always keep showing up, then you'd almost certainly want to track them and persistently evaluate them if there's a change - today's false positive might be tomorrow's PAIN5 after all. That said, we are missing specific guidance on how to report these because we figured there are a few different ways that would make sense in context.

Both VER-RPT-PER and VDR-RPT-VDT would include false positive vulnerabilities by default since they aren't excluded. For VER-RPT-VDT you might simply decide that a number of reporting fields are not applicable if something is a false positive, but it would likely include at least the identifier, detection time/source, and time of evaluation if the vulnerability was first detected and evaluated as a false positive. In the current list of required information for VER-RPT-VDT you could add in item 10 (supplementary information) that it's a false positive, without needing to add it somewhere else. (you're right that there isn't specific instructions here, but there are plenty of ways to approach it)

You can also leverage VER-EVA-GRV (Group Vulnerabilities) to simplify tracking/monitoring/reporting of false positives in a lot of different ways - you could even just have a big False Positives group if you wanted. 

>  Does FedRAMP want to see false positives reported as N0 vulnerabilities?

Not mandatory, but evaluating to N0 would be a reasonable automatic outcome of evaluating to false positive. Agreed that you still also want to flag this as a false positive.

Hope this helps, feel free to follow up with any additional questions!

-Pete @ FedRAMP


MAHavens: We agree that tracking false positives is important.  We will find an option that works best for us and make sure that false positives are clearly identified in our reporting.  Thanks for the quick response.

discussion_title: Rev5 questions and discussion on the Consolidated Rules for 2026 (or Legacy)
author: mpg-CF
text:
Re: Rev5 questions and discussion on the Consolidated Rules for 2026 (or Legacy)

mpg-CF: Hey @pete-gov, 

I believe this was mentioned on a community update discussion but I'd like to confirm. There seems to be some confusion about when an annual assessment needs to start producing CR26 package materials (CPO, SDR, OCR) instead of a legacy Rev5 package (SAP, RET, SAR). Is it expected that all FedRAMP Annual Assessments that kickoff in 2027 should be against all CSP applicable CR26 requirements (all rules and controls/KSIs)? Is there a switch over date when the PMO will no longer accept Legacy FedRAMP Rev5 packages (SAP, RET, SAR etc) and the CSP can ensure their packages are what the PMO is expecting to maintain their certification(s)? 

If this is spelled out in the CR26 material, please let me know. I haven't found it.   

pete-gov [FEDRAMP-OFFICIAL]:  > I believe this was mentioned on a community update discussion but I'd like to confirm. There seems to be some confusion about when an annual assessment needs to start producing CR26 package materials (CPO, SDR, OCR) instead of a legacy Rev5 package (SAP, RET, SAR). Is it expected that all FedRAMP Annual Assessments that kickoff in 2027 should be against all CR26 requirements (all rules and controls/KSIs)? Is there a switch over date when the PMO will no longer accept Legacy FedRAMP Rev5 packages (SAP, RET, SAR etc) and the CSP can ensure their packages are what the PMO is expecting to maintain their certification(s)?
>
> If this is spelled out in the CR26 material, please let me know. I haven't found it.

Each ruleset has Maintaining Ongoing Certification and Grace Period Ends dates (previously "Maintain" and "Grace Ends"). These are all summarized and explained here for Rev5: https://www.fedramp.gov/2026/providers/updating/deadlines/rev5/

They land in a few different ways at a few different times because we expected some folks to invest in them differently. Some of them have explicit maintain dates and grace period end dates that are mandatory regardless of the FedRAMP independent assessment timing - cloud service providers will be expected to make significant changes to implement those. That includes the CCM rules for the OCR, which will be mandatory for everyone on April 2, 2027.

So if you start an assessment on July 31, 2027:

- Grace period has ended for AFC, SCG, MKT, VDR, VER, CMU, IEC, and SCN
- Grace period extends through the FedRAMP independent assessment (so it has to be implemented and included in it) for FRC, IVV, MAS, and CPO
- You can still hold off a bit longer before implementing CCM, CDS, and SDR. 

Those details shift a bit as the date shifts throughout the year. 

By the end of 2027 everything will be switched over for everyone no matter what except for CDS. 

(edit: removed incorrect statement confusing 2027-07-01 with 2027-01-01 for CPO)



pete-gov [FEDRAMP-OFFICIAL]: And adding:

Ideally, if at all possible, cloud service providers are heavily incentivized to simply adopt all of these CR26 rules in advance of their next FedRAMP independent assessment so they don't have to deal with all these grace periods. Any cloud service provider capable of doing so will benefit from doing so. I am aware that there are more than a few cloud service providers planning to do a full CR26 cutover at an upcoming assessment like this because so many of the new rules are written and designed in response to feedback from them about problems with the legacy process so they want to switch over in one big fell swoop.

mpg-CF: Hey @pete-gov, 
I appreciate the quick turnaround. 
One thing I want to flag first. You mentioned "The first assessment starting after 2027-01-01 needs to match CPO, full stop.", but the CR26 Rev5 deadlines page shows CPO's maintain date as 2027-07-01 with a grace period ending on the first assessment started after 2027-07-01. Can you confirm which is correct?

I do understand the maintain and grace period dates. However, by what you stated, if a CSP is starting an annual assessment in early 2027 and completing it in May, they do not need to have a SDR, CPO, or CDS in place since those rulesets have not yet met their maintain dates. With that being said:

1. If these rulesets are not yet required in the above scenario, how can a CSP create a partial CR26 Certification Package without them (especially CPO and SDR)? I agree the cleanest path is to do a full scope, but is there a door for a partial package without key rulesets?

2. I see you hint that a CSP could supplement a SDR with a SSP (unless I misunderstood your comment) and that "You can still hold off a bit longer before implementing CCM, CDS, and SDR" in your scenario. Due to CR26 rules being interconnected, removing one from the package (like CPO and SDR) leads to many more questions and creates a cascading effect on other rulesets. _With no SDR then how is IVV met without verification and validation statements from both the IA and CSP? Where is IVV documented? What does the PMO review without SDR? Will the PMO allow discretion to the CSP with what supplementation looks like in the interim for all rulesets that have not yet hit their maintain dates?_ I hope you see where I am going and the source of confusion here. 


Again, I completely agree that **the cleanest path is doing a full CR26 assessment** but there are providers who just want to know, 1) when is the last date I can submit a Legacy Rev5 package (SAP SAR etc), 2) what do I need to do in 2027 if my annual ends before a maintain date for a ruleset (aka I can just "skip" it since it says its not "required"), 3) when do I need to do my first full CR26 Rev5 certification package? I'd like to think it is one or the other until a certain date (Legacy Rev5 vs CR26 Rev5). After that, it is full CR26 then on and not partial frankenstein packages.

pete-gov [FEDRAMP-OFFICIAL]: > One thing I want to flag first. You mentioned "The first assessment starting after 2027-01-01 needs to match CPO, full stop.", but the CR26 Rev5 deadlines page shows CPO's maintain date as 2027-07-01 with a grace period ending on the first assessment started after 2027-07-01. Can you confirm which is correct?

Honestly we probably should've just set deadlines different than 07-01 - myself and many other folks struggle seeing the difference between 01-01 and 07-01. This was an especially egregious mistake considering I had originally messed up and put all of the +6mo grace periods for 01-01 maintain deadlines at 01-01 instead of 07-01 and it took many weeks for anyone to notice.

The deadlines in each ruleset are accurate. Always follow the rules as the source of truth, not something said elsewhere. :) I will edit my previous response to remove the incorrect dates.

> If these rulesets are not yet required in the above scenario, how can a CSP create a partial CR26 Certification Package without them (especially CPO and SDR)? I agree the cleanest path is to do a full scope, but is there a door for a partial package without key rulesets?

Yes, the expectation is that the cloud service provider finds a simple way to navigate this in a customer-experienced focused way. There is a bit of over-fixation on templates in the historical approach to FedRAMP, but we have deliberately moved away from that in the modern era. Providers are welcome to provide supplemental information about addressing FedRAMP Practices within the context of a legacy package or by simply producing standalone supplemental materials.

For example, VDR/VER does not have templates with how to report that information and there is no place for it in the traditional package, but that doesn't mean a provider can't easily figure out effective ways to share that information even if they haven't adopted the Certification Data Sharing rules.

> With no SDR then how is IVV met without verification and validation statements from both the IA and CSP? Where is IVV documented? Will the PMO allow discretion to the CSP with what supplementation looks like in the interim for all rulesets that have not yet hit their maintain dates? I hope you see where I am going and the source of confusion here.

Yes, this is intentional: [It's Not a Trap!](https://www.fedramp.gov/2026/rules/#its-not-a-trap)

This doesn't seem complicated to us. You can provide separate documents, add **Verification:** statements to the SSP control text, etc. You can progressively manage something like this with a machine-system and store it in a database/JSON/etc. while still manually doing the SSP in Word. 

>  I'd like to think it is one or the other until a certain date (Legacy Rev5 vs CR26 Rev5). After that, it is full CR26 then on and not partial frankenstein packages.

Oh no, we're definitely expecting frankenstein packages. We expect a lot of different approaches, some awesome, some incredibly poorly thought through. It's fine, it's all temporary. Our direction has been to prioritize incremental adoption among industry and government instead of setting an arbitrary cut-over date years in the future and to accept the risk of that mid-transition churn to prioritize earlier adoption of key bits. It needs to be clear that cloud service providers and assessors can't simply put everything off.

mpg-CF: This is great, @pete-gov. Thank you for explaining. 
Just to recap, starting in 2027, CSPs should start creating CR26 packages. For those rulesets that are not yet complete, CSPs can create supplemental items that take the place of those rulesets (SDR, CPO, CDS) but don't necessarily follow all the rules/requirements from those rulesets (since they arent due yet). However, any due rulesets need to be followed and displayed in some form or another (IVV). It is highly recommended that a CSP goes ahead and starts creating a full scope package rather than waiting and spinning wheels on temporary outputs (SSP + V&V) but that is an available route. At the end of it, FedRAMP Packages starting in 2027 should follow CR26 rules/requirements as best they can. 

By frankenstein packages, I mean where CSP decides to pick and choose what CR26 requirements to follow, what Legacy FedRAMP Rev5 requirements/rules/guidance to follow (severity ratings, e,i,t statements, SAP/SAR etc.) and what to ignore from both. Therefore creating a package that doesnt fully follow either. 

Thanks again, Pete.

discussion_title: Rev5 questions and discussion on the Consolidated Rules for 2026 (or Legacy)
author: shon-d-dingman
text:
Re: Rev5 questions and discussion on the Consolidated Rules for 2026 (or Legacy)

shon-d-dingman: @pete-gov 

We’d like to confirm how providers should set up their approach to PAIN ratings.

We noticed that RFC-0031 defined the N-ratings by adverse effect on agency operations, and the final CR26 rules use service-level customer-effect definitions (minimal, narrow, disruptive, debilitating) instead. With that in mind, which approach does FedRAMP expect?

Agency-informed: Providers consult agency customers about how they use the service and how much they depend on it, and use that to calibrate PAIN ratings.
Service-based: Providers apply the customer-effect definitions directly, based on observable effects such as how many users lose access and how much federal customer data is affected. Each agency then judges what that means for its own operations.

If option 1 is acceptable, how should providers document agency input and keep it current as customers and their use of the service change?

Thanks!

nicole-gov [FEDRAMP-OFFICIAL]: FedRAMP always expects you to follow finalized rules, not what was proposed in the RFC. We use RFCs to solicit public comment about planned changes, but rules are never finalized until they're officially published in documentation (like CR26). 

In this case, the final rules changed from the RFC precisely because of questions like this. We don't expect you to know the details of how agencies are using your cloud service. We only expect you to know that agencies are using it. You need to provide your customer agencies timely information about vulnerabilities that may affect them and then it's up to the agencies to determine which compensating controls to implement after that. 

shon-d-dingman: Does the service-base approach mean that a vulnerability capable of causing a complete outage across multiple federal agency customers must receive PAIN-5, even when the service performs only non-mission-critical functions?

pete-gov [FEDRAMP-OFFICIAL]: > Does the service-base approach mean that a vulnerability capable of causing a complete outage across multiple federal agency customers must receive PAIN-5, even when the service performs only non-mission-critical functions?

Nope! We recommend checking into the [Using the Consolidated Rules](https://www.fedramp.gov/2026/rules/#definitions) section of the site to read about how we use defined terms to clarify stuff like this in the rules. In the human-readable version of the site, each rule links to all of the defined terms that it uses for quick reference.

There are a bunch of specifically defined terms used in [VER-EVA-EPA (Estimate Potential Agency Impact)](https://www.fedramp.gov/2026/reference/vulnerability-evaluation-and-reporting/#estimate-potential-agency-impact) that should address this question in the context of the rules:

- N5 specifically is " could be expected to have a **debilitating customer effect** on more than one agency that uses the cloud service offering."
- [Debilitating customer effect](https://www.fedramp.gov/2026/definitions/#debilitating-customer-effect) is defined as "An unwanted customer effect that interrupts use of the cloud service for most users or compromises the integrity or confidentiality of most federal customer data. If the adverse customer effect is unknown then it should be treated as if it is debilitating until proven otherwise."

If you know a service isn't performing mission-critical functions such that it isn't likely to affect most users / most customer data, then you would not evaluate it as a likely debilitating customer effect at PAIN5. More likely it would be something like a [narrow customer effect ](https://www.fedramp.gov/2026/definitions/#narrow-customer-effect)on one or more agencies that use the cloud service offering at PAIN2.

discussion_title: Rev5 questions and discussion on the Consolidated Rules for 2026 (or Legacy)
author: zeesharfcspab
text:
Re: Rev5 questions and discussion on the Consolidated Rules for 2026 (or Legacy)

zeesharfcspab: Hello FedRAMP PMO team, 

Hoping to get some clarification on who incident reports actually go to under the Incident Report rules (IEC-CSO-IIR / OIR / FIR). The rule statement and the notification requirement seem to point to two different, separately-defined groups:

Rule statement: notify all affected parties = "FedRAMP and directly impacted federal customer agencies."
Notification requirement: update all necessary parties via the Trust Center = "FedRAMP and any agency customer using the offering."
For an incident that affects only some agencies, which one governs distribution of the incident reports?

Our reading is that the affected parties receive the incident reports, while all necessary parties review certification-wide reporting like the quarterly OCR (which already summarizes incidents). Sharing full incident reports with all necessary parties would also seem to tension with CDS-CSO-RIS (don't share detail that would enable a threat actor). Could the PMO confirm which is intended?

pete-gov [FEDRAMP-OFFICIAL]: > Our reading is that the affected parties receive the incident reports, while all necessary parties review certification-wide reporting like the quarterly OCR (which already summarizes incidents). 

Ah, this is an oversight - this set of rules doesn't require require notification of `all necessary parties` so the notification requirement shouldn't have that in there either. I've created [FedRAMP/Rules#47](https://github.com/FedRAMP/rules/issues/47) to track fixing this. We will make the notification of `all necessary parties` _optional_ - it's still helpful to have incident information in the trust center but up to the business.

> Sharing full incident reports with all necessary parties would also seem to tension with CDS-CSO-RIS (don't share detail that would enable a threat actor). Could the PMO confirm which is intended?

We use the defined term [**responsibly**](https://www.fedramp.gov/2026/definitions/#responsibly) when directing notifications. An incident notification really really really should not enable a threat actor. Sanitize it as much as appropriate. In most cases it should be fine to post incident reports publicly, though there may be some obscure circumstances where even the knowledge of the existence of an incident could create a threat and in that case I'd say keep it close and share carefully with only affected parties, yup.



zeesharfcspab: Thank you for the quick response, greatly appreciated Pete!

discussion_title: Rev5 questions and discussion on the Consolidated Rules for 2026 (or Legacy)
author: hawksjennifer
text:
Re: Rev5 questions and discussion on the Consolidated Rules for 2026 (or Legacy)

hawksjennifer: For Ready Conversion applicants with a penetration test performed by an independent third party that is not a FedRAMP-recognized independent assessor, may the designated independent assessor conducting the Ready Conversion assessment review, validate, and incorporate those results into the CSP's initial certification assessment, or must the independent assessor independently execute another penetration test?

pete-gov [FEDRAMP-OFFICIAL]: > For Ready Conversion applicants with a penetration test performed by an independent third party that is not a FedRAMP-recognized independent assessor, may the designated independent assessor conducting the Ready Conversion assessment review, validate, and incorporate those results into the CSP's initial certification assessment, or must the independent assessor independently execute another penetration test?

FedRAMP does not _require_ a penetration test from a FR Recognized independent assessor under the Consolidated Rules for 2026. The results of your penetration test from another assessor can definitely be included in your Vulnerability Detection and Response activity reports et al. 

If you're planning on submitting under the legacy rules and then converting to CR26 by February, then we'll let you take a POA&M/finding on not having a FR Recognized penetration test and you can document what you did instead and why you don't think there's a significant resulting risk. Then once you switch over to CR26 it would go poof.

hawksjennifer: Thank you, Pete. This is exactly the kind of practical, risk-based approach we were hoping for, avoiding unnecessary costs to CSPs without compromising security outcomes. Appreciate the clarification and flexibility!

author: KHFedR
text:
Re: 20x questions and discussion on the Consolidated Rules for 2026

KHFedR: What is the preferred path for a provider who has some items on prem and some in AWS?  Rev 5 had the PE, MP, MA families to address those risks, but 20x is very much designed for cloud native products.  With the planned retirement of Rev 5, there doesn't seem to be a path for these services in FedRAMP or am I missing something? 

pete-gov [FEDRAMP-OFFICIAL]: At the moment 20x is for cloud native services built on a FR Certified IaaS/PaaS - Phase 4 will explore expanding this to include on prem and host services including Class D.

KHFedR: Does Level A allow for those services to enter the marketplace or will on prem/host services need to wait until Phase 4?

author: ElaineFR
text:
Re: 20x questions and discussion on the Consolidated Rules for 2026

ElaineFR: I know that @pete-gov is out getting some nature and motorcycle therapy right now, but would love some help with the following questions! :) 

1. It seems that ACM has nothing prescriptive that would include CIS benchmarks or DISA STIGs. I imagine that flexibility is allowed so that configuration standards can be set by the CSP, but I just wanted to run a sanity check on this. How are you seeing CSPs satisfy secure config for 20x? Moving forward will we see these items omitted from FR PMO but likely retained by agencies as an expectation? 
2. For the Class B/C submissions Aug 10 for companies that have achieved RAR/SAR and/or lost a sponsor, do you have a link that outlines the entire process and what the certification process will look like? 
3. For Rev. 5 conversions to 20x, do you have any documentation that you can share about the expected process steps for CSPs to align with 20x by Jan 2027? 

pete-gov [FEDRAMP-OFFICIAL]: > I know that @pete-gov is out getting some nature and motorcycle therapy right now, but would love some help with the following questions! :)

Surprise! I'm back! ;o

>  1. It seems that ACM has nothing prescriptive that would include CIS benchmarks or DISA STIGs. I imagine that flexibility is allowed so that configuration standards can be set by the CSP, but I just wanted to run a sanity check on this. How are you seeing CSPs satisfy secure config for 20x? Moving forward will we see these items omitted from FR PMO but likely retained by agencies as an expectation?

There are a thousand different ways to ensure secure configuration of OS images and neither CIS benchmarks or DISA STIGs are particularly applicable globally. Roll your own following best practices and/or using tools of your choice.

>  2. For the Class B/C submissions Aug 10 for companies that have achieved RAR/SAR and/or lost a sponsor, do you have a link that outlines the entire process and what the certification process will look like?

Information about this is on the [Choose a Path](https://www.fedramp.gov/2026/providers/start/path/#temporary-rev5-program-certification-availability-for-class-b-and-c) page here. The important part is that the provider must agree with follow all updated rules by February 19, 2027. 

>  3. For Rev. 5 conversions to 20x, do you have any documentation that you can share about the expected process steps for CSPs to align with 20x by Jan 2027?

discussion_title: 20x questions and discussion on the Consolidated Rules for 2026
author: TM-Microsoft
text:
Re: 20x questions and discussion on the Consolidated Rules for 2026

TM-Microsoft: Welcome back, Pete! Could you help us with a question?

If a ruleset's grace-end date falls before a CSP's Annual Assessment (AA) date, how does FedRAMP expect the CSP to demonstrate compliance?

For example, the VDR and VER rulesets have grace-end dates in March, but a CSP may have its AA scheduled for August. In that scenario, how is the CSP expected to show compliance with those rulesets in the gap between March and August?

paulagosta [FEDRAMP-OFFICIAL]: TM...  Sorry Pete is out at an event rubbing elbows with Agencies, 3PAOs, and CSPs....  So you get the third string kicker..

Based on your scenario, you are a Rev5 CSP transitioning to the ruleset...  Something important to call out as 20x processes and Rev5 are different in regards to timelines and reviews.

Transition to Rulesets do not require initial 3rd party validation it just requires you to follow the rules.  Yes, transition to some of the rulesets will change control statements that should be validated during your annual review.  Your VDR/VER example is great as it will affect your CA-5 controls, but you can transition to rulesets anytime before the required dates.

Some Rulesets require notification when transitioning.  For example, the CDS Ruleset, under CDS-CSF-TCM, requires you to "Notify FedRAMP via email: [info@fedramp.gov](mailto:info@fedramp.gov)," when you transition.  

Others, we will request your implementation status at various points through the FSI process.  The evidence of your transition for most of these will be prevalent in you trust center or repo.  The VDR/VER example you provide is an excellent example.  Your March ConMon in your scenario should contain VDR/VER requirements (POA&M should change to Monthly activity report with PAIN thresholds, new timelines, etc).  

When you do your annual assessment we will also ask about status of rulesets and implementation dates.  Your agencies should also be tracking your ruleset adoptions and should identify issues and deficiencies as well.

Hope that helps.

Paul

nicole-gov [FEDRAMP-OFFICIAL]: I'm also going to point out that adopting new FedRAMP rules that change your existing processes will almost certainly count as a Significant Change, so you should treat it as such, follow the Significant Change rules, and notify your customers accordingly.

ElaineFR: Hello! To prepare for our RAR conversion submission, I have a couple questions:

1. What kind of qualification evidence is expected for the eligibility form? For RAR conversion, would the FedRAMP Ready listing and a secure share of the RAR suffice? https://help.fedramp.gov/hc/en-us/requests/new?ticket_form_id=52069750514459

2. I imagine that for RAR conversion, our RAR evidence will be enough to get listed, but I am wondering what the timing expectation is for these other Getting Listed requirements, which will take some time to build out. 
https://www.fedramp.gov/2026/providers/implement/marketplace/

pete-gov [FEDRAMP-OFFICIAL]: Hey Elaine, a couple points:

(1) A conversion from FedRAMP Ready to a Rev5 Class B+ Program Certification requires completing all of the tasks to receive a Rev5 Class B+ Certification, including a full assessment with a SAP/SAR, full control implementation, etc. You can apply for this but will still have to do all of the work to prepare a full package for review, including a commitment to be aligned to all of the new CR26 rules for Rev5 by February 2027. The application for conversation is just that, an application to discuss next steps and make sure folks understand that you have to invest considerable effort.

(2) You can't convert to a Rev5 Program Certification until you meet _all_ of the requirements. 

Also, don't forget (3) You can't have a 20x Certification and a Rev5 Program Certification. You have to pick one.

ElaineFR: Got it @pete-gov! Thanks for the added clarity! 

ElaineFR: Pete - one more question. There is a space on the submission form for uploading files. Is the expectation that the SAR will be uploaded there? Is this a secure share mechanism? 

pete-gov [FEDRAMP-OFFICIAL]: No, we have your RAR if you're already FedRAMP Ready. It's for anything else relevant that you might want to attach and is kinda a generic part of the form - that form is just a form to start an application, it's not like The Thing that's a one-and-done ship then we make a determination and you find out. Don't overthink it! ;)

ElaineFR: Old FedRAMP trained me to overthink though! 😂 It's going to take some time to develop FR20x neurocircuitry. 

ElaineFR: @pete-gov, with the RAR/SAR/SAP path, we have our package completely built. We obtained fedramp equivalency, as well. I think it would be faster for us to initially adopt the Rev 5 approach and then move to 20x later. 

That said, does Rev 5 still require a sponsor to get listed? If so, we may need to rethink. 

Thanks for any insights! 🙏🏻 

pete-gov [FEDRAMP-OFFICIAL]: Rev5 always requires a sponsor except for temporary Program Certification options for Rev5 Class B and C that are available based on limited criteria [outlined in detail here](https://www.fedramp.gov/2026/providers/start/path/#temporary-rev5-program-certification-availability-for-class-b-and-c). In this case if you have very specific questions about a very specific set of circumstances it's fine to follow up with us directly, but it should be quite straightforward to know if you meet the criteria or not.

And again, as that page outlines, for FedRAMP to do a Program Certification without a sponsor for Rev5 the company will have to not only meet that criteria but also agree to be following all CR26 Rev rules by February 19, 2027 even if they submit a package before January 1, 2027. 
 

ElaineFR: @pete-gov, it looks like we are one month off, so we won't qualify for the readiness conversion. 

We have our SOC 2, so we are considering applying for the Class A initial listing. Do you have information on what that opens for us? How quickly can that move to a Class C? 

Right now we are Ready at Moderate/Class C in the marketplace, so it feels like a big step backwards to go to Class A. 

As always, thanks for any clarification! 🙏🏻 

nicole-gov [FEDRAMP-OFFICIAL]: The Class A submission window opened on 8/3. FedRAMP Class A is a real FedRAMP Certification, whereas FedRAMP Ready (at any level) is not. You can always note in your service description and/or your FedRAMP package additional efforts you have done. The rules for each class level are a minimum set of requirements - not a maximum. 

The 20x Class C submission window opens on 8/31, which is the only available program path if you don't qualify for ready conversion / lost sponsor. 

ElaineFR: @nicole-gov, thank you! With class A, what are the next steps? Can you build up to Class C quickly? Or is it better just to submit for Class C out of the gate? 

I'm thinking it is probably better to get in line sooner with Class A, but your opinion would be so great. 

ElaineFR: Hey @nicole-gov, I know you guys have more messages than ever now - just bumping this up. ☺️

nicole-gov [FEDRAMP-OFFICIAL]: We can't offer business advice, so it's really up to you. 

You can apply for Class B or C as soon as you want after a Class A certification once the relevant B/C pipelines are open or you can skip Class A and head directly for 20x Class B/C (or Rev5 Class B/C if you qualify for lost sponsor or ready conversion). 

ElaineFR: Totally understand that, just wondering specifically if there is a clear path to C if we start with A, and what that looks like. Is that defined yet or more a WIP? 

nicole-gov [FEDRAMP-OFFICIAL]: Yes, all certification paths from Class A through Class C are already defined in CR26. If you start with a Class A, you can submit for any available Class B or C path that you qualify for whenever you're ready. 

20x Class B and C opens on 8/31/26. 
Rev5 Class B and C are currently open, but require a sponsor. 
Program Rev5 Class B and C opens on 8/10/26, but requires qualifying through lost sponsor or ready conversion criteria. 

ElaineFR: Thank you Nicole! I'm excited to see where we end up landing. It's amazing how many choices there are - it feels like the open frontier. 😊 

dan-fedramp [FEDRAMP-OFFICIAL]: One more clarification.  The Secure Configuration Guide required under SCG-CSO-RSC is intended to instruct an agency customer how to configure your service. So unless you expect to have agency customers configuring the OS on your system components, the OS configuration does not need to be included in the Secure Configuration Guide.

discussion_title: 20x questions and discussion on the Consolidated Rules for 2026
author: aaronhbridges
text:
Re: 20x questions and discussion on the Consolidated Rules for 2026

aaronhbridges: Hi FedRAMP team — a question on the Scope of FedRAMP guidance (https://www.fedramp.gov/2026/scope/#information-providers, originally from RFC-0010). The out-of-scope "Online Learning Platforms" example lists Udemy, Coursera, Skillsoft, and similar platforms. OpenSesame is an online learning and training platform squarely in that same category.

Three questions:

- Is there a process for a provider to be reflected in that illustrative example list, or to otherwise have our service recognized as falling within the "training and online learning platforms" category?

- When an agency (or a reseller supporting an agency) wants documentation of a provider's out-of-scope status, is the published category sufficient on its own, or is anything expected from the provider or the PMO?

- Would a letter from our independent auditor — who is also a FedRAMP-recognized 3PAO — affirming that our service falls within the out-of-scope online learning platform category be a recognized or useful artifact for this purpose, or does scope determination rest solely with the agency?

We want to give agencies and partners what they need without implying an authorization requirement that doesn't apply. Thanks for the work on CR26.

— Aaron Bridges, CTO, OpenSesame

emu-gov [FEDRAMP-OFFICIAL]: Thanks for posting this here in the community as this is a great topic to dive into! 

Scope of FedRAMP really depends on how the service is being used. Any example services are to aid understanding and not to be used as any kind of exclusion list. Even those mentioned in the examples could in certain use cases be within scope. So while "it depends" might feel like a non-answer, this stuff is really circumstantial based on how the agency will be using your service. Different uses exist across different agencies and even within the same one!

A key test here is _general education and training_ . If the same content is being offered to the general public as it is the agency, then you are likely out of scope. If the agency is creating and publishing internal content to your platform for specific agency users and requires the collecting of federal information, you are probably in scope.

Best thing to do is to talk it out with the agency you are working with and you can absolutely reference our [Scope of FedRAMP](https://www.fedramp.gov/2026/scope/#scope-of-fedramp) page to help frame the discussion. We don't offer any kind of blanket out of scope hall pass or anything, but are always happy to help support agencies when they have questions.

author: AshPublicSector
text:
Re: 20x questions and discussion on the Consolidated Rules for 2026

AshPublicSector: Hi FedRAMP team-
Can a feature of a larger product be listed on the Marketplace on its own, or must the parent product be the CSO?

Context: If a capability is sold as a licensed feature inside a larger cloud service — enabled by a feature flag, running entirely on the parent product's infrastructure, not purchasable or operable on its own — can that capability be listed on the FedRAMP Marketplace and pursue a 20x Class A Certification as its own cloud service offering? Or is the expectation that the parent product is the listed offering, with the feature inside the Minimum Assessment Scope?

Follow-ups:

1. If the feature can't be listed on its own, does certifying the parent product cover the feature, assuming it falls within the identified resource set under MAS-CSO-IIR?
2. Would the answer change for a standalone product variant of the same capability?
3. 
Our reading of MAS-CSO-IIR (the identified resource set constitutes the offering) and CDS-CSO-PSM (providers determine what constitutes separate services) suggests there's flexibility - but since the feature depends entirely on the parent's infrastructure, its boundary would pull in the parent's components anyway, making the parent the natural listing. Is that right?

emu-gov [FEDRAMP-OFFICIAL]: Sorry we have not responded yet, this is a good question that requires a thoughtful and nuanced response. We will discuss internally and get back to ya!

emu-gov [FEDRAMP-OFFICIAL]: > not purchasable or operable on its own

Being unable to purchase the service as an individual product without the parent would make it ineligible for it's own listing. It also feels a bit on the sneaky side.

When you certify the parent product, you have the flexibility to add services under that listing, which are services from a marketing feature perspective, not a technical perspective. So as long as any relevant components that feature relies upon are included in the minimum assessment scope, you are OK.

In the other possible scenario that it becomes a product purchasable on its own, but is still heavily dependent on the parent product, you could list and reference the parent as a resource under `MAS-CSO-IIR`  BUT this really stretches the spirit of the rules pretty thin because that parent product would likely have a very high impact to the CIA of federal information processed by the service without being FR certified. This could be severely limiting and have unintended consequences when agencies try to decipher your package, see some trickery and nope out.

pete-gov [FEDRAMP-OFFICIAL]: To emphasize this response with some specific scenarios:

If a company develops a standalone product that has its own team, assurance support, FedRAMP Certification Package, etc. then it's a separate cloud service offering with its own Marketplace listing - even if it is hosted or run on a PaaS/IaaS provided by that company.

All FR requirements must be met to maintain a Marketplace listing, and something like a feature or capability where there isn't a standalone package, continuous monitoring, sales pipeline, etc. is obviously part of the parent cloud service offering and listed as a service within that parent Marketplace listing.

emu-gov [FEDRAMP-OFFICIAL]: Initial Certification means when we originally review your Certification package materials. If you have a Class A and submit for a Class C, our Class C review is still the *"initial certification"*.

Also, as we are doing our Class A Certification reviews, we put a section on your Certification report specifically for any feedback we have for ascending to a Class B or C. discussion_title: 20x questions and discussion on the Consolidated Rules for 2026
author: cclements05
text:
Re: 20x questions and discussion on the Consolidated Rules for 2026

cclements05: Is a CSP required to have a Trust Center to get listed on the Marketplace in the Initial Implementation Phase?

CDS-CSO-PUB and MKT-IIP-DCP make reference to Trust Centers, however, do not seem to specifically require a Trust Center (as machine-readable information via public webpage is an option). However, the CSP Getting Listing narrative (https://www.fedramp.gov/2026/providers/implement/marketplace/) states: "You will need a basic FedRAMP-compatible Trust Center" and 20x CWG meetings have discussed CSPs not needing "a full Trust Center", insinuating some level of a Trust Center is required for the Initial Implementation Phase.

pete-gov [FEDRAMP-OFFICIAL]: You've hit on a small narrative issue but the key thing is that the explicit rules are followed, not the narrative. The rules require you to make information available publicly and a "basic FedRAMP-compatible Trust Center" is explained as a way to do that in the narrative, but there is no rule that applies FedRAMP-compatible Trust Center requirements here.

Per the rules:

1. MKT-CSO-MLR (Marketplace Listing Requirements) applies, linking to CDS-CSO-PUB (Public Information) which says that the public information that is available must be publicly shared in a human-readable and JSON format and lists the expected information. For Initial Implementation, much of that information will not be "available" or "applicable."

2. MKT-CSO-PML (Provider Marketplace Listing Requests) applies, requiring the form to be used.

3. MKT-IIP-AGU (Agency Use Cases), MKT-IIP-DCP (Demonstrating Continuous Progress), and MKT-IIP-DLA (Deadline for Assessment) apply for Initial Implementation phase, and must be available in some fashion.
 
So basically if you have a FedRAMP landing page that publishes all of that information publicly we would consider that to be "a basic FedRAMP-compatible Trust Center."

text:
Re: 20x questions and discussion on the Consolidated Rules for 2026

jbrenton-fits: I'm looking for clarification on how to apply the scope criteria for FedRAMP 20x in cases where locally installed software handles Federal data and is essential for the CSO to function, but operational control resides entirely with the agency.

Based on MAS-CSO-IIR, it appears that such software may be in scope if it handles Federal data or could impact its CIA. Additionally, the Scope of FedRAMP website includes an example where a locally installed agent that handles Federal data is considered within the FedRAMP assessment scope:
https://www.fedramp.gov/2026/scope/#detailed-examples1

However, both the Scope of FedRAMP site and notes within MAS-CSO-IIR also state that FedRAMP is focused on cloud products, and that locally installed software is generally out of scope unless it is operated as part of a shared responsibility model.

In this case, which factor takes precedence for scoping purposes: 
that the locally installed software handles and could impact Federal data, or the fact that the software is fully managed by the agency?

pete-gov [FEDRAMP-OFFICIAL]: > I'm looking for clarification on how to apply the scope criteria for FedRAMP 20x in cases where locally installed software handles Federal data and is essential for the CSO to function, but operational control resides entirely with the agency.

The answer - as you've seen - is that the nuance depends on the implementation. For FedRAMP and the Minimum Assessment Scope, the scoping occurs within the data boundary of the cloud service. If you have command and control from the cloud service, or accept telemetry from devices, or have some other form of control over the deployed software (such as updated) then all of that aspect of the cloud service is in scope for FedRAMP.

The actual software itself, the process of deploying and operating it within an agency enclave or device, the risk and analysis of it, etc. is outside scope for FedRAMP. 

[MAS-CSO-SUP (Supplemental Information)](https://www.fedramp.gov/2026/reference/minimum-assessment-scope/#supplemental-information) allows you to include information like this in your FedRAMP Certification Package for easy distribution, but FedRAMP will not assess the security of something that isn't a cloud computing product or service within the scope of FedRAMP and FedRAMP's rules do not extend to locally deployed software that is placed inside an agency boundary.

Does that help or just have more questions? If there's a specific architecture scenario we can help walk through it.

jbrenton-fits: Thank you very much. I think I'm following.
		
For locally installed software, different aspects may be considered in or outside the FedRAMP scope depending on the level of control the CSO exercises over the software. 
		
So, in cases where the local software can be controlled to some extent from the CSO, the control the CSO exercises over the local software is within the FedRAMP scope. This would mean that KSIs and rules applicable to the actions the CSO can take on the local software must be addressed, but other aspects of the software fully managed by the agency would remain outside the FedRAMP scope.

pete-gov [FEDRAMP-OFFICIAL]: Yes, exactly right!

discussion_title: 20x questions and discussion on the Consolidated Rules for 2026
author: dfulleradsk
text:
Re: 20x questions and discussion on the Consolidated Rules for 2026

dfulleradsk: Following the recent introduction of N0 to the PAIN ratings, I have a question about how N0 interacts with Accepted Vulnerability classification.  If a vulnerability remains detectable but has been fully mitigated such that its likely agency impact is N0, does VER-TFR-MAV still require it to be categorized as an Accepted Vulnerability after 192 days, or does full mitigation satisfy the requirement regardless of continued detection?

pete-gov [FEDRAMP-OFFICIAL]: There does not have to be any interaction between N0 and Accepted Vulnerabilities. A cloud service provider may choose to accept the risk of a PAIN5 vulnerability. 

> If a vulnerability remains detectable but has been fully mitigated such that its likely agency impact is N0, does VER-TFR-MAV still require it to be categorized as an Accepted Vulnerability after 192 days, or does full mitigation satisfy the requirement regardless of continued detection?

Vulnerabilities should live on as a tracked vulnerability until they are remediated. Even a fully mitigated vulnerability that has been accepted needs to be tracked in case there's a future circumstance where it comes into play.

Remember that fully mitigated means it's still there, you can still see it. Remediated means it's gone. Remediation is the only true end state for tracking a vulnerability.

discussion_title: 20x questions and discussion on the Consolidated Rules for 2026
author: shanacronin-grc
text:
Re: 20x questions and discussion on the Consolidated Rules for 2026

shanacronin-grc: We’re preparing a FedRAMP 20x Class C certification for a multi-tenant SaaS platform that lets customers use our tools with data and workloads appropriate to the assessed scope and applicable agency requirements. Class C is our initial step. We plan to pursue Class D or IL4 later, and we’d like the Class C work to be a reusable foundation for that. Since Class D isn’t available in this window, agencies would initially be responsible for securing and authorizing any data storage in their own solutions.

Three scoping questions:

We have a documented SaaS use case but no named agency customer or live federal workload yet. Does that support an initial Marketplace listing under MKT-IIP-AGU, and how should we define the initial assessment scope before an agency customer exists?

Under MAS-CSO-IIR, if agency data stays in agency-managed storage and the platform only processes it in transit, how should we treat that data and the resources that handle it when defining the offering?

If a storage service is added once a Class D path opens, would it be added to the existing certification or assessed separately?

pete-gov [FEDRAMP-OFFICIAL]: Hi! I do want to be clear that the specifics might vary from situation to situation and it's usually a good idea to have an advisory service with some experience to help navigate stuff - but overall if you're intentional and stay up with the rules there shouldn't be any surprises.

Remember... [it's not a trap!](https://www.fedramp.gov/2026/rules/#its-not-a-trap)

> We have a documented SaaS use case but no named agency customer or live federal workload yet. Does that support an initial Marketplace listing under MKT-IIP-AGU...

If you intend for the offering to be used by agencies then you're fine.

> and how should we define the initial assessment scope before an agency customer exists?

Scope it to whatever parts of the offering you expect to make available to agencies that are likely to handle or affect confidentiality, integrity, or availability of federal customer data when they onboard.

> Under MAS-CSO-IIR, if agency data stays in agency-managed storage and the platform only processes it in transit, how should we treat that data and the resources that handle it when defining the offering?

FR can't provide advice and would need to deep dive on your architecture in any case to understand what you're asking here, but the rubric is simple - everything handling it is in play. Everything related that would likely affect CIA of it is in play.

> If a storage service is added once a Class D path opens, would it be added to the existing certification or assessed separately?

This is up to you and would depend on the business case and goals. You can add it to an existing certified assessment scope as a significant change or you could get a separate certified offering if it's a different product. 🤷 

Hope this helps!

discussion_title: Machine-verifiable evidence for human-approval decisions, an open format offered for the KSI process
author: FutureEnterprises
text:
Machine-verifiable evidence for human-approval decisions, an open format offered for the KSI process

I run EMILIA Protocol, a small open project (Apache 2.0) that works on one narrow piece of the evidence problem: proving a named human approved a specific consequential action, in a form a third party can verify by machine.

I have read a lot of compliance modernization plans. 20x is the first one that treats evidence as something to verify rather than something to file, and the Automatic Validation principle is the part I keep coming back to.

It also exposes a hard case. Any indicator that turns on a human decision (change approval, access grants, break-glass, production deployments) is usually evidenced by a ticket screenshot or a log line the provider maintains. So the validation pipeline ends up trusting the provider's own records for the one control class where those records are the thing in question.

The format we build closes that gap. The approver signs the exact action (Ed25519 over RFC 8785 canonical JSON), the receipt binds the named approver to that action's digest, and anyone can verify it offline with a CLI against keys the relying party pins. No call back to us, and no vendor in the trust path. Our standard demo walks a two-person approval on a high-value disbursement, then jumps six months ahead to an audit where the issuing service no longer exists, and the auditor still verifies the authorization from a single file while a forged copy is refused with a stated reason. Honestly, the offline audit moment is pretty cool to watch.

The pieces are public. The specification is posted as individual Internet-Drafts at the IETF (draft-schrock-ep-authorization-receipts, an individual submission, not an adopted standard). The verifier and an 18-suite conformance corpus are in the open repo, and everything is Apache 2.0, so an agency or assessor can adopt it, fork it, or replace it without touching us.

My question for the working group: as Phase 3 formalizes requirements, does human-approval evidence belong inside KSI validation, or is that class of evidence out of scope for 20x as designed? If it belongs, I would like to contribute the format into the open process, and I am glad to bring the runnable demo to a community call. You all see the whole assessment picture in a way I do not.

Iman Schrock, EMILIA Protocol
emiliaprotocol.ai | github.com/emiliaprotocol/emilia-protocol

discussion_title: Data-quality findings from a full-coverage conversion of the CR26 consolidated rules (v2026.07.14.01)
author: christoph-puppe
text:
Data-quality findings from a full-coverage conversion of the CR26 consolidated rules (v2026.07.14.01)

Hi all 

sharing findings from an experiment I ran in personal capacity. I wrote a converter that maps the complete consolidated rules JSON into an experimental semantic model, with a computed coverage report: every source field path inventoried, every path assigned a declared destination. Result: 7,294 leaf values, 100 % declared coverage, zero unexplained fields. The process surfaced a few things that may be useful to the FedRAMP data team:

1. **Nine undeclared subsets.** `CSX` (in `20x` data blocks) and `CSF` (in `rev5` data blocks) appear under `FRR.*.data.*` for CDS, CPO, FRC, IVV and SDR, but are not declared in the corresponding `info.subsets`. Tooling that builds applicability scopes from `info.subsets` will silently miss these rules.
2. **Layered rule counts.** The corpus contains 246 rules = 225 track-independent (`data.all`) + 12 rev5-only + 9 20x-only. Worth documenting, since naive parsers that read only `data.all` will report 225.
3. **29 variant-only rules** exist solely inside `varies_by_class` with no base `statement`/`force` — consumers need a defined interpretation for the base case.
4. **Consistency compliment:** across all 111 class-variant `force` changes, there is not a single easing — every published class delta tightens or specifies. That's a remarkably clean dataset property.
5. **FRD quality:** all 264 term references from rules and KSIs resolve against the FRD via term + `alts` matching — the alias lists demonstrably earn their keep. The 51 variant timeframes without a base timeframe and the 79 CTL overlay entries are documented in the report as well.
6. The 373 KSI→800-53 control links import cleanly as typed, provenance-carrying mapping objects.

The converter script and the full coverage report (JSON: every path → destination, with counts) are available. The wider experiment — a semantic-core architecture hypothesis derived from measuring three national corpora (ISM, BSI IT-Grundschutz++, CR26), with a handbook and worked examples packaged as an AI skill — is here: [Semantic OSCAL Ideas](https://github.com/christoph-puppe/Semantic-OSCAL-2-Ideas). Criticism of the architecture itself is explicitly welcome; happy to file any of the data findings above as separate issues if useful.

A summary can be found on [LinkedIn](https://www.linkedin.com/posts/christophpuppe_oscal-complianceascode-itgrundschutz-ugcPost-7484537947745226754-RTbA/)

— Christoph Puppe (personal capacity)

discussion_title: Data-quality findings from a full-coverage conversion of the CR26 consolidated rules (v2026.07.14.01)
author: pete-gov
text:
Re: Data-quality findings from a full-coverage conversion of the CR26 consolidated rules (v2026.07.14.01)

pete-gov [FEDRAMP-OFFICIAL]: > 1. **Nine undeclared subsets.** `CSX` (in `20x` data blocks) and `CSF` (in `rev5` data blocks) appear under `FRR.*.data.*` for CDS, CPO, FRC, IVV and SDR, but are not declared in the corresponding `info.subsets`. Tooling that builds applicability scopes from `info.subsets` will silently miss these rules.

For this one I'm hoping it's a structural misunderstanding - subsets are declared in `info.subsets` if they apply to both Rev5 and 20x. If a subset applies only to one of those, then it is declared in `info.20x.subsets` or `info.rev5.subsets` instead.

For example, `CSF` is a Rev5-only subset so it is declared in `info.rev5.subsets`. `CSX` is a 20x-only subset so it is declared in `info.20x.subsets`.

> 3. 29 variant-only rules exist solely inside varies_by_class ...

Yep, this is explicit in the schema, there either needs to be a `statement`/etc. OR there needs to be a `varies_by_class` with the `statement`/etc.

Similar to the structure for (1) above - things apply globally by default, but in some cases there are specific applications and those are then defined on their own.

Cheers!

christoph-puppe: Thanks @pete-gov — confirmed, structural misunderstanding on my side, and **finding 1 is withdrawn.**

My check only looked at the common `info.subsets` block. Re-running it including `info.20x.subsets` / `info.rev5.subsets`: zero undeclared subsets — all nine are declared exactly as you describe, with full name, description, and applicability. The global-by-default / specific-when-needed layering is clean design; my checker just wasn't layered enough. The embarrassing part: AGENTS.md states this resolution rule explicitly, and I cited that file in my post without following its clearest instruction. Fair cop.

**I'll adapt my converter code to resolve exactly this misunderstanding:** it will read the framework-specific `info.20x.subsets` / `info.rev5.subsets` declarations alongside the common block — which actually improves the conversion, since the nine framework-specific subsets then carry their real declared titles and applicability instead of synthesized ones. Updated converter and coverage report will land in my repo, and I'll edit the original post above with strikethrough to match.

On (3): agreed — the either/or is explicit in the schema, so the pattern is intentional and finding 3 narrows to a small question rather than an issue: is there (or would you want) presentation guidance for class-agnostic consumers — search indexes, generic exports — on how to display a variant-only rule outside any class context? Entirely optional; happy to drop it if the answer is "class context is always required."

I've also downgraded my own finding 2 to plain statistics — the `all`/`20x`/`rev5` structure is documented; the counts (246 = 225 + 12 rev5-only + 9 20x-only) just stand as descriptive data. What survives review: zero easings across the 111 class-variant force deltas, 264/264 term references resolving via FRD term+alts, and the 373 KSI→control links importing cleanly.

Exactly the kind of review I was hoping for. Cheers!

christoph-puppe: Following up as promised: the converter fix landed, and the whole experiment has now shipped as **[JASCON v1.0.0](https://github.com/christoph-puppe/Semantic-OSCAL-2-Ideas/releases/tag/v1.0.0)**.

For CR26 specifically: the corpus converts with **UNMAPPED = 0** — the layered `info.20x.subsets` / `info.rev5.subsets` resolution from your correction is now the reference behavior — exports back to schema-valid OSCAL 1.2.2, and the 373 KSI→800-53 links round-trip as typed, provenance-carrying mapping objects. The converted corpus and computed coverage report are in [`converted_examples/`](https://github.com/christoph-puppe/Semantic-OSCAL-2-Ideas/tree/v1.0.0/converted_examples).

Verify it yourself — Linux/macOS:

```bash
uv run --with jsonschema python semantic-oscal/scripts/validate_core.py
```

```powershell
powershell -ExecutionPolicy Bypass -File semantic-oscal/scripts/validate_core.ps1

```
Thanks again for the review — it's baked into the release. Cheers!

discussion_title: Unlocking FedRAMP Collaboration: Simplifying CSP-to-CSP Security Package Access
author: pete-gov
text:
Re: Unlocking FedRAMP Collaboration: Simplifying CSP-to-CSP Security Package Access

pete-gov [FEDRAMP-OFFICIAL]: For the legacy model, FedRAMP doesn't manage package access for private companies, only agencies.

Certification packages are entirely the intellectual property of the company that creates them, and FedRAMP has no ability to control or provide access to them for other companies. FedRAMP only has the ability to set rules for how companies can consistently make this information available to agencies.

The Certification Data Sharing rules make it quite clear that FedRAMP does not assert any ownership over packages and will not penalize parties for responsibly sharing these in any way in [CDS-CSO-RPS (Responsible Public Package Sharing)](https://www.fedramp.gov/2026/reference/certification-data-sharing/#responsible-public-package-sharing).

discussion_title: RFC-0032 Offerings By Government
author: rhoesing
text:
RFC-0032 Offerings By Government

# RFC-0032 Offerings By Government

**⁉️NOTE⁉️ 
FedRAMP will not answer questions in this thread as it is reserved for official public comment. If you would like to ask a question or generally discuss this RFC informally, please use the [General Discussion & Q&A on RFC-0032](https://github.com/FedRAMP/community/discussions/157).**

**Status:** Closed  
**Start Date:** August 6, 2026  
**Closed:** September 8, 2026

## **Summary**

Cloud service offerings that are provided by federal government agencies as a shared service for use by other federal agencies are different from cloud service offerings provided by private companies: they are subject to all statutory and policy requirements for federal information systems and must receive an agency authorization to operate following agency-specific requirements. 

The FedRAMP Certification process is designed to establish a standardized process for commercial cloud services operated by private companies to provide agencies with sufficient information to make risk-based decisions when using the cloud service. This process is generally unnecessary for a cloud service that is operated by a federal agency under existing federal requirements.

The Offerings By Government ruleset allows cloud service offerings that are overseen by federal authorizing officials to obtain a FedRAMP Certification following their own agency process without needing to adopt all FedRAMP rules that are designed for private companies. This pathway allows FedRAMP to rely on the authorization, assessment, and ongoing oversight performed by the Agency Provider while preserving the minimum government-wide information and activities necessary to support reuse by customer agencies.

These rules do not constitute a government-wide authorization to operate. Each customer agency remains responsible for determining whether the cloud service offering is appropriate for its use and for authorizing the federal information systems in which the offering will be used.

---

## **Applicability**

These rules apply to a cloud service offering when:

1. The cloud service offering is operated by a federal agency;  
2. The offering is made available for direct use by one or more other federal agencies;  
3. The operating agency maintains responsibility for the security, privacy, assessment, their own authorization, and ongoing monitoring of the offering; and  
4. The responsible Agency Authorizating Official (AO) formally requests use of the Offerings by Government pathway.

For purposes of this ruleset, an Agency Provider is a federal agency responsible for operating a cloud service offering that is made available for use by other federal agencies.

---

## **General FedRAMP Responsibilities**

These rules apply to FedRAMP for granting FedRAMP Certification to cloud services provided by agencies.

### **OBG-FRP-ELG \-Offerings by Government Eligibility**

>FedRAMP MUST apply the Offerings by Government rules only when the responsible Agency Authorizing Official (AO) confirms through official government channels that the cloud service offering meets the applicability requirements of this ruleset.

### **OBG-FRP-EFR Exemption from FedRAMP Rules**

>FedRAMP MUST exempt agency providers from FedRAMP Rules except those in the Offerings By Government ruleset if requested by an agency Authorizing Official during an application for FedRAMP Certification of an agency provided cloud service offering.

### **OBG-FRP-CLS FedRAMP Certification Class Mapping**

>FedRAMP MUST grant FedRAMP Certification at the appropriate agency requested Certification Class UNLESS the request exceeds the FIPS-200 Information System Impact Level in the agency authorization to operate, as follows:
>
>1. Low Impact ATO: Class B  
>2. Moderate Impact ATO: Class C  
>3. High Impact ATO: Class D

### **OBG-FRP-DEC \- Certification Decision**

>FedRAMP MUST review the Offerings by Government Certification Package for completeness and grant FedRAMP Certification when:
>
>1. The Agency Provider meets the eligible requirements;  
>2. The agency Authorization to Operate is current and active;  
>3. The package contains the minimum information required by this ruleset; and  
>4. The package is available to FedRAMP and customer agencies

## **General Agency Provider Responsibilities**

These rules apply to federal agencies providing cloud services to other federal agencies who wish to obtain or maintain FedRAMP Certification.

### **OBG-AGP-ATO Authorization to Operate**

>Agency Providers MUST obtain and maintain an agency authorization to operate for the service offering.

### **OBG-AGP-NAS Notification of Authorization Status**

>Agency Providers MUST notify FedRAMP and customer agencies promptly when the agency authorization to operate is:
>
>1. Allowed to expire;  
>2. Suspended;  
>3. Revoked;  
>4. Replaced by an interim authorization;  
>5. Subject to new material conditions; or  
>6. Otherwise no longer sufficient to support the existing FedRAMP Certification

### **OBG-AGP-CPO Certification Package Overview**

>Agency Providers MUST supply an Agency Certification Package, using any format determined appropriate by the agency,  that includes *at least* the following information:
>
>1. Agency Authorization to Operate letter that includes the FIPS-199 Information System Impact Level  
>2. Agency System Security Plan  
>3. Agency Plans of Action & Milestones  
>4. Agency Privacy Threshold or Impact Assessment  
>5. Agency Security Assessment

### **OBG-AGP-MKT Marketplace Listing**

>Agency Providers MUST supply the necessary information required by [CDS-CSO-PUB](https://www.fedramp.gov/2026/reference/certification-data-sharing/#public-information) to maintain a listing in the FedRAMP Marketplace.

### **OBG-AGP-CCM Collaborative Continuous Monitoring**

>Agency Providers SHOULD establish at least quarterly collaborative continuous monitoring meetings to review ongoing security decisions and risks with their customer agencies.

### **OBG-AGP-UTC Use of Trust Centers**

>Agency Providers MAY use any appropriate trust center or similar sharing mechanism to make the Agency Certification Package available to agency customers and FedRAMP.
