discussion_title: RFC-0033 FedRAMP 20x Phase 4 Development Tracks for 20x Class D
author: Excentium-CPS
text:
Re: RFC-0033 FedRAMP 20x Phase 4 Development Tracks for 20x Class D

Excentium-CPS: **Comments on RFC-0033: FedRAMP 20x Phase 4**
Date: October 8, 2026
To: FedRAMP Program Management Office
Submitted via: RFC-0033 comment thread on GitHub
Comment period: September 9, 2026 through October 9, 2026
From: Excentium, Inc.

Excentium, Inc. is a FedRAMP Recognized Independent Assessment Service and a Service-Disabled Veteran-Owned Small Business headquartered in Reston, Virginia. We have held A2LA accreditation for FedRAMP assessment work continuously since 2015 and served as the independent assessor for one of the cloud services certified through the FedRAMP 20x Low pilot. We partner with government and commercial industry to strengthen our nation's cyber infrastructure.

These comments draw on two bodies of work. The 20x Low pilot gave us direct experience with a compressed schedule and requirements still being developed. Four years as the Independent Assessment Service for a federal agency's multi-bureau shared cloud service offerings, assessed under Rev5 at the Moderate and High baselines, gave us sustained exposure to agency assurance expectations for consequential workloads. The recommendations below address specific terms, dates, and assessment mechanisms so providers and assessors can reach a common reading.

Excentium supports the direction of RFC-0033. Extending FedRAMP 20x to Class D completes the Certification Class range for the 20x Type, while extending it to self-hosted and hybrid-hosted services opens the pathway to providers responsible for their physical infrastructure. Developing these requirements through three simultaneous tracks and public RFCs gives providers, assessors, and agencies an opportunity to resolve implementation questions together.

References to CR26 use the Consolidated Rules for 2026, version 2026.10.08.01, published and verified on October 8, 2026. We use Independent Assessment Service following FRD-ASR. Proposed RFC requirements are identified as proposals; they do not establish current obligations.

### R1. Classification Test for Mixed Hosting Footprints

**Ref:** New FedRAMP Definitions for Cloud-Hosted, Self-Hosted, and Hybrid-Hosted; MAS-CSO-IIR

The proposed Cloud-Hosted and Self-Hosted definitions use where machine-based information resources primarily run and who takes responsibility for the physical infrastructure. Hybrid-Hosted applies where some resources are cloud-hosted and others are self-hosted. Please clarify how the two uses of primarily interact with the Hybrid-Hosted definition and whether a materiality threshold applies.

This classification determines which requirements attach. Anticipated item 2 applies to cloud-hosted and hybrid-hosted Class D services, while Track 2 eligibility includes primarily self-hosted or hybrid-hosted services. An offering that runs almost entirely on certified cloud infrastructure and includes a small component for which the provider takes physical-infrastructure responsibility appears to fit the Hybrid-Hosted definition. Providers need to know whether that component always determines the classification or whether its function and significance affect the result.

The test should account for the resources identified under MAS-CSO-IIR, including resources that can affect the confidentiality, integrity, or availability of federal customer data through security functions. Equipment ownership alone does not establish responsibility for physical infrastructure. A test based only on direct handling of federal customer data would also omit applicable resources with indirect security effects.

**Recommendation:** Publish the classification test and explain how primarily and Hybrid-Hosted apply to a mixed offering. State whether any materiality threshold applies, how physical-infrastructure responsibility is established, and how the result affects item 2 and Track 2 eligibility. Use the MAS-CSO-IIR applicability condition so providers and assessors can reach a consistent classification.

### R2. The Six Month Period Without Corrective Action

**Ref:** Anticipated Requirements item 1; AFC-FRP-COR; SCN-FRP-CAP; VER-FRP-ARP; IEC-FRP-ORV; FRC-CCL-UCC

Item 1 proposes that an offering obtain and maintain a 20x Class C Certification without corrective action for six months before becoming eligible for 20x Class D after the Phase 4 pilot. The proposal leaves open which corrective-action events interrupt that period.

AFC-FRP-COR describes consequences that can range from negative Marketplace ratings to suspension of Certification, depending on severity. SCN-FRP-CAP and VER-FRP-ARP refer to a formal provider Corrective Action Plan. Individual rules also publish corrective actions: IEC-FRP-ORV provides for a Corrective Action Plan and a three-month grace period to implement proper procedures in specified circumstances. These mechanisms can produce different eligibility results. An assessor organizational plan under REC-IAS-CAP addresses a separate subject and should be distinguished from corrective action affecting the provider or offering.

Adoption milestones may fall within the first six-month eligibility windows. Current 20x deadline guidance identifies January 1, 2027 as the Maintaining Ongoing Certification date for many rulesets, with the grace period ending at the first independent assessment started after that date. For existing Certifications, the guidance says providers should adopt by the maintaining date and requires a plan to adopt by the end of the grace period if they have not done so. VDR and VER have a maintaining date of December 7, 2026 and a grace period ending March 7, 2027. Providers need to know how an adoption-related plan affects Class D eligibility.

FRC-CCL-UCC requires a new application to upgrade Certification Class, with applicable requirements met in advance. The six-month condition therefore needs a defined start date and a clear point at which it must be satisfied. A material change to architecture, hosting, a relied-upon security function, or a validation method can also change whether earlier operating history represents the offering that seeks Class D. An assessor should be able to examine a dated record of the change, its affected assurance, and the disposition of the earlier evidence.

**Recommendation:** Identify the corrective-action events that affect the six-month period, who determines their effect, and whether each preserves, pauses, or restarts the clock. Confirm whether the period begins with Class C Certification and must be complete at the Class D application. Explain the treatment of adoption-related Corrective Action Plans and how a Class D Pilot Certification relates to the post-pilot six-month condition. Define when material changes require a recorded determination that the prior operating history remains representative, and the evidence for that determination.

### R3. Certification Profile in Items 2 and 3

**Ref:** Anticipated Requirements items 2 and 3; FRD-CPF; FRD-TPR; MAS-CSO-IIR; MAS-CSO-TPR

We understand from FedRAMP's September 23 response in General Discussion 172 that a reference to Certified, without a specified Type, includes both Rev5 and 20x at the stated Class. That answer resolves the initial Type question. Incorporating the interpretation into the pilot requirements will give providers and assessors a common reference. FRD-CPF also includes Certification Path, so any Path restrictions should be stated.

The same response explains that Rev5 end dates and transition requirements will be finalized during Phase 5. Current guidance closes applications for new Rev5 Certifications on June 11, 2027 and provides that existing Rev5 Certifications remain active until at least December 31, 2028 unless FedRAMP is otherwise directed. Please explain how dependency eligibility will be handled as Phase 5 establishes the transition, including whether reliance continues while an upstream Certification remains valid or ends on a separately announced date.

Item 3 also needs a scope clarification. FRD-TPR defines a Third-Party Information Resource by its incomplete inclusion in the offering's Minimum Assessment Scope. MAS-CSO-TPR addresses third-party information resources used by the offering, subject to MAS-CSO-IIR applicability. That construction covers relevant indirect security functions as well as applicable resources that handle federal customer data.

MAS-CSO-TPR requires documentation of usage and configuration, justification for use, mitigation measures, and compensating controls. Providers need to understand how those provisions relate to the proposed Class B minimum when an applicable resource relies on an offering Certified below Class B or without FedRAMP Certification. For any permitted exception, an assessor could examine the resource's function, relevant data and control flows, privileged access, potential effect on security functions and availability, and the provider's retained responsibilities. The decision should record the relied-upon assurance, compensating measures, and events that require reassessment.

**Recommendation:** Incorporate FedRAMP's existing interpretation that the Class references include Rev5 and 20x, and identify any Path restrictions. Explain the treatment of valid Rev5 dependencies during the transition and the notice associated with any separate eligibility cutoff. Align item 3 with FRD-TPR and MAS-CSO-TPR while preserving MAS-CSO-IIR applicability. State whether the Class B minimum is absolute. If exceptions are permitted, require a documented impact determination, specific compensating measures and evidence of their effectiveness, an approval authority, and conditions for continuing review.

### R4. Assurance Engineering Resources and Agency GRC Integration

**Ref:** Anticipated Requirements item 4; FRC-CSO-JSN; CDS-CSO-PUB; CDS-CSO-CBF; CDS-CSO-HAD; CDS-CSO-PSM; CDS-TRC-PAC; FRD-PFA

Item 4 combines support for agency review of the Certification Package with ongoing integration of assurance data into agency GRC systems. Each commitment needs a stated assessment criterion so providers know what to demonstrate and assessors know what to validate.

The integration commitment can build on existing CR26 interfaces. CDS-CSO-PUB requires public information in human-readable and JSON formats; CDS-CSO-CBF requires automation to keep them consistent. CDS-TRC-PAC requires documented programmatic access to all FedRAMP Certification Data. CDS-CSO-HAD requires snapshots aligned to Ongoing Certification Reports, and CDS-CSO-PSM requires per-service materials at Class D. The October 5 clarification to FRC-CSO-JSN also addresses standard web consumption of public JSON, including appropriate CORS behavior and response headers. These rules provide a concrete basis for describing the additional integration support expected at Class D.

A practical demonstration would have an agency consumer retrieve applicable public JSON through a standard browser, validate it against the corresponding FedRAMP schema, associate the results with the correct offering, service, rule, and reporting period, and retrieve the relevant historical snapshot. The assessor could examine the recorded ingestion result, human-readable and JSON consistency, CORS and response headers, and the documented interface. Access to protected Certification Data should be exercised under the appropriate authorization, separately from public JSON access.

Active support for agency package review also involves people and availability. FRD-PFA describes a Persistent FedRAMP Assessment as focused on Key Security Indicators. A support commitment needs evidence of the agency-facing outcome and the provider's ability to sustain it. Documented support routes, escalation arrangements, and measurable response commitments would let an Independent Assessment Service examine that capability.

**Recommendation:** State whether item 4 will be expressed as a Certification rule, a KSI with a defined validation method, or a documented commitment in Certification Data. For Class D, require a demonstrated agency GRC ingestion exercise using the applicable CDS and FRC-CSO-JSN interfaces, with results an assessor can reproduce or inspect. Define the measurable evidence for agency package review support, including escalation and response arrangements, and identify the additional Class D outcome to validate.

### R5. FOCI and Automated Validation Indicators

**Ref:** Anticipated Requirements item 5; REC-IAS-AFI; REC-IAS-CFI; KSI-CED-RAT; KSI-CNA-OFA; KSI-RPL-RRO; KSI-RPL-TRC; CDS-CSO-AVR; FRC-CSX-VVK; SDR-CSX-KSI; IVV-CSO-SEE; IVV-IAS-VEF

CR26 already addresses foreign interest, influence, and control for assessors. REC-IAS-AFI requires annual reporting, and REC-IAS-CFI requires updated information within 48 hours of a change in foreign ownership or control. These recognition obligations offer a useful reporting model for a provider construct, with its own defined scope and acceptance criteria.

Placing FOCI within the Key Security Indicators also raises a measurement question. Ownership and control information describes an organizational condition. A KSI needs a security outcome that can be persistently validated. The Cybersecurity Education theme shows that organizational matters can be expressed as indicators, so the proposal should explain the provider outcome and the evidence that will establish it over time.

Availability already has anchors in CR26. KSI-CNA-OFA addresses optimization for high availability and rapid recovery. KSI-RPL-RRO addresses recovery objectives, and KSI-RPL-TRC addresses testing recovery capability. CDS-CSO-AVR requires Class B, C, and D providers to maintain a web service showing current and historical availability of core services over at least the past 30 days. Class D can extend these measures with clearly stated assurance expectations.

A provider FOCI indicator should also show whether measures addressing identified risks remain effective as ownership, personnel access, governance, or relevant dependencies change. Existing federal determinations could supply evidence where their organization and offering scope applies; an assessor would still need a mapping of coverage, exclusions, and any additional mitigations.

FRC-CSX-VVK requires at least four automated methods per Key Security Indicator for 20x Class D. Santoshkumarpuppala's September 20 comment in the formal RFC thread recommends an observed failing run to show that a method can detect the condition it claims to detect. We support that test and add an assessment of shared dependencies. For each method, evidence could identify the controlled failing condition, expected and observed result, method version, and evidence source. The assessor should examine whether methods depend on the same upstream signal or processing path, and whether their combined coverage remains useful if one dependency fails. A representative test environment, replay, or other justified technique can demonstrate detection without disrupting production.

**Recommendation:** Publish the intended scope of the provider FOCI theme, including whether it reaches ownership, personnel, supply chain, or a combination. Define the mitigation outcome to be validated over time and how annual and change-triggered reporting supports it. Consider accepting applicable federal FOCI determinations, including those under 32 CFR 117.11, with a scope mapping and gap analysis for the offering. Build new availability indicators on KSI-CNA-OFA, the Recovery Planning theme, and CDS-CSO-AVR. For automated validation, require evidence that methods detect representative failing conditions and identify shared sources or dependencies, leaving the test technique to the provider.

### R6. Class C Review Timing Against the December 1 Deadline

**Ref:** Phase 4 Track 1; FedRAMP response in General Discussion 172 on September 18, 2026

Track 1 requires a CR26-compliant FedRAMP 20x Class C Certification received before December 1, 2026. Providers applying for Class C before November 13 and intending to participate are asked to send a notice of intent after submitting the application. The dates are eighteen days apart, and eligibility depends on completed Certification.

FedRAMP's September 18 response confirms the completed Class C prerequisite and explains that late applications cannot be promised priority review. The notice-of-intent date therefore provides a coordination step; it does not establish a completion window. Providers would benefit from indicative review assumptions when deciding whether their readiness and schedule support Phase 4 participation.

**Recommendation:** Publish indicative Class C review timing and the readiness assumptions that affect it, subject to package completeness and available review capacity. Provide practical guidance on the remaining opportunity to qualify before December 1 and explain how notices of intent are used. Preserve the distinction between submitting an application and receiving Certification.

### R7. The Independent Assessment Service Role in the Phase 4 Pilot

**Ref:** Phase 4 Track 1 items 4 and 5; REC-IAS-ADA; REC-IAS-RQU; REC-IAS-SEP

Track 1 expects participants to engage a FedRAMP Recognized Independent Assessment Service. Providers planning a Class D engagement need to understand the personnel competence and technical capabilities expected of the assessor, as well as how independent assessment will be maintained during pilot collaboration.

Excentium is a FedRAMP Recognized Independent Assessment Service and could be engaged by a Phase 4 participant. We disclose that interest here. These questions apply to the assessors and providers participating across the pilot.

REC-IAS-ADA establishes an ongoing recognition experience floor of at least two initial or ongoing assessments for Class B, C, or D Certifications every two years, without specifying a Certification Type. REC-IAS-RQU separately requires the roles and personnel qualifications prescribed by A2LA R311, subject to a specifically published exception for a limited pilot or other explicitly scoped process. Meeting the recognition experience floor does not by itself describe the competence needed for every Class D engagement. Please state any additional Class D experience or capabilities expected for evaluating automated assurance.

REC-IAS-SEP bars an assessor from independently assessing the same offering within two years after supplying advisory or consulting services, subject to a specifically published scoped exception. Participation in developing or interpreting program requirements and offering-specific advisory or consulting work need clear treatment during the pilot. The collaboration described in Track 1 makes this boundary worth publishing early so providers and assessors can plan their roles.

**Recommendation:** Publish the competence expectations for assessors supporting Phase 4, including any additional Class D experience or technical capabilities. Clarify which pilot activities constitute offering-specific advisory or consulting services under REC-IAS-SEP and which constitute participation in developing or interpreting program requirements. If a pilot exception is needed, publish its scope, permitted activities, independence safeguards, and retained assessment duties. Confirm the direct technical channel to the PMO for assessors supporting participants.

### R8. Publishing Themes From the Direct Engagement Rounds

**Ref:** Phase 4 Tracks 2 and 3

Tracks 2 and 3 pair targeted direct engagement with public RFCs so other parties can participate. The direct tracks will help shape the drafts on which the broader community comments.

Provider Round 1 runs November 4 through November 20, 2026, and Round 2 runs January 4 through January 15, 2027. The proposed self-hosted and hybrid-hosted rules publish for comment on February 10, after both rounds. Publishing the themes discussed would help parties outside the direct tracks understand the basis for that draft.

**Recommendation:** Publish a short summary of the themes from each direct engagement round as it concludes, protecting information that cannot be disclosed. Make those summaries available with the related public RFCs so all commenters can address the issues informing the Consolidated Rules for 2027.

### R9. Question Timing for Assessment Services

**Ref:** Phase 4 Track 3

Track 3 states that assessment services will receive the same general questions and information as providers and respond from their assessment perspective. The first assessor round runs October 19 through October 23, 2026. The RFC carrying the general questions publishes November 4, when provider Round 1 begins.

Sending the questions with the October 12 assessor notification would allow participants to review them against their engagement history and bring specific examples to the first round.

**Recommendation:** Send the general questions to qualifying assessment services with the October 12 notification, including any background material needed to prepare for the October 19 through October 23 meetings.

### R10. Confirming Eligibility for the Assessment Service Track

**Ref:** Phase 4 Track 3

Track 3 publishes its eligibility criterion: a recognized assessment service must be the current assessor of record or have been the primary assessor within the last three years for a provider qualifying for Track 2. FedRAMP will identify qualifying services using the information available to it and the Marketplace, then notify them at the public email address in their Marketplace listing.

Notifications are targeted for October 12, 2026, with an October 16 opt-in deadline. A service that believes it meets the published criterion needs a timely route to resolve a missing invitation or a disputed eligibility determination during that short window.

**Recommendation:** Provide a contact route for assessment services that believe they meet the published Track 3 criterion and have not received an invitation by October 13. Identify the supporting evidence needed, such as the qualifying provider and offering, the assessor relationship, and the relevant dates. Explain how a missing invitation or disputed eligibility determination can be resolved before the October 16 opt-in deadline.

### R11. Aligning Guidance on Class D Availability

**Ref:** CR26 guidance on Choosing a Certification Type; Phase 4 Track 1 target dates

Current CR26 guidance anticipates piloting 20x Class D in late 2026 and making it available as a formal option in early 2027. RFC-0033 places the pilot in FY27 Q1 and Q2, with final review extending into the beginning of Q3. The March 23, 2027 FedRAMP Day is tentative, and the final Phase 4 rules will be incorporated into the Consolidated Rules for 2027.

These statements serve different planning purposes. Providers need an indicative target for general availability outside the pilot, together with the dependencies that could affect it. That information is particularly useful before June 11, 2027, the final date to apply for a new Rev5 Certification.

**Recommendation:** Align the Certification Type guidance with the Phase 4 planning schedule and state an indicative target for general availability of 20x Class D outside the pilot. Distinguish that target from pilot package deadlines and the tentative FedRAMP Day, and identify the review and rule-publication dependencies that could affect it. Keep the guidance current so providers can plan against the June 11 Rev5 application deadline.

### R12. Reusing Physical Infrastructure Assurance in Tracks 2 and 3

**Ref:** Phase 4 Tracks 2 and 3; MAS-CSO-IIR; IVV-CSO-SEE; IVV-IAS-VEF

Tracks 2 and 3 ask which existing certifications and classifications can support self-hosted or hybrid-hosted offerings and what remains to be assessed for FedRAMP. An assessor-reviewed mapping would let FedRAMP reuse applicable infrastructure assurance while making the coverage of that assurance visible to agencies.

The mapping should identify the issuing body, standard and edition, current certificate or assessment report, covered facilities and services, validity period, exclusions, relevant findings, and shared responsibilities. It should connect each relied-upon assessment result to the actual deployed environment and the FedRAMP requirement or security outcome it supports. For example, evidence about a facility's physical access, power, environmental protections, or recovery arrangements has value when the facility and services covered match the offering and the provider's retained responsibilities are clear.

An Independent Assessment Service could examine that mapping, identify residual gaps, and perform targeted verification and validation of the remaining work. A certificate title alone does not establish that a specific offering, facility, or configuration is covered. This record would let the provider, assessor, FedRAMP, and relying agencies understand exactly which assurance can be reused.

**Recommendation:** Use Tracks 2 and 3 to develop an assessor-reviewed mapping for physical-infrastructure assurance. Specify the evidence of coverage and applicability, exclusions and retained responsibilities, relevant findings, and the gap analysis. Reuse covered results with targeted independent verification of residual FedRAMP requirements and security outcomes.

Excentium appreciates the opportunity to comment on RFC-0033 and welcomes further discussion of these recommendations with the FedRAMP PMO.

Class D addresses workloads where threats to the confidentiality, integrity, or availability of federal customer data may lead to catastrophic harm, including loss of life. Clear requirements and assessable evidence will help agencies place confidence in the resulting Certification. We support developing that assurance in the open and resolving the practical questions while the requirements are being written. This work supports our shared mission to reduce the vulnerabilities of our Nation.

Respectfully submitted,

Colin Corlett  
President and Chief Executive Officer  
Excentium, Inc.
1768 Business Center Drive, Suite 220  
Reston, VA 20190

discussion_title: RFC-0033 FedRAMP 20x Phase 4 Development Tracks for 20x Class D
author: wisecryptic
text:
Re: RFC-0033 FedRAMP 20x Phase 4 Development Tracks for 20x Class D

wisecryptic: **New FedRAMP Definitions Comments**

A solid foundation for the present. No suggested changes. Future signals to look for:

Edge and fog computing instances. Currently, 99% of edge computing (CDNs, colos, PoPs) fits nicely into a hybrid model, with workable scopes and interfaces defining the boundary. Future trends that could complicate this model include sensor/mesh networks deployed in smart cities, research areas, or battlespaces; generalized robotification, such as worker or drone machines on a network; and mini data centers. Most of these are forward-looking scenarios in which high-sensitivity CIA may be exposed to risk.
Self-hosted AI integration, a subset of the above, may become a trend over the next few years. Currently, frontier models dominate and interfaces are becoming standardized. Due to cost, future work may be segmented into localized AI models. Even when localized, these models may be offered as a service and forward-deployed, similar to what DOW is doing with battlespace computation today. It will also be interesting to see whether AI-written on-prem apps hyper-converge with traditional SaaS, or whether API interfaces remain the modus operandi.

**Overall Anticipated 20x Class D Requirements**

FedRAMP should prepare for the following scenario: an agency or prime contractor has a use case that is not typically High (D), but instead of requiring C plus an overlay, they require D for a scenario that isn’t truly D. They may want to blanket-require D to avoid building boundary checks. They may feel D will be easier than managing an overlay. They may simply be security posturing, or making the wrong call.

However, this means the authority issuing the requirement may be lax about some D requirements and strict about others. This puts the CSP in the awkward position of potentially overbuilding. How to handle these scenarios may be an excellent question to investigate during the pilot period. Ideally, FedRAMP and the CSP would catch potential issues early and right-size the approach. In any case, I recommend that KSIs be structured to hold to a known standard while remaining flexible enough to capture variable uses within that standard.

Item 1: If the certification is purely a program certification, it may benefit FedRAMP operations and potentially even agency assurance, to run at C for six months before moving to D. However, if an agency wishes to onboard the system immediately because of a past relationship or operational need, this six-month period should in no way hinder the parties from doing business or fulfilling their missions. This should be made clear in the rules and guidance. I recommend not implementing the six-month period. If this is implemented, to signal intent or preparedness for D, FedRAMP could create a designation such as “D Pending,” meaning the CSP attests to D but FedRAMP has not yet reviewed the materials.

Item 3: Similar to sca1235’s comment, this runs close to a problem CSPs had with the old SA-9 controls. FedRAMP used to insert a parameter assignment requiring all external services to apply the same FedRAMP baseline as the system under review. This caused many problems, because many types of systems under many types of authorizations did not fall under FedRAMP. Examples include telephony, public infrastructure integration services (“public” here meaning infrastructure that handles public information, not “public cloud services”), scrapers, and messaging services. While Item 3 relies on the strength of FedRAMP’s minimum assessment scope definition, I expect this to be at least an area of vigorous discussion, and likely one where exceptions to the rule will eventually be raised.

**Phase 4 Track 1: 20x Class D Cloud-Hosted Pilot Comments**

While I support the rapid pace of improvement in FedRAMP, the June 2027 Rev 5 cutoff for Class D seems too abrupt following the pilot. I encourage extending the deadline for Rev 5 High (D) acceptance. I have a client who will likely be negatively affected by this cutoff.

Keeping participants engaged with the TAG and board will benefit all parties. This should be a primary goal, as it will spread lessons learned and encourage greater engagement outside that group as well.

**Phase 4 Track 2: Expanding 20x to Self-Hosted or Hybrid-Hosted Services Comments**

If none of the applicants holding 15+ agency uses are smaller enterprises, I recommend including at least one. In the past, large players were selected because of their impact and then influenced rules that disadvantaged smaller players with leading-edge solutions. This stifled the breadth and novelty of solutions in the marketplace.

**Phase 4 Track 3: Independent Assessment Service Engagement Comments**

No comments.

wisecryptic: Thank you, FedRAMP, as always, for your thoughtful and rapid improvement efforts.

discussion_title: RFC-0033 FedRAMP 20x Phase 4 Development Tracks for 20x Class D
author: socure-control-freak
text:
Re: RFC-0033 FedRAMP 20x Phase 4 Development Tracks for 20x Class D

socure-control-freak: Socure appreciates FedRAMP's work to define a rigorous 20x Class D and supports the higher assurance bar described in this RFC. The following comments focus on continuity for agencies that already rely on Rev5-certified services.

**Re: Overall Anticipated 20x Class D Requirements, item 1 (6 months of 20x Class C without corrective action)**

The 6-month requirement is a sensible way to confirm a provider can sustain 20x-level operations before taking on Class D. For providers that already hold a Rev5 Class C or Class D certification, however, a clean continuous monitoring record of that length (or longer) may already exist and has been reviewed by agency authorizing officials.

We support @cb-axon's request for a direct path for existing Rev5 Class D providers, and ask that the same principle extend to Rev5 Class C providers seeking Class D. Once Rev5 closes to new applications on 11 June 2027, these providers will move to 20x, and without credit for their existing record agencies may face a gap of a year or more before those services can reach Class D, even where the underlying security program has a long, clean history.

**Suggestion:** allow a Rev5-certified provider with no corrective actions in the most recent 6 months to satisfy item 1 using its Rev5 continuous monitoring record, or to complete 20x Class C and Class D in a single combined assessment. This would preserve the intent of the requirement, reduce duplicate assessment cost for agencies and providers, and help agencies reach Class D-level assurance sooner.

discussion_title: RFC-0033 FedRAMP 20x Phase 4 Development Tracks for 20x Class D
author: socure-control-freak
text:
Re: RFC-0033 FedRAMP 20x Phase 4 Development Tracks for 20x Class D

socure-control-freak: **Re: transition from Rev5 to 20x for providers seeking Class D, and the 11 June 2027 Rev5 cutoff**

Many Rev5-certified providers and their agency customers are planning 2027 investments now, and the key input is how Rev5 certifications will transition to 20x. As @Excentium-CPS notes, transition requirements are expected to be finalized during Phase 5. However, a Rev5 Class D application requires many months of preparation, an independent assessment and an agency authorization before 11 June 2027. A provider that cannot complete all of that by the cutoff would, as currently proposed, need to earn 20x Class C, hold it for six months, and wait for 20x Class D to open beyond the pilot, likely a delay of a year or more before agencies can use the service at Class D. Providers and agencies must therefore effectively choose between a Rev5 Class D upgrade and a 20x route in the next few months. Guidance that arrives in 2027 will be too late to inform that choice, and may lead to duplicate assessments or a rush of incomplete Rev5 applications near the cutoff.

**Suggestions:**
1. Publish an indicative Rev5→20x transition path for Rev5 Class C and Class D providers by the end of October 2026, or with the final pilot requirements on 18 November at the latest. Even before the rules are final, a statement of intent would allow informed decisions: whether Rev5 continuous monitoring history will count toward Class D eligibility, whether a direct Rev5 Class D to 20x Class D path is planned, and the expected timeframe for general availability of 20x Class D.
2. Allow providers whose Rev5 Class D independent assessment (initial or upgrade) has formally started by 11 June 2027, as documented in an assessment plan with a FedRAMP Recognized Independent Assessment Service, to submit their complete Rev5 application after the cutoff, within the existing freshness requirement (FRC-APP-FIA) and with the required agency authorization. This would avoid a surge in assessor demand and rushed, incomplete applications in spring 2027. At a minimum, please confirm that a complete Rev5 application in active FedRAMP review by 11 June 2027 will be allowed to finish review if FedRAMP requests corrections.
3. Ensure there is no period in which existing Rev5 providers have no available route to Class D. We agree with @Excentium-CPS (R11) that an indicative general-availability date for 20x Class D is needed, and with @wisecryptic's concern about the cutoff: if 20x Class D is not yet generally open by 11 June 2027, consider keeping Rev5 Class D applications (including upgrades from Class C) open until it is, so agencies with high-impact needs are not left without a certification path.

discussion_title: RFC-0033 FedRAMP 20x Phase 4 Development Tracks for 20x Class D
author: socure-control-freak
text:
Re: RFC-0033 FedRAMP 20x Phase 4 Development Tracks for 20x Class D

socure-control-freak: **Re: Overall Anticipated 20x Class D Requirements, item 3 (only Class B, C or D certified third-party information resources)**

We support the points raised by @sca1235, @cb-axon, @wisecryptic and @Excentium-CPS on scoping this requirement and preserving the documented MAS-CSO-TPR path.

Certification status is one useful signal of third-party assurance, but it is not the only one, and it does not by itself reflect the actual risk a third-party resource introduces. Many best-in-class services have no federal business case for pursuing FedRAMP certification, regardless of its cost. An absolute certified-only rule would require providers to substitute certified but less capable alternatives, or remove functionality entirely, even where the third party handles no federal customer data or has narrowly limited access. In those cases agencies would receive a less capable service without a corresponding reduction in risk.

**Suggestion:** replace the absolute requirement with a risk-based approval path that applies whether or not a certified alternative exists. A provider could use a non-certified third-party resource where it documents:
- the function performed and why it is needed;
- the federal customer data, if any, and the access the resource has to the offering;
- the independent assurance relied on (e.g., SOC 2 Type II, ISO 27001, or other recognized attestations);
- compensating controls and how the dependency is monitored; and
- the conditions that would trigger re-review.

Approval would rest with the agency authorizing official, or FedRAMP, and could be scaled to risk: lighter for resources with no access to federal customer data, stricter or not permitted where a resource processes federal customer data or could directly compromise the offering's security. This preserves Class D assurance where it matters, while letting agencies benefit from the best available capabilities.

Thank you for the opportunity to comment.

discussion_title: RFC-0033 FedRAMP 20x Phase 4 Development Tracks for 20x Class D
author: Alliancefordigitalinnovation
text:
Re: RFC-0033 FedRAMP 20x Phase 4 Development Tracks for 20x Class D

Alliancefordigitalinnovation: The Alliance for Digital Innovation (ADI) appreciates the opportunity to comment on RFC-0033, 20x Phase 4 Development Tracks for 20x Class D. To support FedRAMP’s efforts, we offer the following recommendations:

**_Align FedRAMP 20x with Agency Authorization and FISMA Responsibilities_**

ADI appreciates RFC-0033's inclusion of additional agency engagement during the Phase 4 pilot. Agencies will ultimately need to understand how FedRAMP 20x certifications can be incorporated into their existing risk-management and authorization processes.

As Phase 4 progresses, FedRAMP should provide agencies and CSPs with a clear framework showing how the evidence generated through a 20x Class D Certification can support an agency's own authorization decision and responsibilities under FISMA. The goal should be to ensure that FedRAMP 20x and agency authorization processes operate as complementary components of a common risk-management framework rather than as separate or duplicative processes.

ADI encourages FedRAMP to work closely with agency CIOs and authorizing officials during the pilot and to publish clear guidance or mappings that agencies can use when incorporating 20x certification evidence into their own authorization processes. This coordination should extend to agency Inspectors General and other oversight entities so agencies have a common understanding of how 20x will be recognized within existing authorization and cybersecurity oversight processes.

**_Establish a Workable Transition from Rev. 5 to FedRAMP 20x_**

RFC-0033 appropriately focuses on developing the future Class D model, but the transition from existing FedRAMP Rev. 5 authorizations to 20x will be equally important.

Without a coordinated transition, CSPs that already maintain Rev. 5 authorizations may need to continue supporting those requirements for existing agency customers while also investing in and maintaining 20x processes. This can create significant duplicative compliance costs and operational burdens, particularly as agencies adopt 20x at different speeds. 

This challenge is already emerging in practice, as the pace of FedRAMP modernization may outpace agency readiness to adopt the new model, including where agencies and their oversight bodies continue to evaluate authorization practices against existing Rev. 5 expectations. FedRAMP should therefore make the transition path between Rev. 5 and 20x clear and explicit, including how existing agency authorizations will be treated as agencies move to the new framework.

FedRAMP should coordinate the transition with agency CIOs, authorizing officials, Inspectors General, and other relevant oversight entities so agencies and CSPs have a common understanding of how 20x will be recognized and used. The transition framework should resolve differing federal expectations at the government level rather than leaving individual CSPs to navigate or reconcile them on their own. 

FedRAMP should develop a clear transition framework before finalizing broader Class D requirements. That framework should:
•	Provide sufficient time for agencies to adopt and operationalize the new model;
•	Minimize periods in which CSPs must maintain duplicative Rev. 5 and 20x compliance processes;
•	Clearly identify which Class D requirements represent new assurance obligations and which replace existing Rev. 5 requirements
•	Ensure alignment among FedRAMP, agency authorizing officials, Inspectors General, and other relevant oversight bodies so the transition from Rev. 5 to 20x is consistently evaluated and accepted across the federal government;
•	Clarify how existing agency authorizations and Rev. 5 assessments will be treated during the transition, including clear milestones for transitioning existing certifications; and
•	Avoid creating incentives or requirements that effectively force migration before agencies are prepared to accept and use 20x certification evidence.

FedRAMP should also use the Phase 4 pilot to measure the practical costs and operational challenges associated with transition, rather than evaluating only whether individual CSPs can successfully satisfy the new Class D requirements.

**_Ensure the Phase 4 Pilot Reflects the Existing Federal Cloud Market_**

RFC-0033 would limit the Phase 4 Class D pilot to no more than ten participants and require participants to receive a CR26-compliant FedRAMP 20x Class C Certification before December 1, 2026.

ADI understands the value of selecting participants that have demonstrated an ability to meet 20x requirements. At the same time, the final Class D framework should not be developed based solely on the experience of providers already positioned to move quickly through the 20x process.

Many mature commercial cloud offerings have made significant investments in Rev. 5 authorization and currently support federal agencies under that framework. Their experience will be important in identifying migration challenges, interoperability issues, and agency adoption considerations that may not arise among providers already optimized for 20x.

ADI encourages FedRAMP to ensure that Phase 4 incorporates meaningful input from existing Rev. 5 Class C and Class D providers, including providers that may not be able to obtain a 20x Class C Certification in time to participate directly in the pilot. This could include an additional transition-focused engagement cohort or other structured mechanism for testing proposed requirements against existing authorized services before those requirements are finalized.

FedRAMP should also ensure that participating agencies have a meaningful role in evaluating how Class D requirements operate within their existing risk-management and authorization frameworks.

**_Clarify the Scope of Self-Hosted and Hybrid-Hosted Offerings_**

ADI welcomes FedRAMP's effort to clarify the treatment of self-hosted and hybrid-hosted cloud service offerings. As FedRAMP develops these definitions and associated requirements, however, the program should ensure that their scope remains clear and predictable.

In particular, FedRAMP should clarify how self-hosted and hybrid-hosted offerings fit within FedRAMP's established cloud-service scope, including the circumstances in which customer-managed or on-premises deployments would fall within the program.

Clear boundaries will help agencies and providers determine when FedRAMP requirements apply and prevent uncertainty for commercial products that may support multiple deployment models.

Sincerely,

Alliance for Digital Innovation

discussion_title: RFC-0033 FedRAMP 20x Phase 4 Development Tracks for 20x Class D
author: mkimsy
text:
Re: RFC-0033 FedRAMP 20x Phase 4 Development Tracks for 20x Class D

mkimsy: **Commenter:** Mike Kim, CEO, Mycroft (GRC automation vendor supporting 20x certification packages)

Thank you to the FedRAMP team for running this process in the open. 20x has already changed what our customers can achieve, and we think Class D is the right next step. Mycroft is pursuing 20x Class C and Class D certification, and we offer these suggestions from the perspective of the tooling that produces and transports assurance data.

1. **Reusable validation (item 5).** Where a certified third-party tool performs KSI validation, FedRAMP might consider allowing its methods to be assessed once and inherited by the providers using it, with each provider still assessed on configuration and coverage. This would follow the same logic as inheriting from a Class D IaaS and could improve consistency across packages.

2. **Assurance engineering resources (item 4).** We welcome the emphasis on stronger agency support. It would help to know whether providers can meet part of this expectation through certified tooling and services alongside their own staff.

3. **Tooling perspective in Phase 4.** The direct engagement tracks are a sensible way to draw on provider and assessor experience. If capacity allows, a session for tooling providers, or published themes from each round as @Excentium-CPS suggests in R8, would help the wider community contribute well to the follow-on RFCs.

4. **Third-party resources (item 3).** We support this requirement and agree with @sunstonesecure-robert that resources which implement or validate security belong in the Minimum Assessment Scope. Two clarifications would help: confirmation that validation and evidence tooling is in scope, and whether a resource with a 20x application in progress could be treated as eligible for a limited transition period.

5. **Agency GRC integration (item 4).** We support Excentium's R4. A reference ingestion profile and conformance test on the agency side would complement it, so providers can build the integration once and agencies receive a consistent feed.

6. **Failure evidence (item 5).** We support @Santoshkumarpuppala's observed-failing-run idea and Excentium's shared-dependency check. Fields for both in the Security Decision Record schema would make them easy for agencies and assessors to verify.

7. **Pilot and eligibility details.** When the Oct 14 RFC is published, it would be helpful to see the selection criteria for the pilot, and confirmation of how self-identified, promptly remediated findings are treated under the six-month condition.

We appreciate the pace and transparency of this work and look forward to the detailed requirements.

discussion_title: RFC-0033 FedRAMP 20x Phase 4 Development Tracks for 20x Class D
author: CSP-AB
text:
Re: RFC-0033 FedRAMP 20x Phase 4 Development Tracks for 20x Class D

CSP-AB: CSP-AB submits the following comments to RFC-0033:

**Overall Anticipated 20x Class D Requirements.**

- We ask FedRAMP to reconsider making certified status an absolute requirement for third-party information resources in Class D Minimum Assessment Scope. As written, it forces CSPs to source every dependency, even for non-federal-data workflows, from an already-certified vendor pool. This can block adoption of useful services that never touch federal or CUI data, for example third-party observability and monitoring platforms handling only synthetic or non-customer telemetry, AI-driven feature services like text-to-speech or translation used for product functionality unrelated to federal data. This mirrors a restriction from FedRAMP Rev5, where third-party services had to hold an authorization at the same level as the CSP's own. That approach proved overly restrictive in practice, often forcing CSPs into lower-quality tooling simply because the strongest available vendor hadn't yet pursued certification.

- We also suggest allowing non-certified third-party resources when a CSP can demonstrate the resource never processes federal or CUI data, paired with reporting stipulations that preserve assurance: documented data flow diagrams proving isolation, a assessment scope justification reviewed at each annual assessment, ongoing monitoring and reporting on the third party's security posture (SOC 2 Type II or equivalent, incident history, patch cadence), and a commitment to monitor that provider's vulnerability disclosures as part of the CSP's own vulnerability management program. Any change in the provider's data handling would move the resource back under the standard certified-only requirement. This would let CSPs scale into useful non-federal-facing capabilities without waiting on a niche vendor's FedRAMP business case, while keeping the actual federal data boundary just as tight.

- FedRAMP should ensure guidance accounts for: 

1.) External services that are required for ther operation of the CSO, but that are not themselves strictly CSOs - things like DNS, SMS, Mobile Notification APIs, etc.
2.) External services that are optional and under the configuration and control of a specific customer of a CSO. We should not be limited in our ability to allow customers to use whatever services that want with our CSO.

- Is the FedRAMP working with OMB to mandate standard APIs regarding the requirement to integrating assurance data into agency GRC systems? Individual CSOs should not be on the hook for integrating with agency-specific systems -- unless they are paying the CSP specifically for those integrations (e.g., professional services engagements).

- FedRAMP should also be very clear and specific as to what "additional assurance engineering resources" means and whether there are any costs, service levels, or service availability expectations. What if a CSP has a large number of customer all request support at once?

**Phase 4 Track 2: Expanding 20x to Self-Hosted or Hybrid-Hosted Services**

- The RFC doesn't address how a currently-authorized FedRAMP Rev5 Class D (formerly High) cloud-hosted CSP would obtain a 20x Class D designation. Track 1 appears to require earning 20x Class C first, which effectively asks an already-High-authorized CSP to step down to a Class C 20x certification before re-earning Class D under 20x. It would help to confirm whether that's the intended path, or whether a direct Rev5 Class D to 20x Class D track is planned.

- We request that the anticipated Class D Key Security Indicators and transition options for existing Rev5 Class D cloud-hosted CSPs specifically be included in the October 14 RFC. Many CSPs are trying to budget FY27 and FY28 compliance and engineering investment in the next 8 weeks, and it's difficult to plan responsibly without visibility into the end-state requirements or an interim path for CSPs already operating at the High baseline.

- We request that FedRAMP provide greater detail on the expected level of effort, participation expectations, and any deliverables required of self-hosted/hybrid cloud service providers in the Track 2 direct engagement. Specifically: (a) the anticipated time commitment per participant and per round (e.g., preparation, number and duration of working sessions); (b) what inputs or materials providers are expected to prepare or submit (e.g., existing certifications, written responses to questions); and (c) whether any deliverables or formal work product are expected during or after the engagement. Clear expectations up front will help qualifying providers appropriately resource their participation and make an informed opt-in decision ahead of the October 16 deadline.

Re: RFC-0033 FedRAMP 20x Phase 4 Development Tracks for 20x Class D rhoesing [FEDRAMP-OFFICIAL]: This content came in on October 9, 2026 via email - So I am including as it was submitted before RFC deadline closed. Thank you for the opportunity to review and provide input on this request for comment. Overall, Google supports the structural modernization goals outlined in the draft, but we see several areas where terminology and architectural assumptions require refinement to align with standard industry practices and maintain commercial viability. ## Key Recommendations ### Phased Transition and Equivalency FedRAMP should implement a grandfather clause for Class C certifications and grant High-impact equivalency during the pilot phase to prevent massive provider downgrades while the Class D ecosystem matures. ### Pragmatic Assessment Scoping The Minimum Assessment Scope should be strictly defined by whether a component processes, stores, or transmits federal High-impact data, allowing necessary Class A telemetry and monitoring tools to operate within a Class D boundary without forcing niche vendors out of the market. ### Assurance Engineering Feasibility Mandating active engineering support for all agencies represents a burden that will increase costs and negatively impact service availability for all agencies. Additionally, there are a large depth and breadth of offerings for GRC tools, requiring Cloud providers to offer integration support that would extend beyond GRC agreements the government currently holds. ### Streamlined FOCI Verification To prevent redundant evaluations, FedRAMP should explicitly defer to existing Defense Counterintelligence and Security Agency provisions and accept an eligible status within the National Industrial Security System. ## Proposed Revisions to Language Provided | Section Title | Current Text | Google Proposed Changes | |---|---|---| | Cloud-Hosted | A cloud service offering where machine-based information resources primarily run on third-party cloud service offerings and the cloud service provider is not responsible for the physical infrastructure used. | Google recommends renaming the label to reflect the architecture's reliance on external IaaS and rewriting the definition to eliminate recursion, as the current language conflates the software vendor with the infrastructure provider.

**Proposed Section Title:** Third-Party Hosted Cloud Service Offering

**Proposed Definition:** A service offering where the underlying compute, storage, and networking resources run on infrastructure managed by an external, third-party Cloud Infrastructure Provider (IaaS). The primary service provider is responsible for the application and platform layers, but is not responsible for the physical hardware or data center facilities. | | Self-Hosted | A cloud service offering where machine-based information resources primarily run on physical infrastructure operated by the cloud service provider, either directly or through an agreement with a third party. This includes fully self-managed infrastructure as well as infrastructure running in a colocated facility or fully managed by a third party where the cloud service provider itself takes full responsibility for the physical infrastructure. | Google recommends renaming the label to reflect the architecture's reliance on external IaaS and rewriting the definition to eliminate recursion.

**Proposed Section Title:** Provider-Hosted / First-Party Hosted Cloud Service Offering

**Proposed Definition:** A service offering where the primary service provider operates and maintains direct control over the underlying physical infrastructure. This includes first-party data centers, leased colocation facilities, or bare-metal environments where the primary provider maintains operational control and assumes full responsibility for the hardware layer. | | Hybrid-Hosted | A cloud service offering where some machine-based information resources are cloud-hosted and others are self-hosted. | Google recommends updating the terminology to reflect a mix of first-party and third-party backend infrastructure, as the term hybrid typically refers to cloud and customer on-premises environments.

**Proposed Section Title:** Multi-Environment / Hybrid-Backend Cloud Service Offering

**Proposed Definition:** A distributed service offering that utilizes a combination of Provider-Hosted infrastructure and Third-Party Hosted cloud resources, with workloads, data, or services orchestrated across both environments. | Thank you!
