discussion_title: Clarification requested: Is `Content-Type: application/json` a normative MUST for all FedRAMP-required JSON artifacts?
author: jdettweiler
text:
Re: Clarification requested: Is `Content-Type: application/json` a normative MUST for all FedRAMP-required JSON artifacts?

jdettweiler: Thank you, Pete. I appreciate the response, and I agree with the broader goal of making Certification Data practically consumable by FedRAMP and agencies.

I think the remaining concern for us is less about this particular HTTP header and more about how a CSP is expected to make an engineering decision today based on the published rules. We are actively expending engineering resources implementing CR26. In our case, that includes significant automation around Box as our Trust Center. We selected that architecture based in part on FedRAMP's published position that a FedRAMP-compatible Trust Center can be any secure repository or service that satisfies the CDS-TRC requirements, with the current guidance even describing a WordPress-hosted Trust Center as a possible implementation.

If the actual acceptance criterion is broader than the explicit rules and is instead whether an implementation is ultimately “FedRAMP-consumable,” then I think CSPs need a concrete definition of that interface before building against it. We are not asking FedRAMP to guarantee that Box, or any particular vendor, will be supported indefinitely. We are asking whether an implementation that satisfies the current explicit Consolidated Rules can reasonably be relied upon as compliant today.

If FedRAMP requires additional characteristics for automated consumption, specific HTTP headers, authentication flows, API behavior, credential types, URL behavior, or other interface characteristics, those requirements materially influence architecture and vendor selection and should be part of the published interoperability contract.

Otherwise, a CSP can spend substantial engineering time and money implementing automation that satisfies the published requirements, only to later discover that a technically conforming implementation is not considered usable because of an unstated interface expectation. That is the situation we are trying to avoid.

### Authentication illustrates the broader problem

The Trust Center model also raises a related machine-access question. The rules require documented programmatic access to Certification Data while also contemplating controlled access, agency-user/system inventories, access logging, and mechanisms such as JIT access. For non-public Certification Data, FedRAMP will therefore ultimately need some method of authenticating programmatically to each CSP's Trust Center, whether through service accounts, OAuth client credentials, federation, or another mechanism.

We actually raised this issue with the PMO in September 2025. At that time, we specifically asked whether Login.gov could support agency access to CSP Trust Centers, whether FedRAMP could facilitate a common federation pattern, or alternatively what authentication approach CSPs should implement.

Our question was specifically about federal agency users accessing Trust Center information, not authentication to our commercial service. That distinction was explained in the follow-up exchange.  Our original questions also explicitly asked about a PMO-sponsored federation pattern and recommended authentication mechanisms for Trust Centers. 

That architectural question remains important. If every CSP independently selects a different Trust Center and authentication mechanism, FedRAMP may eventually need to establish and maintain a different machine identity or credential relationship with each CSP. If the intended future state is centralized federation, a standard service identity, an OAuth/OIDC profile, or some other common mechanism, CSPs need to know that before committing significant engineering resources to another pattern.

### Changes to the technical contract also have schedule implications

There is a second issue that I think is becoming increasingly important as CSPs move from reading CR26 to actually implementing it. CR26 is not simply a documentation exercise. For CSPs attempting to implement the machine-readable and programmatic-access portions as intended, it requires real software engineering: schemas, exporters, APIs, authentication flows, validation pipelines, Trust Center integrations, automated evidence generation, and changes to existing GRC processes.

Our experience has been that the amount of engineering required is materially greater than may be apparent from a high-level discussion of “automation.” We have evaluated this in the context of actual implementation, and there is not currently a broad set of off-the-shelf GRC products that simply makes all of these requirements work without integration and development effort. That matters when requirements change after implementation work has already begun.

We certainly understand that CR26 will continue to evolve. But when an interpretation introduces a new technical requirement that changes architecture, invalidates an existing implementation, or requires CSPs to modify code, we believe it should be handled as a versioned change to the technical contract, rather than simply becoming an immediately applicable interpretation of an existing rule.

FedRAMP's own public repository maintenance guidance uses essentially this software-engineering concept when describing breaking changes: changes that cause existing parsers, validators, exporters, queries, or integrations to fail, reject previously valid data, or require code changes to continue processing the machine-readable contract. That is a useful model for CR26 generally.

If a new requirement meets that threshold, we believe the change-management process should include:

- a documented change to the applicable Consolidated Rule or schema;
- identification of whether the change is breaking or non-breaking;
- a clear effective date;
- a migration or grace period appropriate to the engineering impact; and
- corresponding adjustment of compliance deadlines where the change materially affects work already underway.

The Consolidated Rules data model already distinguishes obtain, maintain, optional-adoption, and grace dates, so there is already a mechanism available to manage this kind of transition. This last point is important. The implementation clock and the requirements baseline cannot reasonably move independently of one another.

If CSPs are being held to fixed CR26 implementation dates while the technical interface they are expected to build against remains subject to material changes or new interoperability requirements, CSPs absorb the entire schedule risk created by those changes. That is especially difficult when engineering work completed in good faith against the published rules may need to be redesigned because a later interpretation establishes a technical constraint that was not previously documented. We are not suggesting that FedRAMP freeze CR26. We are suggesting that when FedRAMP changes the engineering contract, the implementation schedule should move with it in a manner proportionate to the impact of that change.

### What would help us move forward

I think four concrete clarifications would help considerably:

1. Can CSPs rely on satisfying the currently published Consolidated Rules as the acceptance criteria for Trust Center implementations?
2. If “FedRAMP-consumable” imposes additional technical requirements beyond those rules, can FedRAMP publish a minimum interoperability profile covering transport, authentication, programmatic retrieval, and related interface expectations?
3. Is FedRAMP considering a standardized authentication/federation mechanism for its own programmatic access to authenticated Trust Center data, rather than requiring unique credential integration with every CSP?
4. When new or changed technical requirements require CSPs to redesign integrations or modify code, will FedRAMP treat those as versioned changes with appropriate effective dates, grace periods, and extensions to affected implementation deadlines?

I recognize that this area is evolving, and I don't expect FedRAMP to predict every future technical decision. What CSPs do need is a stable and testable baseline for the requirements effective today, together with normal software change-management practices when that baseline changes.

We would be very happy to spend 30 minutes with you and the appropriate technical stakeholders to walk through the Box implementation, the authentication issue, and the automation we have already built. I think a short technical discussion could help distinguish between the outcomes FedRAMP is trying to achieve and the implementation assumptions CSPs are currently having to infer.

Thanks again for engaging on this.

pete-gov [FEDRAMP-OFFICIAL]: Johann - we have been quite clear that there will need to be occasional small tweaks to the rules and that we will do so quickly while trying to mitigate the impact. A lot of these will be responsive to problems we discover in the real world during implementation.

We're not looking to make this a big complicated over spec'd thing. The ask at the moment is simple: we, and many other customers, need to be able to access machine-readable JSON data via a web-based application that we expect to directly read and operate on that data using interoperable web standards. FedRAMP and government agencies shouldn't need to build a bespoke custom pipeline just for one company in order to access their certification data. Addressing this is not an engineering challenge, and this type of cross origin resource sharing has been a standard practice for nearly 20 years. We aren't asking you to invent something new, we just expect to be able to access the JSON data via our web-based SaaS applications.

discussion_title: Clarification requested: Is `Content-Type: application/json` a normative MUST for all FedRAMP-required JSON artifacts?
author: jdettweiler
text:
Re: Clarification requested: Is `Content-Type: application/json` a normative MUST for all FedRAMP-required JSON artifacts?

jdettweiler: Thanks, Pete. I appreciate the response. I think the discussion may have drifted a little from the specific issue that caused us to raise this in the first place, so I want to reconnect the architectural questions to the original implementation problem. This started because we attempted to update our FedRAMP Marketplace listing by providing the PMO with our public CPO JSON hosted in our Box Trust Center. The underlying artifact is valid JSON and validates successfully against the applicable FedRAMP schema. However, the submission was rejected because Box serves the file using:

```
Content-Type: application/octet-stream
```

rather than:

```
Content-Type: application/json
```

We were subsequently told that the CPO could only be provided if the HTTP response used `application/json`, and that this expectation applied more broadly to FedRAMP-required JSON artifacts. That is what prompted the question in this thread.

We have already implemented a workaround for the public CPO, so I am not asking FedRAMP to change the Marketplace validator. What concerns me is what that experience tells us about the broader CR26 implementation model: we implemented against the written requirement that the document be valid, machine-readable, schema-conformant JSON, but discovered an additional transport-level acceptance criterion only when we attempted to submit it.

That distinction matters because we are actively spending engineering resources implementing the rest of CR26. I completely agree that agencies obtaining controlled security documentation from CSPs is not new. CSPs and agencies have exchanged authorization packages through portals, secure repositories, file shares, and similar mechanisms for many years.

What seems materially different now is the expectation for machine-readable Certification Data to be programmatically consumed across independently operated Trust Centers. CDS-TRC-PAC requires programmatic access to Certification Data, while the broader Trust Center model also contemplates controlled information, agency users or systems with access, access inventories, access logging, and mechanisms such as JIT provisioning. For non-public Certification Data, a machine therefore needs some way to authenticate.

### We can solve this with Box today

To make this concrete, we can provide FedRAMP programmatic access to our Box Trust Center using Box's native server-to-server capabilities. We can establish an OAuth 2.0 Client Credentials Grant application, authorize it to the appropriate Trust Center resources, and provide FedRAMP with a dedicated machine identity. FedRAMP could then obtain short-lived access tokens and retrieve Certification Data through the Box API without human interaction. From our perspective, that appears to meet the intent of programmatic access.

We are not asking FedRAMP to bless Box as a product or guarantee that Box will always be acceptable. The question is more fundamental: If we implement programmatic access using the native capabilities of our selected Trust Center and satisfy the explicit CDS-TRC requirements, can we rely on that implementation as compliant today?

If yes, we can continue engineering against that contract. If no because FedRAMP ultimately expects some different transport, authentication, API, credential, URL, or retrieval behavior, then those expectations materially affect architecture and need to be known before CSPs invest in implementations.

The `Content-Type` issue is a good example of why that matters. The Box-hosted CPO contained the correct data and passed schema validation, but the architecture was nevertheless rejected because of an additional HTTP behavior that was not apparent to us from the rule we were implementing.

### The scaling question is what I still do not understand

A Box Client Credentials Grant would establish a machine-to-machine trust relationship between our Trust Center and FedRAMP. If an agency also requires programmatic access to protected Certification Data, we would need to establish an appropriate identity or integration for that agency as well, particularly if access must be attributable for inventory and logging purposes. Now multiply that across the ecosystem.

One CSP may use Box. Another may use SharePoint/Graph. Another may use Vanta or Paramify. Another may expose a custom OAuth API. Without some common interoperability model, the resulting architecture appears to be something like:

```
FedRAMP  -> CSP A / Box credentials + API
         -> CSP B / Microsoft Graph credentials + API
         -> CSP C / commercial Trust Center API
         -> CSP D / custom OAuth API
         -> ...

Agency X -> CSP A integration
         -> CSP B integration
         -> CSP C integration
         -> ...

Agency Y -> CSP A integration
         -> CSP B integration
         -> ...
```

I may be missing an intended mechanism, but I do not understand how authenticated programmatic access scales across hundreds of CSPs and federal agencies without at least one of the following:

1. a common federation or service-identity model;
2. a standardized authentication and retrieval profile implemented by Trust Centers; or
3. some centralized brokerage/aggregation capability that normalizes these integrations.

The Trust Centers themselves do not need to be centralized. But it seems that some portion of the trust and interoperability layer has to be standardized if the objective is automated consumption across the FedRAMP ecosystem. This is what we were trying to get at when we previously asked the PMO about Login.gov. Login.gov itself was only one possible implementation. The broader question was whether FedRAMP intended to provide or define a common identity/federation mechanism for federal users and systems accessing independently operated CSP Trust Centers.

### This is why the “20 years” point does not completely resolve the concern for me

Human users obtaining authorization documentation from controlled CSP repositories has been done for many years. But having machines automatically authenticate to, retrieve, validate, and continuously consume structured Certification Data from independently operated repositories is a different engineering model.

That model may absolutely be the right direction, and we support the move toward automation. But CSPs are already investing engineering resources to implement it, which means the interface contract needs to be stable enough to build against.

### The questions I am ultimately trying to answer are:

1. Would the Box Client Credentials Grant model described above be considered a valid implementation of programmatic Trust Center access under CDS-TRC-PAC?
2. Can CSPs rely on satisfying the currently published Consolidated Rules using the native capabilities of their selected Trust Center platform as the acceptance criteria today?
3. Does FedRAMP expect to establish and maintain CSP-specific machine credentials/integrations with each Trust Center, and are agencies expected to do the same independently?
4. Or is FedRAMP planning a common service identity, federation profile, authentication standard, retrieval profile, or aggregation mechanism for machine consumption?
5. If additional technical requirements are introduced that require CSPs to redesign integrations or modify code, will those be treated as versioned changes with appropriate effective dates, grace periods, and adjustments to affected CR26 implementation deadlines?

pete-gov [FEDRAMP-OFFICIAL]: Out of curiosity are you using AI to generate these very long structured responses? I'm struggling to parse them and the language is very demanding, which doesn't really match my experience interacting with either you or @vennemp and makes this thread a bit confusing. It feels like I'm talking with a chatbot not a person. I can do that on my own time any time, but it would be helpful either way if this discussion was way more concise.

I think in the near term we can split the difference in the near term - a strict mandate for web interoperability on JSON data that is required to be public (such as [CDS-CSO-PUB](https://www.fedramp.gov/2026/reference/certification-data-sharing/#public-information) and [CDS-CSO-SVC](https://www.fedramp.gov/2026/reference/certification-data-sharing/#public-service-list)) in the immediate future, following by additional public discussions and an RFC on web interoperability for JSON data that is inside a Trust Center authentication wall. 

> This started because we attempted to update our FedRAMP Marketplace listing by providing the PMO with our public CPO JSON hosted in our Box Trust Center. 

This will apply to the data required for a marketplace listing **because if your Marketplace data isn't compatible with basic web interoperability standards then we can't use it.** Again, this isn't a complicated thing, it's just CORS allow and an appropriate content-type. You can set up this public information in less time than it has taken to have this conversation this morning.

Either way, as always, FedRAMP will continue to encourage folks to consider the experience of their customers (including FedRAMP) as a driving factor in decision making.



vennemp: I was actually writing mine lol which is probably why they were incoherent.  

pete-gov [FEDRAMP-OFFICIAL]: Your comments feel entirely genuine Matt, no worries :) It's the weird long stuff from Johann that feels super wonky.

jdettweiler: Pete - Yes, I'm absolutely using AI to manage these conversations, at the encouragement of FedRAMP. Including .agent files in the new rule libraries was a great idea and I'm taking full advantage of it. 

I recognize that can make some of my comments a little dense, but the detail is intentional. These discussions increasingly become part of the technical context that our automation reasons over, so precision matters. As FedRAMP moves further toward machine-readable requirements and automated validation, the more explicit and unambiguous we can make the underlying requirements and implementation expectations, the better and more reliable the resulting automation will be.

Ultimately, we appear to be on the same page for now as we've made adjustments to how the CPO is served. My disappointment was that in our first interaction with FedRAMP on a new CR26 deliverable, there seemed to be a "hidden" requirement that prevented success and required re-engineering. I'll keep the conversations going as we encounter these issues and hope that you will remain open to hearing about the impacts sometimes seemingly minor decisions can have on automation designs. 

pete-gov [FEDRAMP-OFFICIAL]: > Pete - Yes, I'm absolutely using AI to manage these conversations, at the encouragement of FedRAMP. Including .agent files in the new rule libraries was a great idea and I'm taking full advantage of it.

I would strongly encourage you to use AI to manage knowledge related to FedRAMP, yes, absolutely. And I would encourage using it to prep and think as a partner.

It is not helpful to use it to navigate a conversation on your behalf though - there is still a certain obsequious arrogance to most agent output that creates an uncanny valley effect which makes understanding and processing the actual human intent very difficult. 

One thing I will promise you is that my team and I do not and will not use AI to manage these interactions directly. We dedicate considerable and real human time to this in place of other critical tasks because of how we prioritize it. Please do us the courtesy of engaging directly as a human with us so that we can continue to do this.

> My disappointment was that in our first interaction with FedRAMP on a new CR26 deliverable, there seemed to be a "hidden" requirement that prevented success and required re-engineering.

This is 100% fair, and that's why I immediately identified a need to update the rules when it was brought to me. We thought the rules had been written clearly enough that this wouldn't be considered a hidden requirement but real world testing with you demonstrated this assumption was wrong. That's how we learn and improve.

None of us want FedRAMP to return to a world where we spend 5 years arguing about explicit and unambiguous requirements that can meet every possible situation before giving up and starting over because it's an impossible task in a fast-moving technology-based arena. That means sometimes some folks are going to go hard in one direction that FedRAMP might decide is not the right direction, and participants need to be prepared for that reality.

discussion_title: FRC-CSX-VVK - How does FedRAMP interpret "Automated Methods" for KSI Validation
author: jdettweiler
text:
FRC-CSX-VVK - How does FedRAMP interpret "Automated Methods" for KSI Validation

I was hoping to see if I could get some clarity around FRC-CSX-VVK, which requires automated methods to persistently verify and validate the accuracy and completeness of each Key Security Indicator. Current requirements are noted as: 

```
Class A: MAY implement automated methods; no minimum.
Class B: SHOULD use at least 1 automated method per KSI.
Class C: MUST use at least 2 automated methods per KSI.
Class D: MUST use at least 4 automated methods per KSI.

Source: FRR.FRC.data.20x.CSX.FRC-CSX-VVK, dataset version 2026.09.13.02
```

Would it be possible for FedRAMP clarify how it determines whether two automated validations are distinct methods for this purpose? We are currently building out an automated assessment platform, so I want to provide a real world example of how we are validating/assessing KSI-CNA-EIS "Enforcing Intended State". The platform executes multiple deterministic checks and produces a single assessor-readable "assessment" report. The assessment currently evaluates:

| Assessment area                                          | Intended role                                                |
| -------------------------------------------------------- | ------------------------------------------------------------ |
| Persistent vulnerability and compliance scan telemetry   | Recurring machine-resource security assessment               |
| Organization Policy source-to-effective-state comparison | Validate that deployed effective policies match version-controlled intended state |
| Provider boundary source-to-live-membership comparison   | Validate that provider boundary enforcement is active for the complete scoped population |
| OS policy source-to-live-assignment comparison           | Validate that deployed OS policy assignments match the intended enforcement chain |
| Endpoint/host policy and agent telemetry                 | Validate bounded host anti-malware enforcement               |
| GCP asset and enabled-service inventory coverage         | Establish complete population coverage for the above validations |
| Finding/disposition tracking                             | Confirm that detected drift and findings are tracked         |
| Process documentation                                    | Establish the documented assessment and lifecycle process    |

The automated assessment platform produces machine-readable results/evidence, operates on defined in-scope populations, has distinct logic and failure conditions, and is designed to run repeatedly. 

Since this is all occurring in a single assessment platform, ultimately the question is does this count as a single "automated method" or does the table above represent multiple "automated methods" since deterministic telemetry is being retrieved and correlated from multiple security mechanisms within the environment (e.g., vulnerability scanner, endpoint manager, document repository that contains policy and procedures, ITSM, etc.)?

discussion_title: FRC-CSX-VVK - How does FedRAMP interpret "Automated Methods" for KSI Validation
author: pete-gov
text:
Re: FRC-CSX-VVK - How does FedRAMP interpret "Automated Methods" for KSI Validation

pete-gov [FEDRAMP-OFFICIAL]: > Would it be possible for FedRAMP clarify how it determines whether two automated validations are distinct methods for this purpose?

This is up to the cloud service provider. You are making a choice that is designed to assure customers of your security posture and coverage of the KSI. If you make poor choices, potential customers are less likely to find your assurance adequate. If you make good choices, potential customers are more likely to find your assurance adequate. 

Don't think of this as "what do I need to do to get a FedRAMP Certification" - **think of it as "what do I need to do to assurance customers that I protect their information?"**

During FedRAMP Certification we will include our own report on how usefully assuring and diverse we think the methods used are.

discussion_title: Updates to frrAssessment or ksiAssessment content
author: gmengelberg
text:
Updates to frrAssessment or ksiAssessment content

- Is a CSP allowed to update the frrAssessment/ksiAssessment content provided by an IA during an assessment?
    - If not, how would the content be updated if the CSP changed the implementation to address the discrepancies identified during the assessment?

discussion_title: Updates to frrAssessment or ksiAssessment content
author: pete-gov
text:
Re: Updates to frrAssessment or ksiAssessment content

pete-gov [FEDRAMP-OFFICIAL]: I'm not entirely sure I understand the context of the question but if you are asking if SDR information can change throughout the assessment then the answer is yes, very much so, and it very much should. If an assessor finds an issue with something that the cloud service provider agrees with then the provider should make appropriate changes and get it reassessed before submitting to FedRAMP. 

gmengelberg: Thanks for the reply @pete-gov.

During an assessment, an Independent Assessor may identify instances where the content in the SDR _(frr|ksi)Implementation_ attribute(s) does not address the practice requirements, or instances where it is not faithfully implemented.  In these instances, the assessor would document the discrepancy in the _(frr|ksi)Assessment_ attribute and provide it to the CSP to update the SDR (per IVV-CSO-ICP). 

Over time, the CSP would update the SDR _(frr|ksi)Implementation_ content, and/or the actual implementation, and will want the _(frr|ksi)Assessment_ attribute to be updated to show that there is no longer a discrepancy; however, the assessment has already concluded and the assessor has disengaged.

If the CSP was not allowed to update the _(frr|ksi)Assessment_ attribute in a meaningful way, the documented discrepancy would remain in the SDR until the assessor is re-engaged. In many cases, this may be upwards of a year. If the CSP is allowed to update these attributes once the discrepancy addressed, then the SDR could more faithfully reflect the current state of the system.

Hopefully this helps to clarify why I am asking my question(s).

discussion_title: MKT-IIP-AGU: what evidence shows a cloud service is "intended for" agency use?
author: fitz-taylor
text:
MKT-IIP-AGU: what evidence shows a cloud service is "intended for" agency use?

We're a small SaaS provider preparing for a 20x Class C assessment on the Program Certification path. Our customers today are federal contractors, and we are pursuing federal agency users in parallel. MKT-IIP-AGU says a provider must demonstrate the offering is intended for direct or indirect agency use, but the rules don't say what evidence FedRAMP looks for. Five questions:

1. What evidence demonstrates intended direct use: a letter of intent from an agency program office, a no-cost pilot or evaluation agreement, an SBIR end-user memo, or only a contract? Does it need to come from an authorizing official?
2. If one boundary contains several applications, is an agency use case for one application enough for the whole offering?
3. For indirect use, what shows that an offering is included as a third-party information resource in another agency-used offering: a letter from that provider, or its listing documentation?
4. If an offering serves both agencies and private contractors, does contractor use (including for CMMC) matter once one agency use case is real?
5. Timing: must the use case exist at Initial Implementation listing, or can it be shown by the time we apply for certification?

discussion_title: MKT-IIP-AGU: what evidence shows a cloud service is "intended for" agency use?
author: pete-gov
text:
Re: MKT-IIP-AGU: what evidence shows a cloud service is "intended for" agency use?

pete-gov [FEDRAMP-OFFICIAL]: > MKT-IIP-AGU says a provider must demonstrate the offering is intended for direct or indirect agency use, but the rules don't say what evidence FedRAMP looks for. 

This isn't about what agencies say they will or won't do, this is about what your product is designed to do. It should be relatively straightforward to demonstrate that you expect agencies to directly or indirectly use your product. 

On the flip side, sometimes it's pretty straightforward that products are not intended for direct or indirect agency use. For example, if you offering a gambling machine management service then it might require a bit more clarity on how exactly you expect agencies to use that cloud computing product.

> What evidence demonstrates intended direct use: a letter of intent from an agency program office, a no-cost pilot or evaluation agreement, an SBIR end-user memo, or only a contract? Does it need to come from an authorizing official?

It comes from the business, not an agency. It's an attestation where you are saying that you are not making a false claim about what your product is intended to do in order to trick the government (FedRAMP) into spending official resources on reviewing your product if your intent is not to participate in the FedRAMP Marketplace. Don't make false claims!

> If one boundary contains several applications, is an agency use case for one application enough for the whole offering?

That would be very much against the principles of the minimum assessment scope and appear designed to waste government time and resources, which probably wouldn't go over very well. Don't include things in a cloud service offering that aren't necessary for the cloud service offering. That's not an explicit rule as much as it's just a good idea.

> For indirect use, what shows that an offering is included as a third-party information resource in another agency-used offering: a letter from that provider, or its listing documentation?

The simplest way to provably demonstrate this is to to show us which FedRAMP Certified cloud service offerings use the product in their cloud service offering.

> If an offering serves both agencies and private contractors, does contractor use (including for CMMC) matter once one agency use case is real?

FedRAMP is for commercial cloud service offerings, the same offering can be available to commercial customers and government customers.

> Timing: must the use case exist at Initial Implementation listing, or can it be shown by the time we apply for certification?

You must provide this demonstration when requesting a marketplace listing, yes.

This is one of those things where we get a bit nervous when people start worrying about how they're going to demonstrate that their product is designed to be used by agencies because it shouldn't be that tricky....

discussion_title: RFC-0035 Cryptographic Module Use Rules Updates
author: pete-gov
text:
RFC-0035 Cryptographic Module Use Rules Updates

# RFC-0035 Cryptographic Module Use Rules Updates

- Status: Open
- Start Date: October 14, 2026
- Closing Date: November 17, 2026

> Current Cryptographic Module Use rules for reference: https://www.fedramp.gov/2026/reference/cryptographic-module-use/

## **Summary**

This RFC proposes updates to the Cryptographic Module Use (CMU) rules in the Consolidated Rules for 2026 (CR26) for both 20X and Rev 5. The proposed updates remove a previously firm barrier at Class D but do not require currently operating cloud services to do anything differently.

1. Define “CMVP-validated module” as a cryptographic module that has an active validation in the NIST Cryptographic Module Validation Program (or an update stream of such). This simplifies much of the language and discussion in the rules without using potentially confusing standalone terms like “validated encryption.”
2. Change CMU-CSO-UVM for Class D from MUST to SHOULD, matching Class C.
3. Add CMU-CSO-TSC, which treats replacing a CMVP-validated module with a non-validated one as a transformative change for Class B, C, and D
4. Move the update-stream note from CMU-CSO-UVM to the new definition, and replace the term “Validation” in the CMU rules with “CMVP-Validated Module”.

This RFC also does not change agency obligations under FIPS 140-3, or set post-quantum cryptography requirements. Instead, this RFC acknowledges that many agency customers frequently use cloud services where validated cryptographic modules are not in play and FedRAMP’s role is not to block agency access to this type of service when an agency deems it is appropriate or necessary.

## **Motivation**

Agencies decide where they rely on cryptography to protect federal information. Where they do, FIPS 140-3 applies regardless of FedRAMP Certification Class. There exist many valid technical reasons for agencies to bypass the requirements in FIPS 140-3 today, whether because the data is not sensitive enough to be encrypted with NIST Cryptographic Module Validation Program (CMVP) validated modules or because a specific agency use case requires devices or software that do not have validated modules.

Requiring Class D services to use only CMVP-validated modules can force providers to run separate cryptography for government customers. That cryptography can cost more, lag behind commercial security updates, and perform worse than alternative solutions that still provide sufficient protection for specific use cases.

This proposed change to the FedRAMP Certification rules, especially for Class D, will allow cloud services with specific use cases or valid technical reasons to use other types of cryptography to obtain and maintain a FedRAMP Certification. The existing rule of CMU-CSO-CMD (Cryptographic Module Documentation) requires cloud service providers to clearly document their use of cryptographic modules such that a potential agency customer will always know where and how the cloud service offering uses cryptographic modules and the potential risks of placing sensitive agency data into different parts of the cloud service offering. This proposed change will also allow cloud service providers to integrate emerging cryptographic technologies such as Post-Quantum Cryptography in some parts of their offering at the direct request of agency customers without creating vulnerabilities in the FedRAMP Practices.

Finally, the proposed change forces cloud service providers to treat changes where a CMVP-validated module is removed from an aspect of the cloud service offering as a transformative change to ensure that agency customers have sufficient and timely warning of the change so that they can make updated risk determinations about the continued use of the service if a cloud service offering stops using such modules.

## **Specific Proposed Changes**

### FedRAMP Definitions

**FRD-CVM** CMVP-Validated Module

> A cryptographic module that has an active validation under the NIST Cryptographic Module Validation Program, or an update stream of such a module.
>
> _Note: Cryptographic modules include specific algorithms by definition; if an update stream of a cryptographic module adds new algorithms that were not previously validated then those algorithms cannot be considered within the scope of update stream usage under these rules as they are new algorithms within the module that have never been validated._

### Cryptographic Module Use

**CMU-CSO-CMD** Cryptographic Module Documentation

> Providers MUST document the cryptographic modules used in each service (or groups of services that use the same modules) where cryptographic services are used to protect federal customer data, including whether they are CMVP-validated modules.
>
> _Note: This change simply incorporates the “CMVP-validated modules” definition; no functional change._

**CMU-CSO-UVM** Using CMVP-Validated Modules

> Providers with Class A Certifications MAY use CMVP-validated modules when using cryptographic services to protect federal customer data.
>
> Providers with Class B Certifications MAY use CMVP-validated modules when using cryptographic services to protect federal customer data.
>
> Providers with Class C Certifications SHOULD use CMVP-validated modules when using cryptographic services to protect federal customer data.
>
> Providers with Class D Certifications SHOULD use CMVP-validated modules when using cryptographic services to protect federal customer data.
>
> _Note: This change does not alter agency obligations under FIPS 140-3. Agencies use the documentation required by CMU-CSO-CMD to confirm where CMVP-validated modules protect federal customer data._

**CMU-CSO-TSC** Transformative Significant Changes of Modules

> Providers MUST treat changes from CMVP-validated modules to non-CMVP-validated modules as transformative changes when such cryptographic services are used to protect federal customer data.
>
> _Notes:_
>
> - _This is a new proposed rule that would apply to Class B, Class C, and Class D FedRAMP Certifications of both 20x and Rev5._
> - _Updating a CMVP-validated module through its update stream is not such a change. An algorithm that an update stream **adds** is not within the module's validation; using one in place of a validated algorithm is such a change. Adding a non-validated algorithm while a CMVP-validated module still protects federal customer data, such as hybrid implementation, is not such a change._

**CMU-CSO-CAT** Configuration of Agency Tenants

> Providers SHOULD configure agency tenants by default to use cryptographic services that use CMVP-validated modules when such modules are available.
>
> _Note: This change simply incorporates the “CMVP-validated modules” definition; no functional change._

discussion_title: RFC-0035 Cryptographic Module Use Rules Updates
author: az-kennedy
text:
Re: RFC-0035 Cryptographic Module Use Rules Updates

az-kennedy: I understand the rationale for changing the requirement for Class D in CMU-CSO-UVM from MUST to SHOULD. My concern is how this change will affect CSPs and agencies downstream.

Today, a Class D designation tells us that a CSP offering uses FIPS-validated cryptographic modules. If the requirement becomes SHOULD, that assurance goes away. CSPs and agencies would no longer be able to tell whether a product uses FIPS-validated modules without access to the CSP’s CR26 implementation details.

The SHOULD language also leaves CSPs unsure whether they need to refactor their applications. An agency could still require FIPS-validated modules under FISMA and OMB M-11-33, so a CSP may not find out a refactor is needed until an agency asks for it. That makes long-term technical and financial planning for serving the Federal Government much harder.

I’d ask that the Class D requirement stay at MUST. If it does change to SHOULD, please require CSPs to publicly disclose whether their offering uses FIPS-validated modules, so agencies and other CSPs don’t need CR26 implementation details to find out.

discussion_title: RFC-0035 Cryptographic Module Use Rules Updates
author: ryangmsi
text:
Re: RFC-0035 Cryptographic Module Use Rules Updates

ryangmsi: Commenting as a FedRAMP 3PAO assessor who also works CMMC with DIB contractors.

I support CMU-CSO-TSC and the hybrid carve-out for PQC. A few things I'd like tightened before this is final:

1. FRD-CVM says "active validation," and every FIPS 140-2 certificate moved to the CMVP Historical list on September 21, 2026. Plenty of packages still cite 140-2 certificates for OS-level modules the CSP never touched. Read literally, those providers just went from CMVP-validated to non-validated without making a change. Please state whether CMU-CSO-TSC applies only to provider-initiated module swaps or also to certificate status changes (Historical, revoked). My suggestion is to keep TSC for provider-initiated changes and require CMU-CSO-CMD documentation to be updated within a set window when a certificate's status changes, along with a target date for moving to an active 140-3 module. It would also help to say how FedRAMP treats Historical modules in existing systems, since NIST still allows that use.

2. I agree with @az-kennedy that Class D has been the one place an agency or downstream CSP could assume validated crypto without digging. This matters a lot for DoD. DFARS 252.204-7012 (through SP 800-171 3.13.11) and CMMC SC.L2-3.13.11 require FIPS-validated cryptography for CUI, and DIB contractors already have to dig through Class C packages to confirm it. If Class D moves to SHOULD, please add a public, machine-readable field in the certification data and on the Marketplace stating whether federal customer data is protected by CMVP-validated modules: all, some, or none. Applying it to every class would solve the Class C problem too.

3. CMU-CSO-CMD should spell out what an assessor actually validates. The crypto findings I write most often are certificates cited for modules that aren't running in approved mode, are outside the tested operating environment, or are a version the certificate doesn't cover. Requiring the certificate number, module version, approved-mode status, and the data flow each module protects would make the documentation testable. The update-stream note also needs an evidence standard: is a vendor attestation enough, or does the assessor need to verify lineage back to the validated version?

discussion_title: RFC-0035 Cryptographic Module Use Rules Updates
author: alexmellott
text:
Re: RFC-0035 Cryptographic Module Use Rules Updates

alexmellott: I am in support of modernizing this rule. Forcing CSPs to use FIPS exclusively doesn't provide a tangible security benefit and often furthers fragmentation in service offerings. As FedRAMP has previously discussed as a program goal, getting to the state of parity between commercial and government offerings is far overdue. Removing a "hard" requirement of FIPS exclusively (which tends to lag behind modernized encryption that is _far_ more suited to protect today's threat environments [i.e. post-quantum crypto, elliptic curve, etc.]) is a worthy improvement. I do worry about potential agency adoption of non-FIPS as they evaluate in their RMF/FIPS 199 contexts, so I would suggest guidance to agencies on how to properly evaluate cryptographic protections for their particular use cases.

discussion_title: RFC-0036 FedRAMP 20x Class D Cloud-Hosted Pilot Requirements
author: pete-gov
text:
RFC-0036 FedRAMP 20x Class D Cloud-Hosted Pilot Requirements

# RFC-0036 FedRAMP 20x Class D Cloud-Hosted Pilot Requirements

- Status: Open
- Start Date: October 15, 2026
- Closing Date: November 19, 2026

**Note:** You can discuss this RFC without making formal comment in discussion #181 .

## **Summary & Motivation**

The FedRAMP 20x Cloud-Hosted Class D Pilot will explore the impact and implementation of the highest assurance level of FedRAMP Certification for cloud-hosted services. This RFC proposes specific changes to a variety of rulesets and key security indicators to test during the Phase 4 pilot.

This RFC includes the following:

- 2 new definitions
- Miscellaneous updates to 6 different rulesets
- 10 new Key Security Indicators

Additional rules and Key Security Indicators may be added during or after the Phase 4 pilot, and the existing rules and indicators are likely to change based on direct feedback during the pilot. FedRAMP understands that it would be convenient to know exactly what the rules are likely to be a year in advance, but that is not a realistic approach to developing a new process that is responsive to real world impacts.

**The addition of Foreign Ownership, Control or Influence (FOCI) information:**

FedRAMP seeks to drive a balance between the amount of assurance related to FOCI that agencies might expect and the varying amounts of assurance related to FOCI that different cloud service providers may invest in. The goal is to provide basis rules and indicators that a cloud service provider can follow to provide an appropriate level of assurance, based on their own business strategy, in a fashion that can be shared with all potential agency customers. FedRAMP FOCI practices do not replace agency-specific needs or determinations, but should allow cloud service providers that implement them to save time and effort during an agency review.

FedRAMP will make no determinations on FOCI itself, only confirm whether cloud service providers adequately demonstrate that they persistently review the necessary indicators to understand FOCI and their business.

## **Feedback Requested**

This RFC is intended specifically for the Phase 4 Cloud-Hosted pilot. FedRAMP is looking for feedback on the clarity, applicability, reasonability, and achievability of the proposed rules and Key Security Indicators for companies who wish to meet the highest levels of assurance for federal customers.

This RFC does not address Self-Hosted or Hybrid-Hosted rules or requirements as those are not part of the Phase 4 pilot.

## **New Definitions**

**FRD-FOR:** Foreign Ownership, Control, Or Influence (FOCI)

> A condition that occurs when a foreign entity has the power to direct or influence the management or operations of a cloud service offering used or relied upon by agencies. The full extent of the definition of FOCI includes any federal definition or regulation that defines the extent of possible foreign ownership, control, or influence as it might apply to a cloud service offering.

**FRD-FPS:** Foreign Person

> Has the meaning given in 31 CFR 800.224, that is: “(1) Any foreign national, foreign government, or foreign entity; or (2) Any entity over which control is exercised or exercisable by a foreign national, foreign government, or foreign entity.”
>
> _Note: [Reference URL](https://www.ecfr.gov/current/title-31/subtitle-B/chapter-VIII/part-800/subpart-B/section-800.224)_

## **Miscellaneous Requirements**

Please note that this RFC does not reproduce existing Class D rules that will apply to FedRAMP 20x in the Consolidated Rules for 2026; only new or modified rules are added. Participants are encouraged to review all existing Class D rules, of which there are many, for context while reviewing these updated requirements for FedRAMP 20x.

This section contains individual rules that are new or modified from existing rulesets.

### Vulnerability Detection and Response

**VDR-TFR-MVX** Persistent Machine Verification and Validation for 20x

> Providers with 20x Class D Certification MUST verify and validate the status of machine-based information resources at least once every 3 days.
>
> _Note: This matches the current Class C expectation for this rule._

### Vulnerability Evaluation and Reporting

**VER-EVA-IOC** Indicators of Compromise

> Providers with 20x Class D Certifications SHOULD evaluate detected vulnerabilities, considering the context of the cloud service offering, to determine when the likelihood of exploitation is high enough to initiate forensic activities such as searching for indicators of compromise; then do so.
>
> _Note: This is an entirely new rule. It may also be ported to Rev5 in CR27._

**VER-TFR-MRH** Historical Activity

> Providers with Class 20x D Certifications MUST make all recent historical vulnerability detection and response activity available in JSON format for automated retrieval by all necessary parties (e.g. using an API service or similar); this information SHOULD be updated persistently, at least once every 7 days.
>
> _Note: This proposes a change from SHOULD to a MUST for 20x Class D._

### Security Decision Record

**SDR-CSX-KMT** Key Security Indicator Metrics

> Providers with 20x Class D Certifications MUST also include historical metrics in their Security Decision Record, supplying at least the following information for each applicable Key Security Indicator:
>
> 1. Summary of each metric over the past 30 days
> 2. Summary of metric up to the past year (where available)
> 3. Metric data (including status of persistent validation) every 4 hours up to the past year (where available)
>
> _Note: This should be supplied as a supplemental to the main Security Decision Record via API \- see CDS-CSX-API (API Certification Date)._

### Certification Data Sharing

**CDS-CSX-API** API Certification Data

> Providers with 20x Class D Certifications MUST responsibly supply all machine-readable parts of the FedRAMP Certification Package via web-compatible Application Programming Interface (API).
>
> _Note: This is a NEW rule for 20x Class D to increase the quality of assurance commensurate with the expectations for Class D._

### Cryptographic Module Use

**CMU-CSO-PQS** Post-Quantum Cryptography Status

> Providers with 20x Class D Certifications MUST document the post-quantum cryptography status of digital key establishment and digital signatures used to protect federal customer data, also adding at least the following information:
>
> 1. Whether each algorithm is Post-Quantum Cryptography, part of a hybrid implementation with post-quantum cryptography, or neither
> 2. The target date to transition it to post-quantum cryptography or a hybrid implementation (if available and applicable)
>
> _Note: This is a NEW rule for the Phase 4 pilot and the Consolidated Rules for 2027 and is therefore not included in RFC-0035 Cryptographic Module Use Rules Updates._

### FedRAMP Certification for 20x Class D

_(Note: This section includes proposed formal language for some rules that were mentioned in RFC-0033, and the proposed language was adjusted based on feedback from that RFC)_

**FRC-FRA-FOD** FOCI Determinations are Agency Specific

> FedRAMP MUST NOT request details of the foreign ownership, control, or influence of providers and will not make determinations about whether a provider's foreign ownership, control, or influence is acceptable.
>
> _Note: Agencies determine whether a provider's foreign ownership, control, or influence is acceptable for their use. FedRAMP verifies only that providers know and track foreign ownership, control, or influence. This rule makes it clear that FedRAMP does not intend to collect sensitive business information but does expect cloud service providers to be able to supply that information when required by their customers per a contract with them._

**FRC-CLD-PCD** Progressive Certification to Class D

> Providers seeking a FedRAMP 20x Class D Certification MUST maintain a 20x Class C Certification without corrective action for at least 6 months OR receive a special exemption from FedRAMP to apply directly for a 20x Class D Certification due to an urgent critical need; such exemptions may include cloud services prioritized by the FedRAMP Board and limited pilots.
>
> _Notes:_
>
> - _For the purposes of the FedRAMP 20x Phase 4 Pilot, a full non-pilot 20x Class C Certification is necessary to qualify for participation but six months without corrective action is not required._
> - _FedRAMP is a government program that is not funded by fees or services. Program certification for Class D is very complicated and requires considerable investment and commitment from FedRAMP \- traditional sponsorship for Class D (High) often took many years. This breaks up investment and review by expecting a cloud service to demonstrate a progressive level of assurance over time instead of starting at the highest level. Any cloud service provider seeking a 20x Class D Certification can start at 20x Class C, then once this review is completed and they have demonstrated clear understanding of the requirements they can apply for a 20x Class D with additional support from the government with less risk to the taxpayer._
> - _No one with a Rev5 Class D will be expected to give up their Class D Certification, but transitions from Rev5 Class D will still be expected to move through 20x Class C first (we anticipate most Rev5 Class D offerings will seek to maintain their Rev5 Class D even after obtaining a 20x Class D)._

**FRC-CLD-CCH** Certified Cloud Hosting

> Providers seeking a FedRAMP 20x Class D Certification MUST be deployed on a FedRAMP Class C or FedRAMP Class D Certified Infrastructure-as-a-Service/Platform-as-a-Service offering; OR meet all applicable FedRAMP 20x Class D Self-Hosted or Hybrid-Hosted rules.
>
> _Note: This is a NEW rule that clarifies a gap in the current rules. Self-Hosted and Hybrid-Hosted rules do not exist yet; they will be developed during Phase 4 separately._

**FRC-CLD-CTP** Certified Third-Party Services

> Providers seeking a FedRAMP 20x Class D Certification SHOULD limit the likely handling of federal customer data within the cloud service offering to third-party information resources that are included in a FedRAMP Class B, Class C, Class D, or Class G Certified offering.
>
> _Note: This is a NEW rule intended to ensure that the full lifecycle of federal customer data can be assessed for risk by agencies._

## **Key Security Indicators**

FedRAMP has many rules that include specific assurance expectations for 20x (and Rev5) Class D compared to other FedRAMP Certification Classes. Key Security Indicators go beyond assurance to demonstrate that the cloud service provider is maintaining and tracking critical security information over time. FedRAMP 20x Class D providers will need to use at least 4 different automated methods to track Key Security Indicator status and are encouraged to go well beyond this. FedRAMP 20x Class D is intended to be competitive, such that providers who invest in additional automation, greater assurance, and high speed response and communication will consistently outperform providers that only seek to meet the minimal bar \- though efficient providers at the minimum bar may compete on price or specific use cases.

In addition to all existing Key Security Indicators, FedRAMP proposes adding the following new Key Security Indicators specifically for FedRAMP 20x Class D based on the additional security capabilities expected from a High baseline (note that many automation capabilities are already addressed):

**KSI-CMT-TNP** Testing in Non-Production Environments

> Planned changes are persistently verified and validated in simulated or non-production environments before production environments.
>
> _Related Controls: CM-4(1)_

**KSI-IAM-MST** Monitoring Suitability

> Privileged and high risk information resources have their access, privileges, suitability, and activities persistently reviewed and evaluated.
>
> _Note: This includes personnel, funds, and tech such as AI agents/etc. where access, privileges, suitability, and activity review is appropriate._
>
> _Related Controls: SI-4(19), SI-4(20)_

**KSI-IAM-MPI** Managing Personnel Identities

> The background and identity of personnel is persistently verified and validated, based on their privileges and assigned roles.
>
> _Related Controls: IA-12(4), SI-4(19)_

**KSI-RPL-MCA** Maintaining Cryptographic Access

> The ability to make critical information available in the event of cryptographic key loss or failure is persistently reviewed.
>
> _Related Controls: SC-12(1)_

**KSI-SVC-IED** Inspecting Encrypted Data

> Encrypted data is appropriately and responsibly inspected during transmission for malicious content and compliance with organizational data policies.
>
> _Related Controls: SI-4(10)_

**KSI-SVC-UAS** Using Automated Security

> Processes critical to the security of the system are supported by automated tools to ensure compliance and consistency.
>
> _Related Controls: AU-6(1), AU-7(1), CM-3(1), CM-5(1), CM-6(1), CM-8(2), IR-2(2), IR-5(1), PS-4(2), SI-2(2), SI-4(12), SI-5(1), SI-7(2), SI-7(5)_

**KSI-PIY-DFC** Detecting FOCI Changes

> Changes in foreign ownership, control, or influence are detected and appropriate actions are taken.
>
> _Note: Sensitive details of such changes or actions should not be included in Key Security Indicator metrics._

**KSI-PIY-RFP** Reviewing Foreign Persons

> Foreign persons able to direct or decide matters affecting the cloud service offering are persistently reviewed.
>
> _Note: Sensitive details of such persons should not be included in Key Security Indicator metrics._

**KSI-PIY-RFB** Reviewing Foreign Businesses

> Foreign business relationships that support the cloud service offering are persistently reviewed for ongoing risks.
>
> _Note: Sensitive details of such businesses should not be included in Key Security Indicator metrics._

**KSI-PIY-MFD** Maintaining FOCI Determinations or Mitigations

> Foreign ownership, control, or influence determinations and/or mitigation agreements, issued by U.S. government agencies covering the entity that operates the cloud service offering, are persistently reviewed and maintained.
>
> _Note: Sensitive details of such determinations or agreements should not be included in Key Security Indicator metrics._

discussion_title: RFC-0036 FedRAMP 20x Class D Cloud-Hosted Pilot Requirements
author: sam-aydlette
text:
Re: RFC-0036 FedRAMP 20x Class D Cloud-Hosted Pilot Requirements

sam-aydlette: I think allowing Class D offerings to run on Class C infrastructure is a positive step. It's a practical path, especially for providers already on commercial platforms or whose workloads need specialized infrastructure. But Class D assurance can't simply be inherited from a Class C platform, so the provider has to make up the gap at its own layer. FRC-CLD-CCH should say what that means. At minimum, federal data is encrypted with keys the provider holds outside the platform; plaintext never reaches the platform's managed services; control-plane actions like snapshots, key changes, network changes and log tampering are either blocked or detected independently; and logs and backups live outside the platform, with tested recovery from losing the platform account. The authorization package (the SSP for Rev5/CR26, the SDR for 20x) should also state when the platform underneath is Class C, along with the compensating controls and the remaining risk, so agencies can make an informed call. It would help to clarify whether FRC-CLD-CCH applies to Rev5/CR26 Class D offerings or only to 20x, and how the new FOCI and personnel KSIs apply to the platform's operators in this setup. With clear expectations for equivalent security, this could be a big benefit for CSPs and the agencies that rely on them.

discussion_title: RFC-0036 FedRAMP 20x Class D Cloud-Hosted Pilot Requirements
author: sca1235
text:
Re: RFC-0036 FedRAMP 20x Class D Cloud-Hosted Pilot Requirements

sca1235: I am in agreement with almost all of these requirements. Some might believe these are difficult, but if you are using enough automation and AI assistance then it is actually simpler and more secure to achieve than legacy rev 5. Especially, if you consider the time when class D will be fully released there will be even better tools available to assist in achieving the certification. 

VER-EVA-IOC - I have seen this in practice and definitely useful exercise when discovering a past vulnerability existed in a codebase. Allowing flexibility on level of effort to search for IOCs is good too as long as CSPs document how they searched, as reviewing a years' worth of logs with a script is easier than hiring a forensics team to search for IOCs. All organizations have vulnerabilities at one point or another even if they don't admit it openly so to me this is a valuable check.

FRC-FRA-FOD - The FOCI ones are useful and important going forward as it provides better visibility into the overall setup of an organization. I agree with the setup too where it puts the details in the hands of the agency due to sensitivity of some information. It is clear adversaries have been using FOCI as a way in for a long time as seen in DOW posture to this problem, so it makes sense FedRAMP aligns. FOCI documentation is a positive step in transparency and a powerful security signal when used properly. 

FRC-CLD-PCD - Agree on the progressive steps to achieve class D. Gating the process is useful as we have seen spun up fake startups especially with AI attempt to map out the class D ecosystem. Any company that jumps right into class D without the proper experience should require more review. This allows a vetting period and ensures companies are actually ready and saves everyone time and money. 

FRC-CLD-CCH - Agree with this change, though it opens up an inheritance gap if CSPs don't architect around it properly. If a Class D CSP uses standard Class C serverless or managed PaaS options, an underlying platform support engineer (who may not meet Class D suitability expectations) could potentially access sensitive data or source code.
 
KSI-IAM-MPI and KSI-IAM-MST should block this threat since a CSP typically cannot verify 3rd-party cloud support engineers persistently, the CSP should be forced to use technical controls like Confidential VMs, CMEK, and gated support access. 

FRC-CLD-CTP - Agree with this requirement too since it creates a cohesive secure system when the data can be tracked through vetted providers. It is scoped well to actual risk of federal data which makes it achievable for CSPs.

Overall, these requirements are clear and reasonable for class D.

discussion_title: RFC-0036 FedRAMP 20x Class D Cloud-Hosted Pilot Requirements
author: kelmedina
text:
Re: RFC-0036 FedRAMP 20x Class D Cloud-Hosted Pilot Requirements

kelmedina: My two cents:

KSI-SVC-IED Inspecting Encrypted Data - I believe the intent here is endpoint decryption, but this should be clarified so it is not confused with a requirement for the provider to intercept and decrypt data in transit. It might also need to consider what measures are needed to ensure this ability does not weaken end-to-end encryption.

SDR-CSX-KMT Key Security Indicator Metrics - Does this mean calling the API every 4 hours, or calling it and forcing the check to rerun every 4 hours? For example, would I just call AWS Config to get the latest status of an S3 bucket’s public access block setting, or would I need to rerun that check and then get the status?

FRC-CLD-PCD Progressive Certification to Class D - What does “without corrective action” mean for the six-month Class C period? Is this limited to a formal FedRAMP Corrective Action Plan, or would an agency POA&M or a provider’s routine vulnerability remediation also reset the clock?

discussion_title: RFC-0036 FedRAMP 20x Class D Cloud-Hosted Pilot Requirements
author: kcarr91
text:
Re: RFC-0036 FedRAMP 20x Class D Cloud-Hosted Pilot Requirements

kcarr91: **Feedback on FRC-CLD-PCD: give active Rev5 Class D offerings a direct path to 20x Class D**
We support progressive certification for offerings that are new to FedRAMP. It's a reasonable way to vet providers and manage FedRAMP's review capacity. But it shouldn't apply to cloud service offerings that already hold an active Rev5 Class D certification. They should be able to move straight to a 20x Class D Certification without first getting a 20x Class C Certification and holding it for six months.

Why:
- These providers have already shown Class D assurance. Rev5 Class D providers have put years of effort and significant money into meeting the High baseline, and they keep it up through continuous monitoring and annual assessments. They shouldn't be treated the same as an offering entering FedRAMP for the first time.
- The taxpayer risk argument doesn't really apply here. Agencies already use these systems for High workloads, often under several active ATOs. Making them start at Class C doesn't reduce risk to the taxpayer. It just delays modernizing systems the government already relies on.
- Reviewing twice costs FedRAMP more, not less. The note says Class D review "requires considerable investment and commitment from FedRAMP." Sending an existing High offering through a Class C review and then a Class D review increases that work. A single review of a CSO transitioning from Rev5 Class D to 20x Class D would use FedRAMP's resources better.  Plus these systems have already been reviewed at least once when they first got their FedRAMP Class D (High) certification.
- Contracts and agency expectations are tied to Class D (High). Many contracts require FedRAMP Class D (High). The agency customers we've talked to assume their current High offerings will move to the equivalent 20x class. A 20x Class C Certification, even for a short time, doesn't meet those contract requirements and could confuse agencies about the offering's status.  This could also slow 20x adoption as agencies won’t want to use a 20x package that is Class C when the system is also Rev 5 Class D. 
- Holding both certifications is a heavy burden. The note expects most Rev5 Class D offerings to keep their Rev5 certification even after getting 20x Class D. That means providers maintain two parallel compliance programs for a long time. A smoother transition would avoid this.

Suggested change:
Add an exemption to FRC-CLD-PCD: providers with an active Rev5 Class D Certification in good standing (e.g. no open corrective actions and 1-5+ active agency ATOs) may apply directly for a 20x Class D Certification.

discussion_title: RFC-0036 FedRAMP 20x Class D Cloud-Hosted Pilot Requirements
author: Lowebrew
text:

author: pete-gov
text:
General discussion on RFC-0035 (FIPS) and RFC-0036 (Phase 4 pilot)

Hey all - as a reminder, FedRAMP can't answer questions or generally participate directly in RFC threads to avoid influencing public comment. Sometimes this creates confusion because folks just want to talk about details of something proposed in an RFC to understand it better or learn more about it, so we create these side-threads at times for RFCs.

The two open RFCs in question are:

- #179 
- #180 

Please feel free to use this thread to discuss, ask questions, etc. - but don't forget to add public comment with feedback either way!

discussion_title: General discussion on RFC-0035 (FIPS) and RFC-0036 (Phase 4 pilot)
author: StevenCh99
text:

StevenCh99: With regards to: FRC-CLD-CTP:
"Providers seeking a FedRAMP 20x Class D Certification SHOULD limit the likely handling of federal customer data within the cloud service offering to third-party information resources that are included in a FedRAMP Class B, Class C, Class D, or Class G Certified offering."

discussion_title: General discussion on RFC-0035 (FIPS) and RFC-0036 (Phase 4 pilot)
author: HazemEld
text:
Re: General discussion on RFC-0035 (FIPS) and RFC-0036 (Phase 4 pilot)

HazemEld: The _Notes_ in the rules are undefeated. My favorite is the one in CMU-CSO-TSC: "Adding a non-validated algorithm while a CMVP-validated module still protects federal customer data, such as hybrid implementation, is not such a change." Allows a CSP to add a PQC-approved algo. as an option to the algo that was validated as part of the module without going through a transformative.

pete-gov [FEDRAMP-OFFICIAL]: Hmmm, just to clarify, that note means you can use a CMVP-validated module to protect information _and then wrap it in a PQC resistant algo that isn't CMVP-validated_ (or vice versa) and that's likely not a transformative change (and it's good security). This hybrid implementation can be a bit expensive but it's the most effective way to dot the i's and cross the t's for any customers that are quite picky about sticking with CMVP-validated modules.


HazemEld: Yup, that's exactly what my interpretation of these notes were. You're clarification is a lot more clear than my reaction but we're on the same page here. Thanks you!
