discussion_title: ConMon Observation period
author: brandenc-xai
text:
ConMon Observation period

We're preparing for a Rev5 Class D FedRAMP certification and have a question about continuous monitoring for an initial authorization. Is an observation period required? Specifically, could our independent assessor verify that our continuous monitoring process is in place and the tools are configured correctly, instead of us showing evidence of it running over a set period? Assessors have told us a 60 to 90 day period is needed, but we haven't been able to find where that requirement is written.

discussion_title: ConMon Observation period
author: pete-gov
text:
Re: ConMon Observation period

pete-gov [FEDRAMP-OFFICIAL]: > Assessors have told us a 60 to 90 day period is needed, but we haven't been able to find where that requirement is written.

If an assessor cites a rule or requirement to you but can't show you where that rule is written down officially then that might be a red flag. Historically there were "ghost rules" that assessors learned from bad experiences with FedRAMP and piled on, but we have been quite clear over the past two years that it doesn't work like that anymore.

Ask *them* where this requirement originates from. I'm betting they are referencing old vuln scanning guidance that recommended checking vuln scans in advance of the SAR or something weird like that? Alternatively it may be a requirement from your agency sponsor, or something you agreed to with them, etc.

There is no current FedRAMP rule requiring 90 days of conmon data to be reviewed during assessment, though it's a value add if you have it and can do it.





jsantore-sf: I was a 3PAO in a former life, and I thought would be helpful to add some historical context to this.  This wasn't a 'ghost rule' per se, it was a natural consequence of an strict Federal mandate requirement.  

There were 6 mandates, all published primarily in the RAR (but they weren't arbitrary or secret, and I concur it's weird that the RAR was the main location for listing these).  Those 6 were, paraphrased:
1) Must have FIPS encryption
2) Must have MFA (technically Digital Identity Level 2 for Mod, 3 for High)
3) Must accept CAC/PIV cards (usually done through SAML)
4) Federal records requirements, originally NARA, eventually sort of superceded by M-21-31 (and then M-26-14)
5) Must have DNSSEC in place (SC-20/SC-21) 
6) Does the CSP have the ability to consistently remediate vulnerabilities within 30/90/180 days.  THIS is the one that is relevant to the historical conmon data issue.

In order to determine if someone is consistently remediating vulnerabilies, you need enough of a history to show that any high vulns were addressed in a timely fashion.  That's where the 'we need 60-90 days of conmon data' came from.  When I was assessing a system, my requirement was not necessarily a hard and fast 60-90 days, but sufficient history and/or enough vuln scan cycles to be able to determine that this was consistently addressed.  Regardless, one cannot evaluate this requirement as a simple point in time check; it de facto needs history.

Remember that these were deemed to be Federal mandates (alas I don't remember what the genesis of their authority was, possibly the JAB), but it was consistently applied.  Whether or not these mandates truly had a statutory basis, I don't recall, but these were some of the clearest requirements of FedRAMP.  

@pete-gov "we have been quite clear over the past two years that it doesn't work like that anymore."  

Agreed, and this is one of the best things of the new FedRAMP program.  Just a word of caution that while something may not be a firm black letter rule, sometimes a necessary consequence of evaluating or satisfying that rule (i.e. vulnerability history in this case) has some required-but-unwritten aspect of it.

discussion_title: Clarifying Metadata in Legacy Rev. 5 Systems
author: controlled-chaos916
text:
Clarifying Metadata in Legacy Rev. 5 Systems

I'm working to reconcile MAS-CSO-MDI & MAS-CSO-IIR for my Rev.5/CR26 environment. Can you clarify a few things for me? 

1. Everything included in the minimum assessment scope is subject to the rest of Rev.5/CR26?
2. Is metadata such as IPs, URLs, server names okay to exist in a corporate (read: outside MAS) system? If yes or no, can you give rationale and/or examples of potential use cases you considered? 

Thanks so much!

discussion_title: Clarifying Metadata in Legacy Rev. 5 Systems
author: pete-gov
text:
Re: Clarifying Metadata in Legacy Rev. 5 Systems

pete-gov [FEDRAMP-OFFICIAL]: > Everything included in the minimum assessment scope is subject to the rest of Rev.5/CR26?

Yes, that's right.

> Is metadata such as IPs, URLs, server names okay to exist in a corporate (read: outside MAS) system? If yes or no, can you give rationale and/or examples of potential use cases you considered?

[MAS-CSO-MDI (Metadata Inclusion)](https://www.fedramp.gov/2026/reference/minimum-assessment-scope/#metadata-inclusion) gives you the path to make this determination - we can't say definitively in each particular environment because it will vary from architecture to architecture.

In _general_ though, things like IP addresses, URLs, and server names are not very likely to potentially impact the confidentiality, integrity, or availability of federal customer data if they are managed responsibly, and would not be inside the MAS. Those things are typically not private and their use transits the public internet, and if you were to get a hold of an IP address or host name it shouldn't generally matter. So what if you know something is called `database-useast1`?

On the other hand, if your server names are something like `cia-secret-project-mkultra`and contain actual federal customer data or something (in this fictional example, the name of a secret project that no one would want out there), then they'd definitely be in the MAS. A list of allow-list IPs for a special recovery process might be potentially sensitive if it allows bypassing certain controls. Etc.

Again, if things are configured and designed responsibly, then metadata shouldn't put federal customer data at risk though.

discussion_title: Class A: must the SOC 2 Type II boundary match the offering, and can it carve out subservice organizations?
author: 2bkolohe
text:
Class A: must the SOC 2 Type II boundary match the offering, and can it carve out subservice organizations?

We are a small commercial SaaS provider preparing for a 20x Class A application through the Program path. Before we engage an auditor, we would like to confirm three points about FRC-CLA-ASF and FRC-CLA-EAM:

1. If our SOC 2 Type II (Security criteria) covers exactly the commercial service we would list as the cloud service offering, with the same system description and boundary, does that satisfy FRC-CLA-ASF? Or does FedRAMP expect a boundary built specifically for federal customers?
2. Our service relies on several third parties (telephony, speech, database hosting and an LLM provider) that we would treat as carved-out subservice organizations in the SOC 2. Is documenting them under MAS-CSO-TPR sufficient for Class A, given that none of them holds FedRAMP status?
3. Is a first SOC 2 Type II with a 3-month observation period acceptable for FRC-CLA-ASF, or does FedRAMP expect a longer period?

Thank you.

discussion_title: Class A: must the SOC 2 Type II boundary match the offering, and can it carve out subservice organizations?
author: pete-gov
text:
Re: Class A: must the SOC 2 Type II boundary match the offering, and can it carve out subservice organizations?

pete-gov [FEDRAMP-OFFICIAL]: > If our SOC 2 Type II (Security criteria) covers exactly the commercial service we would list as the cloud service offering, with the same system description and boundary, does that satisfy FRC-CLA-ASF? Or does FedRAMP expect a boundary built specifically for federal customers?

It doesn't have to be exactly the same boundary, but we would expect all of information resources that you list for the MAS-CSO-IIR (Identify Information Resources) to be covered in the SOC 2 Type II. It is likely that the SOC 2 Type II would actually cover resources that you don't include in the MAS for various reasons.

We don't expect a federal-specific boundary at all! The intent is for you to "run what you brung" with Class A. 

> Our service relies on several third parties (telephony, speech, database hosting and an LLM provider) that we would treat as carved-out subservice organizations in the SOC 2. Is documenting them under MAS-CSO-TPR sufficient for Class A, given that none of them holds FedRAMP status?

Yes, that's right. Ensure to document the information flows and risk, such as what type of federal customer data would flow into those services and how that might affect customers (as well as if they can be disabled/etc.). You also might have compensating controls or mitigating measures in place and should document that.

This will help agencies make informed risk decisions - in a situation you described, an agency might want to use the service for communication with the public and would happily accept the risk of third-party telephony because all of the people using the service are coming in through an insecure public phone. Another agency might want to use it for secure phone calls and would not accept the risk of an unknown third-party telephony service. That's all working as intended!

> Is a first SOC 2 Type II with a 3-month observation period acceptable for FRC-CLA-ASF, or does FedRAMP expect a longer period?

This should be acceptable, just note it. 

2bkolohe: Very cool -- thank you, Sir.

discussion_title: Organizational claims do not match FedRAMP Marketplace
author: LPT00-ctrl
text:
Organizational claims do not match FedRAMP Marketplace

I have seen websites where organizations put the FedRAMP logo on their website front page with the words "FedRAMP Compliant" below the logo, yet when I look on the FedRAMP Marketplace, I do not see the organization listed. Is that allowed? It seems somewhat misleading to me.

discussion_title: Organizational claims do not match FedRAMP Marketplace
author: pete-gov
text:
Re: Organizational claims do not match FedRAMP Marketplace

pete-gov [FEDRAMP-OFFICIAL]: > I have seen websites where organizations put the FedRAMP logo on their website front page with the words "FedRAMP Compliant" below the logo, yet when I look on the FedRAMP Marketplace, I do not see the organization listed. Is that allowed? It seems somewhat misleading to me.

The only official place to find FedRAMP status is the FedRAMP Marketplace. We cannot really prevent folks from claiming whatever they want as long as they aren't saying they are "FedRAMP Certified" or "FedRAMP Authorized" because it is descriptive fair use to say that someone complies with FedRAMP rules or is FedRAMP equivalent. GSA's Office of General Counsel will send trademark violation warnings in some cases if someone appears to be violating the FedRAMP trademark by claiming that FedRAMP has given them an official status that FedRAMP has not given them but there's not much to be done beyond the occasional letter.

Only source of truth is fedramp.gov.
